content.content:
It is a bright time for German democracy. After a period of struggle, inflation is finally under control, and the economy is expanding steadily. In foreign policy, we have reached agreements with the Western powers and the Soviet Union that might make genuine peace a reality.

Now, the task of Social Democracy is to prepare for the next election. The bourgeois-right government of Wilhelm Marx is unpopular, and we stand to gain. Perhaps the next government will have a socialist majority.
The current bourgeois-right government has fallen. The next elections are slated for May of this year.

content.content:
The impact of the last election to encourage cooperation between the two liberal parties have culminated in the creation of a parliamentary faction featuring the two parties. This is begrudgingly accepted by the extremes of both parties to increase their parliamentary influence with the declining liberal vote.

A new Liberal Association has been gaining traction with funding from both parties, and are expected to open up state and local chapters and to draft a policy program. This seems to be the prelude to the founding of a new liberal party, but it's not certain if both parties will consent to this.

Our calls for new elections just after the last one have pushed the liberal parties closer together, in order to not face any further decline. A new Liberal Association has emerged coordinating the efforts of the two parties and seems to be the prelude to the founding of a new liberal party, but it's not certain if both parties would fully agree.

The idea of a liberal parliamentary faction has gained considerable traction with both parties and they are likely to negotiate as a single bloc after the election.

content.content: Troubled by the surge of far‑right populism and the emboldened left, Germany’s heavy‑industry financiers have begun quietly pressuring the KVP/DNVP and the DVP to discuss tighter cooperation. The industrialist backers hope that the two parties working closer together will help bolster their leverage in the Reichstag. Members in both the KVP/DNVP and DVP, notably Treviranus and Dingeldey, are optimistic about these potential meetings.After weeks of behind the scenes pressure, the KVP/DNVP and the DVP have formally begun a series of joint meetings aimed at coordinating legislative strategy in the Reichstag. While Treviranus and Dingeldey lead the talks with cautious optimism, reservations linger among the KVP/DNVP’s agrarian wing, who fear further influence from the city focused industrial interests in the DVP. The DVP’s moderate wing is similarly resistant, as they see this as another step away from Stresemann’s legacy.

After weeks of careful deliberation, the KVP/DNVP and the DVP have made unexpectedly rapid strides in aligning their party platforms and coordinating candidate selection. That momentum has put a formal merger squarely on the table. Treviranus and Dingeldey applaud the unprecedented unity, openly acknowledging that a full merger could be on the horizon. Both the DVP’s moderate wing and the KVP/DNVP’s agrarians are still voicing concerns, but find their resistance increasingly sidelined as the broader majority coalesces around deeper integration.

. They argue that this tax, primarily levied on businesses, is an unreasonable burden on job creators given the current economic crisis. Brüning now finds himself caught between appeasing big industry on one side and placating organized agriculture and Hindenburg on the right.

content.content: The Brüning cabinet has introduced the Eastern Aid Act, a policy aimed at relieving the debts of agricultural enterprises in the east—despite the significant financial burden it imposes. This measure directly contradicts Brüning’s broader strategy of economic recovery through budget austerity. To partially fund the policy, the government has retained outdated reparation taxes that became obsolete after the Young Plan. However, the lack of full funding for debt relief has frustrated many influential landowners, prompting them to take their complaints directly to Hindenburg, over whom they wield considerable influence.

Brüning’s decision to sideline the Reichstag and its parties from any meaningful role in shaping his fiscal and economic policies severely undermined the legitimacy of the bourgeois parties in the eyes of their traditional electorates, due to their powerlessness to dismantle his more repugnant policies. One clear example is the plight of civil servants, who have borne the brunt of salary cuts of approximately 20 percent, pushing many toward the Nazis. His deflationary and austerity measures deepened the economic crisis, radicalizing the very social groups upon which these moderate parties relied for electoral support. This has led to heightened tensions between Brüning and his supporting parties, some of whom are even threatening to abandon his coalition.

This is a clear retreat from the unabashed defense of liberal principles that had characterized Stresemann’s tenure as party chairman.

content.content: The Second Spanish Republic has been established, replacing the monarchy of Alfonso XIII. This follows municipal elections in which republican candidates scored significant victories, winning in all 41 provincial capitals. This has forced the king into exile and a new, young republic has been created.

They now claim to be 'correcting' their position by 'reducing the evaluation of fascism to its proper proportions', which means reverting back to their social fascist stance. To them, we are no different than the actual fascists.

Hugenberg's attempts to cultivate a Hitler-style personality have failed, as his upper-class elitism and arrogance leave him out of touch with ordinary people suffering from the economic crisis. Frustrated by his lack of charisma, a group of industrialists has even offered a large reward for anyone who can help depose him, convinced he is steering the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
toward disaster. Adding to his troubles, the economic depression has slashed revenues from his media empire, forcing him to cut the

content.content: The formation of the Austro-German customs union has prompted France to exert significant economic pressure on Austria. Leveraging its sizable influence over the Austrian economy, France is not only refusing to extend financial assistance to the country’s struggling major banks but is also deliberately withdrawing large sums of money, further destabilizing Austria's financial sector.

The major Austrian Bank Creditanstalt has declared bankruptcy, following French political and economic pressures aimed at undermining the plans for the Austro-German customs union. In that respect, they have certainly succeeded. We can only hope that this crisis does not spill over into Germany or, worse, spread across Europe.

content: Following Creditanstalt's bankruptcy, an event that has shaken international financial markets, investors are now rapidly withdrawing funds from German banks. Germany's heavy reliance on short-term foreign loans has turned Austria’s banking crisis into a direct threat to our own stability. In response, Reichsbank President

has implemented measures to curb capital flight by disincentivizing the transfer of money abroad. However, the effectiveness of these policies remains uncertain, and may cause unintended consequences.

content.content: Rumors have circulated regarding Center Party leader Ludwig Kaas's intention to resign, as he has privately expressed a desire to step down from his burdensome position. His frequent absences from Germany, often spent in Rome, have left his deputy leader Joos and parliamentary leader Brüning to effectively manage the party. Kaas also holds one of the worst attendance records in the Reichstag. However, Kaas has attributed his prolonged absences to poor health, and the considerable autonomy he has granted to his colleagues has quelled efforts to replace him with a more active, though controversial, leader.

content: The organizational malaise of the <span style="color: #D3C24D;">

In some urban areas, the party’s shift to the right is estimated to have cost it more than half of its former supporters. In states without a strong liberal tradition, the situation is so dire that even the local branches that had once championed the formation of the
the previous year all but recommended conceding defeat and dissolving the party entirely.

content.content: The first elections of the Second Spanish Republic has been held, with it a great victory for the Spanish Socialists and the Republican Left. Together, they've formed a government with Manuel Azaña as Prime Minister.

Great Britain has abandoned the Gold Standard! The short-lived naval mutiny, caused by pay cuts, led to panic on the London Stock Exchange and a run on the Pound. The British government then adopted this policy as a means to stimulate industrial exports without the harmful side effects of deflation, achieved through the devaluation of the Pound. Germany's top economic experts viewed this as an act of desperation that would ruin England’s banks and insurance companies. Germany's citizens' fear of inflation, along with the obligation to preserve the mark’s value at 0.358 grams of fine gold under the Young Plan, has prevented Reichsbank President

from abandoning the Gold Standard. However, with both the United States and Britain showing sympathies toward our request for more flexible regulations, perhaps this decision was ultimately made on economic grounds after all.

Most of their replacements are conservatives—many of them nationalists. The purge is particularly aimed at socialist provincial presidents and police officials. An estimated 69 republican officials have been stripped of their power. Safe to say, the democratic bulwark has been dismantled.

However, the Nazi leadership's enthusiasm quickly fades when President Hindenburg refuses to appoint
as Chancellor. Papen, deeply offended by Schleicher's apparent willingness to abandon him, has used his growing rapport with Hindenburg to undermine Schleicher’s influence over the President.
Following the results of the Reichstag elections, Papen and President Hindenburg met with
to hear his demands for the party’s participation in government.

requested to be appointed chancellor once again—a demand Hindenburg refused. Buoyed by their electoral triumph, the Nazis have now officially reneged on their earlier promises to tolerate Papen. Going forward, they will pursue an all-or-nothing strategy: the chancellorship for
Papen has released the contents of last week's conversations with

stormed into Hindenburg’s office to demand “total power over the state”—a violent one-party dictatorship—and was met with an angry rebuff from the president. This press release signals aims to signal the start of a counter-offensive against the Nazis. But now, no party is willing—or able—to follow the chancellor into open confrontation with the extremists. Even the Center Party finds
’s version of events more credible than Papen’s.
Coalition talks between the Center Party and
have continued, putting pressure on Papen to outmaneuver his former party in gaining the favor of the Nazis. Brüning, with permission from his party's leadership, has meet with the
's Strasser, promising support if he could convince
to govern via a parliamentary cabinet with Schleicher as Defense Minister and Goerdeler as the commissioner of Prussia.
Under pressure from their principal patron, General von Schleicher, the <span style="color: #0087DC;">

is compelled to support the unpopular Papen government—or risk losing Schleicher’s covert Reichswehr funding. Outraged by the party's backing of such an anti-social chancellor, the Christian Socials resign their positions in protest.
A follow-up meeting to last week’s discussion about a potential Black-Brown alliance, set up by Strasser, has resulted in
agreeing to delay the vote of no confidence against Papen.
also appeared to agree with Brüning’s other demands. Closer cooperation is expected in the near future, if both parties are genuine in their commitment to govern together via parliament.

content.content: Austria has obtained a League of Nations loan that is tied to a 20-year ban on Anschluss, but opposition from the Social Democrats and Greater German Party has stalled the law, before it finally is passed by a single vote.

content: The coalition talks between the Center Party and
have been called off, as Brüning grows increasingly uneasy about the grave risks involved. This decision is also influenced by his friend and our party member, Hilferding, who argued that the

would never restore parliamentary government. Hilferding also pointed out that many of Brüning's own party colleagues have fallen under Nazi influence, a fact confirmed when they all but agreed to impeach President Hindenburg in the planned deal. Hilferding also remains the only one in our party to advocate for toleration of Papen's cabinet as the only means to prevent a Nazi dictatorship. Brüning's goal is now to persuade the Nazis to give the Papen government 'a fair chance' to revive the economy.
The Center Party and its grassroots supporters are becoming increasingly demoralized, largely due to Brüning’s semi-secret negotiations with the

. Locally, party activists have faced the Nazis as violent thugs, disrupting rallies and intimidating opponents—far from the image of a potential coalition partner. Some activists are even taking up arms in self-defense, losing faith in their party and its leadership.

has publicly opposed the party’s recent vote of no confidence and the snap elections it triggered, warning that such moves would only erode the Nazis’ popular support and squander their only real chance to seize power. In response, an unofficial faction of about sixty Nazi Reichstag deputies has coalesced around Strasser—disillusioned by

content.content: General elections were held in Sweden, resulting in a great victory for Per Albin Hansson and his Social Democrats, who now govern in a minority government. The Swedish Social Democrats have embraced the concept of a 'people's home', a form of reformist socialism aimed at reducing class divides while working in the capitalist framework. Perhaps we should consider following their 'nordic' model?

The main proceedings in the case against Papen’s unconstitutional Reichsexekution of the Prussian government have begun, with a verdict expected in the coming weeks. Yet, the historically reactionary leanings of the judiciary place us at a clear disadvantage—despite support from the state governments of Bavaria and Baden, who have joined us in challenging the decree’s legality.

Chancellor of Austria Engelbert Dollfuß has used the "War Economy Enabling Act", a law passed during the days of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, which allowed him to restructure the Creditanstalt without parliamentary approval. While the Austrian Social Democrats have protested, Dollfuß' actions are technically legal.

content: , in an attempt to revive their poll numbers, have outlined the concept of "national democracy," aiming to rekindle the nationalistic impulse that played such a crucial role in the German liberal movement. However, it is essentially a restatement of classical liberal ideology, tailored to appeal to a more nationalistic German middle class. The national democracy program also reaffirms the
's commitment to the Weimar Republic and recommends constitutional changes to strengthen it.
With its electoral alliance with the DNVP, the
's freedom of action has become increasingly constrained. Their rhetoric is aligning more closely with the
, now calling for the "liquidation of the Weimar system," an authoritarian overhaul of its constitution, and the withdrawal of power away from the masses.
Dingeldey and his associates are no longer content with merely renewing their electoral list connection with the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
. Instead, they pushed for a unified Rechtsblock of the

, and various industrialist and business organizations to provide cohesive support for Hindenburg and Papen. However, Hugenberg has shown utter indifference, refusing to commit to anything beyond a renewal of the electoral list connection.
President Hindenburg has once again attempted to sound out the Nazis after the recent election results, with
signaling his readiness to seek the support of other parties if he were to be made chancellor first. Calling
's bluff, the president offered to appoint him, but only if he could secure a working majority in the Reichstag and allow the president to pick the defense and foreign ministers himself. As expected,
declined Hindenburg's proposal and suggested instead that, with emergency powers, he could form a satisfactory government in no time. Convinced that
sought nothing less than a presidential chancellorship, Hindenburg withdrew him from consideration.
Following another disastrous result for the <span style="color: #D3C24D;">
, a group of six former Reichstag deputies and high-ranking party members informed

that if a party congress—specifically meant to dissolve the party—isn't held, they would leave. However, this call has not gained much support, and Carl Petersen, former <span style="color: #D3C24D;">
chairman, has used his mediation skills to prevent the dissidents from publicly announcing their break with the party.

content.content: Democrat Franklin D. Roosevelt has defeated incumbent Republican President Herbert Hoover in a landslide in the United States presidential election. This is attributed by the Great Depression and Roosevelt's campaigning for a "New Deal", proposing expansive public works and government reform.
Rumors are circulating widely that General Schleicher intends to undermine the very chancellor he helped install. Among his contacts, he's already being referred to as the chancellor-designate.

content: to make one final attempt at forming a majority coalition. Reporting back the next day,
confirmed that no such majority could be assembled. His recommendation was blunt: the only way forward is for the President to dismiss Papen, as the Reichstag will never accept him as chancellor.

has suffered yet another crushing setback—this time in the local elections in Thuringia. The results show the party lost nearly a quarter of its vote share compared to the previous state election. While low turnout may be a factor, this and three other recent local elections have only reinforced the growing sense that the Nazis have peaked and are rapidly losing support.

content.content: Despite his ousting, Papen remains in far closer physical proximity to the President than the chancellor does. At Hindenburg’s personal request, he continues to reside in an apartment within the Interior Ministry building—just steps from Hindenburg’s own quarters—while Schleicher lives miles away in a private residence. This arrangement has enabled Papen to scheme full-time, without attracting public attention.

Once a close ally, Oskar von Hindenburg has become an implacable enemy of the new chancellor—reportedly over a tasteless joke that wounded his pride beyond forgiveness. In Prussian times, such insults could end in duels; this time, the fallout may claim the life of the Republic. Two members of the Camarilla now harbor intense hostility toward Schleicher, and are working to sway the President into reconsidering his appointment.

Shortly after Schleicher’s appointment, the Western Allies, following protracted negotiations at the Geneva Disarmament Conference, conceded in principle to Germany’s right to equality in arms. The practical terms of this concession remain unclear, but in Schleicher’s view, it opens the path toward establishing an official militia service.

During Schleicher's addresses to the nation, one central theme rings clear: "Create Work!" He has revived efforts to resettle the urban unemployed on rural homesteads carved from bankrupt estates in the sparsely populated East. Although the Reichstag remains dissolved and he cannot legislate, he has publicly opposed Papen’s changes to the unemployment insurance system, presenting himself as a proponent of neither capitalism nor socialism. His ideological ambiguity has earned him the nickname "social general"—a label he embraces, claiming it aligns with the army’s tradition of solidarity between officers and soldiers.

content: 's resurgence in the polls has led Dingeldey to become overconfident, unequivocally supporting Papen, then Schleicher, and even forming a parliamentary faction with the various splinter parties between it and the
. While this move has bolstered their influence, it has alienated Hugenberg and the
, on whom they still depend on as of their electoral alliance.
For some odd reason, von Schleicher came to believe that nothing came of
’s attempts to be appointed parliamentary chancellor simply because the man didn’t “at the bottom of his heart” want the office. By

, this suspicion had become a firm conviction; he repeatedly confided to journalists and his cabinet that the man simply doesn’t really want power. This belief is leading to Schleicher overestimating his chances of securing <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
Heavy electoral losses for the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

in local elections have further reinforced the disillusionment of the voters who have brought the movement to prominence, many who joined and donated to the party expecting to receive the spoils of victory are beginning to despair, withdrawing their donations. Admission fees for rallies, once a major source of income at the local level, have collapsed despite steep price reductions.

's failure to gain the chancellorship or enter government to constructively relieve Germany's economic woes has caused further frustration among the movement. However, Nazi leaders are quick to suppress any leaks of dissent or rumors of decline to the public.
The global economy is on the upswing—and with it, the erosion of the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
continues. The republican police force surveilling the

in Munich has noted clear signs of disintegration. Resignations are occurring daily, membership dues arrive irregularly, and expulsions over indebtedness are increasingly common. Every branch of the party appears run down. As for morale, the police report observed: “The view that the peak has passed and favorable prospects are missed is commonly held among many members.”
Schleicher still clings to the illusionary hope that the now powerless Strasser might somehow persuade
to allow Nazi participation in his cabinet, now that Strasser has returned from vacation. Strasser’s absence from the public eye has unsettled

, who now fears potential backroom plots to fracture the party—especially given the eagerness of Strasser’s remaining loyalists to do just that. In reality, all Strasser does is to warn former chancellor Brüning that Papen has arranged a secret meeting with Hitler—set to take place within a week or two—to conspire against their mutual enemy: Schleicher.

's financial situation is becoming dire. Increasingly, equipment and supplies are being acquired on credit—credit that's already drying up under the weight of the party's existing debts. Tensions have begun to flare between the

and the party leadership over how to divide dwindling donations, with some members resorting to begging in the streets or organizing lotteries to scrape together funds. One more election, and the party could face a full-blown financial crisis.

Despite promising President Hindenburg not to publicly criticize his favored former chancellor, Schleicher has done just that in a bid to distance himself from the deeply unpopular Papen. Hindenburg, displeased by the breach of trust, grows increasingly estranged from Schleicher. Papen, for his part, has shown little outward hostility toward his ouster—carefully masking his resentment and thirst for revenge beneath a façade of cordiality. In the meantime, Hindenburg has quietly authorized him to serve as his secret liaison to

content.content: Günther Gereke, the energetic special commissioner for public works, has grown frustrated with the chancellor after a request for intervention to clear bureaucratic obstacles was flatly rejected. His ambitious projects remain stalled. Gereke, disillusioned, has confided his disappointment to his close friend—none other than Oskar von Hindenburg.

content: Günther Gereke, the energetic special commissioner for public works, has had his project accelerated after his request for the chancellor to intervene and clear bureaucratic obstacles was approved.

content.content: The disastrous state of the German economy has made rearmament a pipe dream, and Schleicher is eager to get it back on track.

The campaign for the Landtag elections in the microscopically small Free State of Lippe has begun, with the Nazis investing a substantial amount of resources to sway just a hundred thousand voters. However, despite its small size, a victory here could dispel the growing belief that the Nazis are on the brink of a catastrophic decline.

content: At a private dinner with journalists, Chancellor von Schleicher repeatedly expressed confidence that the Nazi leader would eventually come around to tolerating his cabinet—despite

’s public affirmations of an all-or-nothing course. This, even as Schleicher made clear he would dissolve the Reichstag if needed, a move he believes would cost the Nazis further seats (though he seeks to avoid such a step, fearing the
would benefit most from their collapse). “They’ll soon be eating out of my hand,” were the chancellor’s exact words that evening. What Schleicher fails to grasp is that
is no ordinary politician. He will not respond rationally, nor prudently, to Strasser’s break or to the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
’s electoral collapse. He believes destiny is on his side.

Chancellor von Schleicher and his press secretary have deliberately “leaked” plans to appoint Strasser as Vice Chancellor, Interior Minister, and Minister-President of Prussia, alongside naming the Center Party labor leader Stegerwald as Labor Minister. The Agriculture and Economics Ministries were reportedly reserved for Hugenberg himself. It’s highly likely this is a bluff—an attempt to pressure the
into dropping its total opposition, lest they risk being sidelined entirely.
With Dingeldey's pretentiousness, fueled by the <span style="color: #C0A054;">

's uptick in polling, elevating it to the lead party on the "moderate" Right, Hugenberg is growing increasingly irritated by their independence and seeks to terminate their electoral alliance if new elections are called. While the
still hopes to renew the alliance, they begin exploring the possibility of an accommodation with the

and the bourgeois parties as a safeguard against near-certain annihilation if Hugenberg severs ties. Meanwhile, the DNV (German National Association), a non-partisan organization aiming to consolidate the German middle, is starting to repair its relations with the liberals after already securing the support of the non-liberal right, with politicians like Treviranus.

content.content: Von Schleicher's bluffs—such as proposing a cabinet that includes both Stegerwald and Hugenberg—have lost all credibility. The Center Party has publicly ruled out Stegerwald serving alongside Hugenberg, a notorious enemy of organized labor. Moreover, the leak about the President’s meeting with Strasser has led to a permanent break between the Nazi leader and Schleicher, ending any hope that Strasser might persuade him to support a cabinet involving Schleicher. His contradictory tactics and careless remarks have only deepened mistrust and furthered his political isolation. He only now condemns efforts to postpone elections—despite having supported the idea just a week earlier.

With progress stalled across nearly all sectors, Schleicher has attempted to shift focus by bringing the issue of rearmament back into the public eye. He announced plans to establish a compulsory militia within a year, alongside a renewed commitment to arming the Reichswehr with heavy weaponry and instituting universal conscription. However, the impact of this intended public relations triumph is minimal, as news of Schleicher’s political setbacks dominates public attention.

Having failed to extract concessions from the chancellor to turn Germany into a dictatorship, the more radical elements within his party have pressured him into adopting an all-out opposition to Schleicher. A strongly worded resolution has been released, accusing him of "vacillation" in his willingness to "reform" the constitution. Furthermore, his initiative to restart peasant homesteads on bankrupt eastern estates has drawn the ire of conservative elites. With the next vote of no confidence looming, it may well come down to Schleicher versus the entire chamber.
The Rubicon has been crossed, and Schleicher stands on the other side. (keep in mind, all future content is highly speculative)

content.content: Dollfuß has abused his powers given in the "War Economy Enabling Act" to crack down on the workers in a railroad strike, which has resulted in all three presidents of parliament resigning amid a crucial vote. This crisis presented a perfect opportunity for Dollfuß to abolish the parliamentary system and restrict democratic rights, such as the freedom of the press and public protests. Another democracy has fell to authoritarianism.

Dollfuß's Austrofascist dictatorship has banned the Austrian Communists and the paramilitary of the Austrian Social Democrats, the Republican Protection League. He has also established the Fatherland Front, a party promoting a far-right fascist and corporate ideology.

content.content: The Austrian Civil War has begun and ended in a matter of three days, fought between the Republican Protection League and Austria's Austrofascist regime, resulting in a defeat for the socialists across the border. The uprising was sparked by efforts to suppress the remnants of the Austrian Social Democrats and their paramilitary wing. However, the poorly coordinated and weakened movement was swiftly crushed by the army. Perhaps things would have gone more differently if they have taken up arms earlier.

We offer Warsaw what no German government has offered before, which is recognition of the frontier of 1919 as final, in exchange for the restoration of Danzig's freedoms and a timetable for Polish withdrawal from East Prussia and Upper Silesia. Beck accepts the first half at once. On the second he agrees only to "talks on a staged withdrawal, when the security situation permits". It is something.

We offer Warsaw what no German government has offered before, which is recognition of the frontier as final, a joint guarantee of each other's borders and of the rights of minorities on both sides, and arbitration of every dispute. In return, Danzig's Germans may vote on their own future in five years, and German freight will cross the Corridor without customs inspection. Beck, with one eye on the Red Army, signs.
In the Reichstag, the nationalists call it "the second Versailles". Abroad, it is called the most important treaty since Locarno.

content: German machine tools go down the river, and Hungarian wheat and Yugoslav copper come up it. Budapest holds out for six months and then applies to join. The Agrarian League says that cheap Danube grain will ruin every farmer east of the Elbe, and the price of rye in Pomerania falls by a fifth.

content.content: In Rome, the Rome Protocols are quietly allowed to lapse. Mussolini has lost his clients, and he does not forgive the people who took them.
The Western powers would not take a German draft seriously.

e2_disarmament.convention.subtitle: Every army in Europe will grow more slowly, ours too. The generals and the right will be furious.

content.content: The German draft is tabled in Geneva in the spring: no more than three hundred thousand men under arms in any European state, no bombers, no tanks above sixteen tonnes, and a commission with the right to inspect every barracks on the continent. After eight months of argument, twenty-six states sign a weaker version of it. The Soviet Union signs with reservations, and Italy signs last. In the Bendlerblock, the general staff tears up its plans for a larger army.

e2_eastern_crisis.mediate.unavailableSubtitle: No one would come to a conference called by Berlin.

content.content: The conference opens in Geneva in the autumn. It produces a new frontier commission, a League refugee office and a treaty limiting land armies in central Europe, which the Soviets sign and everyone expects them to ignore. It is not much. It is more than the League has done in a decade.

options.title: See what became of Germany.

content: It is the first day of 1950. Twenty-two years have passed since the spring of 1928, when the <span style="color: #c00000;">
returned to government with the largest vote in a decade, and few of us suspected what lay ahead.

content.content: The Weimar Republic, which so many wrote off in 1930, is still standing.
The rubble of the civil war has long been cleared from the streets of Berlin. However, the men who fought in it, on either side, have not forgotten.
The division of Germany still shapes everything we do, whether or not the country has been put back together.
The United Front's experiment began more than fifteen years ago. A whole generation of Germans has grown up with red flags over the Reichstag.
There is a King of Prussia and a German Emperor again—twenty years ago, almost nobody would have believed it.
Papen's New State is still standing, despite every prediction of its collapse. Many of our comrades who made those predictions are now in prison or in exile.
Now it is time to see what became of Germany, and of our party.

The treaty is signed in Paris in the spring, by Germany, France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. The High Authority will sit in Luxembourg, and its first president is a Frenchman with a German deputy. The customs posts on coal and steel come down within the year.

The nationalists call it the end of German sovereignty, and in a sense they are right. On the Saar and the Moselle, where three generations of young men marched off to kill each other, no one is likely to miss it.

e2_evian.open.subtitle: -1 budget. Republicans and the democracies will approve. The nationalists will be loud about it.

content: The German government tells the committee that the Republic will grant asylum to anyone persecuted for their faith, their origin or their politics, and will help them to find work.

content.content: Our deputies carry the vote in the Reichstag with the Centre and the liberals.
some eighty thousand people cross from Austria into Bavaria and Saxony.
some sixty thousand people come from Poland and Romania.

content: The nationalist press counts every one of them.

e2_france_fascist.condemn.subtitle: The Left faction will approve. Paris will remember it.

content: Our chairman calls the new regime in Paris "the Bonapartism of the leagues" and invites Blum to speak at our party congress. The French exiles set up their newspaper in Saarbrücken.

content.content: Paris recalls its ambassador for consultations.
Paris protests to the Foreign Office about "the insults of the German Marxists".

e2_franco_soviet.join.unavailableSubtitle: Moscow does not trust us enough.
e2_franco_soviet.join.subtitle: Moscow will be far less likely to attack us. Poland and the nationalists will be alarmed.

content: The protocol is signed in Geneva: Germany, France and the Soviet Union will consult if any of them is attacked, and none will help the aggressor.

content.content: The Reichstag ratifies it with our votes and the Centre's, against the whole of the right.

content: Warsaw recalls its ambassador for consultations. The nationalist press prints a cartoon of the Chancellor dancing with Stalin.

e2_gw_called.accept.subtitle: Germany will go to war with Poland, France and Britain, at Moscow's side. Our party will split.

content.content: The treaty is signed in the Kremlin. A week later, German and Soviet troops cross into Poland from both sides, and France and Britain declare war on Germany. This is the general war that Europe has feared since 1918, and this time Germany started it.
In the Reichstag, the bourgeois parties walk out together, and several of our own deputies follow them.

e2_hitler_austria.open_border.subtitle: Republic support and the Left faction will approve. The nationalists will not. (-1 budget)

content.content: The Reich government declares that every person persecuted by the new regime in Vienna will find asylum in Germany. By the end of the month, forty thousand Austrians have crossed into Bavaria. The nationalist press complains about "the Jews from Vienna". The trade unions find work for as many of the refugees as they can.

e2_hungary.guarantee.subtitle: Prague will hold. Budapest and Rome will be angry, and the right will ask why Germans should die for Slovakia.

content.content: We sign a guarantee of Czechoslovakia's frontier on the Danube,
The government signs a guarantee of Czechoslovakia's frontier on the Danube, with our votes and against the nationalists',

content: and two German divisions hold maneuvers in Moravia. Horthy pulls his troops back from the border and gives an angry speech about "the betrayal of the German people's old comrades in arms". In the Reichstag, a <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
deputy asks how many Germans live in Ruthenia. The answer is very few.

e2_july_putsch.support.subtitle: The Austrian Nazis will find it harder to try again.

content.content: The Chancellor tells the Reichstag that Germany stands by the government in Vienna, and the frontier police close the Bavarian border to Nazi couriers.
Our deputies move a resolution of support for Vienna, and the government accepts it. The frontier police close the Bavarian border to Nazi couriers.
The Left faction points out that the same government shelled the workers' flats of Vienna five months ago.
Vienna's Social Democrats thank us, and the Schutzbund sends a delegation to Berlin.

e2_gw_declaration.truce.subtitle: The whole nation will stand together. The Left faction will remember 1914.

content: The credits pass with the votes of every party but the <span style="color: #700000;">

. The Chancellor proclaims a political truce: no strikes, no elections and no party quarrels until the war is over. The nationalist press is delighted. In the Left faction, people are reading Liebknecht again.

e2_khalkhin_peace.title: Peace in Manchuria
e2_khalkhin_peace.subtitle: Moscow and Tokyo sign an armistice.

content.content: After more than a year of fighting, the Kwantung Army has been driven back across the Argun and out of northern Manchuria, and Tokyo has signed an armistice that leaves the Red Army on the Sungari. The Japanese generals who started the war have been retired, and Tokyo's attention has turned south, to the colonies of the European powers.
After more than a year of fighting, neither army has gained much. The armistice signed in Harbin leaves the frontier where it was, and both sides claim the victory.

content: The trains on the Trans-Siberian railway are running west again. The Red Army's divisions are coming back to Europe, with officers who have learned how to fight a modern war.

content.content: Moscow has thanked the Republic for its trucks.
Moscow has not forgotten the Zeiss lenses.

content.content: Berlin declares its neutrality in the war in Asia, and forbids the export of arms to either side. Everything else is sold for cash.

e2_league_reformed.treaty.subtitle: Every war will be less likely. The right will be loud.

content: The treaty is signed in Geneva by thirty-one states, the Soviet Union among them. The Reichstag ratifies it by a large majority, with the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
voting against and the general staff keeping its opinion to itself. For the first time, an aggressor in Europe would know in advance what it would cost him.
prints the full text of Tukhachevsky's last letter, smuggled out by a refugee, and our Reichstag deputies stand for a minute's silence for the victims of the purges.

content.content: The government issues travel papers to anyone who can show they are fleeing the NKVD.
We press the Interior Ministry to issue travel papers to anyone fleeing the NKVD, and after weeks of argument it agrees.

The Dewey commission is allowed to hear Trotsky's evidence, and he spends eight days answering its questions. Its verdict, "Not guilty", is printed in every newspaper in Berlin except the Moscow loyalists' sheets.

content: The Soviet ambassador lodges a formal protest, and the
calls us "the lawyers of the Trotskyist wreckers". However, some of its members have quietly started turning in their membership cards.
The Soviet ambassador lodges a formal protest. The
leadership says nothing, but Moscow's loyalists call us "the lawyers of the Trotskyist wreckers".

e2_munzenberg.welcome.subtitle: The KPD loses a third of its support, much of it to us. Moscow will be furious.

content: Münzenberg's group stands its own candidates, but it votes with us in the Reichstag and campaigns with us in the cities. What is left of the <span style="color: #700000;">
denounces him as a Trotskyist, a police spy and a social fascist, in that order.

e2_mosley.moscow.subtitle: The Soviet Union will be friendlier. What is left of the West will trust us even less.

content.content: The Soviet ambassador is received at the Chancellery the following week, and a trade treaty follows within a month: Soviet oil and grain for German machinery, with a clause on "consultation in the event of a threat to the peace". Paris calls it the Rapallo of the Popular Front. The bourgeois parties are horrified, but they have nothing better to offer.

e2_naval_talks.ratio.subtitle: -1 budget. London will be pleased and Paris will not. The shipyards will have work.

content: The agreement is signed in London. The French learn of it from the newspapers, and say so. The first keels are laid at Blohm & Voss in the autumn.

content.content: The Left faction votes against the naval estimates, and the Chancellor carries them with the Centre's votes.
Our deputies split on the naval estimates, and the government carries them with the Centre's votes.

The Hamburg shipyards are soon building freighters for the American merchant marine, and German steel is going to Liverpool. Unemployment in the port cities falls by a third. In Washington, the Secretary of State speaks warmly of "the democratic German Republic". Moscow notes the new friendship and says nothing.

e2_olympics.grand.subtitle: -2 budget
e2_olympics.grand.unavailableSubtitle: The Finance Ministry cannot find the money.

content.content: The new stadium in the Grunewald holds a hundred thousand spectators, and on opening day it is full. The torch relay runs from Olympia through Athens, Sofia, Belgrade, Vienna and Prague, and the black-red-gold flies over all of it.

content: Foreign correspondents had expected a gray, anxious country. Instead they found cafés, jazz and a city very pleased with itself. Jesse Owens wins four gold medals, and the Berlin crowds cheer him on. The nationalists complain that
spent a fortune on a party, but most Berliners are glad of it, and even some Nazi voters are won over.

e2_popular_front_fr.ties.subtitle: France and Germany will draw closer, and the French right will be weaker. The Centre will be uneasy.

content.content: Blum comes to Berlin in the autumn. The two governments sign a trade agreement and a cultural convention, and agree to meet every six months. In the Reichstag, the nationalists walk out during his speech.

Blum speaks at our party congress in the autumn, to a standing ovation. The government signs a modest trade agreement with Paris a month later, under pressure from our benches. The nationalists call it a meeting of the Second International.

e2_rexists.neutral.subtitle: Tension will ease. Paris will be disappointed.

content.content: Berlin declares that it will respect and, if asked, guarantee the neutrality of Belgium, as Prussia did in 1839. Brussels thanks us. The French ambassador observes that the last German guarantee of Belgian neutrality did not end well.

e2_rhineland_zone.remilitarize.subtitle: The nationalists will cheer and the army will be grateful. Paris will not forget it.

content.content: At dawn, three battalions cross the Hohenzollern Bridge into Cologne, with flowers thrown at them from the windows.

The government sends the troops in, and our deputies vote for the motion of confidence that follows. At dawn, three battalions cross the Hohenzollern Bridge into Cologne, with flowers thrown at them from the windows.

content: The French General Staff asks its government for mobilization, and is refused. London says that the Germans have only gone into their own back garden. The nationalist press, for once, has nothing bad to say about the Republic.

e2_spain_partner.credits.unavailableSubtitle: The treasury cannot spare the money.
e2_spain_partner.credits.subtitle: -1 budget. A grateful ally in the south, a calmer France and an angrier Italy.

content.content: A consortium of German banks, with a Reich guarantee, lends Madrid three hundred million marks over ten years. Most of it comes straight back as orders for German locomotives, turbines and telephone exchanges. Siemens opens an office in Barcelona. In Rome, Mussolini, who sent his legions to fight for Franco, says that Germany has "bought itself a red colony".

e2_spain.non_intervention.subtitle: London and Paris will approve. The Left faction and the KPD will not.

content.content: The government signs, and we do not stand in its way.

content: A committee in London meets weekly to record violations, and records them faithfully while doing nothing about them. Italian and Soviet arms keep arriving, and the only country really kept from arming is the Spanish Republic.

At the party congress, a young delegate from Leipzig reads out the names of Spanish Socialists killed in Seville, and the hall stands for a minute's silence. The Left faction is furious with the leadership, and the
accuses us of abandoning Spain. The Center Party, on the other hand, approves of our caution.

e2_stalin_health.thaw.subtitle: Relations with Moscow will improve. Washington will be uneasy.

content.content: The talks open in Stockholm, on neutral ground. They produce a trade treaty, an agreement to exchange prisoners and refugees still held from the thirties, and a joint commission on the frontiers that meets twice and then adjourns. It is very little. It is also the first agreement Moscow has signed with anyone in a year.
We sign a treaty of friendship with Czechoslovakia that recognizes its frontiers as final, and we press Beneš, in private, to treat his German citizens better.

With our votes behind it, the government signs a treaty of friendship with Czechoslovakia that recognizes its frontiers as final. Our comrades in Prague press Beneš, in private, to treat his German citizens better.

content: Henlein's movement is left with nowhere to go. Within six months it has split in two, and its moderate wing is negotiating with Prague over language rights in schools.

content.content: At home, the nationalists call it the betrayal of the Sudetenland. The charge stings. But there will be no war in Bohemia.

The government sent nobody." }, { id: "e2nn_spring_strike", from: [1946, 4], until: [1949, 6], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state" && Q.e2p_spring == "strike" && !Q.e2p_democracy; }, cls: "left", text: "The Neuer Vorwärts printed the names of the dead of the general strike, from Berlin, Hamburg and the Ruhr, on two full pages." }, { id: "e2nn_spring_negotiate", from: [1946, 4], until: [1949, 6], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state" && Q.e2p_spring == "negotiate" && !Q.e2p_democracy; }, cls: "world", text: "Papen's successor as Chancellor, a senior official of the Interior Ministry, promised a constitution \"once order allows\"." }, { id: "e2nn_spring_wait", from: [1946, 4], until: [1949, 6], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state" && Q.e2p_spring == "wait"; }, cls: "right", text: "The government papers began printing readers' letters about a future constitution." }, { id: "e2nn_esterwegen_closed", from: [1947, 1], until: [1949, 12], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state" && (Q.e2p_regime < 45 || Q.e2p_army); }, cls: "world", text: "The government closed the camp at Esterwegen and moved its last prisoners to ordinary prisons." }, { id: "e2nn_franco_kingdom", from: [1947, 7], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state" && Q.e2_spain == "nationalist"; }, cls: "world", text: "Spain voted in a referendum to become a kingdom again, with General Franco as head of state for life." }, { id: "e2nn_mussolini_25", from: [1947, 10], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state"; }, cls: "world", text: "Mussolini marked the twenty-fifth anniversary of the March on Rome with a parade of Blackshirts on the Via dell'Impero." }, { id: "e2nn_1848", from: [1948, 3], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state"; }, cls: "left", text: "On the hundredth anniversary of the March Revolution, the underground laid wreaths at the cemetery of the March dead in Friedrichshain. The police arrested forty people there." }, { id: "e2nn_thaw_unions", from: [1948, 6], until: [1949, 12], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state" && Q.e2p_regime < 45 && !Q.e2p_army; }, cls: "world", text: "The government allowed the trade unions to elect their own officials for the first time since 1934." }, { id: "e2nn_draft_constitution", from: [1949, 2], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state"; }, cls: "left", text: "The executive in London published a draft constitution for a free Germany, written with exiled leaders of the " + Z + "." }, { id: "e2nn_weimar_30", from: [1949, 8], when: function (Q) { return Q.era2_path == "new_state"; }, cls: "left", text: "For the thirtieth anniversary of the Weimar constitution, the underground passed copies of its text around the factories." } ]; // Deaths (post_event, "Deaths in Era II"): shown first, for three months from the month of death. var obits = Q.e2_obit_news ? e2_stresa.join.subtitle: Italy and the West will trust us more. Moving against Mussolini later will be harder. The Left faction will object.

content.content: The Foreign Minister signs the declaration in Geneva, beside Laval, Simon and the Italian ambassador.
The Reichstag approves the declaration with our votes, and the Foreign Minister signs it in Geneva beside Laval, Simon and the Italian ambassador.

content: Mussolini calls the Republic "a serious partner in the defense of order". In our own party, the Left faction's paper prints his words on its front page, without comment.

e2_trotsky_berlin.asylum.subtitle: The Left faction will be delighted. Moscow will be furious.

content.content: Trotsky arrives at the Stettiner Bahnhof with his wife, Natalia Sedova, two secretaries and eleven crates of papers. Within a month he has a flat in Charlottenburg, a guard of Prussian policemen and a German publisher. Moscow recalls its ambassador "for consultations". In the cafés of the Kurfürstendamm, a small Trotskyist circle forms, and its first act is to split.
We have no channels to Spain to speak of.

e2_war_cabinet.national.subtitle: The country will see a united government. The Left faction will see the program put away.

content.content: The new cabinet is sworn in at the Chancellery the next morning. A Centre deputy becomes Vice-Chancellor, and the liberals take the Economics Ministry. Our program is put away "until the victory". The Left faction's paper prints the names of the deputies who voted for the war credits in 1914, and leaves its readers to draw their own conclusions.

e2_war_allies.west.unavailableSubtitle: London does not trust us enough to arm us.
e2_war_allies.west.subtitle: -1 budget. Moscow will not like it.

content: The first British convoy docks at Hamburg three weeks later, with fighter aircraft in crates, trucks and shells. The bill is paid in gold from the Reichsbank's reserves, and with a promise that the Republic will settle its accounts with London after the war.

content.content: In Moscow, *Pravda* calls it proof that the capitalist powers have united against the Soviet Union.

e2_war_battle.defensive.subtitle: The front will hold better, but we will not win outright this way.

onArrival.$code:
Q['e2_war_posture'] = "defensive";
Q['e2_war_home'] = (Q['e2_war_home'] || 0) + 2;

content.content: The army falls back to prepared positions and digs in. The general staff calls it "elastic defense". The nationalist press calls it a retreat. The casualty lists, at least, get shorter.

e2_war_end.parade.subtitle: The nationalists and the army will be delighted. The Left faction will not.

content.content: The victorious divisions march through the Brandenburg Gate under the black, red and gold, with the Reichsbanner's veterans behind them. The President takes the salute. The crowds on Unter den Linden are the largest since August 1914, and some of the older people in them are crying.

e2_war_crisis.purge.subtitle: The front will lose a month. The army will know who commands it.

content.content: Forty officers are dismissed, two generals among them, and the regimental commanders who signed the memorandum face a court-martial. The front loses a month while the new commanders learn their sectors. But the army now knows who commands it, and so does the right.

e2_war_home_front.rationing.subtitle: -1 budget. The home front will hold better.

content.content: A Reich Food Office takes over the grain trade, and every family gets a ration card, the same for a general's wife as for a miner's. Prices for bread, potatoes, coal and rent are frozen. The black market does not go away, but it shrinks, and the queues get shorter. People remember the turnip winter of 1916, and how the government was blamed for it. This time the government has done something about it.

content: Anti-tank guns, mortars and two hundred thousand pairs of skis travel from Stettin to Turku. Some three thousand German volunteers,

content.content: many of them veterans of our own civil war,

content: serve in the Finnish army by February. With German guns on the Isthmus, the Mannerheim Line holds into March. When Finland finally makes peace, it gives up much less than Moscow had first demanded.

content.content: Moscow will not forget who armed the Finns.

e2_war_talks.peace.subtitle: The war ends on the present front.

onArrival.$code:
Q.e2_war_talks_done = 1;
Q.e2_war_final = Q.e2_war_front;

e2_world_recession.free_trade.unavailableSubtitle: London and Paris will not come to a conference called by Berlin.

content.content: The Oslo states, the Low Countries and, after some arm-twisting, France agree to freeze tariffs for three years and cut them by a tenth. Britain stays aloof, but signs a side agreement on coal. It is a modest step, but the first in the right direction since 1929. German exporters breathe again, and German farmers, now facing Danish butter and Dutch cheese, are furious.

e2c_bans.all.subtitle: The Center and the liberals will support it. The Left faction will be furious.
e2c_bans.all.unavailableSubtitle: The country is too unsettled to risk it.

content: holds its first rally in a Munich beer hall with room for two thousand people. Fewer than six hundred turn up. Within six months, three rival leaders are claiming the party, and they spend most of their energy denouncing one another. A new nationalist bloc forms around the old
; it campaigns noisily, but within the law.
The Left faction of our party is furious with us.
accuses us of rehabilitating the men who fought the Republic.
, which has been recruiting the same men for years, accuses us of handing them back to the bourgeois parties.
Still, the political police report that the cellars are much emptier now.

e2c_bredow_coup.arrest.subtitle: Requires the Prussian police, or a seat in the cabinet and a reliable army.

content.content: We have neither the Prussian police nor a reliable army command to carry out the arrests.
We do not control the Prussian police, and the army does not take orders from the opposition.

onArrival.$code:
Q.e2c_bredow_choice = 1;
Q.e2c_bredow_def = 25 + (Q.reichswehr_loyalty || 0) * 40 + (Q.spd_prussia ? 10 : 0);

e2c_constitution.heller.subtitle: Needs a two-thirds majority: the Center, or a strong left.
e2c_constitution.heller.unavailableSubtitle: We cannot muster two-thirds of the convention for a new constitution.

content.content: The Constitution of the Second German Republic is adopted on a warm evening in late summer, and the bells of Frankfurt ring as the result is read out. It has no emergency article. The Reichswehr Minister must be a civilian who answers to the Reichstag, and a chancellor can only be removed if a majority agrees on a successor. Article 151 promises every German "work, a dwelling, and a share in the governance of the enterprise in which he labors".
The generals sulk. We will have to enforce the constitution's promises about the army one promotion at a time.
Most of the officer corps swears the new oath without protest.

content: The Center's newspaper calls it "a socialist charter wearing a liberal coat", but the Center deputies voted for it all the same. Both our Left and Reformist factions are satisfied.

e2c_new_right.front.subtitle: Requires workable relations with the Center. The Left faction will grumble.
e2c_new_right.front.unavailableSubtitle: The Center will not stand on a platform with us.

content.content: The new notes are printed on heavy paper with a sheaf of wheat on the reverse, and within three months prices stop rising. The middle classes, who have already lost their savings once in their lifetimes, are deeply relieved.

However, the building sites go quiet. Half-repaired bridges stand idle on the Elbe, and the dole queues in Leipzig and Chemnitz grow longer every week. The unions accuse us of saving the Mark at the expense of the workers who saved the Republic, and the Labor faction is furious with us.

e2c_outlaw.all.subtitle: The Left and Labor factions will approve, but the bourgeois parties will be uneasy.

content.content: We sign the decree the same night. Police in every Land raid the party offices, seize the membership files and padlock the Brown House in Munich.

The Left and Labor factions are satisfied, but the Center and the liberals warn that this is how dictatorships begin. Unfortunately, the younger men of the far right are already organizing again, in the cellars.

e2c_reconstruction_done.housing.title: Transfer the Office's funds to a public housing program.
e2c_reconstruction_done.housing.subtitle: The building workers keep their jobs. The bourgeois parties want the money returned to the Treasury. (-1 budget)

content.content: The Office's housing department becomes a Reich housing agency and keeps its contracts with the building cooperatives. It will build flats for rent in the industrial towns.

e2c_rhineland.pay.subtitle: (-2 budget)
e2c_rhineland.pay.unavailableSubtitle: The treasury cannot find the money.

content.content: The treaty is signed at Locarno, in the same room as the agreements of 1925. We will pay what we owe, and the left bank of the Rhine will stay free of German troops for twenty years. The last French battalion marches across the Hohenzollern Bridge in Cologne the following spring.
The nationalist papers call it "buying back our own land". However, the Rhinelanders are free of foreign soldiers again, and they ring the cathedral bells.
The treasury cannot cover the compensation bonds.

The Ruhr Coal and Steel Authority takes over a hundred and forty pits and thirty-two steelworks on the first of January. Its board has twelve seats: four for the miners' and metalworkers' unions, four for the Reich and four for the consuming industries. The old owners receive bonds at 4%, which the stock exchange values at about half their face value.
At the Zollverein colliery, the miners raise a red flag next to the black-red-gold, and nobody tells them to take it down. The Left and Labor factions are delighted.

The trials run for more than a year. The newspapers print the testimony every day, including the orders to shoot hostages in Spandau, the lists of trade unionists marked for arrest, and the industrialists' checks. Most of the bourgeois press grudgingly admits that we have behaved like a state governed by law, and the liberals and the Center approve. However, the officer corps is unhappy, because the court calls generals as witnesses and as defendants.
The sentences are severe, but not savage. The evidence is now on the record, and nobody can deny it.

content: The Atlanticists win the vote by a narrow margin, and two hundred delegates walk out singing the
. A week later they found the Socialist Unity Party of Germany, the <span style="color: #9B0000;">
, in a trade union hall in Leipzig. The majority renames itself the Social Democratic People's Party, the
, and keeps the party's offices, its newspapers and most of its voters.

content.content: Within the year Paris has its alliance, and the final clause of the treaty brings the last French soldiers home from the Rhine.

content: is now welcome in the capitals of the West. However, it has lost many of the workers in the factory towns of Saxony.

content.content: The Treaty of Thorn recognizes the present line as the frontier between Germany and Poland, and East Prussia and eastern Upper Silesia pass to Poland. In return, Warsaw guarantees German schools, newspapers and churches in the ceded territories, and any German who wishes to leave may take his property with him. Germany is smaller than it was, but it is at peace with its eastern neighbor.

content: The refugee associations hold a day of mourning, and black flags hang from half the houses in Stettin. The nationalists are outraged, and the

content.content: Strasser's ministers resign in protest, and the cabinet survives without them.

content: The question that has poisoned German politics since the civil war is closed, though many Germans will never accept the answer.

e2d_black_front.ban.subtitle: The Left faction will approve. The liberals will not.
e2d_black_front.ban.unavailableSubtitle: Only the Reich government can ban it, and we are in opposition.

content: 's offices on the Kurfürstenstraße and seize its printing presses. Strasser escapes to Copenhagen and broadcasts from there. The halls go dark, and the black flags disappear from the streets.

content.content: Unfortunately, the cells in the garrisons do not disappear. They simply stop meeting where the police can find them.

e2d_french_withdrawal.timetable.subtitle: Requires the Morgenthau timetable and a settled Ruhr.

content.content: We never signed the Morgenthau pact.
The Ruhr Red Army is still in the field.

content: Paris keeps its word. On a gray morning, the tricolor is lowered over Ehrenbreitstein, and the last French battalion boards its train at Mainz for Metz, its band playing
. The mayors of Koblenz and Mainz give the departing officers a dinner, and the speeches are generous on both sides.

content.content: Keeping our agreements has paid off. Even the nationalist press admits it, if reluctantly.

e2d_march_on_berlin.army.subtitle: Requires a seat in the cabinet, and an army that will fire on Germans in uniform.

content.content: We are in opposition. The Reichswehr does not take our orders.
The Reichswehr will not fire on veterans for this Republic.

onArrival.$code:
Q.e2d_march_def = 20 + Q.reichswehr_loyalty * 50 + (Q.e2d_tp_infiltrated ? 10 : 0);
Q.e2d_march_choice = 1;

e2d_morgenthau.full.subtitle: Requires the West's confidence. The Left faction will be furious.
e2d_morgenthau.full.unavailableSubtitle: The Western capitals do not trust us enough to offer the full plan.

content.content: The first American engineers arrive in Hamburg that autumn, and within eighteen months a new power station is running at Vockerode on the Elbe. Steel bridges go up over the Elbe and the Oder, and the queues at the labor exchanges give way to building sites full of men.

content: Every new bridge has a small bronze plaque saying who paid for it, and the Third Positionists have taken to defacing them with tar. The Left faction and the
are furious about the pact. However, in Paris, the War Ministry has quietly started planning the withdrawal.

content.content: Three divisions take up positions along the Oder and the Netze, and the newspapers print maps of East Prussia with black borders. Warsaw answers with five divisions, and the talks in Geneva end within an hour.
The nationalist press praises our firmness. However, the treasury is now paying soldiers to stand in fields (-1 budget), and the provinces are no nearer to coming home.

e2d_refugees.settle.subtitle: Costs 1 budget.
e2d_refugees.settle.unavailableSubtitle: The treasury cannot finance the settlement banks.

content.content: The Reich Settlement Law gives forty thousand families a holding of fifteen hectares each, carved out of estates whose owners had stopped paying their mortgages long before the war. Many of those owners are in exile with the defeated militias, or in the officer corps. The refugees build their own cottages from the bricks of the manor houses' barns.
In Pomerania, men who expected to spend the rest of their lives in a camp are sowing rye. Their landlords' sons in the Reichswehr regard this as theft and say so in the mess.

The Act of Reunification is passed by four hundred and twelve votes to sixty-one. It creates a federal Republic of fifteen Länder, including a Rhenish-Westphalian Land with its own constitution and its own police. The Reichsrat becomes a real second chamber, and no Land may leave the federation.

content: When the result is announced, the delegates stand and sing. Some sing the
, and most of them do not seem to mind which. Outside, church bells ring across the town, and then across the whole country.
The miners' union persuades the Central Council's moderates to accept, and one afternoon in Essen they simply walk out of the town hall and hand the keys to the Reich commissioner.

content.content: The hardliners have nobody left to command. The last Red Army patrol hands its rifles to a Reichswehr lieutenant on the Ruhr bridge at Mülheim and asks for a cigarette.
The hardliners hold out in Duisburg and the docks at Ruhrort, but their number is shrinking every week.

The second Ruhr referendum passes with sixty-eight percent. The widows get their pensions and the mines stay public. The Land police keep their armbands, which they now wear only on the first of May. Germany is reunited as a federation and on the Ruhr's terms, and it is fairer for that than it might have been.

e2d_ruhr_question.offensive.subtitle: Requires an army we can trust.
e2d_ruhr_question.offensive.unavailableSubtitle: The Reichswehr is not reliable enough to send into the Ruhr.

content.content: The offensive takes Recklinghausen and Gelsenkirchen in a month of street fighting. It stalls in the rubble of Herne, where the Red Army fights shaft by shaft and blows the pitheads rather than surrender them. By the time the front settles again, the council has lost a third of its territory. The towns we have taken have no coal or electricity, and in some of them there are no men left of working age.
The officer corps is pleased. The workers of Berlin are not, and the funerals in Wedding are attended by more people than our May Day rally.

e2d_ruhr_settlement.statute.subtitle: Requires trust between Berlin and Essen.
e2d_ruhr_settlement.statute.unavailableSubtitle: Essen does not trust us enough to disarm on our word.

content.content: The Statute of the Rhenish-Westphalian Industrial Land is signed in the old Essen town hall, under a portrait of the miners' leader Otto Hue. The mines remain the property of the people of the Ruhr. The Red Army becomes the Ruhr Land Police, reporting to the Reich Interior Minister, though it still wears red armbands on the anniversary. The Lippe line is opened at midnight, and miners' families cross in both directions to see relatives they have not seen in years.
The generals say Germany has rewarded rebellion. The coal is flowing, though, and the French have lost their best excuse for staying on the Rhine.

subtitle: The monarchy will be more parliamentary, but our Left faction will be outraged, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
will be hostile.

content.content: Our deputies swear allegiance "to the King and to the constitution", stressing both words equally.
Our party executive and the union chairmen attend the coronation, and declare the labor movement's allegiance "to the King and to the constitution", stressing both words equally.

content: The British ambassador reports to London that the German Social Democrats are becoming "His Majesty's loyal opposition".

content.content: Half our members are relieved. Unfortunately, the other half are tearing up their party cards, and our Left and Labor factions are outraged.

e2k_border.refuse.subtitle: The pacifists and the left will stand with us. The nationalists will call it treason.

content.content: We vote no, all of us, and the credits pass without us.
Our newspapers and the unions denounce the credits, and they pass without us.

content: Seldte calls us the party of the stab in the back. But the war the general staff wanted needs a united country, and without the workers' party, the government settles for a few more border posts and a great deal of rhetoric.

content.content: On a Monday morning, the trams stop, the mines fall silent and the newspapers do not appear.

By Thursday, the Prussian cabinet withdraws the bill. The government calls it a postponement. Everyone else calls it the first defeat of the restored monarchy, and the Center and the liberals start to talk about a constitution in which the ministers answer to the Reichstag.

The army occupies the power stations and the railway yards. After nine days the unions call off the strike, and thousands of their organizers are dismissed, arrested or both. The bill passes in the spring.

e2k_election.stand.subtitle: We will keep some of our seats. (-1 resources)

content.content: We campaign under every restriction they invent. On election night, the monitors report a "national majority" of 60%. However, we keep 120 seats, and the foreign press reports on our arrested canvassers. Our Left faction thinks we have lent the farce our respectability.

e2k_purge.support.subtitle: The government notices our loyalty. So do our voters.

content.content: We vote for the emergency measures. Seldte thanks the "national-minded workers of the Social Democracy" from the Reichstag rostrum, which is the first compliment a Stahlhelm leader has ever paid us. In Wedding and Neukölln, people ask who will be arrested when the emergency is extended to the next opponents.

e2k_prince.reform.subtitle: A parliamentary monarchy, if the prince means it.

content: The regent's first speech from the throne promises responsible ministers, equal suffrage in Prussia and an end to the emergency decrees, and

content.content: our votes give him the majority to keep his word
the unions and our newspapers rally the country behind him, although we have no seats in the Reichstag
Within the year, the Chancellor is chosen by the Reichstag, and the crown has become what the British call a dignified part of the constitution.
The court party fights every clause, and the reforms come slowly, but they come.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
and our Left faction will approve. The Reformist faction will not. (+1 budget)

content.content: By decree, every transfer abroad above a thousand marks now needs a license, and the Reichsbank directorate is replaced by men who answer to the Finance Ministry. The outflow slows to a trickle.

London and Paris protest the freezing of foreign balances, and the middle classes grumble about the paperwork. However, the Mark holds, and the factories keep their credit lines. Our budget situation should improve somewhat.

subtitle: Popular with workers, but the <span style="color: #700000;">
will grumble. (-1 budget)

content.content: The new Bauhaus opens in a converted brewery in Berlin-Weißensee, and within a year its students are designing estates for Siemensstadt, Duisburg and Leipzig. Housing cooperatives run by tenants' councils commission the work and own the results. The flats are small, bright and cheap, with kitchens designed by Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky.

content: The building program has put many people back to work. The <span style="color: #700000;">
complains about formalism, but then quietly allocates the new flats to its own members. Unfortunately, the conservative press has made the "flat-roofed barracks" a rallying cry.

e2l_blocs.east.subtitle: Moscow will be pleased, but the West will be hostile, and our Reformist faction will be furious.

content.content: We take our seat in the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance and sign a Treaty of Friendship with the Soviet Union. Soviet orders keep the steel mills of the Ruhr at full capacity, and Soviet planners arrive to "harmonize" our plan with the plans of Poland and Czechoslovakia.
The Party's grip tightens as the advisers settle in.
Many of our own people are deeply uneasy, and the councils find that their targets are now being set somewhere else. The Reformist faction is furious.

content: In Washington, the newspapers write of "the loss of Germany".

e2l_convention.councils.subtitle: The councils will be much stronger. Our Left faction will be delighted, and the Reformists furious.

content.content: After eleven weeks of argument, the convention adopts the constitution of the German Council Republic. The Reichstag remains, elected by every citizen. Beside it sits the Workers' Chamber, elected by the councils, with a veto over economic legislation and sole control of the planning budget. Every factory, mine, office and estate elects a council, and every council can recall its delegates.

content: Many lawyers say the system is unworkable, and our Reformist faction agrees with them. However, the <span style="color: #700000;">
, which has demanded "All power to the soviets" for twenty years, could hardly vote against it, and our Left faction is delighted.
and the nationalists will be outraged.

leaders. In a villa in Potsdam, they find a draft proclamation and a list of ministers to be "taken into protective custody". The plotters claim it was a staff exercise. It is not quite the proof we wanted, but it is enough to hold them.

press condemns our "Bolshevik methods" against "officers of honor", and the nationalists are in uproar. The conspiracy has lost its leaders. However, we cannot be sure that we have caught all of its members.

e2l_council_bureaucracy.recall.subtitle: The councils will be stronger, but production will suffer for a while. The Labor faction will approve.

content: A new Council Statute limits every full-time delegate to two terms, requires them to return to the workbench or the coalface between terms, and allows any council to be recalled by a petition of a fifth of its electors.

content.content: Half of the Ruhr Coal Council is voted out within a year.
Half of the Ruhr's council delegates are voted out within a year.
Production stumbles while the new delegates learn their jobs, but the Hamborn miners go back to work. Our Labor faction is pleased with us.

content.content: The Finance Ministry issues three-percent Reich Compensation Bonds, redeemable in 1960, to every foreign holder of socialized shares. The terms are not generous, but they are better than nothing, and the City accepts them with a show of reluctance. The embargo is lifted within three months.

content: calls it "tribute to the imperialists", and our Left faction agrees. Our budget will feel the cost for years.

Fortunately, the socialization of coal, steel, energy and banking is written into the constitution, and the new government cannot undo it without a two-thirds majority.
The Workers' Chamber still sits beside the Reichstag, and the new government will have to deal with it on every economic law.
The people's democracy constitution was meant to make this impossible. However, the voters have rejected the National Front list, and the army has made it clear that it will defend the result.
Unfortunately, nothing we have built is protected by the constitution, and the new government has already promised to "review" the socialization laws.

content.content: Land commissions of laborers, smallholders and surveyors divide some three million hectares into holdings of eight to fifteen hectares. The first harvests are poor, and the new farmers will need credit and tractors for years.

content: However, the manor houses are now village schools, and the rural poor are grateful to us. The <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
has lost its last reliable voters in the east, and the officer corps is bitter about the loss of its families' estates.

About a third of the Red Front Fighters refuse to join, and keep their rifles hidden at home. However, the rest accept the new command with surprisingly little grumbling. The <span style="color: #700000;">

content.content: The Interior Minister tells the Reichstag that Germany does not extradite people for their opinions—"not to Rome, not to Vienna, and not to Moscow". Neumann testifies before a Reichstag commission of inquiry, and the transcripts are reprinted abroad.

content.content: Gerlach becomes Minister of Justice, and Wirth becomes Minister of Labor, an office he knows well. Our majority in the Reichstag grows, and Catholic workers in the Rhineland and the Saar are starting to vote for us. Foreign diplomats now describe the cabinet as "broad-based".

e2l_socialisation.councils.subtitle: The councils will be much stronger, and our Left faction will be pleased. Output may suffer at first.

content.content: The law passes after an all-night sitting. In Gelsenkirchen and Bochum the miners elect pit councils, and the pit councils elect a Ruhr Coal Council, which meets for the first time in the old boardroom of the coal syndicate.

Output falls for a quarter while the delegates learn to read balance sheets. Then it begins to climb again. Our Left and Labor factions are delighted, although the Reformists think we have gambled with the economy.

e2l_officers.purge.subtitle: The army will be more loyal, but the nationalists will be outraged.

content: Two hundred colonels and generals are retired on full pension. Their places are filled by officers who stood by the Republic in 1920 and 1923, by former police commanders from Prussia, and by a handful of
veterans with front experience. A new oath binds the army to the constitution and to the Reichstag.
The retired officers gather in the Herrenklub to denounce the "red Reichswehr", and the nationalists are outraged. However, the army is now far more reliable than before. Our Left faction is pleased
