content.content: Within two years, the parity rule is quietly dropped, the "Schumacher clique" is expelled, and the party statute is revised to forbid factions. Some fifty thousand Social Democrats refuse to join the new party. Many of them go into exile in London or Stockholm; some go to the camps.
The Reformist faction is outraged, and the councils have lost much of their independence.

The Reichstag passes the Equal Pay Act, and a law guaranteeing the right to abortion, so that no future government can quietly undo it.

content: The councils amend their statutes so that every third delegate must be a woman. In the textile towns of Saxony, where women are the majority, they take over the councils within a year. The first factory nursery at Siemensstadt has a waiting list of eight hundred names on its opening day.
The bishops preach against "the murder of the unborn" from every pulpit in the Rhineland, and the
is furious with us. However, our Left faction is pleased.

e2p_entente.lobby.subtitle: Our friends in Paris can make this hard for Papen.

content.content: Blum's group and the Radicals make the entente impossible to ratify. Papen comes home empty-handed and turns to Rome and Vienna instead, where the company is less respectable.
The French right wants the entente more than the French left can stop it. Papen signs a declaration of friendship in Paris, and the New State's newspapers print the photographs for a week.

e2p_exile.exile.subtitle: Safe, respected abroad, and far away.

content: The executive sets up in Prague with a newspaper, the

, printed on thin paper so that couriers can carry it over the mountains in their boots. The foreign press quotes it. The comrades at home read it, when it reaches them, and wonder whether anyone in Prague knows what Germany is like now.

e2p_ruhr.support.subtitle: The regime will feel it. So will our networks.

content.content: Our couriers carry money from Prague and leaflets from Berlin. The strike lasts seven weeks, longer than anyone expected, and ends with a pay settlement that Papen's ministers present as their own idea. The police arrest four hundred of our people afterwards. The pit committees survive.

e2p_schleicher.accept.subtitle: Papen falls, but the army rises.

content.content: The unions' underground committees agree, and Schleicher moves in the spring. Papen is escorted from the Chancellery to his estate at Wallerfangen and told to stay there. The unions are legal again within the month. The parties are not, and the new government's ministers wear uniform to cabinet meetings.

e2p_spring.negotiate.subtitle: A safe transition, with the old elites still in their posts.

content.content: The reformers listen politely and then decide that the underground is too weak to need. The regime closes ranks around a new Chancellor from the old elites.

The Foreign Office makes helium a matter of national honor. Washington agrees to sell enough for LZ 130, on condition that it is never used for military purposes. The ship flies in the autumn, full of helium, and every seat on the first crossing is sold. The Zeppelin company announces two more ships. Privately, its own engineers wonder whether anyone will still want to cross the Atlantic at 130 kilometers an hour in ten years' time.

content.content: Zuse gets a contract, a workshop in Adlershof and a deadline. He founds his own company, Zuse Engineering, with four employees and a typewriter. The statisticians start rewriting their models in his strange notation of arrows and boxes.

The Reich Motorway Company is founded as a subsidiary of the Reichsbahn, which leaves Dorpmüller in charge of the thing he hates and quiets him for the time being. The first labor gangs break ground outside Frankfurt in September. Most of them were on the dole a month ago. The surveyors are already working north toward Darmstadt.

content.content: The savings banks offer "household loans" at four percent, which can be repaid over three years. By Christmas, a hundred thousand families have signed up. The shops are empty by the middle of December, and the economists at the Reichsbank are starting to talk about inflation.

A board of twenty-one members, chosen by the Reichstag, the Länder, the trade unions and the churches, will decide what Germans see. Everyone says it will be dull, and everyone wants a seat on the board.

The Reich Institute for Rocket Research opens in Charlottenburg, with von Braun as head of propulsion and Oberth as honorary president. Its first annual report is published in German, English and French. Dornberger is furious that the army's money trained the institute's best man. The old Raketenflugplatz is kept as a test field, and the neighbors in Reinickendorf are told to keep their windows open on firing days.

content: property becomes the default in every new marriage. The women teachers dismissed in 1932 now have a right to reinstatement. Elisabeth Selbert is cheered on the floor of the Reichstag!
The bishops order a day of prayer for the German family, and the
is angry with us. Some Catholic voters are turning away from us, but we have won new support among white-collar voters.
Our party chairman is the first guest speaker at the <span style="color: #000000;">

's founding rally in Essen. He speaks of the Republic that our two parties built together in 1919, and have defended together ever since, and the applause is warm and long. In the Reichstag, the press has begun to speak of a "social bloc". Our relations with the

content.content: However, the Left faction mutters that the party of Bebel is becoming the junior partner of the bishops.

content.content: The 5% clause passes. At the next election, the splinter parties must merge or vanish, and most of the middle-class interest parties simply vanish; their voters drift to the larger bourgeois parties. The next Reichstag will be much easier to govern.

content: The hearing lasts eleven days. The Interior Ministry's file is read into the record page by page, including the lists of our officials' home addresses. The judgment is unanimous: the <span style="color: #D79E2A;">
is "in its program, its organization and its conduct, the successor of the National Socialist movement", and it is dissolved. Its assets are seized, and its deputies lose their seats.
Naumann goes into exile in Argentina. A few of his followers go underground, but most simply go home. The
has some doubts about banning a party, but the ruling has strengthened support for the Republic.

content.content: We do not hold the Justice Ministry.

The Judicial Renewal Act retires more than a fifth of the higher bench in a single year. Their successors will be trained at new judicial academies, where the constitution is taught as living law. The Radbruch code abolishes the death penalty, and treats political violence as violence, whatever uniform it wears. The Association of German Judges challenges the law before the Staatsgerichtshof, and loses by a single vote.

The Reich cannot afford it right now.

The Reich Housing Act passes after a long night in committee. By the following spring, scaffolding has gone up on the edges of every large city: in Spandau and Siemensstadt, in Leipzig-Lößnig, and on the hills above Stuttgart. Thousands of building workers are back at work, and our support among the workers has grown.

content: The landlords' associations call the revived tax "expropriation by installments", and the small property owners are turning against us. The
is also unhappy with the new tax.
The Coal and Steel Co-determination Act passes on a Friday

content: . On the Monday, the strike committees stand down, and the first labor directors take their seats in Essen, Duisburg and Gelsenkirchen. Miners and furnacemen now sit opposite the bankers on the supervisory boards of Krupp and the United Steelworks.
The Labor faction and the workers are delighted. The

content.content: Only the Reich government can propose this.
The Prussian government will not agree to its own abolition, and our partners will not force it.
Our partners will not supply the votes for a constitutional majority.

On the first of April, the black-and-white flag comes down over the Prussian State Ministry for the last time. Its departments move across the street into the Reich ministries, and the provinces, from East Prussia to the Rhine, become Reich provinces with elected assemblies of their own. Prussian conservatives hold a memorial service in the Potsdam Garrison Church, and the Bavarians boycott the Reichsrat for a month.

content: There is now one government in Berlin, one police chain of command and one majority. Nobody will ever again be able to seize Germany by seizing Prussia. However, the
is unhappy that the Rhineland did not get a Land of its own, and many of our Prussian officials in the Reformist faction resent the loss of their state.

e2w_programme.peoples.subtitle: The Left faction will be furious.

content: After a night session that ends with a standing ovation and several walkouts, the Godesberg Program passes by 324 votes to 16. The word "Marxism" does not appear in it. Democratic socialism is defined as a "lasting task", rooted in Christian ethics, humanism and classical philosophy, and private property in the means of production "deserves protection and encouragement, so long as it does not obstruct a just social order".

content.content: Our people's party finally has a program to match.

The Catholic press is cautiously approving, and we are gaining ground with the middle classes, the farmers and the Catholics. The Reformists are delighted. However, the Left faction is furious, and some workers feel that we have left them behind.
We hold neither the Economics nor the Finance Ministry.

The Reich Employment Program puts 400,000 men to work within six months: electrifying the line from Berlin to Hamburg, widening the roads through the Harz, and finishing the housing estates that the slump interrupted. The Reichsbank grumbles, but discounts the bills anyway. By the autumn, the lines at the labor exchanges are shorter, and the workers and the unemployed are grateful to us.

content: warns that we are courting inflation.

content.content: We do not hold the Reichswehr Ministry, and the army command would simply refuse.

The Officer Corps Act lowers the retirement age for generals to 60, abolishes the "election" of new officers by their regimental messes, and sets aside a third of the officer-cadet places for long-serving NCOs. Every soldier swears a new oath, to the constitution by name. Forty-one generals retire in a single month.

The nationalists are outraged, and three of the retired generals found a veterans' league that will cause us trouble for years. However, the colonels who replace them owe their promotions to the Republic. The army is far more loyal than before, and the Left faction is pleased.
We do not hold the Labor Ministry.
The Reich's finances cannot carry it.

The People's Insurance Act passes after the longest debate in the history of the Reichstag. On the first of January, every working German receives a gray cardboard card with a single number on it, which will follow them from their first job to the grave. Widows in Pomerania now receive pensions they can live on, and farmhands in Lower Bavaria can see a doctor without paying. The doctors threaten to strike, but think better of it once they see the new fee schedules.

content: The workers, the rural poor and the Labor faction are delighted. However, the
resent being outvoted, and the middle classes grumble about the cost.

content.content: A new era begins for our party.
The Republic has fallen, but our story goes on.

options.title: Onward to 1950!
Not yet. Go back.

content.content: The crisis years are behind us, or so we hope. Now we face the long work of building something that lasts—through elections and recessions, coups and international crises.

We have brought the Weimar Republic through the Depression without a civil war. Its institutions are fragile, the Reichswehr is restless, and the bourgeois parties still distrust us. However, the ballot box still decides who governs. Now we must show that democracy can do more than survive.

content: The guns have fallen silent. The <span style="color: #3E88B3;">

have been broken in open battle, and for the first time since 1918 the Republic holds a monopoly on force. Unfortunately, the country is exhausted, the Mark is collapsing, and the generals who stood aside are already plotting against us.
We did not win alone, and everyone knows it.

content.content: The Western powers want a reliable democracy on the Rhine, and they intend to have one. The Communists now call us the "Versailles Republic", and under Thälmann they have started to court the nationalists who used to shoot at them.

content: Soviet rifles won the war for the
as much as for us, and the
has come out of it larger and better armed than ever.

content.content: Polish and Czechoslovak volunteers fought on our side, and the nationalists will never let anyone forget it. The officer corps feels doubly humiliated.

The front lines have hardened into borders. Our government holds Berlin and much of the north and center. However, a Ruhr Red Army rules the industrial west, French "peacekeepers" patrol the Rhineland, and Polish troops occupy East Prussia and Silesia. The far-right militias have collapsed into warlordism. Reuniting Germany without destroying it will take a generation.

content: The United Front governs Germany! President
sits in the Reichspräsidentenpalais, and the

share the cabinet table, deeply suspicious of each other. Industrialists are moving their money to Zürich, and the officer corps is sullen. Meanwhile, Moscow is watching to see whether our experiment will bend to its will or stand on its own.
The Republic is gone, and it did not fall to the Nazis. President Hergt and Chancellor Seldte govern with the

and the old officer corps behind them, and everyone in Berlin expects the Hohenzollerns back on the throne within a few years. The Reichstag still meets, and we still sit in it as the largest opposition party—in a state that has no intention of letting the opposition govern. Our task now is to make the coming monarchy answer to parliament, or to bring it down.

content.content: Franz von Papen rules Germany by decree, with the Reichswehr and the industrialists behind him and almost nobody else. Our party is banned, our newspapers have been seized, and our leaders are in prison or in exile. However, we were a million members strong, and most of our members are still here: in the factories, the allotment gardens and the back rooms of the working-class districts. Papen calls his regime the New State. Our task is to outlast it.

content: The game now continues month by month until 1950. Elections, the economy and your cards still matter, and there is a new set of events for this era. On the Status page, you'll find a new
section that tracks stability, international tension and other measures specific to your path.
By 1950, the Weimar Republic had become what its founders hoped for in 1919: a stable social democracy.

content.content: Article 48 was bound by law, and the Constitutional Court now rules on every state of emergency.
Article 48 was bound by law, and no chancellor has governed by decree since.
Article 48 is still on the books, but no chancellor has used its powers in over a decade.
Prussia was dissolved into the Reich, ending the old rivalry between two governments in Berlin.
Prussia remains a state of its own, and a reliable pillar of the Republic.

content: is now the natural party of government

, and it still sings the Internationale at its congresses while winning votes in the middle classes

content: . No major party now disputes unemployment insurance, public housing or the eight-hour day.

content.content: The unified social insurance law of the late thirties is studied in Stockholm and London.
In the mines and steelworks of the Ruhr, workers' representatives sit on the supervisory boards beside the shareholders.
Under the reformed civil code, husband and wife are equals, and a married woman no longer needs her husband's permission to take a job.

content: now swears its oath to the constitution.

content.content: Germany and France now sit together in a European Coal and Steel Authority, which both governments call the first step toward a wider union.
Germany remains in the League, but it has refused to hand any of its sovereignty to a European authority.
The Republic came through the war of the forties with its constitution intact.

options.title: Trigger game over.
Nah.

content.content: After the death of Hindenburg and the presidential election of 1934, it seems as if an era of history is closing. The worst years of political and economic crisis are over, and Nazism's days are numbered. Perhaps Germany will finally enter into a new era of genuine peace...
The bulk of the party does not support funding a Communist paramilitary.
The bulk of the party does not support funding what they view a front organization for an illegal Communist paramilitary.
We have provided funding to Antifaschistische Aktion in the name of a united front against Fascism.

The Agriculture Ministry, led by the respected Martin Schiele, does its best to defend the decree before Hindenburg—but to no avail.

In truth, policy disputes isn’t what will seal Brüning’s fate. Hindenburg had merely planned to give him a few more months to try his luck at Lausanne. But the scheming—and the sense of urgency—pushed by Schleicher, Meissner, and Oskar is forcing his hand toward an early, rash decision.

agrarian_bolshevism.title: "Agrarian Bolshevism"
agrarian_bolshevism.subtitle: A controversial policy involving settling unemployed workers on bankrupt estates in the east.

content: 's Labor Minister Adam Stegerwald’s pet projects is the dismantling of hopelessly bankrupt eastern estates to carve them into peasant homesteads. The problem is that there haven’t been many young workers eager to turn themselves into peasants.

member Hans Schlange-Schöningen newly sworn in as Commissar for Eastern Aid—following Treviranus’s move to the Transport Ministry—he’s struck a deal with Stegerwald: estates deemed “hopelessly bankrupt” will be handed over to the Labor Ministry. Backed by his promise to the unions, Stegerwald has pushed a decree that allows the government to purchase select estates at prices set by the Eastern Aid office.

content.content: Unfortunately for Brüning, a copy of the decree has been leaked to the National Rural League (RLB). Its lobbyists—deeply embedded in Hindenburg’s circle—have denounced it as "Agrarian Bolshevism" slamming the measure as a descent into state socialism. They’ve made sure the President, who along with many friends owns eastern estates, see it as a personal attack.

There is nothing we can do. The peasant unrest rages on, only tempered by its own internal dissension. More and more, the peasant movement is being co-opted by the growing Nazi party, who channel their grievances into demands for the overthrow of the Republic.

content.content: When we ban the film, the Nazis immediately celebrate it as a major victory; they claim that even the red Marxists agree with them! It is a major boost to their morale.

altona_clashes.ban_march.unavailableSubtitle: The judiciary would not allow us to ban the protest, because of free speech.

content.content: We have banned the planned protest. The Nazis appeal the ban in the courts in the name of freedom of speech. Thankfully, the judiciary agrees with us that the Nazis' argument is specious.

content: has yielded to the Nazis' demands, banning the controversial film. The Nazis are quick to proclaim the decision as a significant triumph, leading to a notable boost in their morale and political confidence.

austrian_civil_war.crushed.title: The rebellious Schutzbund has been crushed.

content: The uprising lasted for no more than a few days before it was crushed. The Schutzbund and <span style="color: #A50034;">
were too weak and too divided to stand against the forces of the state.

content.content: The customs union has been formed. Immediately, France and other neighboring countries lodge their protests. The longer-term response is yet to be seen.

The European Union is a largely untested body, and from the beginning contained members that are at best quasi-democratic. Most of its members are more concerned by power politics than democratic values. However, as its founder, Germany holds a special influence in the EU, and we manage to persuade the other members to join in the pressure against Austrofascism.
The Dollfuß regime does not give in, but it is weakened and isolated.
There is, essentially, nothing we can do.

This may end any attempt at reconciliation with the <span style="color: #700000;">

Brüning’s austerity measures will likely intensify from this point forward.

options.title: The affairs of the bourgeois parties don't concern us.

The pause in reparation payments, a budgetary surplus, and a struggling economy have created the conditions necessary to persuade both the Brüning cabinet and many economic experts that a stimulus plan is essential. The economy has hit rock bottom, deflation is in its damaging second phase, and the Lautenbach Plan is considered crucial for a rapid 'ignition' of the German economy, especially as reparations have already been paused. However, due to the German public's fear of inflation, announcing any dramatic expansion of the money supply has proven impossible. As a result, the Reichsbank is forced to scale back the plan to avoid any potential scandal that could threaten the Brüning government.

Labor Minister Adam Stegerwald and Finance Minister Hermann Dietrich have devised a plan to allocate a billion dollars for public works, along with efforts to reduce 'sticky' wages to restore investor confidence. The plan also includes the purchasing of foreign debts to increase liquidity, expanding credit, and reducing interest rates. The deficit generated by these measures is also somewhat offset by the need to pay less unemployment benefits. With these measures, money is beginning to flow once again into the German economy.

content.content: With the abolishment of reparations at Lausanne, the Brüning cabinet finally feels comfortable to expand funding for its recently enacted public works program. A billion dollars in bonds released by the government is used to fund the program, and money begins to flow in the economy again.

This marks a real turning point, and along with the abolishment of reparations, the radicalizing effects of sky-high unemployment and the Versailles Treaty are diminished. The set of conditions that have enabled the Nazis's meteoric rise begins to unravel, depriving them of the fuel that once drove their ascent.

content.content: Paul von Hindenburg has passed away at age 86.

The nation engages in an outpouring of grief for its war hero and former president. Even for committed socialists and republicans, this is a bittersweet moment. Even though he was a manifestation of Prussian militarism and monarchism, he still led the nation through difficult times, without destroying democracy. It could always have been worse.

With the passing of Hindenburg, it seems as if an era of history is closing. The worst years of crisis are over, and Nazism's days are numbered. Perhaps Germany will finally enter into a new era of genuine peace...

content.content: The influx of Protestant conservatives into the Center Party has rendered Jakob Kaiser’s leadership untenable. In a decisive internal vote of no confidence, Kaiser has been ousted—replaced by Stegerwald ally and long-serving Mayor of Cologne, Konrad Adenauer. Adenauer seeks to carry forward Stegerwald’s vision: transforming the party into the dominant force of the German Right.

Unsurprisingly, this development has sparked outrage among the Christian Left and Kaiser’s supporters, many of whom have resigned their posts in protest. The party’s close ties to left-leaning unions have been severely strained, plunging the organization into temporary disarray as labor-aligned factions voice their anger.

are becoming increasingly common—though support is limited to their People's Conservatives and Christian Socials. A merger remains impossible without one of those factions having strong, centralized leadership within their party. At the same time, we must prevent any government cooperation between them and the Center—lest we allow conditions for such a union to emerge.

content.content: Brüning’s decision to postpone the Lausanne conference until June faces sharp criticism from top economic advisors, who argue that the outright abolition of reparations would remain impossible even then. Instead, they urge him to pursue détente and secure access to new French loans—an idea Hindenburg has adamantly opposed, vowing to resign rather than sign such an agreement.
Brüning, however, has reason to believe waiting is the right move. France is facing a severe fiscal shortfall and remains reluctant to cut off a crucial revenue stream.
That is, if Brüning can hold on until June.

lausanne_pre.title: Brüning's Dilemma
lausanne_pre.subtitle: An international reparations congress at Lausanne is scheduled this month.

options.title: Brüning has decided to postpone reparation talks until June.

content.content: Following the disastrous fallout from the Banking Crisis, Brüning has successfully managed to secure key concessions from the Western Allies regarding debts and Germany's economic maneuverability. However, Germany's economic crisis continues to worsen, and the Beneduce Report has stated that Germany cannot afford reparations payments in the foreseeable future. The British government has invited the Western Allies to participate in an international reparations congress in Lausanne, as per the recommendations of the bankers.

With the moratorium on reparations in place, there is considerable uncertainty regarding what will happen to Germany's reparations burden once it expires. Brüning argues that this uncertainty has stifled investor confidence and hindered Germany's recovery from the economic crisis. The dire state of German finances has also contributed to this, with the Beneduce Report painting a bleak picture of Germany's ability to repay reparations in the foreseeable future. The British government has invited the Western Allies to participate in an international reparations congress in Lausanne, as per the recommendations of the bankers.

This is where the dilemma arises: France's government cannot discuss any permanent revision of the Young Plan until after their elections in May. Brüning faces a choice: he can either push for a prolongation of the moratorium on reparations for another three years, or he can wait until June for a potential complete abolition of reparations.

content.content: The decree confirms the overtly anti-social character of the so-called “cabinet of barons,” and has ignited fury across the working class. With nearly two-thirds of the country now irrevocably hostile to the chancellor, it is politically suicidal for any party outside the reactionary right to support him without suffering severe electoral consequences.

papen_cabinet_2.title: Papen's First Emergency Decree
papen_cabinet_2.subtitle: A virtual abolishment of unemployment insurance!

content: Papen has unveiled his first emergency decree—one that keeps most of Brüning’s planned austerity measures but strips away the system of peasant homesteads. Most egregiously, it subjects all recipients of unemployment insurance to a means test after just six weeks. In effect, the system has been dismantled—radicalizing the proletariat, especially toward the <span style="color: #700000;">

content.content: Unlike Brüning, who at least aimed to share the burdens of austerity across classes, Papen’s decree openly targets the working poor. Unsurprisingly, the gutting of the welfare state has triggered a spike in unemployment and a sharp dip in the stock market. As ever, Germany finds itself with no shortage of problems.

content.content: Emergency Ordinance for the Reactivation of Economy

Papen has taken the initiative on economic matters, using the funds generated by the gutting of the unemployment insurance program to finance tax cuts for the wealthy and their businesses. This has solidified the backing of the industrial elite behind his chancellorship, but further cements his image as a chancellor for the barons.
However, it does help draw bourgeois sympathies into the cabinet, as many upper-class members of the Center and various bourgeois parties applaud his effort toward constructive policy.
Yet another disgraceful capitulation to the Nazis. Still, their shameless defense of convicted murderers may alienate voters and cost them dearly at the next election.

papen_cabinet_9.title: Papen Drafts Sweeping Amendments to the Constitution!
papen_cabinet_9.subtitle: Despite his extreme unpopularity, the chancellor has ordered his cabinet to begin drafting sweeping constitutional amendments.

content.content: As part of Papen’s previously announced ambition to create a “New State”—a reform of the constitution aimed at transforming Germany into a dictatorship reminiscent of the former Kaiserreich—the continued political deadlock has led him to pursue changes to the system itself. Lacking both popular support and a parliamentary majority, it's unclear how Papen would institute such changes. Nonetheless, such a move would almost certainly provoke civil war—one the Reichswehr is in no position to easily win.

Papen's increasing independence and assertiveness, distancing himself from Schleicher's control, has alarmed the latter, who had previously sought to manipulate him. His open calls for dictatorship, along with the risks involved in keeping such an unpopular chancellor by circumventing the constitution, would unite the legions of organized labor against the government—something Schleicher is anxious to avoid. After all, a civil war would severely impede Germany's rearmament.

content: The Reichstag has reconvened for the first time since the election, with a significantly larger contingent of <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

members now present. The immediate issue at hand is the election of the President of the Reichstag. While the position has traditionally been a procedural one, it has taken on heightened importance under Papen's presidential government, given the President's authority to influence the agenda and adjourn sessions.
By long-standing custom, the role is granted to the largest parliamentary delegation. That delegation is now the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
. The Center Party holds the balance of power. Will they uphold tradition and hand a key parliamentary post to an openly anti-constitutional party?

These decrees would allow Papen to govern unchallenged, free from the threat of parliamentary repeal or a vote of no confidence.

Papen has quickly become Hindenburg’s favorite, and the president—unwilling to part with him—has signed off on a decree that violates the constitution he swore to uphold. Former Chancellor Brüning, upon learning of this, has threatened Hindenburg with impeachment should he proceed, persuading himself that he'd deterred Papen from presenting the decree in the next session.

content.content: Following the disastrous failure of the Prussian Reichsexekution, Papen has lost the support of Hindenburg and his camarilla, making his position untenable. It's expected that General Schleicher would be the successor to Papen, however, being the Defense Minister and mastermind of the failed coup has severely damaged his standing as well. With new elections coming up soon, Hindenburg may choose to keep Papen in office, until a successor can be found with a new, more right-wing Reichstag.

papen_lausanne_conference_1.lausanne.title: Anyhow, the German delegation is off to Switzerland.

content.content: At the opening session, our delegation demands the complete cancellation of reparations. This position has found sympathy from the British and the Americans. France’s new left-wing government has softened its stance as well—though they still insist that Germany enter a pact with the Western Allies, including provisions for military détente. Negotiations will continue in the coming weeks.

At the Lausanne Conference, the Allies will meet with German representatives to settle the reparations question once and for all. With the global economic crisis still raging, most now accept that Germany cannot resume payments once the current moratorium expires.

But with the reactionary nationalist Papen at the helm, Germany’s negotiating hand is weakened. The absence of the internationally respected Brüning, coupled with Papen’s reckless ambition to press for rearmament and a deletion of the 'war guilt' clause, threatens to derail the entire process.

papen_lausanne_conference_2.lausanne.title: At least we walked away with something.

content.content: Germany’s reparations burden has been slashed by 90%, with no payments due for another three years. This eases the strain on the national budget and gives the government new room to maneuver on monetary and fiscal policy.

Unfortunately for Papen, this does little to ease the near-universal hatred of his government. The far-right has denounced the treaty as a failure, outraged by his inability to secure any political or military concessions. Meanwhile, the republican parties and press have handed the credit to Brüning, who laid the groundwork for the conference in the first place. This development would've certainly been more impactful if Brüning had remained in office.

Papen’s tarnished reputation among the Western Allies has severely undermined Germany’s standing at the Geneva Disarmament Conference. With many now convinced that militarism has triumphed in Berlin, Schleicher’s efforts to negotiate military parity are likely to face steep resistance.

papen_lausanne_conference_2.title: Lausanne Conference Concludes
papen_lausanne_conference_2.subtitle: Germany's reparations payments are virtually abolished!

content.content: After weeks of difficult negotiations with the Western Allies, the German delegation at the Lausanne Conference has finally secured a result—though not the one it had hoped for. When talks hit a snag, Papen made a dramatic offer: a military alliance with France, sealed by an exchange of general staff officers. This only outraged the British and deepened French mistrust.

British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald tried to salvage the negotiations by proposing the repeal of disarmament clauses. But French Prime Minister Édouard Herriot rejected this outright—refusing any political discussions and treating Germany’s offer as an admission it could still pay. Backed into a corner, Papen’s delegation was left with no option but to offer a final payment of three billion marks—in exchange for nothing.

content: Walther Lambach and the Christian Socials have long championed a presidential government and the vision of a non-partisan strongman ruling above political factions. That strongman is Schleicher. With the formation of the
, he sees little remaining reason to maintain the

content.content: He has urged his movement to merge into the German National Unity Front, pointing to their shared goal of a Volksgemeinschaft that includes the workers and their common desire to cast off the chains of Versailles. Lambach and Treviranus, over the objections of old guard figures like Westarp and Hergt, have pushed the party at an emergency congress to vote for immediate dissolution—a vote that passes once a "monetary incentive" is offered to on the fence lower-level members by Schleicher himself.

content: Schleicher continues to walk a tightrope between appeasing organized labor and retaining the favor of Germany’s industrial elite. Nonetheless, the <span style="color: #BFC8CC;">
secures over five million marks in funding from a consortium of German businesses—chiefly those tied to rearmament, who see Schleicher’s survival as essential to their own profits.

content.content: The German industrialists and big business leaders have maintained a friendly stance toward Schleicher, appreciating his prioritization of their interests over those of the agrarians and his efforts to stabilize the economy. However, concerns linger over his growing state intervention and the risk that his public works campaign could trigger runaway inflation.

content: To address this, Schleicher has summoned a secret meeting with his allies and Germany’s leading industrialists. He will offer sweeping concessions: a guarantee of capitalism’s preservation and their continued dominance over labor within a corporatist framework. In return, they are expected to pool their resources for unrestricted use by the <span style="color: #BFC8CC;">

However, relations soured with the chancellery after Schleicher refused to grant him full control over the agricultural and economic ministries. His uncompromising opposition to Schleicher has sparked widespread discontent within the
, eroding Hugenberg’s once unchallenged authority among both party leaders and the rank-and-file.

content.content: Many find it bewildering that Hugenberg would oppose a fellow reactionary, especially one presumably sharing his goal of steering Germany toward authoritarian rule.

With internal party democracy long dead—party congresses stacked with loyalists serving as mere rubber stamps—dissenters have little choice. Now, the majority within the party are seizing Schleicher’s lifeline: the absorption of friendly nationalists into the German National Unity Front, where they hope to finally gain a hand in shaping the chancellor's future policies.

At a leadership conference between national and local chapters, they conceded that the era of paramilitaries and political maneuvering is over, and agreed to align the organization with the state in service of the national interest.

To this end, Schleicher plans to subsidize the organization with state funds, gradually making it dependent on the state and available for use. Still, the general is irritated that its military exercises often overshadow the numerically inferior Reichswehr.

content.content: The various Nazi splinter parties that have emerged are now beginning to collapse entirely. Burdening such a dynamic, revolutionary movement with the compromises of government—and failing to deliver real solutions to their base’s hardships—has sapped their morale and dried up donations.

Yet only a handful of fanatics remain in this rump organization, while the "tamed" Nazis drift into the ranks of the

schleicher_3.schleicher.title: Hear what the general has to say.

content.content: ADGB leaders Theodor Leipart and Wilhelm Eggert have met with Chancellor-designate Schleicher, who promised to rescind Papen’s most offensive emergency wage decrees, launch a public works program, and abandon the former chancellor’s plans to impose his “New State” via presidential decree.

We are pleasantly surprised by these concessions, and Schleicher has earned some goodwill among the union leadership. Still, deep distrust remains—after all, he was the one controlling Papen when those very decrees and the unconstitutional postponement of elections were proposed.
"Republic or monarchy is not the question now, but rather what should this republic look like."

content.content: A few months back, a line of communication was opened between the General and the ADGB's leadership, with the understanding of further meetings.
Following the results of the last election, von Schleicher has reached out to the various Christian and socialist unions once again, presumably in an attempt to broker a political truce.

The Social Patriots advocate full support for Schleicher’s chancellorship and his rearmament program, believing that only through strength can Germany break free from the chains of Versailles and reclaim its rightful lands.
Schleicher, predictably, is pleased with our acceptance of this new political current—but his influence within our party is growing alarmingly fast. Perhaps too fast.

content.content: Schleicher, once reviled by the public, is now hailed as Germany’s savior. Through his public works campaign and ruthlessly pragmatic ideology, he has managed to win support from across the political spectrum. But a key question remains: where can these grateful voters turn to express their support for the chancellor?

content: The reactionary right will never win over the workers, and the
is seen as unreliable when it comes to backing Schleicher’s government.

In the past, Schleicher flirted with the idea of building a new "presidential party"—a direct vehicle for rallying public support behind his cabinet. Until now, he had taken no concrete steps. But with new ties to the working class and the moderate forces on the German Right, he now has an opportunity to bring such a party to life

schleicher_cabinet_1.title: Schleicher Presents a New Government
schleicher_cabinet_1.subtitle: A Commissioner for Employment is established for planned public works...

content.content: Chancellor Schleicher has unveiled his new cabinet—retaining all but two of Papen’s ministers. His top priority, he claims, is putting people back to work. To that end, he has appointed Günther Gereke, President of the Rural Municipal Congress and a reformist economic theorist, as Reichskommissar for Employment, with a full seat in the cabinet.

For now, Schleicher is enjoying a political honeymoon. The relief at Papen’s fall has been widespread, and his public disavowal of any plans to alter the constitution has calmed both the national mood and the republicans who had bitterly opposed his predecessor.

content: The Christian trade unions and their affiliated parties have adopted a conciliatory stance, while the ADGB and
leaderships, viewing Schleicher as the lesser evil, have responded positively to his public works proposals.

content.content: But the real issue isn’t popular unrest—it’s whether Schleicher can survive the no-confidence vote looming in the Reichstag later this week.

schleicher_cabinet_10.z_in_gov.title: Schleicher has found a new puppet in Kaas.

into the fold, which is granted the Postal Ministry.

content.content: With Ludwig Kaas’s connections in Rome, the negotiation of a Reichskonkordat is fast-tracked and set to be ready for signing in a few weeks.
However, their entry into government has strained our relations, as they had previously stood in united opposition with us.

schleicher_cabinet_10.title: The Center Party Enters Government
schleicher_cabinet_10.subtitle: Promises of a Reichskonkordat lures them into cooperation.

content: Schleicher has concluded that he needs broader popular and parliamentary support beyond the <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">

The main obstacle, however, is the Center Party’s deep reservations about sharing a cabinet with the Nazis. To overcome this, Schleicher and the
have signaled their readiness to fast-track a Reichskonkordat with the Vatican—an offer that Kaas, a longtime advocate of such, finds difficult to refuse.

schleicher_cabinet_11.reichskonkordat.title: What will happen to the Center Party?

content.content: Having achieved his lifelong goal, Kaas sees little reason to remain as leader of the Center Party—a position he had long described as a burden and expressed displeasure with. As a result, a new leadership race is set to take place within the party, with Schleicher able to influence the outcome through his connections with Kaas and the Christian Trade Unions.
The candidate backed by the Christian unions and those advocating for a more interconfessional Center Party rallies around Stegerwald.

content: , has rejoined the party and is Schleicher’s preferred candidate. Bracht is a true believer in Schleicher's vision for a new Germany—one less entangled in parliamentarianism—and aligns with the Center's right wing, though not as far right as Papen. However, due to his lack of influence within the party and limited prior experience, having served only as Mayor of Essen for eight years, it is Schleicher's backing that remains the key to elevating him to leadership.

content: In the aftermath of the crackdown against the <span style="color: #700000;">

We know all of this is nonsense, but Schleicher has slowly taken steps toward the Gleichschaltung (synchronization) of his regime, having recently established the "Ministry of National Guidance" in the decree in which he banned the

content.content: For now, the organization remains confined to Prussia, but its presence is felt everywhere. Local party members whisper that their phones are tapped, and troublesome politicians vanish—never to be seen again. With the police now firmly under government control, they decide which crimes to overlook and coordinate raids hand-in-hand with the Reichswehr.
Yet, their reach still depends on the willingness of people to betray their comrades by reporting them to the police.

But with the Reichswehr’s militia now patrolling the streets under Frick and Strasser’s oversight, there is no longer any need for this relic of the Weimar Republic. In its place, the Staatsschutzamt (State Security Office) has been created, staffed by

content.content: Unbeknownst to the public, Schleicher has been suffering from pernicious anemia for several years. As early as 1930, his family doctor warned him that, given the stress and heavy responsibilities of his career, he likely had no more than six years to live. Now, with the added strain of the chancellorship, those who interact with him have begun to notice his steady decline into lethargy. He may only have a few months left.

In a public announcement, Schleicher announces his resignation, stating that he will soon handpick a successor to be appointed by Hindenburg. He never truly enjoyed the role, and in recent months has quietly delegated his duties to trusted allies in the Reichswehr, grooming them to take his place.
The question now: who will carry forward Schleicher's legacy?

title: Carl Friedrich Goerdeler - <span style="color: #BFC8CC;">
schleicher_cabinet_19.goerdeler.subtitle: Former nationalist mayor of Leipzig. Strong conservative.

content: Goerdeler, an outspoken conservative on the German Right, with personal authoritarian and monarchist leanings, represents Schleicher’s signal of a return to partisan rule in essence. Despite breaking with his former party to join the <span style="color: #BFC8CC;">
, his appointment is seen by workers and republicans as little different from naming a

content.content: Yet, the fact that he is not a military figure like Schleicher or his circle has brought some measure of relief. Though a long-time opponent of Alfred Hugenberg and his faction, Goerdeler remains a conservative at heart and is expected to continue the dismantling of the despised Weimar order.

But Goerdeler is no Schleicher. He lacks the vast network of political ties that his patron carefully cultivated across German society, and Schleicher’s personal popularity has failed to pass to his chosen successor. Moreover, Goerdeler is known for his hardline fiscal conservatism and anti-social stance, having once called for the abolition of unemployment insurance during the Papen era.
Perhaps the house of cards Schleicher so carefully built is already beginning to wobble.

Although not directly related to recent negotiations, a scandal was revealed during a session of the Reichstag’s budget committee: a Center Party member leveled sweeping accusations of fraud against beneficiaries of the Eastern Aid program. Meant to rescue bankrupt estates, the funds were allegedly used instead for racehorses, luxury cars, and lavish holidays—at a time when millions of Germans were living in poverty.

content: President Hindenburg himself has been implicated. His

estate—a gift from right-wing industrialists and the RLB in 1927—was transferred into his son Oskar’s name to avoid taxes. Though not legally contestable, the revelation that many of Hindenburg’s close friends also benefited has deeply unsettled the President, who is now inundated with complaints from his old allies.

content.content: Given Schleicher’s reputation for shadowy political maneuvering, and the fact that these revelations surfaced just a day after his break with the RLB, many suspect that he orchestrated the leak as an act of revenge.

schleicher_cabinet_2.title: Schleicher and the Agrarians
schleicher_cabinet_2.subtitle: The RLB is disappointed in Schleicher's agricultural policy.

content.content: Schleicher’s economic and agricultural ministers remain locked in a bitter struggle over tariffs—part of the broader conflict between industrialists and agrarians. Schleicher has refused to take a side, maintaining a façade of unity for the public. However, his failure to uphold a promise to continue Papen’s protectionist policies—meant to shield German farm products from cheap foreign imports—has led the increasingly right-wing National Rural League (RLB) to turn against him.

President Hindenburg, like many conservative Germans of his generation, viewed agriculture as the bedrock of national life—a source of tradition and moral strength. It was he who, of his own accord, summoned the economic and agricultural ministers, along with Schleicher, to a meeting with the RLB. The cabinet temporarily mollified the situation by promising future action.

content: Yet Hindenburg and the RLB remained dissatisfied, particularly over the government’s failure to renew a decree shielding bankrupt farmers from foreclosure. In truth, however, the RLB had long since become a political instrument of the

, more interested in toppling Schleicher than securing concessions. Despite the earlier agreement, they publicly attacked the chancellor—prompting an angry Schleicher to break off further talks. Hindenburg, under the influence of his

content.content: Eventually, Schleicher relented and agreed to issue a new measure protecting bankrupt farmers from foreclosure.

Instead, he recommends the appointment of rising star and Volkskonservativ leader Gottfried Treviranus. With deep ties to German industry, the Right, and a pseudo-republican veneer, Treviranus is a candidate aimed at stabilizing Germany’s worsening crisis.

Though they remain our enemies, as they were in the days of normalcy, whoever Hindenburg selects now is likely to be preferable to Schleicher’s continued hold on office.

The more left-leaning—and quite frankly, eccentric—elements of the movement have formed a new Old Social Democratic Party (

content.content: With Schleicher nearing the end—both politically and personally—he is in no position to stop the unraveling of his own creation. Perhaps this will be remembered as his greatest blunder: that everything he built ends in anticlimax. Yet the Weimar system has already been gutted over the past few years.

content.content: Despite the clear advantages of the third option, Schleicher rejects it. He hints that even if the Reichstag cannot oust him directly, a hostile majority could still repeal his emergency decrees—rendering his position untenable. True to Prussian military tradition, which favors offense over defense and prizes personal courage in the face of adversity, Schleicher may find it too humiliating to swallow his pride and retreat from his earlier threats to dissolve the Reichstag.

Nevertheless, he decides to ask the President for authorization to dissolve the Reichstag and postpone new elections—despite Oskar likely having convinced his father to oppose this course weeks ago. His position is weakened by the fact that he previously brought down Papen, in front of the very cabinet members he retains today, by claiming the Reichswehr could not handle the outrage such a blatantly unconstitutional move would provoke.

Schleicher now argues that circumstances have changed. His outreach to the labor unions, he claims, has neutralized the risk of civil war, and his economic plan will soon reduce tensions. As Defense Minister, he also asserts that he has addressed the Reichswehr’s deficiencies—it is now better prepared, with greatly expanded stocks of tear gas and streetfighting gear.

content: immovable, Schleicher seeks to unconstitutionally postpone elections.

content.content: The nation needs a break from more polarizing elections. Let the chancellor govern.

Schleicher was never a true believer in converting his cabinet into a parliamentary one, and he undercut his own threat to call new elections by suggesting that no one would object if they were delayed beyond the constitutionally mandated 60 days. In reality, nothing could be further from the truth.

Even so, Schleicher now seeks to secure a decree—similar to the one he once offered Papen but which was never enacted, as the Reichstag president simply ignored him. Should Hindenburg refuse to issue such a decree, it won’t signal a renewed commitment to constitutional norms. Rather, it would confirm the scope of the conspiracy against Schleicher—one that now includes the President himself.
Schleicher lays out four scenarios before the President:
3. His own cabinet continuing under presidential emergency powers—his recommendation.
4. A disastrous cabinet led by Papen and Hugenberg—likely to provoke civil war.
He does not request a postponement of elections this time—only a commitment from Hindenburg to dissolve the chamber upon reconvening.
He is denied. Hindenburg acknowledges Schleicher’s efforts to win over the Nazis, but with that effort having failed, the President declares it time to explore “another possibility.”

The plan is approved by the chancellor and signed by Hindenburg without objection. With Schleicher fulfilling a widely popular promise, and the republican parties beginning to soften their stance on the government, it seems that Schleicher may be here to stay.

content.content: With Schleicher granting concessions to the workers on his own initiative—rather than under pressure from the SPD—he alone reaps the political rewards. Even some radicalized Communist workers begin to drift away, as the less ideological and politically disengaged prioritize their livelihoods over loyalty to their traditional parties.

But hey, at least the workers aren’t suffering as much anymore. This alone has led the ADGB to adopt a friendlier stance toward the chancellor, giving Schleicher growing influence within our party, using the unions as his middleman.

content.content: Presumably aiming to win over the unions' affiliated parties—the Center Party and the SPD—and to bolster public confidence in his leadership at the grassroots level, Schleicher has enacted a new decree.

An eight-hour workday is now mandated across most industries, intended to "spread out" employment among more workers. The means test for unemployment insurance has been abolished, and welfare funding has been increased to offset years of austerity.

The Social General has lived up to his nickname. Yet, cynically, the cost is clear—Schleicher now wields significant leverage over the unions, and many workers are beginning to shift their loyalty toward the chancellor, who delivers results, rather than the opposition parties. His image as a strongman, standing above the old parties, is slowly conditioning the workers to accept a more authoritarian system.

content.content: The Reichstag reconvenes under Schleicher, and nearly all parties present are unwilling to move against the popular chancellor on the chamber’s first day back. The opposition chooses to wait, looking for the inevitable misstep—a constitutional violation or a divisive policy—to use as a pretext and rallying point against him.

Meanwhile, Schleicher shows little concern over the threat of a no-confidence vote. He makes his position clear: unless a united bloc emerges with a viable successor, he will continue governing as usual, backed by Hindenburg.

content: Schleicher immediately issues his decree to unconstitutionally adjourn the Reichstag indefinitely, declaring that the chamber will remain closed until the parties prove they can govern constructively again. Reactions inside the chamber are mixed: Schleicher's supporters applaud the chancellor’s show of strong leadership, while the <span style="color: #700000;">
ignite brawls that police are forced to break up.

In the following days, civil demonstrations are violently suppressed. Police disperse crowds with tear gas, street clashes erupt, and several civilians are killed. The strengthened Reichswehr and the divided stance of republicans make any serious rebellion futile. At least half of the

Following the death of Hindenburg from old age and Schleicher due to health complications, General Hammerstein is elected in a landslide in a heavily rigged election. The

content: hated Weimar system is dismantled, and a new March Constitution is passed near-unanimously. The Reichstag is reduced to a rubber stamp for the regime. Germany formally adopts a presidential system, with both the Presidency and Chancellorship held by various
members, who rise through bribes, patronage, and backroom deals. Corruption is endemic. Elections are stage-managed, dominated by fraud and manipulation.
is never formally banned and endures as a powerless "loyal opposition," unable to influence national policy. Though tolerated, they face constant harassment and suppression by the ruling regime.

content.content: Despite the regime’s authoritarianism, social discontent remains subdued. A Wirtschaftswunder—an economic miracle—emerges as the Great Depression fades. In 1935, Germany secures equality in armaments at Geneva and begins agitating for the return of the Polish Corridor separating East Prussia from the Reich.

In 1942, a "special military operation" is launched to seize Danzig. Poland refuses to cede territory, and with backing from France and a hesitant Britain, enters a state of war. A puppet regime is installed in occupied territories. A limited French offensive into the Saar fails, and the Western Allies remain at war only on paper.

Sensing German isolation, the Soviet Union invades eastern Poland, citing abuses against native Belarusians and Ukrainians under military occupation. A new German–Soviet war erupts. Defense Minister Hammerstein cultivates ties with the "Little Entente"—states facing their own Soviet-backed revolutionary threats. An unofficial Mitteleuropa bloc emerges, with Germany at its core, squeezed between a Western capitalist bloc and the Eastern state-socialist order.

In 1946, the war ends in stalemate. Poland is partitioned at the Vistula River. Romania and Bulgaria fall under Communist control. Western Europe grows closer to the United States, and a tripolar global order takes shape.

By the late 1960s, economic stagnation and renewed domestic unrest—driven by the Red Army Faction and neo-Nazi agitation—force Chancellor Kurt Georg Kiesinger to begin relaxing the dictatorship. The corporatist house of cards that had maintained the regime's stability for decades begins to crumble as independent unions discreetly form. However, Germany remains far from a free and democratic country, the Reichswehr maintains constant watch over politics, exercising real control behind the scenes.

. The Mitteleuropa bloc persists as a fragile intermediary between the West and the East—neither liberal nor socialist, but something in between.

content.content: Our party executive escaped to Prague in 1933, and published the *Neuer Vorwärts* there until 1938, when the threat of a German invasion forced it to move to Paris. When the Germans reached Paris in 1940, the executive moved on to London. Otto Wels died in Paris in September 1939. Rudolf Hilferding was handed over to the Gestapo by Vichy France, and died in its custody in 1941. Rudolf Breitscheid, who was arrested with him, died in Buchenwald in 1944.

Our party executive escaped to Prague, then to Paris, and finally to London. It went on publishing a newspaper in exile, but fewer people in Germany could read it every year. The regime that defeated us had the army behind it, and it did not hesitate to use it.

Inside Germany, our underground networks were broken and rebuilt again and again. Julius Leber and Wilhelm Leuschner joined the conspiracy against Hitler, and both were executed after the failed coup of 20 July 1944. Kurt Schumacher spent ten years in the camps. Six million Jews were murdered, and the war that the Nazi regime began killed tens of millions more.

Inside Germany, our comrades kept the networks alive in the factories, the cooperatives and the allotment gardens. Unfortunately, most of them were caught sooner or later, and many were arrested more than once.

content: When the war ended in 1945, our party was refounded within weeks by survivors of the camps, the underground and the exile. In the Soviet zone, it was forced to merge with the Communists in 1946. In the west, Schumacher led the
into the first elections of the Federal Republic in 1949, where it came second.

content.content: By 1950, the exiles who are still alive have spent nearly two decades waiting for a Germany they can return to. Some have given up hope. The rest still meet in London every May Day, and still argue about where we went wrong.

The German Republic, called by some of our detractors as the "Weimar Republic", is a parliamentary republic with a somewhat weak president and a strong parliament, called the Reichstag. The Reichstag is responsible for governing, while the President has a largely ceremonial role but also has some important governing responsibilities.

The Reichstag is elected based on a proportional representation system, giving parties seats roughly proportional to their vote share in each electoral district. The Reichstag then elects the Chancellor and the cabinet by a majority vote, who are responsible for government. A majority vote-of-no-confidence can remove the current government.

The President is elected by a national direct vote, in two rounds. The second round is used if the first round does not result in a majority for one candidate; the candidate who receives a plurality in the second round becomes president (there is no obligation for weaker candidates to drop out). The role of the president is mostly to represent Germany, but he also has some crucial governing powers. The president and chancellor can together use emergency decrees to govern, bypassing the Reichstag. The president can also appoint or remove a chancellor when a parliamentary majority is unable to be established, and can thus influence the formation of a government.
Germany is divided into a number of states, each of which have their own governments with some responsibilities. By far the largest and most important state is Prussia.

e2_brown_exodus.league.subtitle: Paris and London will appreciate it. It may help a little.

content.content: Our note to Vienna, copied to the League Council,
At our urging, the government sends Vienna a note, copied to the League Council, which

content: lists the camps and the names of the men who run them. Vienna answers that it knows of no such camps. However, the publicity makes it harder for the Austrian government to pretend, and some of the camps close.

e2_china.advisers.subtitle: A middle course. Neither side will be satisfied.

content.content: The arms contracts are suspended, and the advisers stay, "in a private capacity". The Chinese are disappointed, the Japanese are not appeased, and Falkenhausen's officers go on helping the Chinese army in everything but name.

e2_bavaria_plot.autonomy.subtitle: Bavaria will feel respected, and the Left faction will call it appeasement.

content.content: The Bavarian courts try the plotters, and most of them are home within a year. In Berlin, a commission of the states sits down to revise the division of powers in the constitution: schools, police and broadcasting go to the states, and Bavaria gets its own seat on the Reichsbahn's board. The separatists find that there is much less to separate from. Our Left faction asks what we would have said if the plot had come from the left.

unavailableSubtitle: will not accept a single American dollar.

content.content: Germany takes the credits and signs the trade agreements, but politely declines the invitation to the Atlantic Defense Council. Washington is disappointed, and gives a little less than it might have. Moscow is suspicious, but it does not break off relations. Germany has one foot in each camp, which is uncomfortable, and so far it has worked.

The League appoints a commission of three jurists, a Swede, a Dutchman and a Swiss, who spend the winter taking evidence. The Polish warship leaves the Westerplatte and the customs inspectors go back to work. Nothing is resolved, but nothing gets worse either. In this part of Europe, that counts as a success.

e2_danube.trade.subtitle: A smaller gain, and fewer enemies.

content.content: Germany signs a most-favored-nation treaty with the new union and stays outside its tariff wall. The Danube states get their market, and Germany keeps its farmers. Hodža says, politely, that half a bridge is better than none.

e2_disarmament.support.subtitle: A smaller convention. Armies will grow a little more slowly.

content.content: London tables a cautious draft, and Germany votes for it. The convention that comes out of Geneva limits bombers and heavy guns, and leaves the size of armies to a later conference. It is something. The arms manufacturers of Essen and Le Creusot are relieved that it is not more.

For nine days the foreign ministers of the Soviet Union, Poland, France, the Baltic states and Germany meet in the old castle at Königsberg. The Red Army waits at the frontier. On the tenth day they sign. The Baltic states accept Soviet naval bases at Paldiski and Liepāja. Poland keeps its borders, but grants autonomy to its Belarusian and Ukrainian provinces under League supervision. Moscow calls it a victory for peace, and the Red Army returns to its barracks.

The settlement is not just. The Estonians and Latvians are not happy about it, and nobody believes the bases will stay bases for long. But there is no war, and for that the Republic will take a great deal of credit.

e2_eastern_end.pact.unavailableSubtitle: Paris does not trust us enough for a permanent alliance.

content: In the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, of all places, Germany, France, Poland, Belgium and the Netherlands sign a treaty of mutual defense. An attack on one is an attack on all. The French premier calls it the burial of 1871 and 1919 alike.
calls it a declaration of war on the Soviet Union.

content.content: Moscow calls it a declaration of war on the Soviet Union.

The negotiations take a year longer than Paris wanted. In the end, the treaty gives the miners' and metalworkers' unions a third of the seats on the High Authority's advisory committee and recognizes the right of member states to keep their industries in public hands. The Ruhr barons, or what remains of them, are furious. The French socialists, who wanted the same thing but did not dare ask, are quietly delighted.

e2_evian.lead.unavailableSubtitle: The other powers do not take our proposals seriously enough.
e2_evian.lead.subtitle: The democracies will be impressed. A few thousand people will be saved who would not have been.

content.content: The German government proposes that every country at Évian take refugees in proportion to its population, with a League office to share the cost. The British and the French agree in principle. The Americans agree to study it. The committee gets a German vice-chairman and a little more money than it would have had, and it gets some twenty thousand people out over the next year.

e2_france_fascist.britain.subtitle: Britain will draw closer to us, which will make Paris think twice.

content.content: Our Foreign Minister travels to London.
At our urging, the Foreign Minister travels to London.

content: The British government will not sign an alliance, but it agrees to consult with Germany "on any threat to the peace of western Europe", and the Royal Navy pays a visit to Kiel. In Paris, the new government takes note.

e2_franco_soviet.welcome.subtitle: Paris and Moscow will be pleased, and nobody will be committed to anything.

content.content: Berlin welcomes "every contribution to the security of Europe" and keeps its own counsel. The French and Soviet ambassadors both report home that the Germans are friendly, and evasive.

e2_gw_called.stall.subtitle: Moscow and the KPD will be angry, but we will have a year.

content: We tell the ambassador that the army needs a year to prepare, and that the harvest must come in first. Moscow does not believe us, and neither does the <span style="color: #700000;">
. However, for now, there is no war.

e2_hitler_austria.frontier.subtitle: The Reichswehr will be pleased, and an attack from Austria will be less tempting. Tension will rise.

content.content: Two Reichswehr divisions move to Upper Bavaria, and the frontier posts on the Salzach and the Inn are fortified. The new government in Vienna calls it a provocation. In Munich, the Bavarian government is quietly relieved.

e2_hungary.arbitration.unavailableSubtitle: Neither Prague nor the Western powers trust us enough to accept our proposal.
e2_hungary.arbitration.subtitle: A small border change, and no war.

content.content: A League commission of a Swede, a Swiss and a Dutchman draws a new line along the language border, and Hungary gets back a dozen market towns and the island of Csallóköz. Ruthenia stays with Prague. Neither side is happy, which the commission takes as proof that it was fair. Budapest's newspapers call it "the little Trianon".

e2_july_putsch.extradite.unavailableSubtitle: Only the government can ask for an extradition.
e2_july_putsch.extradite.subtitle: Vienna may lock him up. The Austrian Nazis will make him a martyr either way.

content: The Foreign Office sends Vienna a formal request for the extradition of Adolf Hitler, to stand trial for conspiracy against a friendly state and for the murders committed by his followers.

content.content: Vienna does better than that. The Austrian police arrest him at his house in Linz, and the government announces that he will be tried in Vienna, by an Austrian court, for high treason.
Vienna will not hand an Austrian-born agitator to a Marxist government in Berlin, but it does intern him in the camp at Wöllersdorf, alongside the Social Democrats it locked up in February.

content: The nationalist press calls it persecution.

e2_gw_declaration.defense.subtitle: The Republic will fight for its life and nothing more. The right will grumble.

content: The credits pass, with a resolution that our deputies wrote: Germany fights to defend its frontiers and its constitution, and will seek no annexations. The <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
votes for the credits and against the resolution. The Left faction accepts it, without enthusiasm.

e2_khalkhin_gol.moscow.subtitle: Moscow will be grateful, and the factories will have orders. The West will be wary.

content: The first trainloads of Büssing and Krupp trucks leave for Moscow in the winter, paid for in gold and timber.
organizes "solidarity shifts" in the truck plants.
In London, the Foreign Office notes that German factories are now supplying the Red Army.

e2_league_reformed.force.subtitle: An even safer Europe. The army and the right will be furious.

content.content: Germany offers two divisions, a squadron of aircraft and a staff college to the League's command, and France and Britain match the offer. The Reichswehr's officers are told that they may one day serve under a Czech or a Norwegian general, and several of them resign. The Peace Pledge Union in London calls it the most hopeful thing a German government has done since Locarno.

Leon Trotsky arrives in Hamburg in a rainstorm, wearing a borrowed overcoat and guarded by a dozen Prussian policemen. He is given a villa outside Potsdam on condition that he stays out of politics. He breaks that promise within the week.

content: Moscow recalls its ambassador "for consultations". The <span style="color: #700000;">

is furious, but it is also losing members, as a small and noisy Trotskyist circle forms around the old man. The bourgeois parties are appalled that we have let in the founder of the Red Army, though some of them are quietly pleased to see Stalin so angry.

e2_munzenberg.distance.subtitle: The KPD still splits, but its defectors go their own way.

content.content: We say that the SPD welcomes every democrat and leave it at that. Münzenberg founds a small party and a large newspaper, and the communist movement in Germany splits into two parties that hate each other more than they hate anybody else.

e2_mosley.east.subtitle: Poland and Czechoslovakia will stand closer to us. Paris will call it encirclement.

content.content: Warsaw and Prague have as much reason to fear the new France as we do, and they know it. The three foreign ministers meet in Breslau and agree to consult on every threat to their frontiers. It is not an alliance, and none of the three trusts the others very far, but it is a beginning.

e2_naval_talks.free.subtitle: -2 budget. The nationalists will cheer. London and Paris will both be alarmed.

content: Berlin tells London that a sovereign state does not ask permission to defend its coasts. The Admiralty answers by laying down two more battleships of its own, and the French Chamber votes a new naval program within the month. The nationalist press is delighted.

content.content: Our deputies vote against the estimates, and lose.

options.title: Otto Braun.
Rudolf Breitscheid.
Carl Severing.
Kurt Schumacher.
Ernst Reuter.

content.content: The parliamentary group meets the same evening to choose a successor.

Germany declares strict neutrality in the Pacific war and sells to anyone who pays in cash. The money is good, and the Americans are irritated. When a German freighter carrying optical glass to Yokohama is stopped by a British cruiser off Ceylon, the Foreign Office has to protest. It does so quietly.

The Games are held in the old Deutsches Stadion, freshly painted and fitted with temporary stands. The opening ceremony is short, and the speeches are shorter. The athletes don't seem to mind, and the foreign press praises a host that remembered there was a Depression on. The right calls it a national humiliation, but nobody listens for long.

e2_popular_front_fr.correct.subtitle: Relations with Paris will improve a little.

content.content: Berlin sends Blum its congratulations and an invitation to talks on trade. The talks are useful, and dull. Blum's friends in our party are disappointed.

e2_rexists.west.subtitle: Paris will be grateful. Belgian nationalists will resent it, and Rex will lose ground.

content.content: The Foreign Minister tells his Belgian colleague that the Republic would regard Belgium's alliance with France as a guarantee of peace, not a threat to Germany.
Our party sends its money and its speakers to the Belgian Workers' Party, and the government, prodded by our deputies, tells Brussels that it has no objection to Belgium's alliance with France.

content: In the Brussels by-election that Degrelle forces in the spring, the Prime Minister beats him by more than three votes to one.

e2_rhineland_zone.negotiate.unavailableSubtitle: The Locarno powers do not trust us enough to negotiate.
e2_rhineland_zone.negotiate.subtitle: The zone will go, slowly and by treaty. The nationalists will call it begging.

content.content: The Locarno powers meet in London in the summer. After two months, they agree that German troops may return to the Rhineland in stages, in garrisons of an agreed size and under League inspection, and that France may keep its fortresses on the other side. The generals call the terms humiliating and accept them. Paris calls them generous.

e2_spain_partner.league.subtitle: Spain will have a voice in Geneva. So, through Spain, will we.

content.content: The German delegation proposes Spain for a permanent seat at the next Assembly, and France seconds the motion. Italy votes against and walks out. Spain takes its seat on the Council in the autumn, and its first vote is for a League inquiry into the foreign volunteers who fought for Franco.

e2_spain.covert.unavailableSubtitle: The Foreign Office is not ours, and the Chancellor will not look the other way.
e2_spain.covert.subtitle: A trickle of arms and volunteers, at little cost.

content.content: We sign the agreement, and customs officers in Hamburg are told not to look too closely at crates marked "agricultural machinery".
The government signs the agreement. However, our comrades in the Hamburg harbor make sure that nobody looks too closely at crates marked "agricultural machinery".

content: A few hundred German volunteers make their way to Spain by way of Paris.

content.content: It isn't much, but it is better than nothing, and it costs us very little.
