content.content: The Foreign Office sends a polite and noncommittal reply, and settles down to read the Soviet newspapers for clues. In the spring, the clue comes: Zhdanov's name disappears from the list of speakers at the Supreme Soviet, and Malenkov's moves up.

e2_sudeten.autonomy.unavailableSubtitle: Neither Prague nor London trusts us to act as an honest broker.

content.content: With British and German mediators at the table, Prague and the Sudeten German Party agree on a statute modeled on the Swiss cantons. The Sudeten districts receive their own assemblies, German-language schools and courts, and a share of the civil service. The radicals denounce it, and the voters approve it. Czechoslovakia becomes a federation of three nations, and Bohemia goes quiet.
Berlin replies that Germany welcomes any declaration in favor of peace, and that it has no need to sign one, having broken no treaty. The answer is correct, and slightly smug. Paris is disappointed.

e2_trotsky_berlin.conditions.subtitle: Moscow will still be angry, though less so. Neither faction will be satisfied.

content.content: Trotsky is given a house on the island of Föhr, in the North Sea, on condition that he gives no interviews and receives no visitors without the permission of the police. He agrees to everything, and begins to write a history of the Soviet bureaucracy. Moscow protests, though in the tone of a government that had expected worse.

e2_spain_end.mediate.unavailableSubtitle: No one is listening to us.

e2_war_cabinet.united.subtitle: The workers will fight for a government of their own parties. The Centre and the West will not like it.

content: For the first time, a Communist sits in a German war cabinet, as Minister of Supply. <span style="color: #700000;">

factory cells organize the night shifts, and the Red Front's veterans go to the front beside the Reichsbanner's. The Centre's deputies abstain in the vote of confidence. The British ambassador asks, very politely, what exactly the Republic is fighting for.

e2_war_allies.soviet.subtitle: Paris and London will not like it.

content.content: Soviet tankers from Leningrad unload at Stettin within the month, and freight trains of Soviet grain follow.
The Red Army sends two tank corps to the Corridor front, and Soviet tankers unload at Stettin under the guns of the Baltic Fleet.

content: Moscow asks for machine tools in return, and for the right to send observers to our general staff. Both requests are granted.

onArrival.$code: Q['e2_war_posture'] = "balanced";

content.content: The army holds the line where it stands. Every train that comes to the front brings more men and more shells, and the general staff is content to wait until it has enough of both.

e2_war_end.memorial.subtitle: The republicans and the Left will approve. The nationalists will call it ingratitude.

content: There is no parade. Instead, the Reichstag votes the money for a memorial to the dead of the war, and the government declares a day of mourning on the anniversary of its outbreak.

content.content: The generals, who had been looking forward to a parade, are not consulted.

e2_war_crisis.concede.subtitle: The army will fight. It will also have a say in politics, and the republicans will not forget it.

content.content: The Reichswehr Minister resigns, and a general takes his place. The Reichsbanner's liaison officers are withdrawn from the headquarters. The regiments go back into the line the next day. In the Reichstag, our deputies ask who is governing Germany, and nobody answers them.

e2_war_home_front.strike_ban.subtitle: More shells for the front. The Left faction and the unions will be furious.

content.content: A decree forbids strikes and lockouts in the war industries, and sends disputes to arbitration boards whose rulings are binding. Production rises within a month. So does the anger. At the trade union congress, a delegate from Hamburg reads out Bebel's speech against the Anti-Socialist Laws, and the hall gives him a standing ovation.

content: with the majority, and the Soviet Union becomes the first great power to be expelled from the League of Nations. German Red Cross trains carry medicines and field hospitals to Finland. In March, Finland, exhausted, cedes the Isthmus and Viipuri and keeps its independence.

e2_war_talks.mediate.subtitle: A compromise peace: better than the front if we are losing, worse if we are winning.

content.content: The Reichstag raises duties on grain, meat and manufactured goods. The farms and the steel mills are safe for now. Bread is dearer, and within weeks France and the Netherlands retaliate against German chemicals and electrical goods. Everyone has learned the lesson of 1930, and everyone is repeating it anyway.

content: may reform as a veterans' association, without arms or uniforms, and its leaders must swear an oath to the constitution. Former members of the nationalist parties may stand for office again. The
and its stormtroopers stay banned, and the Reichstag confirms this by a large majority.

content.content: Most of the "choirs" dissolve into the legal associations. Unfortunately, the hardest men stay underground, and now they have a grievance that the moderates do not share. The Left faction grumbles about the compromise.

e2c_constitution.councils.subtitle: Needs the KPD and a large left majority. The Reformist faction will be furious.
e2c_constitution.councils.unavailableSubtitle: The left does not have the votes, or the KPD does not trust us enough.

content.content: The Chamber of Labor, elected by the works councils of every enterprise with more than fifty employees, gets a veto over economic legislation and the right to propose laws of its own. The Center and the liberals walk out of the Paulskirche before the final vote, and the constitution passes with the votes of the two workers' parties alone.

content: The Left faction and the <span style="color: #700000;">
are jubilant. However, our Reformists are furious, and the employers' associations call it "the November Revolution, completed".

content.content: Only the Reich government can pay for such a program.
The treasury cannot pay for it.

e2c_rentenmark.levy.unavailableSubtitle: Without a seat in the cabinet, we cannot write the tax law.

content.content: The levy takes a tenth of every fortune above two hundred thousand Marks. It falls hardest on the East Elbian estates whose owners financed the putsch, and on the industrial dynasties that hid their money in Zürich. The Junkers call it expropriation by stealth. The Reichstag passes it by 11 votes.

content: The new Rentenmark holds, because this time the people paying for stability are the ones who can afford it. The <span style="color: #C0A054;">
and the Center are bitterly opposed, but the

e2c_outlaw.paramilitary.subtitle: No more private armies, but the party stays legal. The Left faction will grumble.

content: The uniformed formations are dissolved, and their weapons are handed in or hunted down. The <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
keeps its seats and its newspapers, and its leaders denounce the decree as tyranny from the Reichstag rostrum.

content.content: Some in our Left faction think we have stopped halfway.

e2c_reconstruction_done.close.title: Close the Office and return its funds to the Treasury.
e2c_reconstruction_done.close.subtitle: The budget benefits. The building trades will lay workers off. (+1 budget)

content.content: The Office closes at the end of the year, and its remaining funds go back to the Finance Ministry. The building workers' union expects several thousand of its members to be laid off over the winter.

e2c_reconstruction_done.title: Reconstruction Complete
e2c_reconstruction_done.subtitle: The Reconstruction Office publishes its final report.

content: The Reconstruction Office has published its final report

content.content: , covering the territory the Republic controls

content: . The railway bridges destroyed in the civil war are back in service, the Reichsbahn runs to its pre-war timetable, and the last emergency barracks have been cleared. Industrial production has passed its 1928 level.

content.content: The Reconstruction Bloc's program is finished, and the Centre and the liberals ask what the pact is for now.
The Office will be wound up by the end of the year. The building trades expect layoffs once its last contracts run out, and the cabinet must decide what to do with its remaining funds.

e2c_rhineland.pact.subtitle: Requires good relations with the West. The Left faction will be furious.
e2c_rhineland.pact.unavailableSubtitle: Paris and London do not yet trust us enough for an alliance.

content.content: Germany, France and Britain sign a mutual defense pact. An attack on one of them by any European power, which everyone understands to mean the Soviet Union or Fascist Italy, will be treated as an attack on all three. The French have no reason to guard the Rhine against an ally, and their garrisons are withdrawn within the year.

content: Moscow calls the pact "an imperialist encirclement".
agrees, and so does the Left faction of our party.
no longer takes its line from Moscow, but it opposes the pact all the same, and so does the Left faction of our party.

content.content: We cannot pass it without the KPD, and they will not work with us.
The treasury cannot cover even the reduced compensation.

The Socialization Law names the owners whose property is forfeit for financing high treason, with Thyssen at the top of the list. The others, including Dutch and British shareholders in the Gelsenkirchen company, are paid in cash at a valuation set by the commission. Their governments protest to the Foreign Office.

On the Ruhr, the workers celebrate as they did in 1920. However, our Reformist faction is alarmed, and in the boardrooms of Frankfurt and Cologne, men who never supported the putsch wonder whether their names will be on the next list.

The field courts sit in requisitioned schoolhouses, three judges to a bench, and a case rarely lasts an afternoon. By the end of the season, more than two hundred men have been shot, and thousands have been sent to labor battalions clearing the rubble of the eastern districts.

content: The workers who fought for the Republic feel that justice has been done, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
approves. In the villages of Pomerania and the small towns of Franconia, however, people hear a different story, and the far right now has its martyrs. The Center and the liberals are appalled.
The neutralists carry the congress. Reuter, Schmid and forty Reichstag deputies leave to found the Social Democratic People's Party, the <span style="color: #f0456a;">
, with the money of the Hamburg merchants and the sympathy of the British Labour Party. The rest of the party merges with the left socialists to form the Socialist Unity Party, the

content.content: The workers' districts stay loyal to us, but many of the clerks, teachers and Catholic trade unionists do not. The French ambassador asks pointedly whether Germany still considers itself part of Europe.

e2d_east_settlement.plebiscite.subtitle: Requires the League's promise or strong Western backing.
e2d_east_settlement.plebiscite.unavailableSubtitle: Without the League's promise or the West's backing, Warsaw will never allow a vote.

content.content: Under the supervision of Swedish and Swiss officials, the people of the occupied provinces go to the polls. In East Prussia the result is never in doubt: 91% vote to return to Germany, and the church bells of Königsberg ring all night. Upper Silesia is divided district by district, as it was in 1921. Kattowitz stays Polish, while Gleiwitz and Beuthen come home.

content: The Polish garrisons march out along roads lined with silent crowds. The plebiscite has given us a victory that no general could have won, and the
has lost its most powerful argument.

e2d_black_front.infiltrate.subtitle: Requires control of the Prussian police.
e2d_black_front.infiltrate.unavailableSubtitle: We do not control the Prussian police.

content: Department IA of the Berlin police headquarters plants informers in eleven <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">

cells, including two on Strasser's personal staff. Their reports reach the Interior Minister's desk every Monday, and they make worrying reading: the front is organized in armed hundreds, and some of its contacts reach the Bendlerblock.

content.content: For now, though, we know what they know. That may prove useful one day.
No Western government will sign a pact with Strasser's ministers in our cabinet.
Paris and London do not trust us enough.
The new Rhine Pact makes Germany, France and Britain allies, and the French have no reason to garrison an ally's river. Their troops leave over the spring, and the Rhineland celebrates.

content: calls us "the Western bastion against the workers' fatherland"
calls the pact a surrender to the Western bankers
, and the Left faction of our party is unhappy.

e2d_morgenthau.money.subtitle: Requires some standing in the West.
e2d_morgenthau.money.unavailableSubtitle: Without a pact, the West will not fund us at all.

content.content: Washington grumbles, but accepts. The fund is cut in half, the advisers stay in their hotels, and the French make no promises about the Rhine. Some of the money arrives, and with it some of the cranes. We keep our freedom of action, but reconstruction will be slower.

e2d_polish_talks.plebiscite.subtitle: Requires some standing in the West.
e2d_polish_talks.plebiscite.unavailableSubtitle: Without support in London and Paris, Geneva will not listen.

content.content: After four months of drafting, the League Council agrees in principle that the "future status of the territories occupied during the German civil war" will be decided by their inhabitants, in a vote under international supervision "when conditions permit". Warsaw signs because the British insist, but it has no intention of letting conditions permit any time soon.
Still, the promise is on paper, and with the right friends we may be able to enforce it one day.

e2d_refugees.relief.subtitle: Costs 1 budget.
e2d_refugees.relief.unavailableSubtitle: The treasury cannot finance the camps.

content.content: The camps get barracks, schools and clinics, and each elects a committee to run them. It is decent work, and decently done. Families are fed and children go to school, and the Heimatbund men have a harder time handing out their leaflets when a Social Democratic camp committee is standing next to them.
The camps are still camps, though. Ten years from now there will be children who have never lived anywhere else.

content: The Act of Reunification places the Ruhr, the Rhineland

under Reich commissioners appointed in Berlin, with full powers "until the restoration of normal conditions". Prussia gets its western provinces back, and the Reichswehr is given garrisons in Essen and Koblenz.

content.content: Germany is one country again, and it is governed from Berlin. In the Ruhr, people take down the red flags and put up the black, red and gold without enthusiasm, because they have seen Berlin's commissioners before.

e2d_ruhr_endgame.statute.subtitle: Requires trust between Berlin and the miners.

content.content: Strasser's ministers would bring down the government.
The miners do not trust us enough.

The Statute of the Rhenish-Westphalian Industrial Land is signed in a pithead bath house at the Zollverein colliery, because both sides agree it is the most neutral ground in the Ruhr. The mines stay public, the Red Army becomes the Land police, and Essen gets a Landtag of its own. It is the settlement Berlin could have offered years ago, and the miners know it.

The Assembly passes a unitary Act of Reunification and appoints a Reich commissioner for Rhineland-Westphalia, with a Reichswehr division to support him. The Ruhr does not rise again, because it no longer has the strength. In Essen, Bochum and Gelsenkirchen, people remember that their vote was overruled, and they will remember it at every election for the next thirty years.

e2d_reunification_retry.title: The Assembly Reconvenes
e2d_reunification_retry.subtitle: The delegates have come back to Weimar.

options.title: Accept the Ruhr's terms, pass a federal Act and put it to the Ruhr again.
The nation has spoken. Pass a unitary Act on the strength of the national majority.

content.content: The Weimar Assembly is back in session for the first time since the Ruhr voted no. The year in between has not been wasted. Committees of miners' delegates and Reich officials have spent it going through the Ruhr's grievances one by one: pensions for the widows of Red Army fighters, the status of the public mines, and the Land police's red armbands. The Essen delegates are prepared to vote yes, and they say their voters will follow if the Republic meets them halfway.
The Reichswehr and the right are not interested in meeting anyone halfway. A referendum was held, and the country as a whole voted yes. In their view the Assembly should act on that result now.

The trains stop at Münster and Hamm. By February the Ruhr is rationing bread, and the Central Council splits between those who want to negotiate and those who want to break out toward the Rhine. Several thousand fighters slip across the Lippe and surrender, hungry and exhausted.

The blockade cuts both ways. Without Ruhr coal the factories of Hanover and Magdeburg run three days a week, and Red Army radio broadcasts photographs of hungry children in Bochum to anyone who will listen.

Leaflets dropped over Bochum and Dortmund promise that any man who brings his rifle to a Reichswehr post will receive a full pardon, a hot meal and a railway ticket home. Within three months twenty thousand have done so. They queue with their rifles slung upside down, as instructed, and many of them weep.
The hard core of the Red Army, a few thousand men in Essen and Duisburg, are not tempted. The Central Council denounces the deserters and holds on to the city centers.

e2k_coronation.boycott.subtitle: Republicans will rally to us, and our Left faction will approve. The new monarchy will not forgive us.

content.content: The seats reserved for our deputies in the cathedral stay empty.
None of our leaders attend the coronation.

content: In the evening, black, red and gold flags hang from windows across the working-class districts of Berlin. The police take down the flags, and the names of the people who hung them.

content.content: The republicans are with us, and our Left faction is proud. However, the Kaiser's ministers will not forget who stayed away.

e2k_border.vote.subtitle: The government will reward us. History may not.

content.content: We vote for the credits "in defense of the homeland".
The party executive declares its support for the credits "in defense of the homeland".

content: The Emperor receives our leaders at the palace for the first time. The next morning, the youth organization of the party in Berlin resigns as a body, and the old men who remember 1914 say nothing at all.

content.content: We obstruct the bill in every committee and challenge it before the State Court.
We have no deputies to obstruct the bill, so we challenge it before the State Court.

content: The court finds, after eighteen months, that the Prussian constitution permits the Prussian legislature to change the Prussian electoral law. By then the first Landtag of the three classes has already been elected.

e2k_election.boycott.subtitle: We will lose all of our seats in the Reichstag. Our Reformist faction will be furious, but the Left will approve.

content.content: We refuse to take part. Turnout in the working-class districts falls below 40%, which proves our point—but it also costs us every seat. For years to come, the Reichstag will debate the monarchy's laws without a single Social Democrat in the chamber. From now on, we will have to fight through the unions, the party press and the streets.
Our Left faction is proud of us. The Reformists are furious.

e2k_purge.law.subtitle: The principled position. The government will remember it.

content.content: Our deputies insist that even a stormtrooper has the right to a judge. The nationalist press calls us the Nazis' lawyers. A few judges, though, take the hint, and some of the trials are held in public.
We call for a referendum on the monarchy, and the unions call the workers into the streets.

The regent offers reforms, the army offers bayonets, and the middle classes decide that a liberal prince is better than a second revolution. The movement ebbs within a month. The court party uses the scare to bury most of the regent's program.

subtitle: The Left faction and the <span style="color: #700000;">
will be furious.

content.content: The Chancellor gives a sober radio address: property will be respected, compensation is guaranteed, and the budget will be balanced. The stock exchange recovers a little, and some of the money drifts back from Basel.

content: walks out of the cabinet meeting and comes back in an hour later, but its deputies now speak openly of "Hilferding's betrayal of 1923". Our Left faction is furious, and some workers are asking what they voted for. The councils have lost some of their standing.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
will be pleased, but our Reformist faction will not.

content: A Reich Cultural Council is formed, with seats for the factory cultural committees and a large majority for the <span style="color: #700000;">

's cultural commission. Brecht and Eisler write for the workers' theaters, and some of their work is excellent. However, other artists are found to be "insufficiently close to the life of the people", and their grants are stopped.

content.content: Gropius decides to stay in London, and Mies is reported to be considering Chicago. Many of our middle-class voters are put off, and the Reformist faction is unhappy with us.

e2l_blocs.neutral.subtitle: Both blocs will be irritated, but our position at home will be stronger.

content.content: A conference of neutral states meets at Potsdam, with Yugoslav, Indian, Swedish, Austrian and Czechoslovak delegations. It resolves that its members will join no military alliance and allow no foreign bases on their soil.

content: Berlin becomes the place where East and West meet when they cannot meet anywhere else. Both blocs are irritated with us, but both find us too useful to punish.
votes for the declaration after a long and painful debate, but it is not happy with us.

content.content: Our party's left wing votes for the declaration after a long and painful debate, but it is not happy with the leadership.

subtitle: The government will be more stable, but the <span style="color: #700000;">
and our Left faction will be angry.
unavailableSubtitle: and its allies are too strong in the convention to accept a constitution that would leave them a minority party.

content.content: The constitution of the Social Republic keeps the Reichstag sovereign and abolishes the presidential emergency powers. It writes the socialization of coal, steel, energy and banking into its articles, so that no future majority can undo it without a two-thirds vote. Works councils sit on the boards of every enterprise with more than fifty employees, but they do not run them.

content: votes against it and denounces the "bourgeois-parliamentary cage", but it remains in the cabinet for now. Our Left faction is unhappy, but the middle classes are reassured.

e2l_conspiracy.alert.subtitle: The workers will be ready if the army moves. The foreign press will notice.

content.content: The militias are put on alert. Rifles are moved from the central depots into the works of Siemens, AEG and Borsig, and every factory council in Berlin receives a sealed envelope, to be opened on a code word.

Unfortunately, the arrangements are not as quiet as we hoped, and a British journalist has written about "the arming of the Berlin proletariat". However, if the army moves, the workers will be ready for it.

e2l_council_bureaucracy.managers.subtitle: Output will rise, but the councils will be weakened, and the Left faction will be furious.

content.content: The councils keep their seats on the supervisory boards, but the mines, mills and power stations are now run by directors with engineering degrees and five-year contracts. Output rises and absenteeism falls. The councils become a kind of permanent works committee, consulted on safety, canteens and holidays.
Our Left faction says that we have handed the revolution back to the foremen. The Reformists are pleased.

subtitle: Moscow will be pleased, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
will gain influence. Our Reformist faction will be unhappy.

content.content: A Soviet trade delegation arrives in Berlin and leaves with a five-year agreement: German turbines, machine tools and chemicals, in exchange for Ukrainian wheat, Baku oil and Urals manganese. The Saxon factories are busy again.

content: Unfortunately, the agreement allows Soviet "technical inspectors" to visit the plants that fill its orders, and there are soon a great many of them. The
is pleased with the deal. However, our Reformist faction voices its displeasure.

subtitle: The councils and the <span style="color: #700000;">
will gain ground, but the Catholic peasants will be alarmed.

content.content: The estates are handed over whole to the laborers who work them. They elect a council and a farm manager, who is often the old estate steward under a new title. The great fields remain great fields, and the machinery stays in use.

content: In Pomerania, it works well. In Bavaria, however, the Catholic peasant leagues hold torchlight meetings against "the kolkhoz", and no reassurance that smallholders will not be touched seems to make any difference. The <span style="color: #700000;">

e2l_coup.militia.subtitle: This depends on the strength of our militias.

onArrival.$code: Q['e2l_coup_response'] = "militia";

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
will gain influence in the militia, and the Reichswehr will be alarmed.

content.content: The People's Militia is formed with a joint staff. Every command post is doubled and every order countersigned. It is clumsy, but it works. The militia drills in the factory yards after the shift, and its battalions are named after Liebknecht and Bebel.

content: Unfortunately, its political education is in the hands of the <span style="color: #700000;">
's instructors, who are more diligent than ours. The generals call it "the Red Army of Germany", and our Reformist faction is uneasy.

content.content: The refugees are given papers and small pensions and sent to live in Thuringian spa towns, on condition that they give no interviews and join no organizations. Most of them keep the bargain. Moscow complains about the list, but eventually drops it.

content: is only mildly annoyed with us
agree to support the government on confidence and supply. They keep their freedom to criticize us, and they use it.

e2l_socialisation.trusts.subtitle: Production will continue smoothly, but the Left faction will grumble. (-1 budget)

content.content: The Reich Coal Corporation and the Reich Steel Corporation are founded, with boards of engineers and civil servants and a third of their seats reserved for the unions. The managers are mostly the same men as before, with new letterheads and lower salaries. Production hardly changes.

content: Our Left faction complains that the workers have exchanged one boss for another, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
calls the trusts "state capitalism in a red tie". However, the Staatsgerichtshof finds little to object to, and the middle classes are reassured.

e2l_officers.commissars.subtitle: The army will be somewhat more loyal, but the nationalists will be outraged, and the Reformist faction will be furious.

content: Every regiment now has a political officer, appointed jointly by the <span style="color: #c00000;">
, who countersigns orders and reports on morale. The officers hate them. Most of the commissars are earnest young trade unionists who know nothing about artillery. Unfortunately, a few of the
's men seem to take their orders from somewhere other than the cabinet.
is pleased. Our Reformist faction is furious, and the nationalists are making the most of it.

e2l_unity_party.democratic.subtitle: Our Left faction will be pleased; the Reformists less so.

content: is too strong to accept a merger on our terms.
does not trust us enough to accept our conditions.
's apparatus is too entrenched to dissolve itself into a democratic party.
After eighteen months of negotiation, the two parties merge into a <span style="color: #c00000;">
. Its statute guarantees the right to form factions, the election of every office by secret ballot, and the right to publish dissenting opinions in the party press.
's Moscow loyalists refuse to join, and form a small "Communist Party (Bolsheviks)" that Moscow recognizes and almost nobody votes for.
The Moscow loyalists who walked out of the <span style="color: #700000;">
during the purges denounce the merger from outside, but almost nobody listens to them.
The rest of the old <span style="color: #700000;">
becomes the new party's loud, argumentative left wing.

content.content: We are now the largest socialist party in the world. Our Left faction is delighted, although the Reformists have their doubts.

e2l_women.pay.subtitle: The Left faction will be a little disappointed. (-1 budget)

content: Equal pay becomes law, and the socialized industries are ordered to build nurseries. The women's congress accepts the gains and promises to come back for the rest.

content.content: Paragraph 218 remains on the books, although prosecutions become rare.
The abortion law stays as it is, with no new guarantees.
Marie Juchacz tells a reporter that she has been waiting since 1919 and can wait a little longer—"but not very much longer".

e2p_entente.dossier.subtitle: Names, dates and photographs. The New State will call it treason.

content.content: The files go to Paris by courier: the camps in the Emsland moors, the names of the dead, the photographs. The entente dies in the French Chamber. In Germany, the police hunt down the people who could have smuggled the files, and catch some of them.

The party goes into the cellars and the allotment huts. Groups of five, each knowing only one name in the next group, collect dues, pass on news and keep lists of who can be trusted. Within a year, the police have broken two networks in Berlin and one in Hamburg. There are always more.

e2p_ruhr.arm.subtitle: A rising could shake the New State. A massacre could finish us.

content.content: Rifles from the old Reichsbanner caches go out to the pit committees.

The army moves in before the committees can organize. In Bochum, a column of strikers walks into machine-gun fire, and the photographs make the New State's case for it: armed Bolsheviks in the Ruhr. The underground loses hundreds of its best people.

content: The army surrounds the coalfield and then hesitates. The officers do not want to fight a civil war for Franz von Papen

content.content: , and in Berlin, Schleicher makes sure everyone knows it

content: . The strike ends in a truce, and the New State looks weaker than it has ever looked.

e2p_schleicher.refuse.subtitle: Our hands stay clean. Papen stays in power.

content: We send the colonel back with a polite answer: the <span style="color: #c00000;">
will negotiate with a government that restores the constitution, and with no other. Schleicher shrugs and waits for a better partner.

content.content: The army stays loyal to whoever pays it. After a week of shootings in the industrial cities, the strike collapses, and the New State goes on without Papen.

LZ 130 is finished, flown for a season of joyrides over the Bodensee, and then broken up. Its aluminium is used to build Condor airliners. Eckener calls it the saddest day of his life. Lufthansa's order book is full, and the aircraft factories in Dessau, Bremen and Rostock take on another eight thousand workers.

content: card has been added to the Modern Age deck.)

content.content: Only the Reich government can fund this.

Schreyer gets two thousand valves and a laboratory in Charlottenburg, and Zuse gets a joint appointment. The first electronic circuit adds two numbers in a ten-thousandth of a second. Then one of the valves burns out, as one will every few hours. Building the machine will take years. Engineers are already coming from Manchester and Philadelphia to see it.

content: card has been added to the Modern Age deck.)

e2u_autobahn.car.unavailableSubtitle: Only the Reich government can promise to buy the cars.

content.content: We tell the motor industry that the Republic will buy the first ten thousand small cars for the Reichspost, the rural doctors and the district nurses if someone will build them at Ganz's price. Opel and Adler send polite refusals. Porsche sends a telegram that says only "When?".

content: card has been added to the Modern Age deck.)

e2u_fission.secret.unavailableSubtitle: Only the Reich government can classify research.

content.content: The "Uranium Club" meets for the first time in the War Ministry on the Bendlerstraße. Its members are sworn to secrecy. The Reich buys the entire stock of the Joachimsthal mines' uranium oxide through a Swiss front company. Meitner resigns from the project on the first day. Hahn stays, and he does not sleep well.

content: card has been added to the Modern Age deck.)

content.content: The wholesale society of the consumer cooperatives signs a contract with Bosch and AEG for half a million refrigerators. They will carry the cooperative label and be sold at cost to members. The retailers' association calls it "Marxism by mail order". The cooperatives have three hundred thousand new members within a year.

content: card has been added to the Modern Age deck.)

content.content: Only the Reich government can fund this.

The Reich Penicillin Works opens beside the Robert Koch Institute, with Chain in charge of a staff of two hundred. Its product is sold to the sickness funds at the cost of production. IG Farben says it is unfair competition. Chain says it is a public health service, and the doctors agree with him.

content: card has been added to the Modern Age deck.)

content.content: Only the Reich government can fund this.

Viewing rooms open in post offices across Berlin and Potsdam, and the Reichspost's new broadband cable carries the picture to halls in Leipzig as well. The queues go round the block. A tram conductor's family from Wedding and a professor's family from Dahlem sit in the same dark room and watch the same flickering runners. Both of them cheer.

content: card has been added to the Modern Age deck.)

content.content: The society is quietly wound up, and its best members put on civilian clothes paid for by the War Ministry and take the train to Usedom. Peenemünde will have wind tunnels, test stands and a liquid oxygen plant, all hidden behind the pine woods. Nothing about it appears in the budget debate. The French military attaché hears about it within six weeks.

content: card has been added to the Modern Age deck.)

content.content: The amendment passes with 11 votes to spare. The nationalists walk out before the final reading, denouncing "the castration of the presidency", but the galleries are full of Reichsbanner men, and their applause drowns out the protests.

content: The new Reich Constitutional Court will sit in Leipzig, alongside the Reichsgericht. For the first time, the emergency powers are bound by the constitution. The Left faction and the
are both pleased with the result.

content.content: The "double earner" law is repealed, and a married woman's wages are now her own property. The rest of the Selbert draft is referred to a commission of jurists, where it will probably remain for some time.
The women's committees accept the half-victory, though without much enthusiasm.

content: Our press greets the new party as "the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
with holy water". We send our best speakers into the Protestant small towns where the
hopes to grow, arguing that a Christian worker belongs in the workers' party—and some of them come over to us. The Left faction approves.
's leaders are offended, and they will remember it the next time a coalition is formed.

The Reichstag building is under guard, so our deputies and those of the other republican parties slip past the cordon and meet in the old Prussian Herrenhaus on the Leipziger Straße. 260 deputies—a clear majority—vote to declare the decrees void and the

content.content: Within hours, the Constitutional Court in Leipzig issues an emergency injunction to the same effect.
Foreign radio stations broadcast the resolution, and our members paste copies of it on factory walls across Berlin.

From now on, every German has a constituency deputy as well as a party list. Our candidates in the Ruhr and in Saxony win their constituencies by huge margins. In rural Pomerania and Upper Bavaria, they are crushed—but the list seats keep the overall result fair.
Our deputies have begun holding office hours in the back rooms of pubs, and the voters seem to like it.

content: The Reichsbanner, the unions and our youth organizations go to work. Every <span style="color: #D79E2A;">
meeting is met with a larger counter-meeting across the street, and
prints Naumann's old speeches from the Goebbels years next to his new ones. There are scuffles, and one death in Brunswick, which each side blames on the other.

content.content: The party keeps its hard core, but many of the curious drift away.

content: will not support a new court.

content.content: The Staatsgerichtshof was never more than an arbitration panel between the Reich and the Länder. Its successor, the Reich Constitutional Court, can now hear complaints from any citizen whose basic rights have been violated—whether by a ministry or by a court. Its sixteen judges are elected by the Reichstag and the Reichsrat with a two-thirds majority, so neither we nor the Right can pack it.

content: is pleased with the new court.

content.content: The Reich Credit Corporation has opened a housing window for non-profit builders. The union societies break ground within months, and the Labor faction is pleased. Their estates are good ones, if fewer than we had hoped.
However, the poorest families, who cannot afford even a cooperative share, mostly stay where they are.

e2w_mitbestimmung.third.subtitle: The Labor faction wants parity, and will be unhappy with less.

content.content: The Works Constitution Act gives employees a third of the seats on the supervisory board of every company with more than 500 workers. The unions concede that it is an achievement, since it applies across the whole economy—but it falls far short of parity. Böckler calls off the strike, telling the press that "the workers of the Ruhr were offered a chair at the table and given a stool in the corner".

content: The Labor faction is unhappy with us, though the

content.content: Only the Reich government can propose this.

content: will not support a new map.

content.content: The Reich Territorial Act redraws the map of Germany for the first time since Napoleon. Prussia is divided into eight new Länder, among them Rhineland-Westphalia, Lower Saxony, Hesse-Nassau and Schleswig-Holstein; Lower Saxony also absorbs Brunswick, Oldenburg and the two Lippes. content.content: Expectedly, the Lautenbach Plan has failed due to strong opposition from those who adhere to fiscal orthodoxy, which holds that deflation, despite its pain, is healthy because it weeds out inefficient producers. This contrasts with the Keynesian belief that a destructive second phase occurs, where economic recovery becomes possible but fails because of a collapse in investor confidence.

Reichsbank President Hans Luther, who personally sympathizes with increasing the money supply and expanding credit, has shelved the idea. The conference only reached two unanimous conclusions: the German people's fear of inflation made it impossible to announce any dramatic program to expand the money supply, meaning the government would have to act secretly if it ever decided to implement Lautenbach's plan, and the government must continue its campaign to lower wages bound by long-term collective labor contracts and prices set by cartel agreements.

However, Luther has made concessions to the Keynesians, quietly expanding the money supply and increasing credit availability, even abandoning the rule that 40% of money in circulation must be covered by gold and foreign exchange. Furthermore, generous financing of exports to the Soviet Union has helped counteract the effects of the withdrawal of foreign credits on both the money supply and the job market.
"Stimulation can only help if we are already at the bottom....I do not believe that we are that far yet."
- Ernst Trendelenburg, Reich Minister of Economics, 1931.

content: Papen, eager to return to power and thirsting for revenge against his former ally and ouster Schleicher, has been working behind the scenes to arrange a meeting with
. With the help of intermediaries—and ultimately a banker sympathetic to the Nazis—he finally secured an audience with the man himself.

The two met at the banker’s home, where they spent much of the time airing old grievances. Nevertheless, Papen made a concerted effort to court the Nazi leader. He insisted that it was Schleicher, not he, who had blocked

’s path to the chancellorship. He also revealed that President Hindenburg had yet to issue Schleicher a decree to dissolve the Reichstag—evidence, he claimed, of the president’s deep reservations about him. Papen emphasized that the true nature of the Hindenburg-Schleicher relationship was far more strained than the public believed, and he asserted that he himself still wielded considerable influence over the old man. His hatred for Schleicher was unmistakable throughout.

content.content: By the end of the meeting, the two had reached a mutual understanding: they would work together to oust Schleicher and replace his government with a presidential cabinet based on a coalition between the Nazis and the reactionary right, with the goal of crushing the leftist parties once and for all.

content: However, the question of who should lead this new government remained unresolved. Papen argued that Hindenburg’s well-known opposition to appointing
should make him the more viable candidate, offering to give the Nazis control over the Interior and Defense Ministries as compensation.
flatly rejected this, still insisting that his mass movement had earned the right to the chancellorship.

content.content: The meeting concluded with a promise to continue discussions, though no future date was set.
Even in their weakened state, the Nazis are still a threat. We must not be too complacent.

content.content: Franz von Papen has unveiled his new cabinet—assembled almost entirely on Schleicher’s recommendations. Vorwärts wasted no time branding it the “Cabinet of Barons,” with six members drawn from the nobility and only three being commoners. The overtly anti-social character of the cabinet has already alienated the vast majority of the country and firmly sealed Papen’s vast unpopularity among the German people.

content: The only party formally represented in the cabinet is the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">

, which holds three ministries. The remaining posts are occupied by right-wing independents, in line with Papen’s stated goal of forming a government "free from party influence." Schleicher has been promoted to Defense Minister, where he intends to steer the administration from behind the scenes.

content.content: An embittered Papen—convinced that Schleicher orchestrated his downfall and vowing never to forgive the betrayal—has officially submitted his resignation to Hindenburg, who, with reluctance, has accepted it.

As this marks yet another cabinet's fall under Schleicher's influence, Hindenburg's suspicions of his motives begin to grow, particularly with Schleicher’s constant invoking of national security as justification for his actions.

content.content: It has been thirteen years since the adoption of the Weimar Constitution in 1919—a date still marked as a public holiday in its commemoration.

However, Papen has chosen this occasion to unveil his plan for a so-called “New State”: an authoritarian constitution that would merge the offices of chancellor and Prussian minister president, free the chancellor from reliance on Reichstag confidence, and establish an aristocratic upper house of parliament appointed by the president. In practice, this would transform Germany into a dictatorship run by elites.

content: The Reichstag has reconvened for the first time since the election, with a significantly larger contingent of <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

members now present. The immediate issue at hand is the election of the President of the Reichstag. While the position has traditionally been a procedural one, it has taken on heightened importance under Papen's presidential government, given the President's authority to influence the agenda and adjourn sessions.
By long-standing custom, the role is granted to the largest parliamentary delegation. That delegation isn't the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
, but the Center Party backing them nonetheless is a key part of negotiations between the two parties. Without such backing, it is likely that our candidate, Paul Löbe, would be elected once again.
have secured unanimous approval for a change in the order of business to allow an immediate vote on a motion of no confidence against Papen, and not even the

content: President Hindenburg has expressed his reluctance to run for re-election. At 84 years old, he prefers to spend his remaining years in retirement free from the burdens of his high office. While he has been open to serving longer if his term were extended by the Reichstag, the failure of those efforts, combined with his unwillingness to endure a grueling presidential campaign, has caused concern, particularly for Kurt von Schleicher
, on whom he depends to enact his decrees
Heinrich Sahm, the Mayor of Berlin, has formed a re-election committee to persuade Hindenburg to run again. This effort has included the collection of over

million signatures and appeals from a wide array of figures and political parties across German society, including Artur Mahraun of the Young German Order, and controversial former Defense Ministers Otto Gessler and Gustav Noske.

Impressed by the public support, Hindenburg is reconsidering his decision but insists that his candidacy must be backed by the German Right and veteran organizations rather than the German Left and Center.

content: Otto Braun, former Minister-President of Prussia and leader of our reformist wing, has—without informing the <span style="color: #c00000;">

leadership—met privately with Chancellor von Schleicher. Braun proposed cooperation, on the condition that Schleicher relinquish federal control over Prussia and restore him to office with full authority, including the power to dissolve the Landtag. Braun suggested that, together, they could rule by decree and wage a determined campaign against the Nazis.

Schleicher, however, was unenthusiastic. Having led the Prussian coup himself, he is reluctant to undo the federal consolidation of power. More importantly, unlike Braun, he is not committed to weakening the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

We have leverage, and we should use it to extract concessions. No one wants civil war.

We have decided to cooperate with the government by preemptively dissolving the organization and turning over weapons before the ban is to take place. A notable amount of socialists have decided to fight on however, but without numbers or weapons, this ad-hoc group is destined for failure.

content: Following months of state repression, the hollowed-out remnants of the Reichsbanner are officially banned. With the more moderate fighters having retired or been absorbed into the state’s militias, only die-hard socialists remain in the self-defense organization. This has given Schleicher the pretext to brand the
and the Reichsbanner as jointly conspiring toward revolutionary overthrow—and to extend the ban to both.

content.content: If this ban goes through, we will be left defenseless against state oppression. Many in the party urge us to resist, while others claim that the era of paramilitaries is over and argue for preemptive disarmament to placate Schleicher.

content.content: Presenting himself as a continuation of Schleicher and as another non-partisan military man, von Bredow has won his close friend Schleicher's favor. Although former chancellor Schleicher is officially retired, he still pulls many strings behind the scenes, unwilling to give up that scheming of his.

However, von Bredow is certainly no Schleicher, he possesses no vast network of political connections throughout all walks of life, and Schleicher's personal popularity has largely failed to transfer over to his hand picked successor.
Perhaps the house of cards Schleicher has carefully built will come tumbling down?

With his resignation announced last week, speculation over who will succeed the monumental leader now dominates the minds of citizens across the nation. Some believe he is prepared to pass power to a civilian, while others expect another military man to take the helm. In the end, it hardly matters—Germany has been changed forever.

content.content: Schleicher requests for a decree dissolving the Reichstag, pointing out the chamber in all likelihood approve a no-confidence motion at the end in the next reconvocation. Also predicting that a new election wouldn't alter the Reichstag in his favor much, he also asks for a decree postponing the planned election.

Hindenburg remains unresponsive. His personal estrangement from Schleicher is already far advanced, and there have been little personal contact between the two men for a majority of Schleicher's term. Schleicher advocating for the same course of action that he himself opposed when it was advocated by Papen.

In the end, Hindenburg is only willing to provide a dissolution decree, but then he refuses to provide it to Schleicher as of right now. But to the public, Schleicher's hold on the chancellorship remains firm.
Schleicher returns to his waiting ministers and relays the outcome. An announcement of his resignation—prepared weeks in advance—is released to the press.

content: At this stage, the options have narrowed to two: a return of Papen, or the ascension of
. Both promise disaster for Germany—and the latter, disaster for all of humanity.

schleicher_cabinet_7.schleicher_3.title: Defund the Reichsbanner; the threat is no longer present.

content.content: With the Reichswehr keeping order in the streets, we have no further need for the Reichsbanner's self-defense role. Better to spend our scarce funds on electoral propaganda rather than weapons.

content: 's dramatic escalation of seemingly pointless violence has gripped the streets, with many innocent civilians caught in the crossfire. Their increasingly open clashes with leftist groups, driven by frustration and insubordination, have spiraled out of control.
Although Schleicher admires the patriotic militarism of the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

, he now dismisses it as little more than Röhm's tool for a socialistic "national revolution"—a gang of thugs turning their violence against ordinary citizens. Röhm's open agitation for such a revolution has left Schleicher no choice but to ban the organization outright.
But Schleicher's objective is already achieved: former "desirable" <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

fighters have been integrated into a newly built militia attached to the Reichswehr, composed of ex-fighters and the unemployed. This force has been deployed to maintain order in the streets, working alongside the local police. However, they remain lenient toward their former comrades and display significant bias against the Reichsbanner and

content.content: Nonetheless, this has succeeded in shifting public opinion toward the "law and order" chancellor, and further against the parliamentary system that failed to protect them.

content.content: Without control of the Prussian Interior Ministry, their reach is limited—though they have already begun turning the federal police into a force loyal to the Nazis.
The Prussian Interior Ministry, however, is the real prize—its police force now answers entirely to them, with widespread purges of republican officials taking place.

content: Fortunately, Schleicher has barred Nazi Party members from joining the police, maintaining the same restriction already enforced in the Reichswehr.
Lately, we have observed the police exclusively targeting Reichsbanner and <span style="color: #700000;">

fighters, while openly shielding far-right demonstrations from our protests. They have even persuaded Schleicher to transfer command of the Reichswehr's militia to the Interior Ministry, citing the need for centralized control.

content.content: The Reichsbank, long known for its strict fiscal conservatism and obsessive anti-inflation stance, had already slashed Schleicher's initial public works decree by 15%. So, it was no surprise when news of even greater government spending met with their disapproval.

However, the endorsement of the campaign by Hjalmar Schacht—a respected banker and recently retired Reichsbank President credited with ending hyperinflation—has done much to calm the business community. Under government pressure, the Reichsbank is ultimately coerced into backing the plan, though not without forcing another 20% cut in funding.

content.content: As expected, the objections raised by Schleicher’s spokesman—acting on direct orders—have sunk the Nazi motion. In response, the Center Party has introduced a compromise: a one-week extension of the recess to allow for further negotiations.

Papen’s scheme has become considerably easier, as Schleicher is now forced to test the President’s support by requesting a decree to dissolve the Reichstag and postpone elections. But if Hindenburg denies the request, the question becomes unavoidable: who would succeed him? Papen? Hitler?

content: Schleicher has squandered a critical opportunity to salvage his cabinet—and perhaps Germany itself. Had the elections been postponed just a few months, his position would likely have improved significantly. He stood to gain from the launch of Gereke’s public works program and the natural recovery of the global economy. content: Ernst Meyer died in Potsdam on the second of February, of a pneumonia that his lungs, after years of tuberculosis, could not fight off. He was forty-two.

content.content: He was still working on the joint campaign with our executive in the week before he was taken to hospital.
The joint lists in the Ruhr pits were his last piece of work.

Thousands of Communist workers follow the coffin through Berlin, and a good number of ours walk with them. The Central Committee elects Arthur Ewert, Meyer's closest ally, as chairman. The Comintern's representative abstains. The party's line will not change, but its new chairman is a very different man.

content.content: The executive keeps its majority, but takes no action against the opposition. Seydewitz is applauded for a fierce speech on the crisis of capitalism—and so is Fritz Tarnow, for his reply: do Social Democrats stand at capitalism's sickbed as its doctor, or as its cheerful heir?
The congress ends in an uneasy truce. The Left faction is satisfied for now, but the Reformist faction is not happy with our leniency, and the bourgeois parties are watching us with some suspicion.

e2_defense_policy.rearm.subtitle: No limit on the army. Tension will rise sharply, and France and Poland will arm faster. The Left faction will be furious.

content.content: The Chancellor tells the Reichstag that Germany will no longer be bound by a disarmament that nobody else has kept. The cheers come mostly from the right of the chamber.

In Paris, the government calls the decision a breach of the peace of Europe and asks parliament for new military credits. Warsaw and Prague follow within the week. The Left faction says that we have done the nationalists' work for them.

e2_currency_reform.loan.subtitle: Prices will stop rising, and the reconstruction will speed up. However, a foreign commissioner will watch the Reichsbank, and the nationalists and the KPD will call it a bankers' dictate. (+2 budget)

content.content: A consortium of British and American banks lends the Reich 800 million Marks against the customs and tobacco revenues, and a new Mark is issued on the strength of it. As in 1924, a foreign commissioner will sit on the Reichsbank's General Council until the loan is repaid. Prices stop rising within a few months, and the money from abroad keeps the building sites busy.

content: both attack the loan as a second Dawes Plan, and the Left faction is unhappy with us.

e2_presidents_ear.reconcile.subtitle: He will stay in office, and the Republic will have peace. The Left faction will be furious.

content.content: Our Chancellor went to the President's palace, and the two men talked for two hours.
Our party chairman went to the President's palace, and the two men talked for two hours.

content: In the end, they came to an understanding: the President will serve out his term, and he has pledged on the radio to govern "only with the Reichstag, and never against it". In return, we will not press for charges, and the officers who obeyed the Directory's orders will be pensioned off rather than tried.

content.content: The bourgeois parties are relieved, and so is much of the officer corps. However, the Left faction calls it a pardon for treason, and many of the workers who stopped the trains are asking what they struck for.

options.title: Demand that the President resign.
Make peace with the President.
Leave it for now.

content: The coup has failed, but its author is still Reichspräsident.

has withdrawn the decrees and blamed his advisers. The Directory's generals are in Moabit awaiting trial, while the man who signed their appointment still receives ambassadors and signs the laws the Reichstag passes.

Nobody in Berlin believes he was misled. However, removing a President against his will takes two-thirds of the Reichstag, either to indict him before the Staatsgerichtshof or to put his recall to the people.

content.content: The republican parties have that majority, if they hold together.
The republican parties do not have that majority.

content.content: The workers know that we tried, and the Labor faction is satisfied with us. However, the bourgeois parties are annoyed that the government is quarreling with its own central bank, and business confidence has suffered.

thousand join the police, and the Red Front is dissolved.

content.content: Our Left faction is delighted. The Reformists are less sure, and the bourgeois parties are furious that former Communist street fighters now carry the Republic's rifles.

content.content: National and sectorial workers councils have been part of the Weimar Constitution, but they were disempowered in the past, acting as nothing more than advisory bodies. We can change that.

Our spending on public works has reduced the need for unemployment insurance and welfare, while also increasing tax receipts through the multiplier effect as the new money circulates in the economy, helping to recover some of our spending. We continue to reinvest most of this new revenue into the program.

content: The economy is finally showing signs of improvement. The bourgeois parties are pleased to see that we’re following through with their economic recovery plan and are offering their full support. The investor confidence generated by our successes has led to a small-scale revival of the private sector, along with capital inflows from foreign investors.

content.content: However, the workers are dissatisfied with our slow pace in raising their wages.

With a great expansion of funding, we hope to keep it that way, and expand on our achievements.

content.content: Furthermore, the liberals in our governing coalition will also face backlash from their support base for participating in the government that increases their own taxes.

labor_affairs.support_employers.subtitle: Popular among the bourgeoisie, much less so among the workers.

content.content: The more radical workers despise our suppression of their strikes, recalling the days of Friedrich Ebert.

While a 40-hour work week was declared during the German Revolution in 1918, enforcement has become increasingly porous over the years. The capitalists have successfully added numerous exceptions and loopholes, returning to the old regime of forced overtime for workers.
Now, with the force of the Labor Ministry, we are finally enforcing the rights of workers to their own time. The bourgeoisie and their political representatives are displeased.

Their argument is that the Nazis are not a passing fever. The Young Plan campaign has given Hitler money and respectability, and his party is winning seats in town councils across the country. The Republic, they say, will not be defended by Marxist arguments alone. We need a mass movement for democracy that speaks to people's feelings as well as their interests.

content.content: A consortium of banks and cement firms builds the road and collects a toll at each end. It is finished on time and under budget, and at two marks a trip it is used mostly by commercial travellers and lorries.

The party backs a public loan, and Friedrichshafen lays down LZ 131 and LZ 132. They are bigger and slower than any aeroplane, and every crossing is fully booked. People seem to want to see the Atlantic from a promenade deck with a glass of hock in their hand. They will not be able to do so for very much longer.
Alwin Walther's Institute for Practical Mathematics in Darmstadt and the mathematicians in Göttingen get machines of their own. Graduate students learn to program before they learn to drive.

The savings banks start offering instalment loans for household goods. Sales double. So do the arrears, after the first winter. The party's left complains that we have taught the working class to borrow.
IG Farben and Schering sublicense the method and divide the market between them, which surprises no one. Penicillin is soon plentiful. It is not yet cheap.

The five big manufacturers agree to build a single standard set, the E1, and they sell it at 650 marks. That is still too dear for most workers, but it is half the price of anything else on sale. Shops start to sell them on instalments.

Grants go out to Dahlem, Leipzig, Heidelberg, Hamburg and Göttingen. There is no central direction, plenty of duplication, and a great deal of very good science. Every result is published within the month.
Dornberger gets his rocket men after all. They leave for Usedom with their slide rules and a good deal of guilt. The research is now a military secret, and so is the budget.

ending_slides.weimar_win.title: The Weimar Republic Limps Forward
ending_slides.weimar_win.subtitle: Ending 2

content: Following the scarring experience of the Nazi movement’s rapid rise and implosion, the flaws of the Weimar system became impossible to ignore. But in the end, the fascists and communists who once battled in the streets now stand together in soup lines. Though a number of neo-Nazi movements would emerge after
’s mask of sanity slipped, the ideology itself remains irrevocably discredited.

No war as destructive as the Great War would come again. Slowly, Germany and the Western Allies began to rebuild relations, choosing to forget and forgive. Fascism never takes root as a dominant force, and the primary threat to European democracy becomes the resurgent Soviet Union. The Spanish Civil War ends in 1936 with a Republican victory.

Africa remains colonized until the 1970s and 80s. Independence, when it comes, is negotiated largely on the terms of the colonizers. Exploitation persists under a different guise. The Cold War unfolds along different lines, as a "state capitalist" Soviet Union remains intact, forming a bloc with the authoritarian Kuomintang-ruled Republic of China and post-independence India, which fought a bloody war to escape British rule in the 1950s. This tri-polar alliance has solidified into a global axis of its own.

Timeline of the SPD and the Republic (until 1928)

content: : The SPD is formed as a merger of the General German Workers' Association, founded by Ferdinand Lassalle, and the Social Democratic Workers' Party of Germany, led by Wilhelm Liebknecht and August Bebel. Eventually, the SPD grows to become the largest party in the German Empire.
: The Great War begins. The SPD votes in favor of war credits, with substantial internal dissent. This begins a policy of
, a general peace between all political parties and trade unions.
: The USPD, a left-wing anti-war split from the SPD, is formed.

: Following defeats in the war and uprisings by soldiers, sailors, and workers, SPD leader Philip Scheidemann proclaims the German Republic, and Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicates from his throne. An armistice is declared, ending the Great War. Conflict between center-left social democrats and far-left radicals erupts in the streets of Berlin and elsewhere.

: The Spartacist Uprising, in which communist workers attempt to seize control of government, is launched. The uprising is defeated by the Social Democratic government, now led by President Friedrich Ebert and Chancellor Philipp Scheidemann, with the support of the far-right Freikorps militas. The two key leaders of the uprising, Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, are murdered by the Freikorps. The Treaty of Versailles is signed under great protest from all political factions in Germany, officially ending the Great War. The Weimar Constitution is signed. The first "Weimar Coalition" government is formed, led by the SPD, DDP, and Center (Z) parties.

: The Kapp Putsch, an attempt by reactionary actors within the military to take power, is launched, and is defeated by the workers with a general strike. This is followed by left-wing uprisings in the Ruhr, which are defeated by the Reichswehr and Freikorps. The Weimar Coalition is defeated in the elections, with the right and far left increasing in vote share. Elected governments in this period are very unstable, often only lasting a matter of months. There is a split in the USPD, with the majority faction joining with the KPD and the Soviet Union's Communist International (Comintern) alliance.
: Communist uprisings in Saxony and Hamburg are defeated. Matthias Erzberger, the Center Party leader who signed the Versailles Treaty, is assassinated.
: The Treaty of Rapallo is signed, which normalized relations with the Soviet Union. Walther Rathenau, the DDP Foreign Minister, is assassinated. The SPD reunites with most of the remaining USPD.

: Hyperinflation begins, largely due to the economic policy of "passive resistance" against the French occupation of the Ruhr and the Versailles reparations. The currency is rapidly devalued as prices for necessities rise to billions of Reichsmarks. The government launches a Reichsexekution against Saxony, which was led by a joint SPD-KPD government. The Nazi "Beer Hall Putsch" is launched in Munich, and fails, with the arrest of Hitler. Eventually, new policies manage to stabilize the currency, and the French occupation ends.

: Parliamentary elections are held in May and December, the latter leading to the bourgeois-right governments that last until 1928. Hitler is released from prison. The Dawes Plan for the repayment of the Versailles reparations is negotiated, which reduces payments and increases economic growth. Germany begins to enter a period of relative stability, with the end of the hyperinflation crisis.

: President Friedrich Ebert dies, and new presidential elections are held, leading to the narrow election of Paul von Hindenburg in the second round. Hindenburg is a war hero and a right-wing reactionary. The SPD adopts the Heidelberg Program as its party platform. The Locarno Treaties are signed, which confirmed Germany's post-war western borders.
: A referendum on the expropriation of the princes, supported by the SPD and KPD, fails.

options.title: Back

content.content: Hindenburg keeps sacking me! How do I prevent it?

It's hard to prevent him from sacking you if you plan to stay in office for the full four years, but pausing reparations (by not exposing rearmament), keeping the Reichswehr loyal, maintaining a budget surplus, keeping a high pro republic support, a low coalition dissent, avoiding land reform, and keeping unemployment and NSDAP poll numbers low, all help. Remember, him sacking you is not the end of the world, and being free from the burden of government could be a blessing in disguise. Sometimes you have to accept it.

A main problem with newer players is that, they overestimate the negative effects of not completing government burden. It is not the end of the world if you miss a goal or two or three, some sacrifices are needed if you need to garner the budget for an economic plan. That said, you also can't afford to completely ignore the Labor Ministry; repeated failures there will significantly increase internal dissent.
How do I impact a party's ideologies and get certain paths? Is it RNG?

content: Nothing in Dynamic relies on RNG, aside from card draws. The Support for the Republic value plays a crucial role in determining party congress outcomes, particularly within the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">

. The liberal parties, on the other hand, are primarily influenced by governmental actions—moving toward economic democracy and left-wing policies will push them rightward, while maintaining good relations and avoiding major socialist policies will bring them closer. Relations also matter significantly, making the negotiation skills of Müller and Braun highly valuable.

content.content: What happened to the WTB Plan?

Woytinsky only came up with the plan in late 1931 after the Banking Crisis, so to represent this, you need to get the event where Woytinsky proposes the concept in order to support it. The event is dynamic, and can trigger depending on factors such as: the state of the economy, deflation, labor faction strength, and most importantly internal party dissent. Appointing Woytinsky as an advisor aids significantly, as his presence passively increases the rate.

Dynamic mode is the intended way to play the mod, combining elements of both easy and historical modes. It reduces RNG with the shuffle leadership and card dismissal features of easy mode while retaining the starting variables of historical mode, such as relations and Reichsbanner strength.
You will have to get Stegerwald as the leader of Prussia, either through Braun resigning, or having a right-wing coalition form.
How do I cross the rubicon?

content: Hindenburg needs to dismiss Chancellor Brüning following the 1932 Presidential elections. This unlocks Rubicon Mode, which remains active for the rest of the game. Since this is the historical sequence of events, you'll need to follow a similar political path, such as securing a Hugenberg-led <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
, to have a better chance of unlocking it.

content.content: Why is the left path so hard?

content: Unlike Redux, this mod does not include any post–civil war content or additional <span style="color: #700000;">

or revolutionary paths. This is primarily due to time constraints—by the time of release, the mod had already been in development for over 9 months. As a result, the only truly "viable" path is the Reformist one, given the immense difficulty of building socialism within a bourgeois democracy—especially with figures like Hindenburg as president and the hostility of the bourgeois parties.

content.content: Why can't I form a coalition with a moderate Christian-Socialist DNVP or KVP?

The Christian Socials of the DNVP, and the party as a whole, remain a racist and antisemitic party, though they are more willing to operate within a democratic framework. The "Christian Socialism" of Weimar Germany is not the Christian Socialism of today; a better comparison would be Austria’s Christian Social Party. It is a nationalist, corporatist, and deeply religious right-wing ideology. The KVP is still a strongly anti-Marxist and nationalistic party at heart, and it would be against everything they stand for to coalition with the socialists.

options.title: Put a German draft convention on the table, and lead the conference.
Support a convention, but let London take the lead.
Leave Geneva to its committees.

content.content: The Treaty of Versailles took away Germany's tanks, its aircraft and its general staff, and in Part V it promised that this was "to render possible the initiation of a general limitation of the armaments of all nations". Fifteen years later, the general limitation has not begun. The Disarmament Conference that opened in Geneva in 1932 adjourned two years later without agreement, and every army in Europe has grown since.
The conference's bureau, carrying on the work of the late Arthur Henderson,

content: has written to every government that signed the Covenant: if one great power will put a draft convention on the table, he will call the conference back. The draft would limit every army to a fixed number of men and guns, with inspectors from Geneva. It would also bind Germany's own army, which the general staff hopes to see grow.

content.content: The government will decide whether to answer, but a convention would need the Reichstag, and our votes count.
