options.title: Declare armed neutrality and guard our own borders.
Stand with Poland and France, in a limited war of defense.
Stand with the Soviet Union.

content.content: Moscow refuses to come. The Soviet note calls the proposal "a maneuver to give the Polish landlords time". Two days later, the ultimatum expires and the Red Army crosses the Polish frontier at dawn on a front of four hundred kilometers. There is no more time for diplomacy. Germany must choose.

The frontier is opened. Camps go up outside Frankfurt an der Oder and Breslau, and then, as the camps fill, families are housed in requisitioned barracks across the Reich. They are Poles, Belarusians, Jews from the shtetls of Volhynia, and Baltic Germans who have lost their homes for the second time in a generation. The right complains about the cost. The refugees, many of them doctors and engineers, are soon earning their keep.

e2_europe_talks.federation.unavailableSubtitle: Europe does not yet trust Germany enough to share a parliament with it.

content: Germany answers the French proposal with one of its own

content.content: , after our deputies make their votes for the treaty conditional on it

content: program of 1925, a United States of Europe, with a common parliament elected by universal suffrage and a European executive answerable to it. The coal and steel pool would be only its first institution.

content.content: The British will not hear of it, and the Italians want time. But France and the Benelux countries agree to a constituent assembly at Strasbourg, and the coal and steel treaty is signed as its first act. A German, a Frenchman, a Dutchman and an Italian sit together on the platform at the opening session. Half the delegates are in tears.

e2_evian.quotas.subtitle: Nothing will change. Our own members will be ashamed.

content.content: The German government regrets that, with unemployment where it is, the Republic cannot do more than it already does. Its answer is no worse than anyone else's. The committee files it with the others.

e2_evian.title: The Évian Conference
e2_evian.subtitle: Thirty-two nations meet to discuss refugees, and agree on very little.

options.title: Open Germany to the refugees.
Propose a common scheme, with every country taking its share.
Keep the present quotas.

content.content: Since Hitler took power in Vienna, Austrian Jews have been beaten in the streets, thrown out of their jobs and made to scrub the pavements with toothbrushes while crowds watched. Tens of thousands want to leave, and Social Democrats and Catholics who fought the Nazis are leaving with them.

In Romania, the government has reviewed the citizenship of its Jews and stripped a third of them of it. In Poland, the government talks openly of mass Jewish emigration, and the universities have set aside separate benches for Jewish students.

content: In July, at the call of President Roosevelt, thirty-two countries sent delegates to the Hôtel Royal at Évian, on Lake Geneva, to decide what to do about the refugees.

The answer was nothing. The Americans would not change their quotas, and the British would not open Palestine. Australia's delegate explained that his country had no racial problem and did not wish to import one. Only the Dominican Republic offered to take more than a handful. The conference has left a committee behind it in London, and the committee has asked each government what it will do.

content.content: The decision belongs to the government, but our votes count, and so do the Jewish and Catholic voters who have written to us.

e2_france_fascist.correct.subtitle: Paris will have no excuse. The Left faction will be furious.

content.content: We say nothing about the new regime and keep our ambassador in Paris.
We say nothing about the new regime, and neither does the government, which keeps its ambassador in Paris.

content: The Foreign Ministry argues that the less reason Paris has to fear us, the less reason it has to attack us. The Left faction says that the French workers will not forget our silence.

options.title: Condemn the coup, and welcome the French exiles.
Seek an understanding with Britain.
Keep correct relations with Paris.

content.content: In February 1934 the right-wing leagues marched on the Chamber of Deputies, and the police held the bridge. This time the police stood aside. The Croix-de-Feu, the Action Française and the veterans' leagues crossed the Pont de la Concorde, the government resigned before midnight, and the President has asked Colonel de La Rocque to form a "government of national authority". The Chamber has been adjourned indefinitely.

content: Léon Blum and the leaders of the <span style="color: #F0001C;">

have fled to Brussels. The Communist deputies have been arrested. The new government has announced that France will "reconsider" its alliances in the east, and its first ambassador abroad has gone to Rome.

content.content: For fifteen years France has been the guarantor of the Versailles order, and our most suspicious neighbor. Now its government is the enemy of everything our party stands for, and it still has the largest army in western Europe. London is asking Berlin, very discreetly, what we intend to do.

e2_franco_soviet.protest.subtitle: The nationalists will approve. Paris and Moscow will not.

content: The Foreign Office protests that the pact is incompatible with Locarno and aimed at Germany. Paris replies that it is aimed at nobody who does not attack France. In Moscow,
calls the German note "the voice of the Ruhr barons".

e2_franco_soviet.title: The Franco-Soviet Pact
e2_franco_soviet.subtitle: Paris and Moscow sign a treaty of mutual assistance.

options.title: Join the pact as a third party, as Barthou intended.
Welcome the pact, but sign nothing.
Protest that the pact is aimed at Germany.

content.content: On the second of May, Pierre Laval and the Soviet ambassador signed a treaty of mutual assistance in Paris. Each power promises to help the other if it is attacked in Europe. Two weeks later, Czechoslovakia signed a treaty of its own with Moscow. The pact is what is left of Louis Barthou's plan for an "Eastern Locarno", in which Germany, the Soviet Union, Poland and the Baltic states would all have guaranteed each other's frontiers. Barthou was killed in Marseille last October, beside the King of Yugoslavia.

content: Paris and Moscow have said that the door is still open to Germany.
wants us through it at once.
calls the pact a victory for peace.
Warsaw sees a treaty that would let the Red Army cross Poland to help anybody, and has said that it will never allow it. The <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
says that France has brought Bolshevism to the Rhine.

content.content: The decision belongs to the government, but any treaty needs the Reichstag, and our votes count.

e2_gw_called.refuse.subtitle: Moscow will not ask again. The KPD may never forgive us.

content: Our Chancellor tells the ambassador that the German Republic will defend itself against anyone, and attack no one. The <span style="color: #700000;">
calls it "the second betrayal of 1914", and its ministers threaten to resign. In Paris and London, the news is received with relief, and with some surprise.

onArrival.$code: Q['e2_gw_call'] = 0;

options.title: Accept. The Red Army and the German army will march together.
Ask for time to prepare.
Refuse. The Republic will not start a war.

content: The Soviet ambassador came to the Chancellery with a document of twelve pages. The Soviet Union proposes a joint action, "in the spirit of proletarian internationalism", to liberate the workers and peasants of Poland and the Baltic states from their landlords and generals. The Red Army would cross the Bug, and the German army would cross the Corridor.

content.content: Since the Western powers cut off our trade, Moscow argues, the capitalist encirclement of both our countries is already a fact, and it will only grow tighter.

content: 's Politburo endorsed the proposal before we had read it. In the Reichstag, its deputies speak of "the last war of the old world".
The councils will do what the <span style="color: #700000;">
Paris and London have let it be known that a German army in Poland would mean war with both of them.

e2_hitler_austria.league.subtitle: The West will appreciate it. Tension will fall a little.

content.content: At our urging, the Foreign Minister brings

content: the coup to the League Council with the support of France, Britain and Czechoslovakia. Italy blocks any sanctions. However, the Council's report names the Austrian Legion and its German origins, and Hitler's regime begins its life as an outcast.

options.title: Open the border to Austria's refugees.
Reinforce the Bavarian frontier.
Take the matter to the League, together with Paris, London and Prague.

content.content: At noon on a weekday, a hundred and fifty men of the Austrian Legion in Bundesheer uniforms drove into the courtyard of the Chancellery on the Ballhausplatz. By evening they held the Chancellery and the radio station, and the Heimwehr, instead of fighting them, had joined them. The Chancellor is under arrest. The President has appointed Adolf Hitler, whose Austrian citizenship was quietly restored a year ago, as head of a "government of national rebirth".

The Heimwehr and the Austrian Nazis ran together as a "National Bloc", and they won. The President has appointed Adolf Hitler, whose Austrian citizenship was quietly restored a year ago, as Federal Chancellor. Within a week the Nationalrat has passed an enabling law, and the parties that voted against it have been dissolved.

Hitler's first speech as Chancellor was broadcast from the Heldenplatz. He spoke of "the German people of Austria and Bavaria", of the "Marxist Republic in Berlin", and of a Germany that would one day be reunited "under the right flag". Mussolini has sent his congratulations.
The first refugees are already at the Bavarian border: Jews from Vienna and Graz, socialists, trade unionists, and Catholic politicians who stood in the Heimwehr's way.

e2_hungary.stay_out.subtitle: Czechoslovakia will be weaker, and Italy's friends will be stronger.

content: Prague gives way. At a conference in Vienna,

content.content: with an Italian foreign minister in the chair,

content: Czechoslovakia hands southern Slovakia to Hungary, and in the spring Hungarian troops march into Ruthenia as well. The Czechoslovak army has lost its fortifications in the south and a good part of its morale. In Belgrade and Bucharest, governments start to wonder whose friendship is worth having.

e2_hungary.title: Budapest's Claims
e2_hungary.subtitle: Hungary wants back the lands it lost at Trianon.

options.title: Guarantee Czechoslovakia's southern border.
Propose arbitration under the League.
Let Budapest and Prague settle it between themselves.

content: The Treaty of Trianon left a million Magyars inside Czechoslovakia, most of them in a strip of farmland along the Danube in southern Slovakia, and Hungary has never accepted it. Regent Horthy's government now demands that strip back, and Ruthenia as well. Hungarian troops have been moved up to the border, and

content.content: Rome has promised Budapest its "full diplomatic support".
Rome has let it be known that it sympathizes with Budapest.
Czechoslovakia, which has already given up its German borderlands, is in no state to fight.
Prague's new federal constitution has not been tested yet, and the Slovak autonomists are listening to Budapest.
The army in Prague is ready to fight, but it would rather not fight alone.

content: President Beneš has asked Berlin what it intends to do.

content.content: The answer belongs to the government, but a guarantee would need the Reichstag's votes, and ours count.
The government expresses its condolences and its confidence in the Austrian authorities.
The government expresses its condolences and its confidence in the Austrian authorities, and we do not ask for more.

content: The Austrian Nazis' couriers keep crossing the Bavarian border at night.

e2_july_putsch.title: The July Putsch
e2_july_putsch.subtitle: Austrian Nazis storm the Chancellery in Vienna.

options.title: Stand by the Austrian government against the Nazis.
Demand that Hitler be handed over for trial in Germany.
It is an Austrian affair.

content.content: On the twenty-fifth of July, a hundred and fifty Austrian Nazis in borrowed army uniforms drove into the courtyard of the Federal Chancellery in Vienna. Chancellor Dollfuss was shot in his study, and left to bleed to death on a sofa while the putschists held his ministers at gunpoint. Another group seized the radio station and announced that the government had resigned. By the evening the army and the police had retaken both buildings, and the putsch was over.

On the twenty-fifth of July, a hundred and fifty Austrian Nazis in borrowed army uniforms tried to seize the Federal Chancellery and the radio station in Vienna and arrest the Social Democratic cabinet. The ministers had been warned an hour earlier. The Schutzbund and the Vienna police surrounded both buildings, and by the evening the putschists had surrendered.

content: In the Alpine provinces, local Nazi bands fought on for several days. In Rome, Mussolini sent four divisions to the Brenner Pass and let it be known that Austria's independence was an Italian interest.

content.content: In Linz, where he has lived since Germany deported him, Adolf Hitler has denied everything. The putschists' orders say otherwise.

content: The putschists took their orders from the leaders of the banned <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
, who have been organizing across the Austrian border since the ban.

content.content: Vienna wants to know where Berlin stands. The answer belongs to the government, but our votes and our press count.

e2_gw_declaration.mediation.subtitle: The war may end sooner, though not necessarily on good terms. The West will approve. The nationalists will call it defeatism.

content: The credits pass. On the same day,

content.content: at our insistence, the Foreign Minister asks

content: Sweden, Switzerland and the United States to offer their good offices. The nationalist press calls it "a white flag on the first day of the war". Our members, at least, know that we tried.

content.content: The Red Army has crossed the frontier.
Italian and Austrian troops are marching on Munich.
French troops have crossed the Rhine.

options.title: Vote the war credits, and call a political truce.
Vote the war credits for the defense of the Republic, and nothing more.
Vote the war credits, and ask the neutral powers to mediate at once.

content.content: At dawn, the Red Army crossed the Polish frontier on a front of five hundred kilometers, and Soviet aircraft bombed the railway yards at Königsberg and Allenstein. Moscow's note accuses Germany of "preparing, together with the Polish landlords, an attack on the land of the workers and peasants". Nobody in Berlin believes it, but that hardly matters now.
Our guarantee to Poland has fallen due, and we have been attacked as well.

In the night, Italian divisions crossed the Brenner, and together with the Austrian army they crossed the Bavarian frontier at Salzburg and Kufstein. Rome's note calls for a "free Bavaria" under the house of Wittelsbach, "delivered from Marxism".
From Vienna, Hitler has broadcast an appeal to "the German people of Bavaria" to rise against Berlin.
In the night, the French garrisons on the left bank marched out of their barracks, French troops crossed the Rhine bridges at Kehl and Mannheim,
In the night, French troops crossed the Rhine bridges at Kehl and Mannheim,
and French armored columns have entered the Palatinate. Paris speaks of "securing the Rhine against the Marxist danger", which is the language of 1923.
Two days later, the new regime in Paris declared war as well, and French troops are crossing the Rhine.
Two days later, Mussolini joined the French, and Italian divisions are marching through Austria toward Bavaria.
Warsaw has seen its chance. Polish troops have crossed into Upper Silesia and East Prussia, and we must fight on two fronts.
Warsaw has honored its word and declared war on our attackers.
Poland has mobilized, but it stays out of the war for now. We must keep divisions in the east to watch it.
Poland is fighting for its life on the Bug, and its army and ours now stand on the same side for the first time.
All over Germany, the men of the Volkswehr take their rifles out of the cupboard and report to their regional units.
The reserve classes are called up, and the trains are full of young men going to the front.
The Reichswehr has almost no trained reserve to call on, so veterans of the Great War and the Reichsbanner are volunteering by the thousand.

content: calls the war "an imperialist crusade against the Soviet Union" and tells its members to refuse service.
is split. Its leaders have called on their members to defend the Republic, and Moscow has called them traitors.
has called on its members to fight fascism with a rifle.

content.content: The Reichstag has been summoned to vote the war credits. In August 1914, our party voted for them, and within three years it had split over that vote. The whole party remembers that vote, and many of our older members remember making it. This war is not that war, but the question is the same: what are we fighting for?

e2_khalkhin_gol.tokyo.subtitle: Trade will go on. Moscow will be angry.

content.content: The Japanese orders for optical glass and chemicals are filled. Moscow protests that Zeiss lenses are being fitted to Japanese artillery. The Foreign Office replies that German firms sell lenses to anyone, which is true.

e2_league_reformed.reserve.subtitle: A safer Europe, and fewer promises.

content.content: Germany signs, with a reservation that the Reichstag must approve any sanctions against a neighbor. Britain makes the same reservation for the Dominions, and France for its colonies. The treaty is weaker than its authors hoped, but it is still stronger than the Covenant was.

e2_league_reformed.title: The League Reformed
e2_league_reformed.subtitle: Geneva wants to give the Covenant teeth.

options.title: Sign the treaty, with binding sanctions.
Go further, and offer German divisions to a League force.
Sign, but keep the right to decide on sanctions case by case.

content.content: For twenty years the League of Nations has been able to condemn an aggressor and do very little else. Article 16 of the Covenant allows sanctions, but every member decides for itself whether to apply them, and in Manchuria and Abyssinia most of them decided not to. Now, with Europe at peace and the Republic on good terms with London and Paris, the British and French governments have asked Germany to join them in rewriting it.

content: The draft treaty makes sanctions binding on every member once the Council has named an aggressor, by a majority and without a veto. It sets up a permanent staff in Geneva to plan them, and invites members to put forces at the Council's disposal. Our party has called for exactly this since 1919. The nationalist press calls it "Versailles with a bureaucracy".

content.content: The government will negotiate the treaty, but it needs the Reichstag's votes to ratify it, and ours count.

content: We make no public statement on the trials.

content.content: However, the Interior Ministry quietly stops returning anyone to the Soviet Union.
However, we quietly persuade the Interior Ministry to stop returning anyone to the Soviet Union.
Several thousand refugees settle in Berlin and Hamburg: engineers, doctors, translators and a great many embittered former communists. Many of them have stories to tell, and some begin writing books.
We say nothing. Without allies, Münzenberg's revolt stays a revolt of editors and intellectuals. Most of the party's members stay with the apparatus, and the apparatus stays with Moscow.

e2_munzenberg.title: Münzenberg Breaks with Moscow
e2_munzenberg.subtitle: The KPD's greatest propagandist has refused a summons to Moscow.

options.title: Offer Münzenberg's people an alliance with the SPD.
Keep him at arm's length. A communist is still a communist.
Let the Communists tear themselves apart without us.

content: 's newspapers, its film company and its illustrated weekly, and for fifteen years he was the most effective communist propagandist in Europe. Now he has been summoned to Moscow, and he has read the reports from the trials there carefully enough not to go.

content.content: He has another reason. Under Thälmann's red-brown course, Münzenberg's newspapers have been printing editorials about the "national liberation of the German people" next to his own exposés of the Nazi past of the party's new recruits, and he has had enough of both.
Even under the Conciliators, the party leadership will not defend him against the Comintern, and he has stopped expecting it to.
He announces his break in his own newspaper, and a good part of the party's intellectuals and trade unionists announce it with him.

e2_mosley.rearm.subtitle: A stronger army, paid for out of the social budget. The Left faction will be furious.

content: The Reichstag votes a special armaments credit, against the votes of the <span style="color: #700000;">
and part of our own Left faction. The money comes out of the housing program. The general staff, which has spent fifteen years asking for exactly this, is quietly delighted.

options.title: Look to Moscow.
Build a bloc with Warsaw and Prague.
Rearm, and trust in no one.

content.content: The National Government did not survive the winter. The Conservatives split over whether to stand by the new regime in Paris or against it, the pound fell, and the unemployed marched on London from the coalfields of Wales and Durham. When the King's ministers could not form a majority, a "Government of National Reconstruction" took office with Sir Oswald Mosley as Prime Minister, half the Conservative backbenchers behind him and the British Union of Fascists in the ministries.

content: Mosley says that Britain will mind its empire and leave Europe to the Europeans. His first act in foreign policy is a treaty of friendship with the new France.

content.content: His second is a visit to Rome.

content: Our ambassador in London reports that the Foreign Office no longer returns his calls. For the first time since 1918, the Republic has no friend among the great powers of the West.

content.content: The government will decide how to answer, but the Reichstag will have to pay for it, and our votes count.

e2_naval_talks.versailles.subtitle: +1 budget. The Left faction and Paris will be pleased. The nationalists will not.

content.content: Berlin thanks London for its offer and declines it: the Republic has no quarrel with any naval power, and better uses for its steel. The money set aside for the navy goes into the housing program. The admirals resign in a body, and the nationalist press prints their photographs with black borders.

e2_naval_talks.title: Naval Talks with Britain
e2_naval_talks.subtitle: London offers to revise the naval clauses of Versailles.

options.title: Accept the British ratio.
Refuse any limit, and build what we need.
Keep the Versailles limits, and spend the money on housing.

content: The Treaty of Versailles allows Germany six old battleships, six cruisers, a few destroyers and torpedo boats, no submarines and fifteen thousand sailors.

content.content: The army's limits have already gone, but the navy's are still on paper.

content: Now the British Admiralty, which would rather know what the German navy will look like than guess, has invited our naval staff to London. Its offer is simple: a German fleet of thirty-five percent of the Royal Navy's tonnage, with a German promise never to go beyond it.
France has not been consulted, and will be furious. The shipyards in Hamburg, Kiel and Bremen would be full for a decade.

content.content: Our own party remembers what the Panzerkreuzer cost us in 1928.
Our own party remembers what the Panzerkreuzer cost us in 1928. The decision belongs to the government, but the money for the ships must pass the Reichstag, and our votes count.
The Prussian Minister-President. The bourgeois parties dislike one man holding both offices.
Otto Braun is sworn in as Chancellor.

e2_pacific_war.mediate.unavailableSubtitle: Washington would not take our offer seriously.

content.content: At our urging, the German ambassador

content: in Geneva proposes a League conference on the Pacific. Tokyo refuses, and Washington is polite. Nothing comes of it, and nobody expected anything to. But the Republic has positioned itself as a voice for peace, and in a world sliding toward war that may yet matter.

e2_pacific_war.title: War in the Pacific
e2_pacific_war.subtitle: Japan strikes at America, and the world's attention turns east.
