options.title: Embargo Japan and sell to the Americans and the British.
Stay neutral and keep trading with everyone.
Offer Geneva's good offices for a ceasefire in Asia.

content.content: On the morning of the seventh of December, Japanese carrier aircraft struck the American fleet at anchor in Pearl Harbor. Within hours Japanese troops were landing in Malaya, the Philippines and Hong Kong. The United States and the British Empire are at war with Japan, and the war will be fought across half the globe.

content: For Europe, the consequences are immediate. The Royal Navy is sending its battleships to Singapore, and America's factories are turning to arms for its own forces. The Western powers' attention, and much of their strength, has gone to the far side of the world.

content.content: Every diplomat in Berlin is asking what Moscow will do in Europe while the West is busy in Asia.

content: Washington has asked Berlin to stop all trade with Japan and to sell America machine tools, ships and steel on credit. Tokyo, which has bought German optics and chemicals for twenty years, asks only that we stay neutral.
calls it a war between two imperialisms and wants nothing to do with either.

content.content: We refuse Baillet-Latour's terms. The Committee moves its Games to Helsinki at a few months' notice, and Berlin holds a Workers' Olympiad instead. Athletes come from the workers' sports clubs of thirty countries, and for the first time a Soviet team competes in the West.

The Games go ahead, but the opening ceremony includes a march-past by the Arbeiter-Turn- und Sportbund, and Soviet athletes are invited to compete as guests. The Committee protests, and the bourgeois parties are scandalized.

content: The stadium is full of red flags and union banners, and the singing goes on long after the last race. It is a wonderful week for the labor movement, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
is delighted. However, the Western governments take a dimmer view.

onArrival.$code:
Q['e2_pe_choice'] = "Schumacher";
Q['e2_pe_spd'] = 1;

e2_popular_front_fr.distance.subtitle: The Centre and the nationalists will be satisfied. Our own Left faction will not.

content.content: The letter is answered politely and late. Blum says nothing in public. The Left faction's paper prints his speech on the Matignon Agreements in full, under the headline "This Is What a Social Democrat Does".

e2_popular_front_fr.title: The Popular Front in Paris
e2_popular_front_fr.subtitle: Léon Blum forms a government of the left.

options.title: Answer Blum's letter with an offer of close friendship.
Keep relations correct and friendly.
Keep our distance from a government with Communist support.

content.content: The Popular Front of Socialists, Radicals and Communists has won the French elections, and on the fourth of June Léon Blum became the first Socialist to lead a French government. Three days later, after a wave of sit-down strikes that brought two million workers out, his ministers, the unions and the employers signed the Matignon Agreements: collective agreements, elected shop stewards and wage rises of up to fifteen percent. Laws for a forty-hour week and two weeks' paid holiday followed within the month.

content: Blum is an old friend of our party, and he opposed the occupation of the Ruhr in 1923. He has written to our chairman to propose a treaty of friendship, a trade agreement and regular meetings between the two governments.

content.content: The Center Party is nervous about a pact with a government that the French Communists support.

content: sees a United Front on both banks of the Rhine.
The French right hates him. In February, royalist thugs dragged him from his car in Paris and beat him in the street.

content.content: We are not in government, but the party can still offer the Socialists of Paris its friendship, and push the government to follow.

onArrival.$code: Q['e2_belgium'] = "none";

content.content: Berlin says nothing. In October the King announces that Belgium will return to neutrality, and the French General Staff starts to plan for a long frontier without an ally on its northern flank.

e2_rexists.title: Rex in Belgium
e2_rexists.subtitle: A young demagogue has shaken Belgian politics.

options.title: Welcome Belgian neutrality and offer to guarantee it.
Urge Brussels to stand by Paris, and against Rex.
Say nothing. It is Belgium's business.

content.content: In the Belgian elections in May, Léon Degrelle's Rex movement came from nowhere to win twenty-one seats. Degrelle is thirty years old, a Catholic publisher who campaigned with a broom against "the rotten parties" and their bankers, and his crowds look very like the ones that marched on the French Chamber two years ago. The Flemish nationalists doubled their seats as well. The Belgian Workers' Party of Vandervelde and Henri de Man is still the largest party in Brussels, but the old governing coalition is shaken.

content: Now the young King Leopold is talking of leaving the alliance with France and returning Belgium to the neutrality it had before 1914. Paris is alarmed: without Belgium, its frontier defenses end at the Ardennes.

content.content: Both Brussels and Paris have asked where Berlin stands.
Both Brussels and Paris have asked where Berlin stands. The answer belongs to the government, but our sister party in Brussels is asking us too.

e2_rhineland_zone.leave.subtitle: Paris and London will be reassured. The generals and the nationalists will not.

content.content: The Chancellor files the memorandum. The Rhineland stays demilitarized, and the Republic keeps the word it gave at Locarno. The general staff's planners draw their defensive line along the far side of the Ruhr, and complain to anyone who will listen.

e2_rhineland_zone.title: The Rhineland Zone
e2_rhineland_zone.subtitle: The generals want soldiers on the Rhine again.

options.title: Send the troops in, and tell the powers afterwards.
Ask the Locarno powers to revise the zone.
Leave the zone as it is.

content.content: The last French troops left Mainz in 1930, but the Rhineland is still not quite German soil. Under the Treaty of Versailles, and again under Locarno, the Republic may keep no soldiers and build no fortifications on the left bank of the Rhine or within fifty kilometers of its right bank. Cologne, Düsseldorf and Frankfurt are policed, but not defended.

content: The Chief of the Army Command has sent the Chancellery a memorandum.

content.content: Since the powers granted us equality of rights, he argues, the zone is the last mark of inequality left, and the army cannot plan a defense of the Ruhr from behind it.
The army is still held to a hundred thousand men, he writes, and cannot defend the Ruhr from behind a line it is forbidden to cross.

content: Three battalions could be in Cologne by morning, and the French, he believes, would do nothing.

content.content: The new regime in Paris has said that it would treat any German soldier on the left bank as an act of war.
The Quai d'Orsay has let it be known that it would much prefer to be asked.
The decision belongs to the government. We can support it or oppose it in the Reichstag, and our votes count.

e2_saar.europe.unavailableSubtitle: France does not trust us enough to share the Saar.

content.content: After hurried talks in Geneva, the League Council agrees to add a fourth option to the ballot: a European Saar, demilitarized, with its mines run by a joint Franco-German board and its people citizens of both states. To general surprise, it carries. The Saarlanders are tired of being fought over.

The nationalists call it a second Versailles, signed this time by Germans, and they are gaining support for it. Some of our own workers are unhappy too. However, Paris has taken the vote as proof that we mean what we say about Europe. The new mining board meets for the first time in Saarbrücken in March, with a French chairman and a German deputy.

onArrival.$code:
Q['e2_spain_partner'] = "trade";
Q['economic_growth'] = (Q['economic_growth'] || 0) + 0.1;

content.content: Germany and Spain sign a trade treaty: oranges, cork and Asturian iron ore for German machinery. Negrín's government is disappointed, and says so, but it signs.

e2_spain_partner.title: An Iberian Partner
e2_spain_partner.subtitle: The Spanish Republic has won its war, and it needs friends.

onArrival.$code:
// WW2_SCOPE.md §6, alternate history. A Republican victory alone makes France's fascist turn less likely.
if (!Q.e2_spain_partner_base) { Q.e2_spain_partner_base = 1; Q.e2_pf_mod = (Q.e2_pf_mod || 0) - 0.005; }

options.title: Lend Spain the money to rebuild.
Sponsor Spain for a permanent seat on the League Council.
Sign a trade treaty, and no more.

content: Madrid has held, and the Spanish Republic has won.

content.content: The generals accepted an armistice brokered in Geneva, and Franco has gone to Lisbon.
Republican troops took Burgos in the spring, and Franco has fled to Portugal.

content: The country is in ruins. Half a million Spaniards are dead or in exile, the railways are wrecked from Bilbao to Málaga, and the Republic owes money to everyone who sold it a rifle.

Prime Minister Negrín has written to Berlin with two requests: credits to rebuild Spain's railways and power stations, and German sponsorship for a permanent Spanish seat on the League Council. In Paris, the Popular Front parties are celebrating, and the Croix-de-Feu has lost its favorite argument, that democracy cannot defend itself.

content.content: The answer belongs to the government, but any credit must pass the Reichstag, and our votes count.

e2_spain.relief.subtitle: The Left faction will think it too little. Nobody else can object. (-1 resources)

content.content: The Republic signs the Non-Intervention Agreement, and keeps to it.
The government signs the Non-Intervention Agreement, and keeps to it.

content: However, the Workers' Welfare and the trade unions raise money in every factory for "Spain's children", and by the autumn there are German field hospitals behind the Madrid front, with German doctors in them. Food ships leave Hamburg for Valencia every fortnight, carrying flour, condensed milk and no rifles at all.

content.content: The Center Party's charities send nuns to Burgos. The Left faction says that milk will not stop Franco.

e2_stalin_health.west.subtitle: The West will trust us more. Moscow, when it recovers, will remember.

content.content: While Moscow is looking inward, the Republic signs the agreements it has been putting off for years: a defense consultation treaty with London and Paris, and a currency agreement with Washington. The Soviet chargé d'affaires calls it "taking advantage of a family bereavement". Nobody has told him that there has been one.

e2_stalin_health.title: The Kremlin Falls Silent
e2_stalin_health.subtitle: Stalin has not been seen in public for two months.

options.title: Take up the offer of talks.
Wait and see who wins in the Kremlin.
Use Moscow's weakness to bind the Republic closer to the West.

content.content: Stalin did not stand on the Lenin Mausoleum for the November parade. Since then he has not been photographed, has not received an ambassador, and has not signed a decree that anyone in Moscow will admit to having seen. Our embassy reports that he suffered a stroke at his dacha at Kuntsevo in the autumn, and that the doctors who treated him have not been seen either.

content: In the Politburo, Malenkov, Beria, Molotov and Zhdanov are watching each other. Nobody is giving orders, and so nobody is giving the orders that frighten Moscow's neighbors. The Red Army has cancelled its summer maneuvers, and Molotov's deputy has asked our ambassador, in a corridor, whether Berlin would be interested in talks on trade "and on other questions".

content.content: The answer belongs to the government, but it will want to know where the Reichstag stands, and our votes count.

Beneš is glad to be rid of them. Czech gendarmes raid the guesthouses at dawn, and forty-one fugitives are handed over at the Bad Schandau crossing. The trials in Leipzig run through the winter. Without its officers, the Volunteer Corps falls apart, and the Sudeten crisis with it.
Prague refuses. Beneš does not trust Berlin enough to do its police work, and he says so. The fugitives move a few valleys further from the border and carry on. The crisis smoulders on unresolved.

e2_stresa.denounce.subtitle: The nationalists will cheer. Every capital in Europe will take note.

content.content: The Chancellor tells the Reichstag that Germany will not be encircled by a new Entente.
The Chancellor tells the Reichstag that Germany will not be encircled by a new Entente, and our deputies join the applause.

content: The nationalist benches stand to cheer him. In Paris and London, the speech is read as proof that the Stresa Front was needed after all.

e2_stresa.title: The Stresa Conference
e2_stresa.subtitle: Britain, France and Italy meet on Lake Maggiore.

options.title: Sign the Stresa declaration as a fourth power.
Stay out, politely.
Denounce the Stresa Front as an alliance against Germany.

content: In April, the Prime Ministers of Britain, France and Italy met in the Borromean Palace at Stresa, on Lake Maggiore. Their communiqué promised to oppose "by all practicable means" any unilateral repudiation of treaties, and to stand by the Locarno guarantees and the independence of Austria.

content.content: Everyone in Europe understood which treaty they had in mind, and which country had already revised it.
Germany has kept to the Versailles limits, and the powers say that their declaration is aimed at nobody in particular.

content: Now Paris has proposed that Germany sign the declaration as well, as a fourth guarantor of Locarno and of Austria.
The Center Party and the liberals like the idea. The
calls it a second Versailles, signed this time of our own free will.

content.content: The Left faction asks why a Social Democratic Germany should sign a guarantee with Mussolini.
The decision belongs to the government, but any treaty needs the Reichstag, and our votes count.

e2_trotsky_berlin.refuse.subtitle: Moscow will be grateful. The Left faction will not.

content: refuses the request, citing "the security of the Reich". Trotsky sails from Oslo for Mexico on an oil tanker. The Left faction's paper prints his letter on its front page, under the headline "The Republic Was Afraid".

e2_war_cabinet.emergency.subtitle: Decisions will be quicker. The Reichstag will be told about them afterwards.

content.content: The Reichstag passes a War Powers Act by a wide majority, valid for six months at a time.
The President signs the first emergency decree the same evening.

content: A cabinet of five ministers now meets every morning with the Chief of the Army Command, and decisions that used to take weeks take an hour. The Reichstag's committees still meet, and they are told what has already been decided.

e2_war_allies.us.unavailableSubtitle: Washington will not lend to a government it does not trust.
e2_war_allies.us.subtitle: +1 budget, and American credits will pay for the war.

content.content: After a month of debate, Congress passes an act to lend arms to "any country whose defense the President deems vital to the defense of the United States". The first ships arrive at Bremen in the spring. The war will be paid for later, in dollars, and the Republic will owe Washington a great deal.

e2_war_battle.offensive.subtitle: We could win the war outright, or lose it much faster.

content: The order goes out the same night. At dawn, the guns open up along the whole front, and the infantry goes forward behind them.

content.content: By the evening, the first villages have been taken.
By the evening, the attack has stalled in front of the enemy's wire, and the field hospitals are full.

options.title: Dig in on a shorter line, and let the enemy wear himself out.
Hold the line and build up the reserves.
Go over to the offensive at once.

content.content: The Red Army's tank columns reached the Vistula below Warsaw and were stopped there. German divisions from East Prussia struck their flank on the Narew, and the Polish army held the river crossings. For now, Warsaw is safe.
The Red Army has reached the Bug and the Narew, and there the front has stopped. Every crossing has changed hands twice. Neither side has the strength to break through, yet.

The Red Army broke the Polish line on the Bug in the first week, and its armored columns are on the Vistula. Our divisions from East Prussia were thrown back across the Narew. In Warsaw, the government is packing its files.

The Italian and Austrian offensive reached Rosenheim and was stopped there. Our divisions held the line of the Inn, and the mountain troops have taken back the passes above Berchtesgaden. In Munich, the church bells were rung.
The front runs through the Chiemgau and along the Inn. Every hill has changed hands twice, and the Alpine winter will soon close the passes to both sides.
Italian Alpini hold the passes, and the Austrian army has taken Rosenheim. Munich is sixty kilometers from the front, and the trains going north are full of families.
The French offensive has stalled in the Black Forest and on the hills of the Palatinate. Our counter-attack has retaken Kaiserslautern, and the French bridgehead at Kehl is under our guns.
The front runs along the Rhine and across the Palatinate. The French hold their bridgeheads at Kehl and Mannheim, and we hold the hills. Neither side can move.
French armored divisions have crossed the Palatinate and taken Kaiserslautern. Their bridgeheads at Kehl and Mannheim are growing, and Karlsruhe is under fire.

Our divisions crossed the Corridor in ten days and joined hands with the East Prussian army at Graudenz. Danzig is surrounded, and the Red Army is approaching Warsaw from the east. In the west, the French have attacked in the Saar and made little headway.
The Polish army is fighting for every town in the Corridor. In the Saar, the French have taken a little ground and lost it again.
The Polish army has held the Corridor, and French divisions have broken into the Saar and the Palatinate. The Red Army is still a long way from Warsaw, and Moscow says that the plan has not changed.
On the Rhine, the French have crossed at Kehl, and we are fighting on two fronts.
In the south, the Italian army is in the Tyrol, and we are fighting on two fronts.
In the east, the Polish army is in Upper Silesia.
The Volkswehr's regional units fight best close to home.
The reserve divisions are arriving at the front by the trainload.
The Reichswehr fights well, but it is small, and the volunteers are still learning to march.

The decision belongs to the cabinet and the general staff. However, the Chancellor needs our votes for every new war credit, and our deputies sit on the Reichstag's war committee, so our view will count.
The Chief of the Army Command has come to the Chancellery for a decision. How should the army fight the war?

The conference opens in Geneva in the autumn. It produces a frontier commission, a League refugee office and a treaty limiting land armies in central Europe. It is not much, but it is more than the League has done in a decade.

e2_war_crisis.talks.subtitle: The strike will end. Peace talks will open within two months.

onArrival.$code:
Q.e2_war_talks_at = Math.min(Q.e2_war_talks_at || 18, Q.e2_war_months + 2);
Q.e2_war_home += 10; Q.left_dissent -= 8; Q.nationalism += 2; Q.dnvp_relation -= 5;

content.content: The Chancellor meets the strike committee and promises that the government will open peace talks through the neutral powers within two months. The strikers go back to work the next morning. The nationalist press calls it a second November, and the general staff calls it worse.

e2_war_home_front.profits.subtitle: +1 budget. The employers will not like it.

content.content: A war profits tax takes everything a company earns above its prewar average, and trade unionists sit beside the industrialists on the supply boards that hand out contracts and raw materials. The employers' associations say it is socialism by the back door. The workers who are earning the profits seem to think it is only fair.

e2_winter_war.mediate.unavailableSubtitle: Neither side would accept us as a mediator.

content.content: German and Swedish diplomats carry messages between Helsinki and Moscow through January. The peace signed in February costs Finland the Isthmus and saves it Viipuri and Hanko. Thousands of young men on both sides will live because the war ended a month early. Neither side thanks us much, but neither holds it against us.

e2_war_talks.fight_on.unavailableSubtitle: The country will not fight on.
e2_war_talks.fight_on.subtitle: The war will go on for at least nine more months. The home front will suffer.

onArrival.$code:
Q.e2_war_talks_at = Q.e2_war_months + 9;
Q.e2_war_home -= 5; Q.nationalism += 1; Q.left_dissent += 4;

content: The Chancellor tells the Swedish minister that the Republic will negotiate when its terms can be met, and not before.

content.content: The general staff promises a victory by the next spring.
The general staff promises that the next offensive will turn the war around. Nobody in the cabinet asks what happens if it does not.

e2_war_talks.title: Peace Talks
e2_war_talks.subtitle: The neutral powers offer their good offices.

options.title: Accept an armistice on the present front.
Ask the neutral powers to mediate a settlement.
Break off the talks and fight on.

content: The Swedish minister in Berlin has brought a message from
: the other side is ready to talk.

content.content: Our armies stand on enemy soil, and the enemy knows it. Any armistice now would be signed on our terms.
The front has hardly moved in months. An armistice now would leave it where it is.
The front is falling back, and the enemy knows it. An armistice now would cost us dearly.
The answer belongs to the government, but the Chancellor will not give it without consulting the Reichstag's party leaders, and our votes count.
The home front is holding, though everyone is tired of the war.
The home front is weary. There are queues outside every bakery, and the casualty lists take up two pages of every newspaper.
The home front is close to breaking. There have been hunger riots in Hamburg and Chemnitz, and the soldiers on leave are not going back.
The country will not fight another year.

content: Hungary, Romania, Yugoslavia and Bulgaria sign clearing agreements. German machines are paid for in wheat, bauxite and oil, and no gold changes hands. The trade keeps the factories running, but it also ties the Danube basin's economies to ours, and Paris and Prague notice. In the Foreign Office, a few old men are heard using the word

content.content: The motion fails. The political police get a larger budget and a new department at the Alexanderplatz headquarters, and the raids on "choirs" in Hanover and Breslau make the newsreels.
The motion fails without our votes, and the government lets the matter drop.

content: The Left and Labor factions are relieved, but the Center and the liberals are disappointed in us.

content.content: However, every banned society seems to be replaced by two new ones. The young men who join them are too young to have fought in the civil war. To them, the bans only prove what their fathers have always said: that we are afraid of them.

e2c_bans.title: The Question of the Bans
e2c_bans.subtitle: Should the defeated get their parties back?

title: Lift all the bans, even the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
's. Let them be beaten at the ballot box!
Legalize the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
and the nationalist parties, but keep the
and
outlawed.

options.title: Why should we give our enemies anything? Keep the bans.

content: have been outlawed since the civil war. The bans have kept the old uniforms off the streets. However, the men who wore them have not gone away. The political police count some four hundred "veterans' choirs", "rifle clubs" and "hiking societies" across the Reich, meeting in back rooms and passing around mimeographed newsletters. Nobody knows exactly what they are planning.

The Center and the liberals have tabled a motion to lift the bans, as long as the members of the legalized organizations swear to uphold the constitution. They argue that a movement in the Reichstag can be argued with, while a movement in the cellars can only be hunted. The
veterans in our party see the motion as a betrayal of the comrades who died fighting these men.

content.content: Many of us also remember that the Bredow conspiracy started in a "veterans' choir".

e2c_bredow_coup.bargain.subtitle: Requires a seat in the cabinet. The Left and Labor factions will be outraged.
e2c_bredow_coup.bargain.unavailableSubtitle: Only the government can offer to change the Reich Defense Law, and we are in opposition.

content.content: A retired colonel who served with Bredow in the Abwehr carries our message to Wannsee, and the answer comes back within two days. The conspirators will stand down if the Reich Defense Law is amended. The army is to keep sole control of promotions and of its own courts, the purge commission is to be dissolved, and no officer is to be prosecuted for "political opinions" held before today.
We accept. On the ninth, the Reichstag sits and nothing happens, and Bredow retires to Silesia to write his memoirs.

content: However, every officer in Germany now knows that we can be blackmailed. When the terms leak, the Left and Labor factions are outraged, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
accuses us of selling out to the generals.

content.content: After four months of debate, the convention produces a list of amendments. Article 48 is struck out, the President's power to dissolve the Reichstag is restricted, and the Reichswehr's oath is rewritten. Everything else stays as it was.
The Center and the liberals are pleased. Heller goes back to his lectures in Frankfurt disappointed, and so does the Left faction of our party.

e2c_constitution.title: The Paulskirche Convention
e2c_constitution.subtitle: A constitution for a Second Republic?

options.title: Heller's draft: a social Republic, with no Article 48!
Heller's draft, plus a Chamber of Labor elected by the works councils.
Surely it is enough to revise the old constitution and strike out Article 48?

content.content: With the civil war won, we have a chance to repair the flaws that nearly destroyed the Republic. The Weimar constitution was written in a theater in a provincial town, by men who feared the Berlin mob. It let the President rule by decree, left the army as a state within the state, and allowed any coalition of enemies to bring down a government without agreeing on a replacement. All of these were used against us in the last few years.

The government has called a constitutional convention to the Paulskirche in Frankfurt, where Germany's first parliament met in 1848. Hermann Heller has brought a draft for a "social Rechtsstaat". It abolishes Article 48, makes the army answerable to the Reichstag, requires a constructive vote of no confidence, and writes the rights to work, housing and co-determination into the basic rights.

content: and the Left faction of our party want a second chamber of workers' councils alongside the Reichstag. The Center and the liberals will accept only a revision of the old text. Unfortunately, any new constitution needs a two-thirds majority.

content.content: The generals have let it be known that they consider the bargain we made in the Bredow affair to be part of the constitution, whatever the convention decides.

e2c_new_right.ban.subtitle: The Left faction will approve, but the Center and the liberals will not.
e2c_new_right.ban.unavailableSubtitle: Only the Reich government can ban an organization, and we are in opposition.

content.content: The presses at the Reichsdruckerei run day and night. Wages go up, the scaffolding goes up, and the shelled tenements of Wedding are rebuilt within a year.

Unfortunately, prices go up too. Clerks, shopkeepers and widows on fixed incomes watch their savings melt away for the second time in their lives, and many of them are starting to say that the Republic has betrayed them twice.

e2c_rentenmark.title: A Second Rentenmark
e2c_rentenmark.subtitle: Is the Mark going the way of 1923?

options.title: The Reichsbank's plan: a hard currency and a balanced budget.
A new Rentenmark, backed by a capital levy on the great fortunes!
Keep printing. We'll rebuild first and stabilize later.

content.content: Inflation is out of control. A loaf of bread costs four times what it did before the fighting. Pensioners queue at the post office on the first of the month and hurry to the grocer before the afternoon rate comes in, and in Hamburg the dockers are demanding their wages twice a week. Older people say they have seen all this before, in 1923.

content: The war was paid for with paper money

has brought the cabinet a plan for a new currency: a second Rentenmark, backed by a mortgage on land and industry, like the one that ended the great inflation. However, a new currency is only worth what the government behind it is willing to give up. The Reichsbank wants a balanced budget and a freeze on public works.

content.content: Our finance experts, led by Rudolf Hilferding, propose paying for the new currency with a one-time levy on large fortunes and estates. The union federation wants us to keep the presses running until the rebuilding is finished.

e2c_outlaw.none.subtitle: The Center and the liberals will approve. The Left and Labor factions will be furious.

content.content: We ban nothing. We will defeat our enemies the way we promised to: in the open, under the law. The Center and the liberals applaud us.

content: However, in the working-class districts, men who fought in the civil war watch the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
veterans walk free. The Left and Labor factions are furious, and the
says we have learned nothing since 1918.

e2c_outlaw.title: Outlawing the Far Right
e2c_outlaw.subtitle: We have won. What should we do with the losers' parties?

options.title: Ban nothing. Can't we beat them again at the ballot box?

content: have been beaten in the field.
On paper they still exist, and so does the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
Both were outlawed before the war, but the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
was outlawed before the war, but the
was outlawed before the war, but the
Under the Republikschutzgesetz, the cabinet can dissolve

and the unions want it done tomorrow. However, the Center and the liberals are uneasy—they fought for the constitution, not for a republic that bans the parties it dislikes. The far right's voters have not disappeared, either. They are sitting at home, defeated, waiting to see what we will do with our victory.

content.content: Every coal and steel enterprise with more than a thousand employees must give half the seats on its supervisory board to representatives elected by the workforce. The owners keep their property, and the chairman keeps the deciding vote.
It is a real reform, and the Center is pleased with it. However, the miners who spent the war defending their pits with rifles had expected more, and the Left faction is unhappy with us.

Two hundred ringleaders go before the court. The rest sign the oath, collect their discharge papers and go home to the farms and shops their wives kept running. Many of them are sullen and some are ashamed, but very few want to fight again. The Center and the liberals welcome our decision.

content: is furious, and so is the Left faction. At a veterans' rally in Magdeburg, a speaker asks whether his comrades died so that their killers could be home for Christmas, and he is cheered for ten minutes. The
calls the amnesty "the second betrayal of 1918".

e2c_tribunals.title: Judgment on the Putschists
e2c_tribunals.subtitle: The prisons are full. What will we do with the men inside?

options.title: Revive the State Court. Every defendant gets a public trial.
Field courts and swift justice! We can't afford mercy.
Amnesty for the rank and file, and trials for the ringleaders.

content: Moabit prison holds more than three thousand men who took up arms against the Republic: <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

district leaders, and the officers of the regiments that marched on Berlin. The camps at Döberitz and Zossen hold tens of thousands more. Every morning their families gather outside the gates with parcels of bread and sausage. Across the street stand the widows of the

The Reich Ministry of Justice has drawn up three proposals. Gustav Radbruch wants to revive the State Court for the Protection of the Republic and try the ringleaders in open court, so that every act of treason goes on the record. The <span style="color: #c00000;">

want field courts, which would be quick and leave no room for clever lawyers. The Center's jurists and some of our own moderates propose an amnesty for the rank and file in exchange for an oath to the constitution, with trials only for those who gave the orders.

content.content: Whatever we decide, a whole generation of defeated men will be watching. What should we do?

e2c_spd_split.divorce.subtitle: Requires a share of power to divide.
e2c_spd_split.divorce.unavailableSubtitle: There are no ministries to share. Without government posts, neither faction has a reason to sign a pact.

content: Willi Eichler's commission spends the summer dividing the party's assets as if it were settling a divorce. The <span style="color: #f0456a;">
and the Hamburg party school, and the <span style="color: #9B0000;">
and the youth movement. The two parties agree not to run against each other's incumbents, and to keep governing together after the election.

content.content: The bourgeois press finds the whole thing hilarious. However, the cabinet stays in office.

e2d_east_settlement.neutrality.subtitle: Requires leverage in Moscow.
e2d_east_settlement.neutrality.unavailableSubtitle: Warsaw does not believe we have any influence in Moscow worth paying for.

content.content: The bargain is cynical, and both sides know it. Germany promises never to join an alliance directed against Poland, and to let no foreign army cross its territory. In return, Poland, freed from the fear of a war on two fronts, withdraws from East Prussia. Upper Silesia, with its mines and the Polish majority in its eastern districts, stays Polish under the treaty.
The people of Königsberg welcome the returning German police with flowers. However, diplomats in Paris and London have begun to describe Germany as "a neutral of uncertain sympathies".

e2d_black_front.steal.subtitle: (-2 budget) The Left faction will grumble.

content.content: Only the Reich government can launch such a program.
The treasury cannot afford a program on that scale.

The National Reconstruction Service employs two hundred thousand men, half of them veterans and half refugees, to drain the Oderbruch marshes and rebuild the railways up to the Lippe line. It pays union wages, and its badges are black, red and gold. However, our speeches about it use the word "nation" more often than our members are used to, and the Left faction is uneasy.

content: 's best organizers end up as foremen in the Service. Strasser denounces them as traitors, but fewer and fewer people come to hear him.

content.content: France receives a thirty-year lease on the Saar coal mines
France receives our formal renunciation of any claim to the Saar coal mines
France receives sole control of the joint Saar mining board for thirty years

content: , along with a final payment of reparations in gold that empties the Reichsbank's vaults. The French soldiers leave by Christmas.
The Rhinelanders are free. However, the nationalists call the price "the Saar Ransom", and the
's posters show Marianne counting German coins on top of a slag heap.

e2d_march_on_berlin.bargain.subtitle: Requires a seat in the cabinet. The Left and Labor factions will be furious.
e2d_march_on_berlin.bargain.unavailableSubtitle: We are in opposition. The cabinet's seats are not ours to offer.

content: Strasser's delegates arrive at the Wilhelmstraße in field gray and are given coffee. By dawn there is an agreement: the <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">
will receive the Ministries of Reconstruction and Refugees and the new office of Reich Commissioner for the Lost Territories. In return, the columns will turn back at Bernau.

Strasser is not quite a minister, but he has his office on the Wilhelmplatz and his own guard at the door. We have avoided a battle by letting our gravediggers into the cabinet. The Left and Labor factions are furious, the <span style="color: #700000;">
denounces us, and the governments in London and Paris have taken note.
The Reconstruction Loan is advertised on every billboard:
Workers buy bonds out of their wages, and the unions put their strike funds into it. Unfortunately, it raises only a quarter of what the Americans had offered.

content.content: At least the Third Positionists cannot call us the lackeys of Wall Street. Rebuilding will be slow, and it will be paid for in paper money.

e2d_morgenthau.title: The Morgenthau Plan
e2d_morgenthau.subtitle: Washington, London and Paris offer to pay for Germany's reconstruction.

options.title: Accept the full plan, defensive pact and all!
Accept the reconstruction fund, but not the pact.
Germany will rebuild with German bonds! Refuse it.

content.content: The United States is offering to pay for our reconstruction. Henry Morgenthau, the American Treasury Secretary, has drawn up a plan for Germany, and the British and French have agreed to it. A European Reconstruction Fund run by the League would spend eight hundred million dollars over five years on bridges, railways, housing and power stations in our territory, and the remaining reparations would be canceled. "A starving Germany is a danger to every democracy," Morgenthau told the Senate. "A rebuilt one is a bulwark."

content: However, there are conditions. Germany must join a defensive pact with France and Britain, accept Western advisers in the Reich Finance Ministry, and keep the Rhineland demilitarized. In return, Paris will commit to a timetable for withdrawing its "peacekeepers" once the Ruhr question is settled.

content.content: The Western governments remember that they stood by us during the war, and they are offering the full package.
The Western governments did not help us during the war, and they are still not sure we are worth the money.

content: and the nationalists both denounce the plan as a new Versailles. However, our economists see no other way to rebuild the country quickly. What should we do?

content.content: The Geneva protocol fixes a demarcation line "without prejudice to a final settlement". German schools reopen in Allenstein, and Upper Silesian coal is to be traded for Pomeranian grain. Sealed trains run again between Berlin and Königsberg, through the Polish zone.

It is a sensible agreement. Unfortunately, the refugee associations call it "the Treaty of Shame", the nationalists are outraged, and a former Freikorps officer fires two shots at our delegate on the steps of the Reichstag.

The provinces do what they can, which is very little. In Stettin the refugees riot over the bread ration, and in Frankfurt an der Oder they occupy the town hall. The Heimatbund men no longer have to explain whose fault it is. The refugees can see for themselves that Berlin has abandoned them.

e2d_refugees.title: The Treks from the East
e2d_refugees.subtitle: A million people have lost their homes.

options.title: Settle them on the land. Break up the bankrupt Junker estates of Pomerania and Mecklenburg.
Build proper camps, with relief committees run by the refugees themselves.
Berlin cannot pay. The towns and provinces must manage.

content.content: They come in handcarts and farm wagons and in cattle trucks with the doors nailed shut against the cold. There are farmers from Masuria, miners from the Upper Silesian pits now under Polish administration, and shopkeepers and clerks from Essen and Bochum who did not want to live under the Central Council. The Red Cross counts nine hundred thousand refugees in the Republic's territory and expects more.

content: They sleep in gymnasiums in Stettin, in disused barracks in Frankfurt an der Oder and in tents on the Tempelhof field. The cities that take them in were already short of food, coal and work. Local officials beg Berlin for money, and in the camps, men with
armbands are already handing out leaflets that explain whose fault all this is.

e2d_ruhr_endgame.offensive.subtitle: Requires a loyal army.
e2d_ruhr_endgame.offensive.unavailableSubtitle: The Reichswehr is not reliable enough to send into the Ruhr.

content.content: It takes six weeks. The Red Army is too weak for a battle of maneuver, so it fights in cellars and pit galleries. The Reichswehr floods the deepest mines rather than go down into them after the fighters. When it is over the Ruhr is quiet, and much of it is under water. It will be years before the pits of Herne and Castrop produce coal again.

The delegates meet in a railway carriage on a siding outside Haltern, where neither side has jurisdiction. The ceasefire they sign is only four paragraphs long. Prisoners are exchanged, coal trains run north under Red Cross supervision, and both sides agree to "further discussions on the future status of the Rhenish-Westphalian industrial region".
The nationalist press calls it a treaty with Bolshevik bandits, and the generals call it worse. The coal is moving, though, and that winter Berlin is warmer than anyone had expected.

e2d_ruhr_question.title: The Lippe Line
e2d_ruhr_question.subtitle: The Ruhr Red Army holds the industrial heart of Germany.

options.title: Order the offensive. Germany has one army, and it answers to Berlin.
Blockade the Ruhr: no food trains, no grain from the east, until the council negotiates.
Open talks through the KPD and the miners' union. A ceasefire first, then terms.

content: The front in the west runs along the river Lippe, past slag heaps and flooded mine shafts. To the south lies the territory of the Ruhr Red Army: Essen, Bochum, Dortmund and Duisburg, a million and a half people ruled by a Central Council of miners' delegates in the old Essen town hall. Its fighters wear red armbands over their pit clothes. They took their rifles from the arsenals of the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
in the first weeks of the war, and they have no intention of giving them up to Berlin.

The Central Council says it defended the Ruhr against fascism when the Republic could not. That is true, and it is also why Berlin cannot ignore it. Every ton of coal that Germany burns this winter will either be mined behind the Lippe line or imported at prices we cannot afford. The French in the Rhineland cite the "red enclave" as their reason for staying. The
in Berlin claims it has no control over the Essen council, and no one believes it.

content.content: The Reichswehr says it could take Essen by spring. The miners' union says there would be nothing left to take.

e2d_ruhr_settlement.offensive.subtitle: Requires a loyal army, and a weakened enemy.

content.content: The Reichswehr is not reliable enough.
The Red Army is still too strong to defeat in one campaign.

The offensive starts in March. By May the Reichswehr has reached the Essen town hall, and the Central Council's last broadcast ends in mid-sentence. The Ruhr is part of the Republic again, as it was in 1920, and as in 1920 it is held by an army that has just been shooting at its people.

Hundreds of fighters go into the Westphalian forests or over the Dutch border. In Bottrop the miners bury their dead under red flags, and the Reichswehr lets them, which is the only sign of mercy in the whole campaign.

e2k_coronation.price.unavailableSubtitle: We are not strong enough to bargain.
e2k_coronation.price.subtitle: If it works, the monarchy will become much more parliamentary. If it fails, we will be weaker.

content: We let it be known that the <span style="color: #c00000;">
a constitutional monarch, and no other kind.
The new Emperor wants the labor movement's support for his reign, and the

backs our demand. The coronation edict promises a written constitution in which the Chancellor needs the confidence of the Reichstag. It is only a promise, not yet a law, but it carries the King's own signature. Our Left faction is still unhappy that we are dealing with the crown at all.

content.content: Unfortunately, the court refuses to bargain with socialists. The coronation goes ahead without us, and the government spends the next month explaining that our absence makes no difference. Unrest is growing in the working-class districts.

onArrival.$code: Q['president'] = "Wilhelm III";

content.content: Swear the oath, and claim the monarchy for the constitution.
Declare our allegiance, and claim the monarchy for the constitution.

options.title: Stay away. We are republicans!

content.content: Name our price: we'll swear the oath for a written constitution with responsible ministers.
Name our price: we'll declare our allegiance for a written constitution with responsible ministers.

The former Crown Prince has been proclaimed German Emperor and King of Prussia as Wilhelm III, with the old Kaiser's blessing sent from exile at Doorn. The coronation will be held in the Berlin cathedral.
Every deputy of the Reichstag has been invited, and every deputy must swear a new oath of allegiance. Our deputies will have to decide whether to swear it.

Since our election boycott, we have no deputies in the Reichstag. However, the party executive and the chairmen of the free trade unions have been invited, and the government expects the labor movement to declare its allegiance to the new monarch.

e2k_border.control.unavailableSubtitle: The Reichstag is too weak to make such demands.
e2k_border.control.subtitle: The army will hate it, but it would be a constitutional revolution.

content.content: We offer our votes on one condition: the army's budget, its appointments and its deployments must answer to a minister responsible to the Reichstag. The general staff refuses, the Center and the liberals back us, and the government chooses parliamentary control over losing the credits. The border is quieter within the year.

e2k_border.title: War Credits
e2k_border.subtitle: The government wants money for the eastern border.

content.content: Vote yes. We cannot be called traitors in wartime.
Declare our support. We cannot be called traitors in wartime.

options.title: Offer our votes for parliamentary control of the army.

content.content: After a year of shooting incidents along the Polish border, the government has asked the Reichstag for extraordinary credits to "secure the eastern frontier". Nobody believes the money is for defense. The general staff has maps of Posen and the Corridor on its walls, and the Kaiser's speeches are full of the lands his family once ruled.

content: remembers the fourth of August 1914, when the <span style="color: #c00000;">
voted for the Kaiser's war credits and split the workers' movement for a generation.

content.content: Since our election boycott we have no seats in the Reichstag, and the credits will pass whatever we do. However, the government wants the labor movement behind it, and it is waiting to hear what we say.

e2k_franchise.accept.subtitle: We keep our organization intact. Our members will ask what it is for.

content.content: The bill passes with our votes against it and nothing more.
The bill passes without a single Social Democratic vote against it, because we have no deputies left to cast one.

content: In the next Prussian election, the <span style="color: #c00000;">
wins thirty-eight percent of the vote and eleven percent of the seats.

e2k_franchise.title: The Three-Class Franchise
e2k_franchise.subtitle: The government wants Prussia's old electoral law back.

options.title: Call a general strike.

content.content: Fight it in the Reichstag and the courts.

options.title: Accept it, and fight for the votes we have left.

content.content: The Prussian government has introduced a bill to restore the electoral law of the old kingdom. Voters would again be divided into three classes by the taxes they pay, each class electing a third of the Landtag. In Berlin, a factory owner's vote would count for as much as those of hundreds of his workers.
The old Kaiser promised in 1917 to abolish this law. His son's government means to bring it back.

content: does not trust us enough to share a platform.

e2k_election.pact.subtitle: A real chance at reform, but our Left faction will call it a betrayal.

content: We stand down in Catholic districts, the
stands down in ours, and both parties campaign on one demand: whatever crown Germany gets, its ministers must answer to the Reichstag. The monitors cannot stop two of the largest parties at once.

content.content: The government keeps its majority, but only just, and the demand for responsible ministers is now in the newspapers every day. However, our Left faction calls the pact a betrayal of the working class.

e2k_election.title: The Monitored Election
e2k_election.subtitle: The government has promised free elections—under supervision...

options.title: We'll stand in every constituency, and make them steal it in public!
We won't take part in a rigged election. Boycott it!

content: Make an electoral pact with the
, for a constitution with responsible ministers.

A new Reichstag is to be elected in the spring, under the watch of "electoral monitors" appointed by the Interior Ministry. Our candidates will need permits to hold meetings, our posters will need approval, and in the countryside the monitors are <span style="color: #3E88B3;">

content.content: The result has been arranged in advance. The only open question is how many seats we will be allowed to keep. What should we do?

onArrival.$code:
Q['e2k_purge'] = "silent";
Q['e2k_unrest'] = (Q['e2k_unrest'] || 0) + 3;

content.content: We let the government do its work without our votes or our objections. The emergency decree stays on the books, and nobody is quite sure any more which emergency it was for.

e2k_purge.title: The Night of the Stahlhelm
e2k_purge.subtitle: The SA has risen against its old allies, and lost.

options.title: Support the crackdown. The Nazis are the greater danger.
Demand that every prisoner be tried in open court.
Say nothing, and let them fight among themselves.

content: expected a share of power for helping to bring down the Republic. When it became clear that Hergt and Seldte meant to share nothing, the brownshirts tried to take it. Reichswehr units and Stahlhelm auxiliaries crushed the rising in three days. Now the prisons are full of Nazis, and the government has suspended habeas corpus "for the duration of the emergency".

content.content: The question in our parliamentary group is simple, and nobody likes it. Do we cheer the defeat of our worst enemies, even when it is done by our other enemies, with powers that can be turned on us next?

options.title: See what became of Germany.

content.content: For six days, Germany stops. On the seventh, the regent leaves Berlin by train for Doorn, where his grandfather spent his exile, and the Reichstag proclaims the German Republic for the second time in thirty years.

e2l_bankers_strike.councils.subtitle: The councils grow stronger, but business will be chaotic.

content.content: The councils are not yet strong enough to take this on.

content: Neither our left wing nor the <span style="color: #700000;">

content.content: Every branch of the Deutsche Bank and the Dresdner Bank now has an elected council of clerks and tellers, with the right to inspect any transfer abroad. They are surprisingly zealous. Within a month, the councils have stopped several hundred million marks at the counter and reported a dozen directors to the prosecutors.

Business is chaotic and the bank boards are outraged. However, for the first time, the white-collar employees of Berlin feel that the new order has something to do with them. The Left faction is pleased, but the Reformist faction voices its displeasure.

e2l_bauhaus.freedom.subtitle: Our Reformist faction will approve, and the West will take notice. (-1 budget)

content.content: The Ministry of Culture endows a dozen academies and asks nothing of them in return. Berlin fills with painters, architects and composers fleeing the dictatorships of Rome, Vienna and Budapest.

content: The working class is not obviously involved, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
grumbles about bourgeois art. However, the middle classes are pleased, and the foreign press has started to write about socialist Berlin with some respect.

e2l_bauhaus.title: The Bauhaus Comes Home
e2l_bauhaus.subtitle: Glass, steel, and a quarrel about realism...

options.title: Make the Bauhaus the design office of a great housing program!

title: Follow the <span style="color: #700000;">
's line: art for the masses, on the Soviet pattern.

options.title: Fund the arts generously, and keep the state out of the studio.

content.content: The Bauhaus was driven out of Dessau in 1932 by a hostile town council, and it limped on in an abandoned telephone factory in Steglitz until Mies van der Rohe ran out of money. Now its exiles are coming back. Walter Gropius has written from London and Hannes Meyer from Moscow. Ernst May, who built ten thousand flats for the workers of Frankfurt and then went to build steel towns in the Urals, has returned with a proposal: let the Bauhaus design the housing program of a socialist Germany.

content: Not everyone is enthusiastic. The <span style="color: #700000;">

's cultural commission has adopted the line of the Soviet Writers' Congress of 1934: art must be "socialist realist", understandable to the masses and free of "formalist decadence". In practice, "formalist decadence" means the Bauhaus. Meanwhile, the bourgeois papers have discovered a sudden love for the half-timbered house, and the Catholic bishops are preaching against the "barracks of godlessness".

content.content: What should we do with the arts?

e2l_blocs.tito.subtitle: The councils will be strengthened, but Moscow will be furious, and the country will be shaken.

content.content: The country is too unsettled to survive a break with Moscow.
Without strong councils or a loyal army, a break with Moscow would end in Soviet tanks.

The decision is taken at a closed session of the leadership. The Soviet advisers are given forty-eight hours to leave, and the Moscow loyalists in the security service are arrested before they can act. Then, as Tito has done in Belgrade, the leadership hands the factories back to the workers' councils, as proof that German socialism has its own road.

Moscow denounces "the Berlin revisionists" in terms usually reserved for Trotsky. For a few weeks, Soviet divisions hold maneuvers in Poland, and we fear the worst. Then they go home. Our Reformist faction is relieved.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
will take the lead. Our Reformist faction will be outraged.

content: The constitution of the German People's Republic declares that the working class, "led by its parties", holds state power. Elections will be held on a single National Front list, with seats allotted in advance to the <span style="color: #c00000;">
, the unions and the smaller allied parties. The councils survive as "transmission belts" for the decisions of the parties.

content.content: Moscow sends its congratulations the morning after the vote. Several of our own delegates abstain, and a few walk out of the theater and do not come back. Our Reformist and Centrist factions are furious with the leadership.

e2l_conspiracy.warn.subtitle: This might scare them off, for a while.

content.content: The Defense Minister summons the generals and tells them, in front of the press, that the government knows that "certain gentlemen" have forgotten their oath. The generals say they are astonished and offended.
The meetings in Potsdam stop for a few weeks. Unfortunately, they do not stop for good.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
will gain ground, and our Reformist faction will be alarmed.

content.content: Every council now has a party group, which meets before the council does and decides what the council will decide. Discipline improves at once, and the quotas are met. The Hamborn strike leaders are moved to other pits.

content: 's cells are better organized than ours, and within a year they hold the leadership of most of the great industrial councils. The commanding heights of the economy now answer to the Party.
For now, our cells hold their own against the <span style="color: #700000;">
's. However, the councils are no longer the voice of the shop floor, and both our Reformist and Left factions are unhappy.

e2l_council_bureaucracy.title: The New Bosses
e2l_council_bureaucracy.subtitle: The miners of Hamborn strike against their own council...

options.title: Restore democracy in the councils: rotation of office and a right of recall.
Hand day-to-day management to trained professional directors.
Let the workers' parties take charge of the councils through party cells.

content: A strike has broken out at the Friedrich Thyssen pit in Hamborn, the colliery that once belonged to Fritz Thyssen. However, the miners are not striking against Thyssen.

content.content: They are striking against the Ruhr Coal Council, which has raised the shift quota for the third time in two years
They are striking against their own works council, whose delegates on the board of the Reich Coal Corporation have agreed to raise the shift quota for the third time in two years
They are striking against their own district council, which has passed on the Reich Planning Office's demand to raise the shift quota for the third time in two years
They are striking against their own district council, which has raised the shift quota for the third time in two years
to meet the demands of the war economy.
to meet the targets of the export plan.

content: A hand-painted banner at the pithead reads: "The new bosses have the same cars as the old ones."

content.content: The miners have a point. The council system has grown a bureaucracy of its own. Its full-time functionaries are re-elected unopposed, its offices are in the old company headquarters, and many of its delegates have not worked a shift in a decade. The economists complain that the councils are slow and parochial, and the workers complain that they have become remote and self-serving.

content: has its own answer: democratic centralism, with party cells at the head of every council to "give it direction".

content.content: What should we do about the councils?

e2l_embargo.autarky.subtitle: The councils will grow stronger, but the economy will suffer.

content.content: Ration cards return for coffee, rubber and textiles for the first time since 1923. The factory and district councils take over distribution, and mostly run it honestly. The chemists of Leuna are told to make substitutes for everything, and they manage a surprising number.
Life is gray and frugal, and the middle classes resent it. However, the councils have never been more important.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
and our Left faction will be unhappy. (-2 budget)

content.content: The Reich Settlement Bank buys some four hundred insolvent estates, at prices their owners could hardly have hoped for on the open market, and parcels them out over a decade. The great families of the east keep their best land, their manor houses and their commissions.

content: The agricultural laborers' union calls it a ransom paid to the Osthilfe thieves, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
agrees with them at length in the Reichstag. Our Left faction is also unhappy.

e2l_land_reform.title: Junkerland in Bauernhand
e2l_land_reform.subtitle: The great estates east of the Elbe...

options.title: Break up the estates into family farms for the laborers and settlers!
Turn the estates into cooperatives run by farmworkers' councils.
Buy out only the bankrupt Osthilfe estates, with full compensation.

content.content: East of the Elbe, little has changed since the last century. Some eighteen thousand families own nearly half the farmland of Pomerania, Mecklenburg and East Prussia.
East of the Elbe, the old order has been shaken, but not broken. A few thousand families still own a third of the farmland of Pomerania, Mecklenburg and East Prussia.

content: Their estates are worked by day laborers who live in tied cottages and vote as the manor tells them. The Osthilfe scandal revealed that millions of marks in state relief had gone to these same estates, and some of it was spent on racehorses and holidays on the Riviera. The Junkers' sons fill the officer corps, and their wives fill the committees of the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">

content.content: Our land reform during the Depression bought up some of the estates and gave the land to farmworkers' associations and small peasants. However, it only scratched the surface, and most of the great estates are still intact.

Our land reform during the Depression broke up many of the bankrupt estates and gave the land to farmworkers' associations and small peasants. However, it paid for every hectare, and the richest families kept their best land, their manor houses and their political power.

content: has revived an old slogan, "Junkerland in Bauernhand", and the agricultural laborers' union has drawn up maps. The question is what should replace the estates. Small family farms would win the gratitude of the land-hungry, but many of them would be too small to survive. Cooperative estates run by farmworkers' councils would keep the land productive. Unfortunately, the peasants of Bavaria and Westphalia are already being told that collectivization is coming for their cows.

content.content: How should we carry out the land reform?

e2l_coup.loyalists.subtitle: This depends on the loyalty of the army and the police.

onArrival.$code: Q['e2l_coup_response'] = "loyalists";

content.content: The two formations remain apart, joined by a liaison committee that meets once a week. They coordinate well enough for parades. Whether they would coordinate in an emergency is another question.

content: Our Reformist faction will be outraged.

content.content: Eleven people are put on a sealed train across Poland and handed over to Soviet officials at the frontier station of Negoreloye. None of them is heard from again. Shortly afterwards, an NKVD "liaison office" opens on the second floor of the Berlin police headquarters on the Alexanderplatz.

content: Several of our own deputies resign their seats in protest, and
runs a black-bordered front page. Our Reformist, Left and Centrist factions are all furious with the leadership.
, which broke with Moscow to escape exactly this, is appalled.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
and our Left faction will approve, but the Reformists will not.

content.content: We thank the splinter parties for their courage, and decline their offer. They will vote with us on most questions anyway, since they have nowhere else to go, but they are bitter. Wirth tells a press conference that "the United Front has chosen to be a sect rather than a nation".

content: is delighted, but our Reformist faction is disappointed.

e2l_new_allies.title: The Splinters Come Over
e2l_new_allies.subtitle: Bourgeois democrats knock at the United Front's door...

options.title: Bring both parties into the Front, and give them seats in the cabinet.
We'll welcome their votes, but keep them out of the cabinet.
The United Front is a front of the working class! Turn them away.

content.content: The files we seized from the Bendlerblock have done more damage to the bourgeois parties than any election. The newspapers have printed, letter by letter, the promises that bourgeois politicians made to the conspirators: to "accept the facts", to "restore order in cooperation with the army", and to serve in a cabinet of national salvation. Not every bourgeois leader wrote such a letter, but none of them denounced the putsch until it had clearly failed.

content: Their parties have split under the strain. The left wing of the
, led by the old pacifist Hellmut von Gerlach, has walked out to found a <span style="color: #E0B0FF;">
, Joseph Wirth and the Catholic trade unionists of the Rhineland have broken away to form a <span style="color: #FF7F00;">
are asking to join the United Front.
is not keen. It did not fight on the barricades, it says, to share the cabinet with priests and professors.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
will be pleased, but the councils will lose ground, and our Reformist faction will be unhappy. (-1 budget)

content.content: The Reich Planning Office opens in the former Prussian War Ministry, staffed by economists from both parties and a delegation of advisers from Gosplan. In the spring it issues its first Four-Year Plan, which is very ambitious and not always realistic.

Unemployment falls as the Ruhr is set to work on the new targets. However, the pit councils have been told to meet quotas they never voted for, and the Reformist and Labor factions are unhappy with us.

e2l_socialisation.title: The Socialization Law
e2l_socialisation.subtitle: Coal, steel and the big banks come before the Reichstag...

options.title: The mines to the miners! Management by elected councils.
Public trusts under professional boards.
A Reich Planning Office to direct the economy from the center.

content: In 1919, a Socialization Commission chaired by Karl Kautsky recommended that the coal mines be taken into common ownership. Its report was printed, praised and filed away.

content.content: Sixteen years later, the United Front has brought socialization back to the Reichstag.

content: During the Depression, we began buying up idle enterprises

content.content: and running them with the works councils

content: . Now the United Front wants to go much further.
During the Depression, we bought up idle enterprises

content.content: and ran them with the works councils

content: , until a significant portion of the economy was in public hands. Now the United Front wants to finish the job.
The bill before the Reichstag would transfer the Ruhr collieries, the Vereinigte Stahlwerke, and the three great Berlin banks into public ownership.

Everyone in the Front agrees on that much. However, nobody agrees on who should run them. The miners' union and our left wing want the pits handed over to elected councils of workers, engineers and consumers. Our economists, led by the old Hilferding school, want public trusts under professional boards, answerable to a minister. The <span style="color: #700000;">
wants a Reich Planning Office on the Soviet pattern, setting targets from Berlin.

content.content: Meanwhile, Fritz Thyssen and Albert Vögler have hired the best lawyers in Germany, and are preparing to take the matter to the Staatsgerichtshof.
Whose model of socialization should we adopt?

subtitle: The army will stay quiet, for now. Our Left faction and the <span style="color: #700000;">
will be angry.

content.content: General von Fritsch receives the Defense Minister in his office and promises, with perfect courtesy, that the army will do its duty. No officer is dismissed, and nobody asks about the private papers in the Bendlerblock's safes.

content: The army is quiet, and the bourgeois press is relieved. However, the <span style="color: #700000;">
accuses us of leaving a loaded gun on the cabinet table, and our Left faction agrees with them.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
will be angry, but the Reformist faction will be relieved.
unavailableSubtitle: controls too much of the state for us to refuse it outright.

content.content: The party congress votes down the merger by a large majority, and Schumacher's speech is cheered for eleven minutes.

content: complains bitterly about "the splitters", but it stays in the Front, since its own members would never forgive it for going into opposition. The two parties will continue to share the cabinet table. Our Left faction is disappointed.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
will be pleased. Our Left faction will be furious.

content: We announce generous maternity grants, a Mother's Medal for women with five children, and new restrictions on divorce.

content.content: The abortion law stays on the books, but the health offices are told to discourage the procedure wherever they can.

content: The women's congress is not, and several of its delegates are expelled from the <span style="color: #700000;">
for "petty-bourgeois feminism". Our Left and Reformist factions are both unhappy with us.

e2l_women.title: The Women's Councils
e2l_women.subtitle: Half the working class demands its half of the revolution...

content.content: Adopt the whole program: equal pay, nurseries, council seats and the abolition of Paragraph 218!
Adopt the whole program: equal pay, nurseries, council seats and a guaranteed right to abortion!
Equal pay and nurseries now. Can't Paragraph 218 wait for another day?
Equal pay and nurseries now. Can't the abortion question wait for another day?

options.title: Follow the Soviet family line: support for mothers, not abortion.

content: German women won the vote in 1918, and ever since then they have been told to wait. Nearly a third of the workers in the socialized industries are now women, but barely one council delegate in twelve is a woman, and women are paid a fifth less than the men beside them on the line.

content.content: Paragraph 218 of the penal code still sends women to prison for ending a pregnancy, as it did when Käthe Kollwitz drew her posters against it in 1924.

Abortion has been legal since our reform of the Depression years. However, many doctors still refuse to perform it, and the Catholic bishops and the right have never stopped campaigning to restore the ban.

content: A National Congress of Working Women has met in Leipzig under Marie Juchacz, the founder of the Arbeiterwohlfahrt, together with Clara Zetkin's old comrades from the
. Its demands are simple: equal pay, nurseries in every factory, a third of all council seats, and

content.content: a guarantee that the right to abortion will never be taken away again.

content: 's leadership has been reminded by Moscow that the Soviet Union restored its ban on abortion in 1936, and that the socialist family is now the line.
, which campaigned against Paragraph 218 in 1931, backs the congress. The Catholic bishops are preparing pastoral letters.

content.content: How should we answer the women's congress?
We say nothing. Papen's entente is signed, ratified and mostly forgotten within two years, but for those two years the New State is received in Paris with honors.

e2p_entente.title: Papen's Entente
e2p_entente.subtitle: The Chancellor wants a French alliance against Bolshevism.

options.title: Ask the French Socialists to block the entente.
Give Paris our files on the New State's prisons.
Stay out of it. Germany's foreign policy is not ours to sabotage.

content.content: Papen has gone to Paris with an offer: a Franco-German entente against the Soviet Union, with German recognition of the western frontier thrown in. If it succeeds, the New State will have the respectability it has always lacked, and French credits to go with it. Léon Blum's Socialists, our sister party, sit in the French Chamber.

e2p_exile.front.subtitle: Twice the strength, and twice the risk of infiltration.

content: In the factories, Social Democrats and Communists who spent the twenties calling each other traitors now hand each other leaflets.

content.content: The communist underground answers to Berlin rather than Moscow, and the two parties' groups learn to trust each other.
The communist cells still take their orders from Moscow, and our people never quite know who is reporting to whom.

e2p_exile.title: Prague or Berlin?
e2p_exile.subtitle: The party is banned. Where does it lead from?

options.title: Build the party in Prague, and smuggle our newspapers into Germany.
Put everything into the underground at home.
Build the underground together with the communists.

content: was published on a Saturday. By Monday, the party's offices were sealed, its presses seized and half its executive under arrest. Otto Wels and the rest have reached Prague, where the Czechoslovak government lets them work as long as they are discreet.

content.content: The question is what kind of party we will be now. An executive in exile can raise money, publish and speak to the world. An underground at home can organize the factories, but every meeting risks Papen's political police, and every arrest can unravel a whole network.

e2p_ruhr.restrain.subtitle: Our networks stay intact. The miners will remember.

content.content: We tell our people in the pit committees that the time is not right. The communists tell theirs the opposite. When the strike collapses, the miners know which party told them to give up.

e2p_ruhr.title: The Ruhr Is Burning
e2p_ruhr.subtitle: The miners have walked out against the New State.

options.title: Back the strikes with everything the underground has.
Arm the strike committees.
Tell our people to go back before the army comes.

content.content: It started in Gelsenkirchen, over a cut in the miners' pay, and spread to every pit between Duisburg and Dortmund within a week. The strikers have no unions any more, because Papen dissolved them, so they elect pit committees instead. Some of the committees are ours. More are communist. All of them are asking the underground what to do next.

e2p_schleicher.leak.subtitle: The regime turns on itself. It may turn on us too.

content: prints the offer in full. Papen dismisses a dozen of Schleicher's officers, and Schleicher's friends in the officer corps never forgive him. The police use the same weeks to arrest everyone they think might have carried the message.

options.title: Accept. Anything is better than Papen.
Refuse. We will not trade one general's dictatorship for another's.
Leak the offer, and let the generals fight each other.

content.content: A colonel in civilian clothes has brought a message to one of our underground leaders in Berlin. General von Schleicher, who still commands the loyalty of half the officer corps, believes that Papen is ruining Germany. He proposes an arrangement. The army will remove Papen. In return, the trade unions will call off their strikes and support a government of "national reconstruction" under Schleicher, which would legalize the unions but not the parties.
It would end the New State and put the generals in its place.

options.title: See what became of Germany.

content.content: The New State ends without a battle: a broadcast announcing a constituent assembly, a column of trucks taking political prisoners home from the Emsland camps, and red flags and black, red and gold flags flying side by side in the Lustgarten.

content: On the evening of the sixth of May, the airship LZ 129

came in to moor at the naval air station at Lakehurst, New Jersey, after a stormy Atlantic crossing. The ship was named for a president who is now dead, and was finished for a Republic he never loved. At 7:25 a flame appeared near the upper fin. Thirty-four seconds later the ship was a burning skeleton on the sand. Thirty-six people died. A radio reporter from Chicago recorded the whole thing and wept into his microphone, and newsreel cinemas around the world have been showing the film ever since.
The ship was filled with hydrogen because the United States, which has a monopoly on helium, has refused to sell it to Germany.

content.content: President Eckener, who commanded the *Graf Zeppelin* round the world in 1929, has left the Reichspräsidentenpalais for the first time in weeks to stand bareheaded at the memorial service in Friedrichshafen.

Classify the research and give it to the Army Ordnance Office.
Set up a Reich Uranium Commission for civilian energy research.

content: Just before Christmas, in a basement laboratory of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry in Dahlem, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann bombarded uranium with slow neutrons. Among the products they found barium, an element only about half as heavy. Hahn could not explain it. His colleague of thirty years, Lise Meitner, could. She spent the holidays walking in the snow with her nephew Otto Frisch and doing calculations on the back of an envelope. The uranium nucleus, she concluded, had split in two, like a drop of water, and released an enormous amount of energy as it did so. Frisch has borrowed a word from biology to describe it:

content.content: The news has crossed the Atlantic within a month. In Copenhagen, Niels Bohr has confirmed it. At the University of Berlin, the Hungarian physicist Leo Szilard is going from office to office arguing that if each split releases more neutrons, a chain reaction is possible, and then a bomb. He wants the results kept secret. Paul Harteck in Hamburg has already written to the War Ministry, pointing out that "the country which first makes use of it has an unsurpassable advantage over the others."

content: Meitner wants none of that. "We are physicists," she tells the Prussian Academy, "not armourers." Werner Heisenberg in Leipzig thinks a uranium "machine" could boil water and drive turbines. Einstein, back from his winter in Princeton, has written to the Chancellor in his own hand. He asks only that, whatever is decided, it be decided in the open.

content.content: In the Planning Office, the economists have one question: could uranium one day replace Ruhr coal?

Germany's nearest uranium lies across the Czech border at Joachimsthal, and with the Ruhr's coal out of reach, some officials are already asking what a "uranium machine" could do for a country short of fuel.
The officers who stood aside in the civil war are taking a sudden interest in physics.

German refrigerators go to Argentina, Sweden and Egypt. The currency reserves grow, and the Mark is rock-solid. In the working-class districts people grumble that they build the things and the foreigners get to keep them.

content.content: Contract IG Farben to mass-produce penicillin.
We are in opposition. Let IG Farben mass-produce penicillin.
