content.content: Eight years ago, Gerhard Domagk of Bayer gave a red dye called Prontosil to his six-year-old daughter, who was dying of a streptococcal infection from a needle in her hand. She lived. The sulfonamide drugs that followed have since cut deaths from childbed fever and pneumonia by a third. Domagk went to Stockholm in 1939 to collect his Nobel Prize, and IG Farben has made a fortune from it.

content: Now there is something better. A mold that Alexander Fleming noticed in London in 1928 has been turned into a drug at Oxford by Howard Florey's team, and Ernst Chain, a Berlin-born chemist, is part of it. It is called penicillin. It cures infections that the sulfonamides cannot touch, including resistant gonorrhoea, gas gangrene and the blood poisoning that can kill a child in a day. The Americans are making it in huge fermentation tanks in Peoria. In Germany there is barely enough to treat a dozen patients a week.

content.content: The surgeons who came back from the war know what a few grams of it would have meant on the hospital trains.

content: Chain is in Berlin this summer, visiting his mother, and he has said he would be willing to come home for the right laboratory.

content.content: The sickness funds and the councils of the chemical workers at Leverkusen and Höchst want the drug made in public hands, at cost.
The sickness funds want the drug made at cost. IG Farben wants a patent and a price.

content: Meanwhile, the British and the Americans are offering licences, for a fee.

content: On a disused army ammunition dump in Berlin-Reinickendorf, which its tenants have proudly named the

, the members of the Society for Space Travel have spent six years blowing things up. Their liquid-fuelled rockets have climbed more than a kilometer into the sky. One of them came down on the roof of a police barracks. Hermann Oberth, the Transylvanian schoolmaster whose book started it all, writes from Mediaş that a rocket could one day leave the atmosphere altogether. The society's treasurer writes back that it cannot pay the gas bill.

Its most promising member is a twenty-four-year-old aristocrat named Wernher von Braun, who wrote his doctorate on combustion in rocket motors. The doctorate was paid for by the Army Ordnance Office, and he did the work behind the walls of the artillery range at Kummersdorf. Major Walter Dornberger of Ordnance now proposes to take the whole society under the army's wing. He would give it a secret test site on the island of Usedom, near the fishing village of Peenemünde, and more money than the society has ever seen. The army has not said what it wants the rockets to carry. It does not need to say.
That the offer comes from the officer corps, after everything, makes some of our

content.content: The rocket men would rather have a civilian patron. Willy Ley, the society's writer, has drafted a plan for a Reich Institute for Rocket Research attached to the Technical University in Charlottenburg. It would publish its results and work on weather rockets, high-altitude research and, one day, flight beyond the atmosphere. Meanwhile a young inventor from the Harz, Gerhard Zucker, is promising the Reichspost a rocket mail service.

content.content: At our suggestion, the ADGB proposes something unheard of: a single trade union federation, independent of every party, open to socialist and Christian workers alike. After six months of negotiations in a Frankfurt hotel, the Christian unions agree. The new German Trade Union Federation has six million members, and its first congress opens with both the Internationale and a Catholic hymn.

content.content: In 1920, the Christian trade union leader Adam Stegerwald called on the Center Party to leave the Catholic ghetto and become a party for every Christian German, Protestant or Catholic. For twenty years, nobody listened. The Center remained what it had been since Bismarck: the party of the Catholic minority, strong in the Rhineland, Silesia and the south, and almost absent everywhere else.

content: Now this is changing. The nationalist Right has been in decline since the crisis years, and its Protestant voters in the small towns of Hesse, Franconia and Württemberg are looking for a new home. At a special congress in Cologne, the Center has voted overwhelmingly to dissolve itself into a new Christian People's Party, the
deputies sit on its first executive alongside Catholic union leaders.

presents itself as the natural party of the center. Its program speaks of "Christian socialism" in one paragraph and of "the sanctity of private property" in the next. Whether it leans toward us or away from us could decide German politics for a generation.

content.content: How should we deal with the new party?

content: The standoff lasts four days. On the third, a battalion in Potsdam refuses to march against the strikers. On the fourth, the commander of the Berlin military district informs the
that he can no longer vouch for his troops.
withdraws the decrees and goes on the radio to say that he was "misled by irresponsible advisers". The Directory's members are arrested, but the President himself is still in office.
The officers of the Committee surrender to the

content.content: The coup has failed! Support for the Republic—and for us—has grown, and the Reichswehr has been reminded where its loyalty belongs.

The bourgeois parties have begun negotiating joint candidates in earnest. In the meantime, the

content.content: From now on, two lay assessors will sit with the professional judge in every criminal case, and they can outvote him. The labor courts, with their union and employer benches, gain jurisdiction over every dispute about wages and dismissals.
Workers who would never have set foot in a courtroom now sit in judgment, and the workers and the Labor faction approve of our reform.

content.content: The socialization program we began in the crisis years is finally complete: the commanding heights of German industry belong to the public.
For the first time, the commanding heights of German industry belong to the public!

content.content: The Chancellor is sworn in as Prussian Minister-President as well, and the Interior, Justice and Finance ministries of the Reich and Prussia are merged under single ministers. Prussia survives on paper, with its Landtag and its flag, but its administration and the Reich's now run as one. This was Otto Braun's old solution, and the Reformists are pleased with it.
However, our jurists warn that a future Chancellor of a different stripe would inherit the Prussian police along with the Reich.

e2w_programme.economic_democracy.subtitle: The Labor faction will be pleased.

content.content: The congress adopts a program built around Fritz Naphtali's old idea of economic democracy. The class struggle disappears from the text, but socialism does not. In its place is a long-term plan to democratize the economy through works councils, co-determination, public enterprises and a planning council in which unions and employers sit as equals.

content: The trade unions and the Labor faction are delighted. However, both the Left and the Reformists are disappointed, and most observers conclude that the <span style="color: #c00000;">
has become a people's party without quite admitting it.

e2w_programme.title: The Godesberg Congress
subtitle: Is the <span style="color: #c00000;">
still the party of the working class, or the party of the people?

content.content: Adopt the reformers' draft. We must become a people's party!
Adopt the reformers' draft, and put our people's party in writing at last.

content: We are the party of the working class!

options.title: Surely there is a third way? Put "economic democracy" in place of the class struggle.

content: Our party still lives by the Heidelberg Program of 1925, drafted by Rudolf Hilferding in the confident language of the old Marxist center. It describes the "historical struggle of the working class" against capitalism, promises the socialization of the means of production, and predicts that capital will be concentrated into ever fewer hands.

content.content: Since the Leipzig congress of 1931, it has stood alongside the left's radical crisis program: socialization of the banks and heavy industry, public works on credit, and joint action with every workers' organization that defends the Republic.
We declared ourselves a people's party in the crisis years, but the program itself was never rewritten to match.

Twenty years later, the hands have not become fewer. Many workers now have savings books and allotment gardens, and our own voters include schoolteachers, civil servants, shopkeepers and, more and more, Catholics.

The executive has called an extraordinary congress in the spa town of Bad Godesberg, on the Rhine, to write a new program. Unfortunately, the drafting commission is split down the middle. Carlo Schmid and Willi Eichler want to drop Marxism as the party's official philosophy, accept competition "as far as possible and planning as far as necessary", and make peace with the churches. Their opponents—the Left faction, and much of the Saxon and Berlin organizations—warn that a party that stops talking about class will soon forget who it is for.
After a decade in which we have been the natural party of government, the question is what kind of party we want to be.
Our vote has barely moved in a decade. Many delegates believe that a new program is the only way to break out of the working-class districts.

When the march arrives in Altona, they are immediately confronted by an angry crowd of communists and socialists, who throw objects at the Nazis. This incident has been called "Altona Bloody Sunday" in the media. The Communists assail the incompetence of the police, who are supposedly under our command.

content.content: Second Emergency Decree for Economy and Finance

His aim is to implement a new constitution via plebiscite—or, perhaps, simply through a presidential decree, with Hindenburg’s continued support.

Amid rising labor protests and growing hostility from all corners of German society, Schleicher can no longer support his former ally. Papen’s reckless pursuit of political suicide, backed only by President Hindenburg, has pushed Schleicher to distance himself from Papen’s unpopular policies in preparation for his own chancellorship. He has engaged with trade unions and a variety of political figures, including Gregor Strasser, to build the necessary support.
One thing is clear: Papen must go for German democracy to survive.

And his threat is clear: the Reichswehr’s militia stands ready to act if no decision is reached before the deadline.
Our good relations have kept him from forcing the issue—so far—but his patience is running out.

Stegerwald has won the leadership vote! By rallying the republicans behind his candidacy, he has successfully blocked Bracht from seizing control of the Center Party. Backing such a right-wing conservative proved unacceptable to the Christian unions, who continue to resist Schleicher's growing influence.

Although Stegerwald favors immediately opening the Center Party to Protestants, the party simply lacks the funds to establish regional branches across Protestant Germany, with recent elections having already exhausted its resources.

content.content: During weeks of intense negotiations in Rome headed by Ludwig Kaas, the Reichskonkordat has officially been signed between Germany and the Roman Catholic Church. The treaty defines a formal relationship between the Church and the German state, guaranteeing freedom of worship for Catholics, and the right of the church to appoint their own clergy. Catholics in Germany are pleased, as are their representatives in the Center Party.

content.content: The course Schleicher pursues is one of three options developed by his colleagues in the Defense Ministry. The first two involve unconstitutional maneuvers: either postponing elections or forcing the Reichstag into indefinite adjournment.

content: The third option, however, is more intriguing—a constructive vote of no confidence. Legal advisors have identified a loophole in the Republic’s constitution: while a hostile Reichstag majority can pass a no-confidence vote, it cannot unite to support a new cabinet. In the event of <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

content.content: To remedy this, the Defense Ministry proposes a constitutional amendment requiring the Reichstag to propose a viable replacement cabinet alongside any no-confidence motion—thereby curbing purely negative obstruction.

content: This option is favored within the Defense Ministry: it has the potential to attract republican support and avoid the civil unrest that the other two would likely provoke. Schleicher could remain in office as a caretaker indefinitely.

content.content: A precedent has even been set in Württemberg, where the Bolz government ignored a no-confidence vote from a purely negative majority and continued to rule by decree.

content: Crucially, this approach requires nothing from Hindenburg beyond passive acquiescence.

content.content: After weeks of delay, Gereke finally presents his public works program to the cabinet. Though too late to save Schleicher’s tenure, it is approved by the chancellor and signed by Hindenburg without objection. The plan allocates half a billion marks to infrastructure projects across the Reich.
In the coming months, as millions of unemployed Germans return to work, it is not Schleicher, but his successor, who will reap the political rewards.

In what is likely his final cabinet meeting, he informs his ministers that he will request a decree to dissolve the Reichstag, as a no-confidence vote is now inevitable. He fully expects his request to be denied and is prepared to submit both his and the cabinet's resignation.

I have been taught obedience.”

content.content: The Nazis have continued cracking down on even lawful leftist activity, on bogus claims of "inciting violence." It seems Frick is doing Schleicher's dirty work for him—cracking down on democrats and all, while Schleicher is still viewed highly in the eyes of many workers.

The Reichsbank, long known for its strict fiscal conservatism and obsessive anti-inflation stance, had already slashed Schleicher's initial public works decree by 15%. So, it was no surprise when news of even greater government spending met with their disapproval.

However, the endorsement of the campaign by Hjalmar Schacht—a respected banker and recently retired Reichsbank President credited with ending hyperinflation—has done much to calm the business community. Under government pressure, the Reichsbank is ultimately coerced into backing the plan, though not without forcing another 20% cut in funding.

Adam Stegerwald at the Labor Ministry, working closely with Günther Gereke, has been formulating a massive billion-mark public works program to expand on Schleicher’s previously modest efforts. They recognize that large-scale public projects and state spending are Germany’s path out of the slump—and Schleicher is eager to approve more to propel the nation back to great power status.

However, the chancellor has been persistently pressing his ministers to focus on rearmament and infrastructure that would support it—such as the construction of the Autobahn, a new nationwide highway system, and state funding for armament companies. To Schleicher’s frustration, however, most of the funds will still be directed toward civilian development.

In 1914 he emigrated to Canada, where he spent the war underground rather than report for internment, until the Toronto police deported him in 1919. He also knows the Comintern's apparatus from the inside: which offices in Moscow matter, who reports to whom, and how long a German party can ignore a telegram before someone is sent to Berlin to ask why. content.content: For better or for worse, the party cannot exist without money. Without the support of wealthy industrialists, we depend on membership dues to sustain our efforts.
We receive dues at the end of each year, but can adjust them throughout. Low party dissent can secure more funds, and vice versa.
The labor wing of the party supports continued participation in government in order to provide benefits to the workers, and the creation of public works programs for employment.

The programs of the Nordic socialists involve active government intervention in the economy. We can learn from their economic strategies, and how they moved beyond their working-class base to attract a broader set of constituents.

content.content: Class Consciousness of the New Middle Class

content: Due to our investments in media, socialism is becoming more popular, including among the new middle class.

content.content: Marxist intellectuals such as Bernstein and Kautsky have long debated about the status of the new middle class and whether they constitute a different class from the proletariat.
Despite becoming a people’s party, our party has traditionally prioritised the industrial working class.

content: Our propagandizing has meant that the new middle class are increasingly considering themselves part of the proletariat, or at least having more in common with them. Whilst they’re more moderate than the industrial proletariat, we could awaken their class consciousness as a way to expand the <span style="color: #c00000;">
and to build solidarity with all workers.

content.content: We have promised to take more policy suggestions from the centrists. Both the left and reformist wings of the party might be displeased.
The communists are suspicious of our overtures, especially the Stalinist leadership, who persist in calling us "social fascists". However, connections are made at the grassroots and local levels.
The communists are still wary of us after years of bitter rivalry. However, their leadership no longer calls us "social fascists", and connections are made at the grassroots and local levels.

It is an arduous and contentious process, but we have pushed through the proposal to become a people's party. The Left and Center claim that our new party platform is a betrayal of our founding principles, a turn away from Marxism towards bourgeois opportunism. Whatever the case, we are now a party representing all of the people, not just the proletariat.
Should we run a new campaign to publicize our new platform?
The police successfully protected our rally, so it can go ahead as usual.

We do not need any special treatment for minorities.

options.title: Antisemitism is the "socialism of fools". We will defeat them with real socialism.
Antisemitism is a crisis. Direct the full force of the Iron Front against antisemitism.
All Germans will suffer from fascism, not just the Jews. We do not need a separate policy for them.

content: Antisemitism has long been a latent feature of German society, but since the beginning of the economic depression, it has grown to a horrifying extent. The Nazis are the worst of it, but all the right-wing parties are deeply antisemitic. Regarding the
specifically, our right-wing enemies love to deploy their racist rhetoric against our many Jewish comrades, magnifying criticism of any minor transgression, and they call the entire
a Jewish party. We are a favorite target of their invectives.

content.content: The Reichsbanner is already serving the purpose it needs to serve. There is no reason to change what already works.

rural_consciousness.awaken_2.subtitle: We can invest 1 budget into building more powerful radio transmission stations so that we can expand our radio network to the countryside.

content.content: We sadly do not have enough budget for this.
We need to be in government to do this.
We might want to consider building up our radio network.

We have taken advantage of the situation and have awoken the class consciousness of the peasantry and the rural working class. Increasingly, they flock to our party and more rural labourers have joined the DLV - the German Agricultural Workers' Union.

By awakening the class consciousness of the peasantry and the rural working class, failing a secondary burden will lessen the extent to which their support is reduced. In addition, our media campaigning and rallies will have more of an effect amongst rural voters, now that they are conscious.

content: It is not enough for the <span style="color: #c00000;">

to solely be a political party. The Worker Singer's League, Worker's Sports, and our schools and libraries are crucial to our members' lives. Funding these organizations makes our members more committed to the party, even when our policies might not be to their liking.

content.content: However, it feels frivolous to spend on sports and choirs when the fascists are murdering us in the streets.

content.content: The Nazi and Communist propaganda machines have poisoned the public’s view of the Republic. Our goal is to counter their narrative with propaganda of our own.

The building workers' councils elect their own site committees, set their own shifts, and argue with the Planning Office about everything. The road is three months late. But nobody can remember a public works project where the men were this proud of the job.

Cities compete to build the best airports. Tempelhof's great curved terminal is finished at last, Hamburg-Fuhlsbüttel and Munich-Riem get concrete runways, and Frankfurt builds an airfield right beside the new motorway.
The Army Ordnance Office leases Zuse's machines to compute firing tables, at a good rate. The money keeps Zuse's company going. The results go into a safe.
The cooperative lorry, painted red and loaded with radios and electric irons, becomes a familiar sight on village market days. The village shopkeepers hate it, and the villagers do not.
Only the Reich government can fund this.

Mobile X-ray vans tour every district and stop outside every pit head and factory gate. Eight million chests are screened in two years. A hundred thousand cases are found early enough to treat. The sanatoria in the Black Forest start to have empty beds.

In a thousand union halls, men who have spent the day at the lathe spend the evening soldering. Every factory gets a set that the workers built themselves. The pictures are not very good, but they belong to the workers.

ending_slides.weimar_win_a.title: Subending A - The World's Most Unstable Republic

content: The political deadlock that defined the gravest crisis of the Weimar Republic has persisted over the years. The

has never been fully reconciled with a system it was fundamentally opposed to from the start. Meanwhile, the estrangement of the Center Party from the Weimar Coalition has only deepened right-wing hostility toward the
The presidency has remained out of reach for the <span style="color: #c00000;">

, with successors to Hindenburg's worldview continuing to preside over Germany and obstruct our return to executive power. In 1939, a recession—sparked by European instability and rising tensions with the Soviet Union—triggered another wave of extremism. The Reichswehr was forced to step in to prevent a "March on Berlin" by both communists and fascism.
Though real democracy was formally restored in the 1960s following massive public discontent, the <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">
has remained a persistent force on the far-right. Recently rebranding itself as the
, it has capitalized on growing public anger over a refugee crisis driven by continued war and instability across Africa.

content: The coal ships sail, the Italian army takes Addis Ababa in the spring, and the King of Italy is proclaimed Emperor of Ethiopia.

content.content: Unfortunately, the League has been shown to be powerless, and every revisionist in Europe has taken note. Many of our own workers are disappointed in us.

e2_abyssinia.title: The Abyssinian Crisis
e2_abyssinia.subtitle: Italy invades Ethiopia. Will the League act?

options.title: Demand full sanctions, including an embargo on coal and oil!
Support limited sanctions, but keep the coal flowing.
Call on the unions to boycott Italian trade.
This isn't our fight—Germany has troubles enough.

content.content: On the third of October, Italian columns crossed the Eritrean frontier into Ethiopia without a declaration of war. Mussolini has promised his people a new Roman empire, and he means to start with the last independent kingdom in Africa. Emperor Haile Selassie has appealed to the League of Nations, of which Ethiopia, like Germany, is a member.

The League has named Italy the aggressor and is debating sanctions. Britain and France talk loudly in Geneva and quietly with Rome—Paris wants Mussolini as a partner against Germany, and London wants no war in the Mediterranean. Whether sanctions bite depends largely on us. Germany has long sold Italy much of its coal, and an embargo on Ruhr coal and on oil would hurt Rome far more than any speech.

content: The Center Party has no love for an attack on a Christian kingdom, but it likes losing coal contracts even less.

content.content: Our coalition partners are uneasy about sanctions of any kind.
The cabinet is divided, and it is waiting to see which way the Reichstag leans.

content: Many of the men who fought the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
in our civil war see the blackshirts in Ethiopia as the same enemy in a different uniform. The Finance Ministry, still printing money to pay for reconstruction, sees only the coal revenue.

content.content: The Ruhr pits that once fed Italy's furnaces are in the hands of the Red Army, and our own coal exports are a fraction of what they were. All we can really offer is a vote in Geneva and an example.

content: For the United Front, this is fascism on the march, and the
wants the dockers to refuse Italian cargo by morning. However, the Foreign Office warns that open hostility to Rome will drive Mussolini into the arms of every reactionary in Europe.

content.content: Full sanctions would break the Stresa Front that we joined in the spring, and Rome would not forgive it.
Paris and Prague will not budge.

content: Renner postpones the referendum, and the two republics have to settle for a customs and currency union instead, which the Council grudgingly allows. The nationalist press howls that we went begging to Geneva and came home with nothing. Austrian socialists are bitterly disappointed, but at least we kept within the law.

e2_bavaria_plot.raise.subtitle: The plot will be made public. What happens next is the government's decision.

content.content: Our deputies read out the plotters' list of ministers in the Reichstag, name by name. The government, under pressure, sends the Reich prosecutor to Munich. The trial is held in Bavaria, and the sentences are light, but the Defense League's members now know that their names are in the newspapers.

e2_bavaria_plot.title: A Plot in Munich
e2_bavaria_plot.subtitle: The Bavarian police have found a plan for a Bavarian kingdom.

options.title: Arrest the plotters, and put the Bavarian police under Reich supervision.
Let Munich deal with it, and open talks on more autonomy for the states.
Call the plotters' bluff, and let Bavaria vote on staying in the Reich.
Raise the alarm in the Reichstag, and demand that the government act.

content.content: The Munich political police have raided a villa on the Starnberger See and found a draft proclamation, a list of ministers and a timetable. On a day still to be chosen, a "Bavarian Defense League" of monarchists, former Freikorps men and a few disaffected officers of the Bavarian division would seize the Wittelsbach Palace, declare Bavaria's departure from "the Marxist Reich" and invite Crown Prince Rupprecht to take the throne. The Crown Prince has said nothing, in public or, so far as the police know, in private.
The money came from Linz. Hitler's Austrian party has paid for the printing presses, and its men have been crossing the border at Salzburg for months.
The money came from the Italian consulate in Munich, by way of a bank in Innsbruck.

content: The Bavarian government, embarrassed, has asked Berlin to let it deal with the matter itself.

content.content: The decision belongs to the government, but the Interior Minister needs our votes, and our deputies are making themselves heard.

e2_cold_war.east.unavailableSubtitle: The United Front is no longer in government.

content.content: The government refuses the American offer and joins the Information Bureau's economic council. Soviet engineers arrive to help draw up a Five-Year Plan, and German factories begin retooling for Soviet orders. The councils are told that the plan is now the business of the planners. On the Rhine, American and British officers watch the new border with field glasses.

e2_cold_war.title: The World Divides
e2_cold_war.subtitle: Washington offers dollars, and Moscow draws a line.

options.title: Accept the dollars and join the Western defense system.
Accept the dollars, and refuse any military commitment.
Refuse both blocs, and build a neutral "third force" in Europe.
Stand with the Soviet Union.

content.content: The war in the Pacific ended in 1945, and America has come home from it the richest power the world has ever seen. The American Secretary of State has stood up at Harvard and offered every country in Europe, "east or west, without exception", a vast program of credits for reconstruction. There is a condition. Each country must open its books to the others, coordinate its plans, and lower its trade barriers. A second condition goes unspoken, but everyone understands it. Those who take the dollars are expected to stand with the West against the Soviet Union.

content: Moscow's answer came within a week. The Soviet delegation walked out of the Paris talks, and a new Information Bureau of the Communist Parties has been set up to coordinate the "struggle against American imperialism".

content.content: As a member of the People's Democracies, Germany has been instructed to refuse.
With the Red Army now on the Vistula, the question is no longer academic.
The bourgeois parties want to accept on any terms. The trade unions are wary of American conditions on wages and public ownership.
Reconstruction is still unfinished, and dollars would finish it.
Washington has said that aid to the Republic will continue only if Berlin stands firm against the Ruhr Soviet, which Moscow supplies.
The Republic has rebuilt itself almost from nothing, and Washington is keen to make it a showcase.

content: The United Front is split down the middle. The <span style="color: #700000;">
will not hear of American money. Many in our party want to take the aid and keep our independence.

content.content: The United Socialist Party is split down the middle. The former Communists in our ranks will not hear of American money. Many others want to take the aid and keep our independence.
The bourgeois cabinet wants the dollars. The councils and the unions are afraid of what Washington will ask in return.
The decision belongs to the government, but it needs a majority in the Reichstag, and our votes count.

e2_danzig.moscow.unavailableSubtitle: The United Front is no longer in government.

content.content: Berlin and Moscow issue a joint declaration guaranteeing the "independence and free development" of the Free City of Danzig. Warsaw backs down at once. It is also terrified. A Polish government that has spent twenty years fearing that Germany and Russia would one day reach across it to shake hands now believes that day has come.

e2_danzig.title: Danzig and the Corridor
e2_danzig.subtitle: Polish customs guards, a Free City and a very old grievance.

options.title: Offer Warsaw an "Eastern Locarno".
Refer the dispute to the League of Nations.
Back Danzig to the hilt, and make Warsaw feel it.
Accept Moscow's offer of a guarantee.

content.content: The Free City of Danzig is German in all but sovereignty. It is a Hanseatic port of four hundred thousand people, run by its own Senate under a League of Nations High Commissioner, with Polish customs officers on its quays and a Polish munitions depot on the Westerplatte. For twenty years it has been the sorest point on the map of Versailles. Poland reached the sea by a corridor of land that cut East Prussia off from the Reich, and Danzig was the price of that arrangement.

Since Polish troops moved into East Prussia during our civil war, Danzig has been an island. Now Warsaw has gone further. A decree from Colonel Beck's Foreign Ministry places the Free City's railways and post under Polish administration "for the duration of the emergency". The Danzig Senate has appealed to the League and to Berlin. Berlin has very little to offer it.

This summer, Danzig's nationalist Senate expelled two Polish customs inspectors. Poland has answered by closing the Corridor to German freight and sending a warship to the Westerplatte. Colonel Beck says that Polish rights in Danzig are not negotiable. He is also, the embassy in Warsaw reports, more frightened of the Red Army massing on his eastern border than of anything Germany might do, and that may give us an opening.
Moscow has quietly suggested that a Soviet guarantee of Danzig's "independence" might concentrate Warsaw's mind.

content: and the veterans' leagues are holding rallies under the slogan "Danzig is German". The Reichswehr has helpfully drawn up plans.
The government declares that Germany will defend its own frontiers and no one else's.

content.content: Frontier guard units are called up in East Prussia and Silesia,
East Prussia and Upper Silesia are still under Polish occupation, so frontier guard units are called up along the demarcation lines in Pomerania and Lower Silesia,

content: and the Reichsbahn is forbidden to carry arms for either side.

content.content: Moscow's request for transit rights is politely refused.

The French ambassador calls it a betrayal. The Soviet ambassador calls it wisdom. Most Germans, remembering the casualty lists of 1914 to 1918, simply call it a relief. In the east, the guns have begun firing, and the first refugees are already on the roads toward our border.

Germany joins the Council of the People's Democracies, with its joint command in Moscow and its planning commission in Berlin. The People's Army's general staff now takes its orders from the Arbat. The councils, which once argued about everything, are learning that some questions are no longer open to discussion.

Germany declines. The Six become Five, and the pool goes ahead without us, centred on Lorraine, the Saar and Belgium. German steelmakers enjoy their independence for a year or two, until they find that their French and Belgian competitors are buying coal more cheaply inside the pool than they can outside it.

e2_khalkhin_gol.mediate.unavailableSubtitle: Neither side would take our offer seriously.
e2_khalkhin_gol.mediate.subtitle: The war will end sooner, and Moscow's hands will be free sooner.

content.content: The German delegate in Geneva proposes a ceasefire on the old frontier, under a League commission. Japan left the League six years ago, but both governments receive the German envoys, and both say that they are interested in peace. The fighting goes on, a little more slowly.

e2_khalkhin_gol.title: War on the Khalkha River
e2_khalkhin_gol.subtitle: A border battle in Mongolia becomes a war between Moscow and Tokyo.

options.title: Declare strict neutrality.
Sell trucks and machine tools to the Soviet Union.
Keep selling to Japan.
Offer the League's good offices for a ceasefire.

content.content: All summer, Soviet and Mongolian troops fought the Japanese Kwantung Army over a strip of grassland along the Khalkha River, where Mongolia meets Manchuria. In August a Soviet corps commander named Zhukov encircled and destroyed the Japanese force with tanks and aircraft. Tokyo was expected to ask for a ceasefire. Instead, the generals of the Kwantung Army sent three more divisions to the border, and in September Japanese troops crossed into the Soviet Maritime Province near Vladivostok. The two powers are now at war along three thousand kilometers of frontier.

content: For Europe, the war means that the Red Army's best divisions are going east on the Trans-Siberian railway.

content.content: The general staff in Berlin, which has watched Soviet maneuvers near Minsk with some alarm, is quietly relieved.

content: Both sides want German goods: Moscow wants trucks and machine tools, and Tokyo wants optical glass and chemicals.

content.content: The decision belongs to the government, but our votes count.

content: We say nothing, and the refugees at the Schlesischer Bahnhof are told to apply through the normal channels, which takes months. The Soviet trade delegation thanks the Foreign Office for its "correct attitude".

content.content: The bourgeois papers ask why the Republic shelters the man at the centre of the trials but will not say a word about them.
Several of our own deputies, who have friends among the missing, tell the party leadership exactly what they think of this. Both the Left and the Reformist factions are angry with us.

e2_obituary.breitscheid.subtitle: The party's foreign policy spokesman, from the Center Marxist wing.

content.content: Rudolf Breitscheid is sworn in as Chancellor. The Center Party and the liberals call him too close to the Left.

Our team marches into the Montjuïc stadium behind a single black-red-gold flag. Among the athletes are a boxer from Essen and two swimmers from Cologne, who crossed the lines to compete for the Republic. When the Essen boxer takes silver, the Berlin papers print his photograph on the front page, and even the Ruhr's own papers carry the story.

content.content: We refuse to sign. Spain's government is lawful, and we will sell it what it needs on credit. Rifles, field guns and a few dozen aircraft are shipped from Hamburg to Cartagena.
the Center Party threatens to leave the cabinet.
the Center Party denounces us from every pulpit.

content: However, in Madrid the crowds that meet the first German freighter sing the

content.content: Britain, desperate to avoid a war over "a quarrel in a faraway country", leans on Prague until it gives way. At a conference in Munich, Czechoslovakia agrees to cede the German border districts after a plebiscite. The nationalists cheer the Republic for the first time in living memory. Jaksch's social democrats, who voted against union, are among the first to flee to Prague.

Prague mobilizes. France reminds us of its alliance with Czechoslovakia, and the Soviet Union of its own. For eleven days Europe waits for war, and then the government backs down. The nationalists, who demanded the confrontation, now say that a real German government would have seen it through.

e2_sudeten.title: Trouble in the Sudetenland
e2_sudeten.subtitle: Prague declares martial law in the German borderlands.

options.title: Stand with Prague and guarantee Czechoslovakia's borders.
Back an internationally mediated autonomy statute.
Demand that Prague hand over the civil-war fugitives.
Demand self-determination for the Sudeten Germans.

content.content: Three and a quarter million Germans live in Czechoslovakia, most of them in the mountain borderlands of Bohemia and Moravia, and most of them have voted for Konrad Henlein's Sudeten German Party since 1935. Henlein wants autonomy, he says, and nothing more. His more radical lieutenants want the border moved. In September a Czech gendarme was shot dead at a rally in Eger, and Prague has declared martial law across the German districts.

The Sudeten valleys have become a haven for the men we beat in the civil war. Former SA and Stahlhelm leaders run Henlein's "Volunteer Corps" from guesthouses near the border, and they are not interested in autonomy. Their aim is to start a war in Bohemia and finish the one they lost in Germany.

content: has declared the defense of "our brothers in the Sudetenland" a national duty, and its papers print atrocity stories, some of them true.

Our sister party in Czechoslovakia, Wenzel Jaksch's German Social Democrats, begs Berlin not to fall for Henlein's game. A democratic Prague, Jaksch says, is the best protection the Sudeten Germans have. The <span style="color: #700000;">

content.content: President Beneš has asked Berlin to restrain the agitators. Britain has offered to send a mediator. The German right demands that we do the opposite.

e2_trotsky_berlin.campaign.subtitle: The Left faction will approve. The government will decide as it pleases.

content.content: Our deputies put down a motion for Trotsky's asylum, and our papers print an appeal signed by three hundred writers and professors. The government refuses all the same, and Trotsky sails from Oslo for Mexico. The Soviet embassy sends our party executive a long note of protest, which is framed and hung in the Left faction's office.

e2_trotsky_berlin.title: Trotsky in Berlin?
e2_trotsky_berlin.subtitle: Norway has expelled Leon Trotsky, and he has asked the Republic for asylum.

options.title: Grant him asylum.
Grant him asylum, on strict conditions, far from Berlin.
Refuse.
Campaign for his asylum.

content.content: Under pressure from Moscow, which has threatened to stop buying Norwegian herring, the government in Oslo has interned Leon Trotsky and told him to leave the country. No government in Europe wants him. His lawyer has sent a letter to the Reich Ministry of the Interior: Trotsky asks for asylum in Germany, and promises to take no part in German politics.

content: He has reason to think he might get it. The <span style="color: #700000;">
's break with Moscow has been denounced in

as "Trotskyism in the service of the German bourgeoisie", although the party's leaders have never had much time for Trotsky either. Our Left faction wants him admitted on principle. The Reformists point out that the founder of the Red Army is not a man who stays out of politics, and that Moscow will take his arrival personally.

content.content: The decision belongs to the Interior Ministry, not to us.

e2_war_cabinet.current.subtitle: The coalition will run the war as it ran the peace, by negotiation.

onArrival.$code:

content.content: The Chancellor tells the general staff that the constitution does not stop for a war, and that the Reichstag that voted the credits will see how they are spent. The generals complain that a war cannot be run by committee. The coalition partners, who had feared being pushed aside, are grateful.

e2_war_cabinet.title: The War Cabinet
e2_war_cabinet.subtitle: Who governs while the war lasts?

options.title: Form a government of national defense with the Centre and the liberals.
Bring the KPD into the war cabinet.
Govern with a small war cabinet and emergency powers.
Keep the cabinet as it is.

content: Every party leader in the Reichstag has asked the Chancellor the same question: who governs while the war lasts?

content.content: The political truce has put the quarrel off, but it has not settled it.
The Centre and the liberals offer to join a government of national defense, on condition that our ministers drop every reform the war does not need.
The bourgeois parties have not come back since they walked out of the Reichstag.

content: has offered ministers of its own, and its members are already in the factories and at the front.
The general staff would prefer a small cabinet that can act without asking anyone.

content.content: Since Article 48 was bound by law, a cabinet that wants to govern by decree must ask the Reichstag for a War Powers Act, to be renewed every six months.
Article 48 still lets the President govern by decree, as Ebert did in 1923 and Brüning did in 1930. A war cabinet could use it every day.

e2_war_allies.alone.subtitle: The Republic will owe nothing to anyone.

onArrival.$code:
Q['nationalism'] = (Q['nationalism'] || 0) + 2;
Q['e2_war_home'] = (Q['e2_war_home'] || 0) + 2;

content.content: The Chancellor tells the Reichstag that the Republic will fight its own war with its own resources. The factories go over to three shifts, and the women who worked in them in 1917 are back, with their daughters. The general staff's list of shortages gets longer.

e2_war_allies.title: Arms from Abroad
e2_war_allies.subtitle: Our factories cannot keep up with the front.

options.title: Ask Britain for arms.
Ask the Soviet Union for fuel and arms.
Ask the United States for credits.
Fight with what we have.

content: The army is firing shells faster than the Ruhr can make them, and the general staff's list of shortages runs to forty pages: aircraft engines, fuel, rubber, trucks, boots.

content.content: The Foreign Office has sounded out the neutral and friendly capitals.
The Western powers have blockaded our ports, and only Moscow can help.
The cabinet will decide where the arms come from, but the credits to pay for them must pass the Reichstag, and our votes count.

e2_war_end.pact.unavailableSubtitle: Paris does not trust us enough for a permanent alliance.

content.content: In the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, of all places, Germany, France, Poland, Belgium and the Netherlands sign a treaty of mutual defense. An attack on one is an attack on all. The French premier calls it the burial of 1871 and 1919 alike. Moscow calls it a declaration of war on the Soviet Union.

e2_war_crisis.concessions.subtitle: -1 budget. The strike will end, and the war will go on.

content.content: The bread ration is raised, wages in the war industries go up by a tenth, and every war factory gets an elected works council with a say in hours and safety. The strike committee recommends a return to work, and the vote is close. The war goes on, and so do the meetings.

e2_war_home_front.press.subtitle: The republican public will approve. The right will cry censorship.

content.content: The public prosecutor charges the editors of three nationalist papers with spreading false reports likely to endanger the conduct of the war. The trial shows that one of them was paid by a foreign embassy. Nobody will ever know whether the others believed what they wrote. The story about the stab in the back stops appearing in print, though not in the beer halls.

options.title: Ration food and fuel fairly, with price controls agreed with the unions.
Ban strikes in the war industries for the duration.
Tax war profits, and give the unions seats on the supply boards.
Prosecute the stab-in-the-back agitators.

content: Bread is rationed in the cities, and the coal ration will not last the winter. The unions report that wages have fallen behind prices, and the metalworkers at Leuna have stopped work for a day.
leaflets in the factories call the war "the bosses' crusade against the workers' fatherland", and tell the workers to go slow.
's factory cells are working the night shifts, and they want the unions to have a say in how the war is run.
members are arguing with each other more than with us.

content.content: These are the cabinet's decisions, but each of them needs a majority in the Reichstag, and our votes count. The unions will also listen to us before they listen to the government.
In the nationalist press, an old story has come back: the army is fighting well, and the Reds at home are stabbing it in the back.
The nationalist press is pleased with the army and nobody else. It asks why the Republic's ministers are still in Berlin while its soldiers are at the front.

Germany abstains in Geneva and ships nothing to either side. In March, Finland signs away its eastern provinces and keeps its independence. In the Reichstag, the right asks what the Republic will do when it is Poland's turn. The government has no answer ready.

e2_world_recession.soviet.unavailableSubtitle: We cannot afford the export credit guarantees.
e2_world_recession.soviet.subtitle: -1 budget

content.content: The Reich guarantees a credit of 500 million marks for Soviet orders. Turbines from Siemens, presses from Krupp and locomotives from Henschel are all bound for the Urals. The order books fill. The Foreign Office warns that Germany is now building the factories of a power that has been massing troops on the Polish frontier, and that it will be hard to stop.

e2_world_recession.title: The World Trade Slump
e2_world_recession.subtitle: The American recession crosses the Atlantic, and the tariff walls go up.

options.title: Call a European conference for a tariff truce.
Protect German farms and factories behind higher tariffs.
Build a clearing bloc with the Danube and Balkan states.
Offer the Soviet Union long-term credit for German machinery.

content: The American recovery has collapsed. Washington cut spending too soon, the stock market fell by a third, and the orders that American firms had placed with German machine-tool makers have dried up. Europe has caught the cold.

content.content: Fear of what the Spanish example might mean has sent capital fleeing from every bourse on the continent.
The talk of war in the east has sent capital fleeing from every bourse on the continent.

content: Britain has drawn the Empire tighter behind Imperial Preference. France has raised its quotas again. Prices for German exports have fallen for nine months in a row.
The Ruhr order books are thinning, and the shipyards in Hamburg and Kiel are laying off men.
The Republic's export trade was small to begin with, and now it is shrinking fast.

content.content: The Ruhr Soviet's propaganda says that this is what capitalism always does.

content: The bourgeois press blames the socialized sector. The <span style="color: #700000;">
blames the bourgeois world market and says the solution lies to the east.

content.content: Every economist in Berlin remembers 1930, and none of them wants to see it again.
The cabinet has to decide which way to turn.
We are not in the cabinet. However, the government is divided, and our votes in the Reichstag may decide which way it turns. What should we press for?

e2c_new_right.campaign.subtitle: It costs us nothing but effort, and the Left faction will approve.

content.content: The Council in Geneva appoints a commission of a Swede, a Dutchman and a Czech, which spends six months touring the Rhineland. It finds that German democracy is "established and secure", and that the occupation no longer serves any purpose recognized in international law. France could ignore the finding, but it does not. The troops go home.
We have won a quiet victory with lawyers instead of soldiers, and the League's standing has grown with it.

content: The commission is told to keep studying. Thyssen's trustees go on running his mills, and the Ruhr's pit committees are told that they have no legal standing. The <span style="color: #700000;">
prints the 1919 report next to the new one in its newspaper; apart from the date, they say almost the same thing.

content.content: The Left and Labor factions are furious with us.

e2c_ruhr_socialization.title: Socializing the Ruhr
e2c_ruhr_socialization.subtitle: The men who paid for the putsch still own the mines.

options.title: Nationalize coal and steel, and compensate the owners in Reich bonds.
Expropriate the putsch financiers without compensation, and buy out the rest!
Co-determination only: works councils get half the seats on every board.
The economy is too fragile. Can't this wait?

content: The tribunals have shown who paid for the putsch. Fritz Thyssen of the Vereinigte Stahlwerke, the aged Emil Kirdorf and the directors of the Gelsenkirchen mining company spent millions on the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

in the years before the war. Thyssen is now in Switzerland. His mills in Duisburg are run by trustees appointed by the government, and the miners of Gelsenkirchen have been electing their own pit committees since the fighting ended.
In 1919, the first Socialization Commission, with Kautsky and Hilferding among its members, recommended placing coal under public ownership. Its report was shelved.
During the Depression, we began buying up idle enterprises

content.content: and running them with the works councils

content: , but the great Ruhr concerns are still in private hands.

Now the commission has been reconvened. The unions want coal and steel run by a public Ruhr Authority, with workers, consumers and the state sharing the board. The Center will accept co-determination, but not expropriation. The
says the putsch financiers should get nothing, and the other owners no more than the pensions paid to miners' widows.

e2c_spd_split.hold.subtitle: Requires a fairly united party.
e2c_spd_split.hold.unavailableSubtitle: The factions are too bitter to accept a compromise.

content.content: After an all-night session, Otto Wels's successors in the party executive find a formula. Foreign policy will be a matter of conscience, the parliamentary group will vote freely on treaties, and both factions keep their seats on the executive.

The party stays together. However, the Foreign Office complains that it now gets two answers to every question, and both Paris and Moscow have noticed that a German government that cannot make up its mind is easier to ignore.

e2c_spd_split.title: West or East?
e2c_spd_split.subtitle: Our party congress in Hanover is coming apart over foreign policy.

options.title: Side with Reuter and Schmid. Germany belongs with the West!
Side with the neutralists. Germany must not become anyone's frontier!
If we must split, can't we at least part amicably, and agree to govern together?
Hold the party together, and allow a free vote of conscience on foreign policy.

content.content: The party survived the barricades, the inflation and the Bredow affair. Now it may not survive the peace. For three days, the delegates at our Hanover congress have been arguing about a single question: where does Germany belong?

content: The party's right, led by Ernst Reuter and Carlo Schmid, wants Germany bound to the Western democracies

content.content: in a permanent alliance with Paris and London

content: , because they see the Soviet Union as the greatest threat to democratic socialism in Europe. The party's left, around Max Seydewitz and the trade union youth, wants Germany armed, neutral and friendly to Moscow.

content.content: They argue that the workers who won the civil war did not fight to become the junior partner of the French bankers.
They admit that French guns helped us win the civil war, but they argue that the workers did not fight so that Germany could become the junior partner of the French bankers.
The war has sharpened every argument. Each side claims its lessons, and each accuses the other of having learned nothing.
Unfortunately, both factions have printed their own ballot papers, and both have hired halls for a "continuation congress" in case they lose. What should we do?

The Foreign Office sends a polite note saying that the time is not ripe. Warsaw takes this to mean that the occupation will go on indefinitely, and begins settling Polish families on the confiscated farms of Masuria.

options.title: Sign a treaty of recognition. We will accept the losses, in exchange for minority rights and peace.
Insist on the League plebiscite! Let the people of the provinces decide.
Offer Warsaw a guarantee of neutrality, in exchange for East Prussia.
We will not sign away German land!

content: Polish governors have ruled Allenstein and Kattowitz since the civil war, under an occupation that Warsaw still calls provisional. A generation of children in Masuria has grown up learning Polish at school and German at home, and the Upper Silesian pits now send their coal to Gdynia instead of Breslau.

content.content: The demarcation line agreed in Geneva has held, and with it a cold sort of peace.
Our divisions still stand along the Oder, as they have for years, at ruinous cost.

content: However, the situation in the east has changed.

content.content: The war has shaken every government between the Baltic and the Black Sea.

content: Poland is looking anxiously at the Soviet Union, and has little appetite for a second hostile frontier in the west. Its new foreign minister has let it be known that Warsaw is ready for a final settlement, one way or another.

content.content: The League has not forgotten its promise of a plebiscite, and London is now willing to insist on it.
Strasser, our Reich Commissioner for the Lost Territories, has warned that his men will leave the cabinet if Germany "signs away one square meter".
