content.content: We have more urgent business than a crank with a pamphlet. Unfortunately, Strasser's audiences grow from hundreds to thousands, and his newspaper starts printing a list of the "November criminals" of the civil war. Many of the names on it are ours.

e2d_black_front.title: The Black Front
e2d_black_front.subtitle: Otto Strasser has come home from Prague.

title: Ban the <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">
under the Republikschutzgesetz.

options.title: Have the Prussian political police infiltrate it, and wait.
Steal their recruits with a national reconstruction drive and jobs for veterans!
Isn't this just a movement of cranks and malcontents? Ignore it.

content: Otto Strasser is back from Prague, and his <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">
is filling halls in Berlin, Stettin and Breslau. Strasser left the
in 1930 because he thought Hitler had sold out to the industrialists, and he spent the civil war in exile, writing pamphlets about a "German socialism" that would be neither Marxist nor capitalist.
The movement is a strange coalition. Former <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

men from the shattered militias march alongside Ernst Niekisch's National Bolsheviks, who left our party in the twenties, and refugees from the lost provinces. Most worrying of all, a growing number of

veterans and young trade unionists are joining—men who fought for the Republic and feel that it has given them nothing. Their program is simple: reconquer the Ruhr, expel the French and the Poles, nationalize the banks, and replace the "party state" with a corporate chamber of estates. Their black flag carries a sword and a hammer.

content.content: The refugee camps have become their recruiting grounds.

content: The political police report that <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">
cells have formed in several Reichswehr garrisons in Pomerania.

onArrival.$code:
Q['nationalism'] = (Q['nationalism'] || 0) + 2;
Q['e2d_tp'] = (Q['e2d_tp'] || 0) + 1;

content.content: We thank the ambassador for his interest. The French conscripts stay in the wine taverns of the Moselle for another winter, and the nationalists grumble.

e2d_french_withdrawal.title: The Peacekeepers Go Home?
e2d_french_withdrawal.subtitle: Paris is tired of paying for the Rhine garrison.

options.title: Invoke the Morgenthau timetable! The Ruhr is settled, and Paris must keep its word.
Offer France and Britain a defensive pact: a Rhine Pact for a new decade.

content.content: a long lease on the Saar mines
our claim to the Saar mines
control of the Saar mining board

options.title: Not now. The time isn't right.

content.content: French troops have been on the Rhine since the civil war, on a "temporary" peacekeeping mission. They are still there. Their commander lives in the Electoral Palace in Koblenz, and French customs officers inspect every barge on the river. The young conscripts posted there spend most of their time in the wine taverns of the Moselle, and more and more deputies in Paris are asking why they are there at all.

content: The French ambassador has made it clear that the mission could end, provided that France's security is guaranteed.

content.content: The Morgenthau agreement already includes a withdrawal timetable, which takes effect once the Ruhr is no longer a threat.
However, as long as a Red Army sits in Essen, the generals in Paris will say that the Rhine needs watching.
The French have also pointed out that our cabinet now includes men who have promised to "drive the French into the Rhine".
How can we get the French to leave?

e2d_polish_talks.moscow.subtitle: Requires good relations with Moscow, or with a KPD that still has Moscow's ear.
e2d_polish_talks.moscow.unavailableSubtitle: The Kremlin has no reason to do us favors.

content: Litvinov receives our ambassador with great courtesy. Within two weeks, the Red Army's maneuvers on the Polish border are larger than usual, and
carries an article about "the oppression of the German workers of Upper Silesia". Warsaw takes the hint and becomes more flexible in Geneva, though it gives nothing up.

content.content: Paris and London take the hint as well. They will not be quick to help a German government that invites the Soviet Union into Central Europe.

e2d_polish_talks.title: Talks with Warsaw
e2d_polish_talks.subtitle: Poland is prepared to discuss the occupied provinces.

options.title: Demand a complete withdrawal, and mobilize the eastern frontier!
Accept League arbitration, on condition of a plebiscite in the occupied provinces.
Accept a provisional demarcation line, in exchange for minority rights and a trade treaty.
Couldn't we ask Moscow to lean on Warsaw?

content.content: Polish troops crossed into East Prussia and Upper Silesia during the worst months of the civil war, to "protect the Polish population" from the militias. They are still there. Polish governors sit in Allenstein and Kattowitz, Polish is taught in the schools, and the zloty is the only legal currency. Warsaw says the occupation is provisional, but it keeps printing new maps.

Now Poland is prepared to talk. Since Piłsudski's death, the colonels' government has been looking for a settlement that it can present as a victory, and Foreign Minister Beck has proposed talks in Geneva, under the eyes of the League. His opening position is a permanent demarcation line in exchange for trade and minority guarantees.

The nationalists say the only acceptable line is the border of 1914, and the refugee associations want nothing signed until they can go home. Unfortunately, as the Foreign Office points out, we have no army capable of making anyone leave anywhere. What should we do?

content: On a single Sunday, from Aachen to the Oder

, Germans vote on whether to live in one Republic. Eighty-four percent say yes. The Ruhr votes seventy-nine percent in favor, and the Moselle valley ninety. Even in the old Red Army strongholds of Herne and Bottrop, a clear majority supports the Republic.

content.content: No general and no assembly made this decision. The people made it, and nobody can say otherwise. The Republic that comes out of the Weimar Assembly has a legitimacy that the Republic of 1919 never had.

onArrival.$code: Q['kpd_relation'] = (Q['kpd_relation'] || 0) - 2;

content.content: The government waits. The Ruhr Soviet does not collapse. It keeps going, more slowly each year, like a clock nobody has wound.

e2d_ruhr_endgame.title: The Last Red Army
e2d_ruhr_endgame.subtitle: The Ruhr Soviet is running out of time.

options.title: A general amnesty and a place in the Republic for every fighter who lays down his arms.
Offer the miners' union the autonomy statute: a self-governing Ruhr with public mines.
Send in the army and end it.
Wait for the Soviet to collapse on its own.

content.content: The Ruhr Soviet has outlived almost everyone's predictions, but it cannot last much longer. Soviet supplies, once smuggled in through Rotterdam, have dried up as Moscow turns its attention to the east. The pits are worked out at the shallow levels, and nobody has money to sink new shafts. The young men of Essen leave over the Lippe line at night to find work in Hanover. The Central Council has split. One faction wants to fight to the last pithead, and the other, led by the miners' union, is quietly sending messages to Berlin.
The amnesty of the late thirties emptied the Red Army's ranks once already. Those who stayed are the hard core.
Strasser's men in the cabinet want the Ruhr retaken by force, and they want the Central Council hanged.
It may be possible to bring the Ruhr home without another battle, but it will probably be the last chance to do so.
The delegation goes home empty-handed. In Essen, the hardliners on the Central Council say they told everyone so.

e2d_ruhr_settlement.title: The Ruhr Statute
e2d_ruhr_settlement.subtitle: Essen is ready to talk about the future of the Ruhr.

options.title: Grant the autonomy statute. The Ruhr comes home on its own terms.
Offer an amnesty to every fighter who hands in his rifle.
The Red Army is weaker than ever. Finish it.
We are not ready. Send the delegation home.

content: The Ruhr Red Army is older and more tired than it was. The miners who took up rifles in the civil war are now in their forties, with families. Soviet arms come through Rotterdam less often, and the Central Council in Essen has to ration electricity.

content.content: The offensive of the early years is still remembered in every street of Herne and Gelsenkirchen, and so are its dead.
The ceasefire signed at Haltern has held, more or less, and the coal trains still run.

A delegation from Essen has come to Berlin under a safe-conduct. Its leader is a white-haired union official who was a Social Democrat until 1919. He says the council will consider a settlement. The Ruhr would become an autonomous Land within the Republic, with its mines in public ownership and its Red Army reorganized as a Land police. The generals reply that no German state can tolerate a private army of Bolsheviks. They want an amnesty for the rank and file, a tribunal for the leaders, and every rifle handed in.

onArrival.$code:
Q['e2k_prince'] = "wait";
Q['e2k_parliament'] = (Q['e2k_parliament'] || 0) + 3;

content.content: We neither cheer nor oppose. The regent governs cautiously, and the court party gets time to regroup.

e2k_prince.title: The Prince from Detroit
e2k_prince.subtitle: The Emperor is ill, and his heir has ideas.

content.content: Back the regent's reforms, and make them law.
Back the regent's reforms from outside the Reichstag.

options.title: The monarchy is weak. Push for a republic.
Wait and see what the prince actually does.

content.content: Wilhelm III has suffered a stroke, and his son Louis Ferdinand has been named regent. The prince is not like the rest of his family. As a young man he worked on the assembly line at Ford's plant in Detroit, and he likes to say that he is the only Hohenzollern who has ever drawn a wage. He has let it be known that he would govern "with the Reichstag, not against it".
In the working-class districts, people have started to ask whether Germany needs a regent at all.
For the first time in years, the Social Democratic press writes about a Hohenzollern without contempt.

subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
will cheer, but the middle classes and the Reformist faction will be alarmed. (+2 budget)
unavailableSubtitle: could carry a measure this harsh through the cabinet, and it is not close enough to us to try.

content.content: The criminal police raid the villas of Grunewald and Dahlem at dawn. Forty bankers and industrialists are charged with currency offenses under the emergency decrees, and their foreign holdings are seized for the Treasury.

content: The working-class districts cheer, and the <span style="color: #700000;">

's newspapers run photographs of directors in handcuffs. Unfortunately, the middle classes are frightened, and some of them are turning to the nationalists. Abroad, the arrests confirm every warning that Germany has fallen to the Bolsheviks.

e2l_bankers_strike.title: The Bankers' Strike
e2l_bankers_strike.subtitle: Gold is leaving Germany by the trainload...

options.title: Impose exchange controls, and put the Reichsbank under the cabinet.
Reassure the markets: there will be no expropriation without compensation.
Why not let the bank employees' councils watch the vaults?
Arrest the currency smugglers and seize their foreign holdings!

content.content: Capital has been leaving Germany ever since the United Front came to power, and the trickle has now become a flood. Every night the express train to Basel carries attaché cases full of bearer bonds, and the Reichsbank's gold and foreign-exchange reserves have fallen by a third over the past year. The big Berlin banks have quietly frozen new credit to firms with works councils "of a political character", and the stock exchange is in a slump.

content: The bourgeois press treats it as a vote of no confidence in our government. To the <span style="color: #700000;">
has printed the names of bank directors whose families have suddenly taken long holidays in Zürich and Amsterdam.

content.content: Our own economists are divided. Some want to stop the bleeding with exchange controls. Others warn that if a socialist government locks the vaults in its first crisis, nobody will ever trust it with their savings again.
What should we do about the flight of capital?

e2l_blocs.west.subtitle: Our economy will grow, but the Left faction will be furious.

content.content: Washington and London do not trust us enough to offer aid.

content: The Front is too close to the <span style="color: #700000;">
for us to accept American money.

content.content: The Marshall dollars come with conditions: a balanced budget, an open door for American exports, and an assurance that no more industries will be socialized. We accept the first two and fudge the third. Grain ships unload at Hamburg, and new rolling mills are built with American credit.

content: walks out of the cabinet for a week.

content.content: The party's former Communists walk out of the parliamentary group for a week.

content: Our Left faction is furious, and quotes Rosa Luxemburg on imperialism. However, most workers are simply glad of the bread, and the Reformists are pleased.

e2l_blocs.title: Between the Blocs
e2l_blocs.subtitle: Moscow and Washington both want an answer...

options.title: Join the Eastern bloc and its Council for Mutual Economic Assistance.
Build a neutral bloc with Belgrade, Stockholm and New Delhi.
Break with Moscow, as Belgrade has, and take the third path!
Accept Marshall aid and lean toward the West.

content.content: The world is dividing into two camps, and both of them want Germany. In Washington, the Marshall Plan is pouring dollars into France, Italy and the Low Countries, and its administrators have let it be known that a socialist Germany could also share in it, "subject to appropriate guarantees". In Moscow, the Cominform has summoned the communist parties of Europe to close ranks, and a Council for Mutual Economic Assistance is being formed to plan the economies of the East as one. A German seat is waiting at its table.

Meanwhile, Tito's Yugoslavia, once the most loyal of Moscow's allies, has been expelled from the Cominform for its independence—and has survived. Tito's envoys are now in Berlin, as are envoys from Nehru's India and from the Swedish Social Democrats. They propose a third path: a league of neutral states, socialist and democratic, that belongs to neither bloc.
For the Party, this should be no question at all: our place is in the socialist camp. However, there are some, even in the Party's leadership, who look at Belgrade and wonder.

content: demands that we join the socialist camp. Our trade unionists want the dollars, and the councils want to be left alone.

content.content: The former Communists in our own party demand that we join the socialist camp. Our trade unionists want the dollars, and the councils want to be left alone.

subtitle: A risky gamble against the <span style="color: #700000;">
's apparatus.

content: protests that constitutions are not made by "petty-bourgeois plebiscites", but it cannot be seen to fear the people. The vote is held in

content.content: The result is decisive: the voters choose the Council Republic, with a Workers' Chamber beside the Reichstag.
The result is decisive: the voters choose a parliamentary republic with a socialized economy.

content: accepts the result with very bad grace, and its grip on the state weakens as its allies in the unions and the militia see the figures.

's apparatus has done its work in the factories and the villages, and the people's democracy wins the vote. Our campaign was outspent and outmaneuvered by our own allies. Our Reformist faction is furious.

e2l_convention.title: The Constitutional Convention
e2l_convention.subtitle: What kind of socialist republic should we build?

options.title: The Council Republic: all power to the councils—and to the Reichstag too!
A parliamentary republic with a socialized economy.
A people's democracy under the leadership of the workers' parties.
Why not put the question to the people in a referendum?

content.content: The putsch has swept away the last defenders of the old order, and many of us believe the Weimar constitution should go with them. Its Article 48 gave the President power against the Reichstag, its courts let the murderers of Rosa Luxemburg go free, and its army nearly overthrew us. The Front has called a Constitutional Convention to Weimar, in the same National Theater where the old constitution was written in 1919.

The Compromise of the Wilhelmstraße has shaken the country and humiliated the Front. Our only answer is to go forward. Despite the generals' furious objections, the Reichstag has voted to call a Constitutional Convention to Weimar, in the same National Theater where the old constitution was written in 1919.
There are three drafts before the delegates:

The first, drawn up by the council movement and our left wing, would create a Council Republic. A Workers' Chamber, elected through the factory, farm and office councils, would share sovereignty with the Reichstag and run the socialized economy.

The second, written by our constitutional lawyers in the tradition of Hugo Preuss and Hermann Heller, would keep a sovereign parliament elected by universal suffrage, with a socialized economy and works councils inside the factories.

content: The third, tabled by the <span style="color: #700000;">
, would establish a "people's democracy". The leading role of the workers' parties would be written into the constitution, and candidates would stand on a single National Front list.
and its allies hold the commanding positions in the convention, the trade unions and the militia. It will be very hard to deny them.

content.content: We are still the larger party in the convention, but no draft can pass without allies.
Which constitution should we fight for?

e2l_conspiracy.ignore.subtitle: Our Left faction will not be happy.

content.content: The lieutenant is thanked and sent back to his unit. Three weeks later, he is transferred to a garrison in East Prussia. The Interior Ministry's file on the matter is marked "no further action", and our Left faction is uneasy.

e2l_conspiracy.title: Whispers in the Bendlerblock
e2l_conspiracy.subtitle: A lieutenant asks to speak to the Interior Minister...

options.title: Arrest the officers he named, tonight!
Quietly put the militias on alert, and move arms into the factories.
Warn the generals publicly that we are watching them.
This is just officers' gossip. Thank the lieutenant and send him home.

content: spring, a young lieutenant from the staff of Wehrkreis III in Berlin has come to the Interior Ministry with a frightening story. He says that senior officers have been meeting in private houses in Potsdam and Grunewald with <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
leaders, Ruhr industrialists and two deputies of the

. He has seen movement orders for the Döberitz garrison that make no sense for an exercise. He also says that the name "Kapp" came up, and that one of the officers promised that this time they would not repeat Kapp's mistakes.
The Prussian political police have heard similar stories for months, and

content.content: our purge of the officer corps evidently did not catch everyone
our agreement with General von Fritsch now looks much less reassuring
several of our regimental commissars have reported officers holding meetings to which they were not invited
the officers we discharged have clearly not been idle
the officer corps has never accepted the United Front

content: . However, the lieutenant has no documents, and the generals he named are respected men. If we move against them and they turn out to be innocent, the bourgeois parties will have the scandal of the decade.

e2l_embargo.neutrals.subtitle: A modest loss of growth, but we will not depend on London or Moscow.

content.content: The neutral governments regard us as a Soviet satellite, and will not take the risk.
Without strong cooperative trading councils, we have no partners to deal with the cooperative movements abroad.

The councils' wholesale cooperatives sign contracts with their counterparts in Sweden, Denmark and Czechoslovakia, while the Foreign Ministry negotiates barter deals with Mexico and Argentina: steel rails for copper and hides.
It is not enough to replace the British market, but it is enough to keep the factories open. We have shown that a socialist Germany doesn't need to be anybody's satellite.

e2l_embargo.title: The Embargo
e2l_embargo.subtitle: London and Paris close their ports to German goods...

options.title: Compensate the foreign shareholders in Reich bonds.
Sign a long-term trade agreement with the Soviet Union.
We'll tighten our belts: rationing and self-reliance through the councils.
Redirect our trade to the neutrals: Scandinavia, Czechoslovakia and Latin America.

content: The foreign shareholders of the socialized mines and banks have waited five years for compensation, and the City of London has run out of patience.

content.content: Our people's democracy has convinced the British and French governments that Germany is now a Soviet outpost on the Rhine.
Our Council Republic has convinced the British and French governments that the revolution will not stop at the German border.
Even our parliamentary constitution has not convinced the British and French governments that German socialism can be trusted.

This week, Britain and France announced an embargo on German manufactures and a freeze on German balances in London and Paris, "until such time as the property of British and French nationals is restored or justly compensated". The Netherlands and Belgium are expected to follow.

content: Our exports to the West, which still pay for most of our copper, rubber and cotton, will fall by half. The Ruhr has plenty of coal, but not enough of anything else. The <span style="color: #700000;">
says this is the moment to turn east. However, our trade unionists in the export industries of Saxony and Württemberg say that their members cannot eat slogans.

content.content: How should we answer the embargo?

e2l_coup.everything.subtitle: Our best chance of crushing the putsch.

content.content: The councils are not strong enough to bring the whole country out.
Our militias do not command the streets.
Too few army units can be relied upon.

onArrival.$code: Q['e2l_coup_response'] = "everything";

subtitle: The army and police will be more loyal, but the <span style="color: #700000;">
and our Left faction will be furious.
e2l_militia.disband.unavailableSubtitle: Neither the police nor the army is reliable enough to be trusted with a monopoly of force.

content: Both formations are dissolved by decree, and their weapons are collected into police armories. The <span style="color: #c00000;">
hands in its rifles. The Red Front Fighters hand in perhaps half of theirs.

The generals send a note of appreciation, and the foreign press praises our "return to normal civic life". However, in the working-class districts, people are asking who will defend us now, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
and our Left faction are furious.

e2l_militia.title: The People's Militia
e2l_militia.subtitle: Two armies of the working class, or one?

options.title: Merge them into a People's Militia under the Interior Ministry.
Merge them under a joint command, with parity between the two parties.
Keep them separate, coordinated by joint committees.
Disband both, and strengthen the regular police.

content: On paper, the working class has two armies. Our own <span style="color: #c00000;">

content.content: lost much of its old membership, though its core remains

content: and a long memory of street fights with the Communists. The

's fighting league, is smaller and far more militant, and until recently it called our people "social fascists". Since the United Front took power, the two have marched side by side. However, their quartermasters still keep separate armories.
proposes to merge both into a single People's Militia under a joint command. The

leadership under Karl Höltermann will only accept a merger if the Interior Ministry commands it—and the Interior Ministry is ours. The Reichswehr, for its part, has let it be known that it regards any "second army" as an intolerable provocation.

content.content: What should we do with the workers' formations?

subtitle: This could split the <span style="color: #700000;">
, and Moscow will not forgive us.
unavailableSubtitle: We have no friends inside the <span style="color: #700000;">
who would dare to break with Moscow.

content: We give the refugees shelter, and we let the <span style="color: #700000;">
's doubters know that a break with Moscow would not cost them their ministries.
The Conciliators who lead the party seize the moment. At a stormy Central Committee meeting they reject the Comintern's "advice", throw its representative out of the building and declare that the
will follow "the German road to socialism". The Moscow loyalists walk out, taking a fifth of the membership with them.
The party leadership does not break with Moscow, but it does bend. A sizeable group of <span style="color: #700000;">
functionaries now owes its safety to us rather than to the Comintern, and the party's line in the cabinet has become noticeably more flexible.
's working-class voters have come over to us in the confusion.

e2l_moscow.title: Moscow's Shadow
e2l_moscow.subtitle: Refugees from the purges knock at our door...

options.title: We will grant them asylum openly, and refuse every extradition!
Grant them asylum quietly, but bar them from political activity.
Hand over the people on Moscow's list. We can't let the Front break over this.

title: Shelter the refugees, and help the <span style="color: #700000;">
's independent wing break with the Comintern.

content: The purges in Moscow have reached the German Communists. In the Hotel Lux, where the Comintern houses its foreign cadres, German Communists are being taken away at night—veterans of the Hamburg rising of 1923, editors and printers from the party press, couriers of the party's old illegal apparatus. Some have managed to get out. Heinz Neumann and Margarete Buber-Neumann arrived in Berlin last week with one suitcase between them, and with a story that the
's newspapers have refused to print. Others are following them: Mensheviks, Left Oppositionists, a Ukrainian poet, and a Comintern cipher clerk who claims to know a great deal.
The Soviet embassy has presented us with a list of "Trotskyist terrorists and Gestapo agents" and expects their extradition as a matter of socialist solidarity.
The Comintern has also made it clear that the
's place in the cabinet depends on its "vigilance". The
ministers said almost nothing during the cabinet discussion, and at least one of them is visibly afraid.

, which broke with Moscow before the purges began, wants the refugees protected. However, Moscow's loyalists outside it are holding rallies for "vigilance", and the embassy has made it clear that our trade with the Soviet Union depends on our answer.

e2l_officers.cut.subtitle: The workers' militias will grow, but the army will be resentful, and the nationalists will be furious. (+1 budget)

content: Twenty thousand men are discharged, the cavalry is all but abolished, and the money goes to rifles, uniforms and training camps for the <span style="color: #c00000;">
and the workers' formations. Geneva welcomes a rare act of German disarmament.

content.content: Unfortunately, the officers who remain feel humiliated and surrounded. The discharged men are drifting into veterans' associations, which the police have started to watch.

e2l_officers.title: The Officers' Question
e2l_officers.subtitle: The Bendlerblock salutes, but does not obey...

options.title: Retire the old guard, and promote republican officers.
Attach political commissars from both workers' parties to every regiment.
Accept the generals' offer, and leave the army alone.
Why not cut the army to the bone, and put the money into the militias?

content.content: The Reichswehr has never served a government like ours. Its officers learned their trade under Seeckt, who taught them that the army stood "above politics"—by which he meant above the Republic. They still toast the Kaiser in the officers' mess at Potsdam. Now they are being asked to salute a cabinet with Communist ministers in it, and they do so very stiffly.

content: The Defense Ministry has given us a list of three hundred officers whose loyalty it considers "doubtful". The <span style="color: #700000;">
has given us a list of three thousand. The generals, for their part, have sent word through intermediaries: if we leave the army to the soldiers, the soldiers will leave politics to the politicians.

content.content: What should we do about the officer corps?

subtitle: This will split the <span style="color: #700000;">
and enrage Moscow.
unavailableSubtitle: We do not have the strength in the militia or the army to risk a confrontation with the <span style="color: #700000;">

content: We present the cabinet with the files:

content.content: the NKVD liaison office at the Alexanderplatz,

content: the secret party apparatus inside the militia that still reports to Moscow, and the lists. The Interior Ministry dismisses three hundred officials in a single night, and the militia's political department is dissolved.
Ulbricht and his closest associates are expelled from the Front, and Ulbricht is on a plane to Moscow by morning. The <span style="color: #700000;">
splits. Its Moscow loyalists go into furious opposition, while the rest, under leaders who have had enough of the Comintern, stay in the government as an independent communist party.
The Moscow men who stayed inside the <span style="color: #700000;">
's apparatus after the split are expelled from the Front, and several of them are on a plane to Moscow by morning. The
leadership stays in the government, but it is bitter that we acted without consulting it, and many of its members have left in disgust.

content.content: Many workers have come over to us, and the Reformist faction is pleased. However, the purge has shaken the country.

e2l_unity_party.title: One Party of the Working Class?
subtitle: The <span style="color: #700000;">
proposes a merger...

options.title: Accept the merger. One Socialist Unity Party!
Unity, but on democratic terms: open factions, secret ballots and no Leninist statute.
Two parties, one Front. We must decline the merger.
Break the Moscow faction's hold on the Front once and for all!

content.content: One Party of the Working Class?
The war is over, and the United Front has survived it.
Germany has kept out of the wars of the forties, and the United Front has outlasted every prediction of its collapse.

content: After twelve years of governing together, the old lines between the two workers' parties have blurred. Many workers belong to a council, a cooperative, a militia battalion and a trade union, all of them run jointly by the <span style="color: #c00000;">

content.content: Now Wilhelm Pieck and Walter Ulbricht have proposed that the two parties merge into a single Socialist Unity Party, with joint chairmen, parity on every committee, and a program built on "the principles of Marxism-Leninism".

content: Now the Conciliators who have led the <span style="color: #700000;">

since its break with Moscow have proposed that the two parties merge into a single Socialist Unity Party, with joint chairmen, parity on every committee, and a program built on "the principles of Marxism-Leninism".

Some of our own people are tempted. Otto Grotewohl in Brunswick says that the split of 1917 was the great tragedy of the German labor movement, and that it is time to heal it. However, Kurt Schumacher, who lost an arm at the front, warns
that a party built on democratic centralism will swallow Social Democracy whole.

's people already hold the security services, the militia command and most of the great councils. Many of our own district secretaries have been told, discreetly, that their careers depend on supporting the merger.
We are still the larger party, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
cannot force the merger on us. However, refusing outright could wreck the Front.

content.content: We tell our people to wait. The regime goes on decaying, more slowly than we hoped.

options.title: Negotiate a transition with the regime's reformers.
Call a general strike for a free election.
Let the regime decay further before we move.

content: Franz von Papen is dead, and nobody in the New State knows who should succeed him. Students march in Berlin and Breslau for a constitution, the illegal unions call stoppages in the Ruhr, and the regime's own ministers have started meeting the underground's representatives in hotel rooms.

content.content: The generals who rule beside the civilian cabinet are divided.
Our people are ready, or as ready as they will ever be. The question is how we use the moment.

Henschel buys the Z3 and Zuse's time. The machine computes wing tolerances for guided missiles and bombers, and the results are stamped "Secret". The rest of Germany hears nothing more about calculating machines for some time.

e2u_computing.title: The Calculating Machine
e2u_computing.subtitle: An engineer in Kreuzberg has built a machine that follows a program.

options.title: Commission a machine for the Statistical Office and the economic ministries.
Fund Schreyer's electronic machine at the Technical University.
Stick with Hollerith. The punched cards work.
Let Henschel keep Zuse for aircraft design.

content.content: In a back room in the Methfesselstraße in Kreuzberg, behind his parents' flat, a thirty-year-old civil engineer named Konrad Zuse has built a machine out of 2,600 telephone relays. It reads its instructions from punched film, cinema stock bought second-hand. It works in binary and handles floating-point numbers, and it can do a multiplication in three seconds. Zuse calls it the Z3. It is, as far as anyone can tell, the first machine in the world that can be programmed to carry out any calculation without a human hand on the crank.

He built it because he was bored. His day job is computing wing-flutter tables for the Henschel aircraft works, and he grew tired of doing the same sums by hand. His friend Helmut Schreyer, at the Technical University, thinks the relays are too slow. Schreyer wants to build the next machine from radio valves, which could make it a thousand times faster.

content: Most of the officials who come to see it are unimpressed. The Statistical Office of the Reich runs on punched-card machines from Dehomag, which is the German subsidiary of IBM, and its president says Hollerith machines do everything a government needs.

content.content: The Planning Office does not agree. Its economists are drowning in production tables, and they want to know whether Zuse's machine could balance a national plan in days instead of months.
The Economics Ministry's statisticians think differently. They have been trying for years to forecast the business cycle, and their best model takes a room full of clerks six weeks to run.

content: Henschel has asked whether the next machine can be built for the aircraft works, and no one else.

content.content: The Reich will license toll roads but not build them. Hesse and Baden sign concessions with a consortium of banks and cement makers for the stretch from Frankfurt to Heidelberg. It will cost a driver two marks to use it, which is an afternoon's wages for a bricklayer.

e2u_autobahn.title: The Motorway Question
e2u_autobahn.subtitle: Roads for cars that nobody can afford, or cars for roads that nobody has built?

onArrival.$code:

options.title: Build the motorways as a public works program.
Back the people's car first. Roads will follow the drivers.
The railway comes first. Electrify the Reichsbahn instead.
Leave it to the HaFraBa, the Länder and private toll companies.

content: For nine years the HaFraBa association has been drawing the same line on the same map: a road for motor cars alone, without crossings or carts or cattle, running from the Hanseatic ports through Frankfurt to Basel. Its managing director, Willy Hof, has lobbied every Chancellor since Marx. In 1932 Konrad Adenauer opened a twenty-kilometer "Kraftwagenstraße" between Cologne and Bonn, and it has been full of sightseers every Sunday since.

content.content: Half of the HaFraBa's route now runs through French-patrolled Rhineland and the Ruhr Soviet, so Hof has redrawn it to run from Hamburg through Hanover to Berlin.

content: The engineers have found allies. Ferdinand Porsche in Stuttgart and Josef Ganz, the editor of

, have both built prototypes of a small car that a skilled worker could buy for under a thousand marks. Ganz's little "May Beetle" has already logged thousands of test kilometers on the roads of the Taunus. Neither man has the capital to build it in numbers.
Julius Dorpmüller of the Reichsbahn is firmly against the whole idea. He says the railway carries Germany, and a motorway is a toy for doctors and industrialists.

content.content: In the Reich Planning Office, the economists ask whether a socialist country should be pouring concrete for private motor cars at all.
The Labour Ministry sees something else: tens of thousands of jobs that need nothing more than shovels and gravel.
The Labour Ministry sees something else: demobilized men who need work and roads that need rebuilding.

Refrigerators, radios and washing machines join coal and steel in the national plan. Every household goes on a waiting list run by the local council. The lists are fair, and they are long. The jokes about them are already being told in the beer halls.

e2u_consumer.title: The Things People Want
e2u_consumer.subtitle: Refrigerators, radios and a little car in front of the door.

onArrival.$code:

options.title: Consumer credit through the public savings banks.
Back the cooperatives: appliances sold at cost.
Exports first, consumption later.
Put consumer goods into the national plan, allocated by the councils.

content: The queue outside the AEG showroom on the Kurfürstendamm starts forming at six in the morning. In the window there is a white enamel refrigerator, priced at 480 marks, which is three months' wages for a fitter. Most of the people in the queue cannot afford it. They have come to look at it.

content.content: Outside, the people's cars are parked nose to tail along the curb, and the city has painted its first parking bays.
In the shop next door a television set is showing the afternoon program, and a crowd of schoolboys has gathered on the pavement to watch.

content: , the German worker wants what the American worker already has: a radio in every home, a refrigerator in every kitchen, a washing machine in the cellar and a holiday by the sea. Market research, a new science imported from Chicago, says that six households in ten would buy a refrigerator tomorrow if they could pay for it in instalments.

Opinions are divided on what to do about it. The savings banks want to lend. The cooperative movement wants to sell at cost through its six thousand shops, cutting out the middleman. The Reichsbank wants the factories to export first and earn hard currency before Germans start spending.

content.content: The Planning Office has drawn up a consumer goods plan of its own: a refrigerator for every household on the waiting list by 1952, allocated by the councils.
With the Ruhr's steel out of reach, every refrigerator made in the Republic uses sheet steel that the reconstruction program also wants.

content: The Workers' Radio League receives the license. The viewing rooms are to be in union halls, and the program councils will be elected in the factories. The <span style="color: #700000;">
is delighted, because it has half the league's branch secretaries. Our own people are less delighted, for the same reason.

e2u_television.title: Pictures Through the Air
e2u_television.subtitle: The Reichspost wants to know who will own television.

onArrival.$code:

options.title: A public broadcaster, with a board drawn from the parties, the unions and the churches.
Fund public viewing rooms in every large city, so that everyone can watch the Games.
License private stations, paid for by advertising.
Give the screens to the workers' radio movement and the councils.

content.content: Since March, the "Paul Nipkow" transmitter at the Witzleben radio tower has been sending out ninety minutes of pictures three evenings a week. It is named after the Pomeranian engineer who patented the scanning disc in 1884 and who now, aged seventy-five, is an honorary member of everything. The images have 180 lines. They flicker, and they are about the size of a postcard. A few hundred enthusiasts in Berlin watch them on home-built sets, and anyone can see them for free in the Reichspost's new public viewing rooms, the first of them in the Postal Museum on the Leipziger Straße.

content: The engineers are not satisfied with that. Manfred von Ardenne has shown an all-electronic picture tube, and Telefunken and Fernseh AG are racing to build a receiver that a family could afford.

content.content: The Reichspost has promised to broadcast the coming Olympic Games live from the stadium, which no country has ever done.
Next summer's Olympic Games will not be in Berlin, so the Reichspost wants to film the athletes' send-off at the Lustgarten instead, to show the world the Republic still has something to broadcast.

content: The real question is who will own the medium. The Postal Ministry believes it owns all signals in the ether. The Reich Broadcasting Company, with its board of civil servants, thinks television is just radio with pictures. The electrical trusts want to sell sets and advertising, as the Americans do.

content.content: The workers' radio clubs, which built half the receivers in Berlin themselves, want the councils to run it.

content: Our own people remember how the old radio supervisory boards kept the <span style="color: #c00000;">

content.content: The referendum carries comfortably! The President signs the law with obvious reluctance, and the new Constitutional Court owes its existence to a direct vote of the German people. Our campaign has won us new support among both workers and white-collar employees, and the Left faction is delighted.

We introduce the Selbert draft as a private member's bill, and it is voted down. Then the letters begin to arrive at the Reichstag—from women's associations, from works councils, from individual wives and widows—until the post office has to deliver them by the sackload.

content: No government can ignore this forever. Our campaign has won us support among white-collar voters, though the

e2w_civil_code.title: Equal in Principle
e2w_civil_code.subtitle: The constitution says men and women are equal. The Civil Code disagrees.

options.title: Enact the Selbert draft in full!
Repeal the "double earner" law and give wives control of their own earnings, but leave the rest of family law alone.
Not now. Can we really afford a fight with the bishops?
We are in opposition, but we can take the draft to the country.

content: Article 109 of the constitution states that men and women have "in principle the same civic rights and duties".

content.content: However, the Civil Code of 1900 was never brought into line with it.

Our reforms of marriage, divorce and inheritance law in the crisis years were a start. However, they were passed as separate amendments, one at a time and against fierce Catholic opposition, and the core of the Civil Code of 1900 survived them.
A husband still has the final say in "all matters of married life". He administers his wife's property and keeps the income from it, and he can give notice

Our reforms struck out the husband's final say in "all matters of married life", but they never reached the law of marital property. A husband still administers his wife's property and keeps the income from it, and he can still give notice

content: on her employment contract if he decides that it harms the household. A mother cannot even sign her own child's school enrollment form. Furthermore, the law of 1932 that allows married women civil servants to be dismissed as "double earners" is still in force, and has cost tens of thousands of teachers and post office clerks their jobs.
Twenty years after German women first voted, the women of our party have run out of patience.

content.content: Marie Juchacz and the Kassel lawyer Elisabeth Selbert have
The Kassel lawyer Elisabeth Selbert has

content: drafted a complete revision of family law: no final say for the husband, shared ownership of property acquired during the marriage, joint parental authority, and the repeal of the 1932 law.

content.content: The women's committees of the liberal parties support the draft, and the Catholic women's associations support parts of it. Unfortunately, the bishops are completely opposed; last Sunday, a pastoral letter read from the pulpits warned against "the dissolution of the Christian family by legislative decree".

options.title: The Republic has fallen.

content.content: Unfortunately, it is not enough. The army holds firm, the resistance crumbles in the provinces, and by the end of the week the trains are running again under military guard. Many of our leaders are arrested at the Inselstraße; others escape across the Czech border.
The committee report is noted and filed.
We vote with the small parties against every proposal, and the committee report is filed away.

content: The small parties send us letters of thanks, and even the <span style="color: #700000;">
approves. However, the Reichstag remains as fragmented as ever, and every coalition will be as hard to form as the last.

e2w_electoral.title: The Splinter Problem
e2w_electoral.subtitle: Should we reform the electoral law?

options.title: Introduce a 5% threshold.
Introduce personalized proportional representation, with constituency deputies.
Why not first-past-the-post, on the British model?
Leave the electoral law alone. Every vote should count!

content: The Weimar electoral law is the purest system of proportional representation in the world. Every 60,000 votes earn a seat, wherever they are cast,

content.content: and there is no threshold at all.
and only the 5% threshold from our constitutional reform keeps the smallest parties out.

content: In 1928, it filled the Reichstag with fifteen parties—among them the Reich Party of the German Middle Class, the Christian-National Peasants' and Farmers' Party, and the People's Justice Party, which existed to fight for the victims of the inflation. In the crisis years, it gave the extremists a platform from their very first percent.

content.content: The Reichstag committee on electoral reform has finally reported. It offers three options. The first is a threshold: no seats for any party that wins less than 5% nationally, unless it wins a constituency outright. The second is a "personalized" system, with half the deputies elected in single-member constituencies and the rest from party lists, so that the result stays proportional. The third, favored by a few Anglophiles in every party, is to elect the whole Reichstag in single-member constituencies on the British model, and let the largest party govern alone.

content: The small parties are in uproar.
Some of our own strategists have noticed that under the British system, the <span style="color: #c00000;">
would win an outright majority at the next election.

content.content: Under the British system, everything would depend on whether the bourgeois parties could agree on a single candidate in each seat. They have never managed it before.
Since we already have a threshold, only the other options are on the table.

content: We have decided that the Republic is strong enough to tolerate its enemies, and that a ban would only make martyrs of them. The
wins seats on town councils and provincial assemblies from Hanover to Schleswig-Holstein, and its gray shirts are becoming a common sight at war memorials on Sunday mornings.

e2w_far_right.title: The National Democrats
e2w_far_right.subtitle: A new party of the far-right is filling the halls the Nazis left empty.

title: Ask the courts to ban the <span style="color: #D79E2A;">
under the Law for the Protection of the Republic.

options.title: Fight them in the open—in the streets, the press and the meeting halls!
Dissolve the party by emergency decree, before it grows any further!
Banning parties is what dictatorships do. Give them enough rope.

content: never recovered from the 1930s. Its leaders discredited themselves, its funders went back to the bourgeois parties, and what was left of it dwindled into a sect.
However, the men who marched with it did not vanish. Many of them are now in their thirties and forties, with jobs and families—and a grievance that has never quite gone away.
Now they have found a new home. The National Democratic Party of Germany, the <span style="color: #D79E2A;">

, was founded last year in Hanover by a group of former Nazi functionaries, Freikorps veterans and a handful of disillusioned conservatives. Its leader, Werner Naumann, was once a rising star in Goebbels's propaganda office, but he is careful never to mention Hitler. Instead, he speaks of "national renewal", "the betrayal of 1918" and "Germany for the Germans".

content.content: The war has given him a new audience among embittered veterans and the families of the fallen.
The rising cost of living has given him an audience.

content: The party's meetings are packed, and its stewards wear gray shirts that look suspiciously like the old brown ones.
The Interior Ministry has a thick file on the <span style="color: #D79E2A;">
: secret membership lists, links to the old
networks, and an "intelligence service" that collects the home addresses of our party officials.

content.content: Our lawyers believe that the Constitutional Court would ban the party as an enemy of the constitution.
Unfortunately, the Staatsgerichtshof has never banned a political party, and nobody is sure whether it even can.

e2w_judiciary.independence.subtitle: The Left faction will be angry.

content: The cabinet issues a statement deploring the Breslau verdict, and affirming its respect for the independence of the courts. The
Unfortunately, our members in Silesia feel abandoned, and the Left faction is angry. The <span style="color: #700000;">
is quick to point out that Social Democratic ministers have been "respecting" these courts for eighteen years.

content.content: Without the Reich, we do what we can from the town halls. Social Democratic councils in Berlin, Frankfurt, Hamburg and Magdeburg pool their borrowing and buy land on the edges of their cities.

content: It is only a fraction of what the country needs. Still, every new estate shows the voters what an <span style="color: #c00000;">
government in the Reich could do.

e2w_housing.title: Light, Air and Sun
e2w_housing.subtitle: A million families still live in the courtyards of the Mietskasernen.

options.title: Adopt the Wagner plan! A Reich housing program, paid for by reviving the house-interest tax.
Lend cheap Reich credit to the union building societies, and leave the rest to the market.
Give the private builders the tax breaks the liberals want.
We are not in the government, but we can build from the town halls we hold.

content: Before the crash, we built. The house-interest tax on pre-war property paid for Bruno Taut's horseshoe estate in Britz, for Ernst May's "New Frankfurt", and for the white terraces of Onkel Toms Hütte in Zehlendorf. Two million new dwellings went up between 1924 and 1930, with bathrooms, balconies and windows that faced the sun.

content.content: Then Brüning's decrees diverted the tax to plug the budget,
Then the Depression came, and the tax was diverted to plug the Reich budget;

content: the cranes stopped, and the building trades sank to the highest unemployment rate of any industry in Germany.

content.content: Unfortunately, the recovery has not reached them. In the working-class districts of Berlin, families of six still share two rooms off a dark rear courtyard, and the tuberculosis wards are full. Martin Wagner, Berlin's former city architect, has sent us a memorandum that is half engineering report and half sermon: 300,000 dwellings a year, built by the municipalities and the cooperatives, on land bought before the speculators can get to it.

The Reich Finance Ministry has done the arithmetic, and does not like it. The liberals would rather give tax breaks to private builders and let the market do the rest. Meanwhile, the trade unions' building societies, DEWOG and GEHAG, say they can start tomorrow if someone lends them the money.
The pits and furnaces of the Ruhr go cold for nine days. Our Reichstag deputies join the pickets at the Zollverein colliery, and the Labor faction is proud of us.

The reform bill dies in the Reichsrat, which suits nearly everyone for now. The Prussian civil service breathes again, and the Reformists are relieved. Luther's League issues a statement regretting "another lost decade".
The dualism remains—and so does the danger that a single decree against Prussia could bring down the Republic. The Left faction is not happy about it.

e2w_prussia.title: Reich and Prussia
e2w_prussia.subtitle: Three-fifths of Germany answers to two governments in the same city.

options.title: Carry out the Länder Conference plan, and dissolve Prussia into the Reich!
Break Prussia up into new Länder—and merge the small states while we're at it.
A personal union only. The Chancellor will also serve as Prussian Minister-President, and the ministries will be merged.
Leave Prussia as it is. It has been the Republic's bulwark, and may be again.

content: Prussia covers three-fifths of the Reich and holds three-fifths of its people. Its government sits a few hundred meters from the Reich government on the Wilhelmstraße, with its own police, its own civil service and its own majority, which is not always the same as the Reich's.
For most of the crisis years, Prussia was the <span style="color: #c00000;">

content.content: Whoever holds Prussia holds the largest police force in Germany.
However, everyone in politics knows that a single decree against the Prussian government could bring down the country, and the Right drew up plans for exactly that more than once.
However, the coup against the Prussian government in the crisis years showed everyone in politics that a single decree against Prussia can bring down the country.

content: The Länder Conference of 1928–1930 produced a plan that every party claimed to support and none ever passed. Prussia would be dissolved into the Reich, and its provinces would become Reich territories under Reich ministries, while Bavaria, Saxony, Württemberg and Baden kept their own governments. Hans Luther's League for the Renewal of the Reich has kept the plan alive ever since.

content.content: With the crisis over and the Republic on its feet, the moment may finally have come.
Unfortunately, the Republic is weaker than the reformers would like, and every change to the map is a change to who holds power.

Munich is already in uproar; the Bavarian government warns that "the destruction of Prussia is only the first course of a centralist meal". In Cologne, the Rhineland Catholics see a chance at a Land of their own. And in our own Prussian party, thousands of officials and police officers are wondering what will become of them if their state disappears.

As expected, the bourgeois cabinet cuts spending. We table the Woytinsky plan as an amendment to the budget, and lose by 30 votes. However, our economics spokesman's speech—"We have seen this before, and we know how it ends"—is reprinted in every union newspaper in the country, and our support among the workers and the unemployed is growing.

e2w_recession_1939.title: The Recession of 1939
e2w_recession_1939.subtitle: The order books are empty again. Will 1930 repeat itself?

options.title: Launch a public works program on credit—roads, rail electrification and housing!
Strengthen the unemployment insurance, and pay short-time allowances to keep workers in their jobs.
We must balance the budget and defend the Mark. Won't the slump pass on its own?
Fight the government's austerity from the opposition benches!

content.content: The downturn began in America, where Roosevelt's attempt to balance the budget in 1937 tipped the recovery back into a slump. Now it has crossed the Atlantic. The shipyards in Bremen and Kiel have canceled their night shifts, the Ruhr pits are working four days a week, and the textile mills of Chemnitz have sent home a third of their workers. Unemployment has risen sharply in a single winter, and the lines at the labor exchanges look disturbingly familiar.

content: Nobody in Berlin has forgotten what happened last time. The Reichsbank and the Finance Ministry want to keep the budget balanced and the Mark sound. The trade unions are dusting off the plan of Woytinsky, Tarnow and Baade

content.content: , which the party rejected in 1932 and has regretted ever since
, which pulled us out of the last slump

content: : public works financed by credit, at once and at scale. The Labor Ministry would rather let the unemployment insurance do the work, with short-time allowances to keep workers in their jobs.

content.content: Thanks to the People's Insurance, at least the unemployed will not starve this time.
Unfortunately, the insurance funds are already stretched, and the municipal welfare offices are bracing for the worst.

e2w_reichswehr.conscription.subtitle: (-2 budget) The Left faction will be furious.

content: Universal military service returns for the first time since 1919.

content.content: Geneva accepts it as part of our equality of rights, and the army may now grow to 200,000 men.

content: The barracks fill up with the sons of the unemployed. The Reichswehr is grateful to us, in its own way.

content.content: Unfortunately, the Left faction is furious, and our youth organizations hold a silent march through Berlin in protest. The French ambassador has asked for an urgent meeting at the Foreign Office.

The government has buried the Wissell report, so we dig it up again. We print a million copies of a summary, illustrated with a gray insurance card and the slogan "One card for every German". The idea is popular among workers, white-collar employees and the rural poor alike. Whoever governs after the next election will have to answer to it.

e2w_social_insurance.title: One Insurance, One Card
e2w_social_insurance.subtitle: Should we rebuild Bismarck's social insurance from the ground up?

options.title: Enact the Wissell Plan in full!

content: Surely there is a compromise with the
? Keep the separate funds, but add a Reich minimum pension and child allowances.

content.content: Simply reverse the Brüning cuts, and leave the structure alone.
Simply reverse the crisis-year cuts, and leave the structure alone.

options.title: We are in opposition. Let's make the Wissell Plan the center of our next campaign!

content: German social insurance is the oldest in the world, and also the most confusing. Bismarck's sickness, accident and old-age schemes, the white-collar insurance of 1911 and the unemployment insurance of 1927 run through nearly 7,000 separate funds, each with its own contributions, officials and rules. A Silesian miner and a Hamburg clerk with the same illness may receive entirely different treatment, while farm laborers, domestic servants and the self-employed fall through the gaps altogether.

content.content: Furthermore, Brüning's emergency decrees cut benefits across the board, and most of those cuts have never been reversed.
Furthermore, benefits were cut across the board in the crisis years, and most of those cuts have never been reversed.

A commission chaired by the former Labor Minister Rudolf Wissell has spent two years on a cure. Its report proposes a single People's Insurance—Volksversicherung—covering everyone in work, with a single contribution and a single insurance card. It would also pay a guaranteed minimum pension, financed from taxes, so that no German who has worked a lifetime ends it in the poorhouse. The report has sold out three printings, and delegations have come from Stockholm and London to study it.

However, the opposition is formidable. The doctors' associations fear a state medical service, and the white-collar unions will not give up their separate fund. The Catholic welfare associations warn that the plan would sweep away the principle of subsidiarity and "replace the family and the parish with the Reich cashier's office". And the Finance Ministry has already asked how it is to be paid for.

content.content: Ludwig Kaas has never truly embraced his role as party chairman, viewing it as a burden. He was elected as a compromise candidate, without actively campaigning for the position. Privately, he has made no secret of his desire to be relieved of the party chairmanship. With the stabilization of the Weimar Republic, Kaas believes he can retire without facing any significant consequences.

Despite pleads from his party members and colleagues, Kaas has officially resigned as head of the Center Party. This decision will have little impact, as he spent most of his time in Rome anyway, delegating the management of the party to his allies Joos and Brüning. No other Center member has missed as many Reichstag sessions as Kaas. Now, the party must find a successor, with potential candidates being his deputy leader Joos, Brüning, Stegerwald, or perhaps another compromise candidate.

options.title: The Nazis are the fault of the petit bourgeois. It is not our responsibility as a working-class party to stop them.

content.content: The Nazis' rise is unprecedented for a political party in modern Germany, and socialist intellectuals are doing their best to come to terms with the rapid rise of this dangerous party.

The trade union researcher Theodor Geiger has written an article titled "Panik im Mittelstand", in which he describes the Nazis as being primarily a movement of the middle class, especially lower-middle civil servants and professionals who fear the proletarianizing effects of the Depression. Geiger argues that the middle class has been economically and politically unmoored, long split between many competing parties, squeezed between the big businesses and the proletariat. The mix of nationalist, anti-democratic, and loosely anti-capitalist rhetoric of the Nazis appeals to this group, perhaps only temporarily before the middle class discovers its true class interests.

By contrast, the theoretician Alexander Schifrin understands the Nazis as a new, unprecedented type of political movement, a fascist party that has non-economic appeal across class lines. He calls to attention its use of violent propaganda and street demonstrations as central to their rise.

Carlo Mierendorff, a leader of the "new revisionists", understands the Nazis as a politically incoherent but nevertheless powerful movement. They are kept together by the strength of their organizing machine and the emotional appeal of their nebulous ideology, which is able to attract less informed voters who voted based on feeling. Countering them would require a new style of campaigning, focused more on symbols and emotion rather than reason.
It is possible that all or none of these hypotheses are correct. Whatever the case, there must be something we can do to stop their rise.

content.content: Class Consciousness of the Peasantry and the Rural Working class

content: Due to our introduction of agrarian policies and the increased popularity of socialism, we now have a chance to raise the consciousness of the peasantry and the rural working class.

content.content: As Marxists, we are predominantly a party of the industrial proletariat and believe that they are the driving force of the transition to socialism. Engels and Kautsky saw peasants as unreliable allies at best and as a relic of a bygone era, whilst Lenin's Bolsheviks saw revolutionary potential in the peasantry. Ideologically, we do not see the peasantry as a revolutionary class, though we could try to radicalise poorer peasants, small farmers, and agricultural workers against the Junkers and to sway them towards socialism.
Despite becoming a people’s party, our party has traditionally neglected rural workers and peasants, with the industrial working class previously being our main focus.

content.content: There is a clinic in every city where nobody asks for a name, and a single injection of penicillin. The Catholic bishops issue a pastoral letter about "public immorality" and the moral consequences. Syphilis cases fall by two-thirds in three years, and the morals of the nation are not obviously any worse.

The Reichstag votes, narrowly, to allow cameras in the chamber. The first broadcast debate is about milk prices. Twelve million people watch it anyway, and several deputies are surprised to find their constituents now know what they look like when they are asleep.

A young assistant at Dahlem notices that Bothe's graphite was made with electrodes containing boron, which swallows neutrons. Siemens-Plania produces a batch of graphite that is pure to a few parts in a million, and the measurements come out right. Graphite is cheap and German, and the first pile is built from it in eighteen months.

The Aggregat-4 carries instruments, not explosives. The gyroscopes developed to steer it are sold to Lufthansa and the merchant marine, and they soon pay back half the research budget. Meteorologists can now measure winds at heights no balloon has reached.
Fine. We enacted a massive austerity program to cut welfare, in order to maintain the stability of our coalition. The vote has been called off.

ending_slides.weimar_mega_win.title: The Weimar Republic Marches On
ending_slides.weimar_mega_win.subtitle: Ending 3

content.content: At the turn of the decade, the Great Depression and widespread disillusionment with the Weimar system left few optimists in Germany. Yet, the Republic—forged by the will of the people all those years ago—has weathered a crisis of unprecedented proportions. Social Democracy endures, as do its detractors.

content: No war as destructive as the Great War would come again. Slowly, Germany and the Western Allies began to rebuild relations, choosing to forget and forgive. Fascism never takes root as a dominant force, and the primary threat to European democracy becomes the resurgent Soviet Union. The Spanish Civil War ends in 1936 with a Republican victory.

content.content: In 1939, Austria's Austrofascist regime collapses under popular revolt.

content: successfully holds a referendum confirming their Anschluss into Germany.

content.content: The war in Austria is eventually won by the Austrofascists, who receive generous aid from a fascist Italy.

content: Isolated and denied any success in his expansionist aims in Yugoslavia and Greece, Mussolini is deposed in a royalist coup led by King Victor Emmanuel III, and Italy returns to democratic governance

content.content: , leading to Austria’s government democratizing as a consequence of losing its benefactor

Africa remains colonized until the 1970s and 80s. Independence, when it comes, is negotiated largely on the terms of the colonizers. Exploitation persists under a different guise. The Cold War unfolds along different lines, as a "state capitalist" Soviet Union remains intact, forming a bloc with the authoritarian Kuomintang-ruled Republic of China and post-independence India, which fought a bloody war to escape British rule in the 1950s. This tri-polar alliance has solidified into a global axis of its own.

content.content: The Schilling is pegged to the Reichsmark, the customs posts at Salzburg and Passau are taken down, and the two governments meet in joint session twice a year. Renner calls it "union in everything but name". France calls it a breach of Saint-Germain, but it is not a breach worth a war. On both sides of the border, the right complains that we have done things by halves.

content: would bring down the government, and the councils would strike.

content.content: After Danzig, Warsaw will not let German troops onto Polish soil.

content: The Reichstag votes war credits for the first time since the Great War, and this time the <span style="color: #c00000;">

votes for them knowing exactly what it is doing. This is not 1914. There is no general mobilization and no war in the west. Twelve Reichswehr divisions entrain for East Prussia and the lower Vistula, and a French expeditionary corps lands at Gdynia. Germany is at war, but only on Poland's soil, and only for Poland's frontier.
Within three weeks, the last Polish garrison marches out of Allenstein, heading east. German police take over in Königsberg and Gleiwitz to cheering crowds. The occupation is over.

content.content: In the Ruhr, the Red Army declares the Republic "a lackey of Anglo-French imperialism".
The Republic's small army marches east under a flag that was not long ago fought over by Germans.

content: ministers walk out of the cabinet in protest, and there are strikes in Halle and Hamburg. The United Front is hanging by a thread.

content.content: The officer corps marches east with an enthusiasm that some of us find more alarming than the enemy.

content: The government thanks Moscow for its friendship and declines to join any permanent alliance. German troops leave the Polish territories east of the Corridor within the month. Moscow is displeased, and the <span style="color: #700000;">
is furious. But Germany has kept its hands free, and for a country that has just fought beside the Red Army, that is a remarkable thing.

content.content: Germany joins the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, and German coal and steel are written into the plans drawn up in Moscow. The Silesian mines, the Saxon foundries and the Ruhr furnaces now work to quotas set two thousand kilometers away. The trains run full to the east.

e2_europe_talks.title: Coal, Steel and Europe
e2_europe_talks.subtitle: Paris proposes to pool the sinews of war.

options.title: Sign the treaty as Paris proposed it.
Sign, but insist on public ownership and workers' co-determination in the High Authority.
Go further, and propose a European federation with an elected parliament.
Stay out. German coal is for Germans.
Join the planning council of the People's Democracies instead.

content.content: The French Foreign Minister has proposed something no one in Berlin expected. France and Germany, and any other European country that wishes to join, should place their entire production of coal and steel under a common High Authority, whose decisions will bind the member governments. Once the two countries' heavy industry is fused together, the proposal argues, a war between them would become "not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible".
The offer is addressed to "all the peoples of Europe", but it is meant for the West, and Moscow has made it clear that Germany will not be joining.
After everything the Republic has done to earn the trust of its neighbors, Paris has come to Berlin first.
Paris is not sure that Berlin can be trusted with it, and says so.

content: The steel barons of the Ruhr are appalled at the idea of answering to a High Authority in Luxembourg. The Center Party's Konrad Adenauer
has made himself the plan's loudest champion. The unions are torn.

content.content: In private, the Quai d'Orsay has linked the plan to the future of the French troops on the Rhine. Integration, it suggests, would make the occupation unnecessary.
The French troops have gone home from the Rhine, and Paris wants to make sure that no German army ever has a reason to follow them.

The Ruhr has only lately been won back from the Red Army, and Paris proposes that it go straight into the pool, with every other coalfield the Republic holds. It would bind the reunited west of Germany to the West for good.

The Ruhr, the heart of German coal and steel, is still in the hands of the Ruhr Soviet. Paris proposes that the pool cover whatever the Republic now holds, and the Ruhr too, "on the day it returns to the community of free nations". For the first time, the West would have its own reason to want the Ruhr back in German hands.

content: Our coal and steel are in public ownership. Joining a pool with the private trusts of Lorraine and Belgium would mean bargaining with capital at a European level.
calls it a Wall Street cartel in a French hat.

content.content: The former Communists in our own party call it a Wall Street cartel in a French hat.
The treaty is the government's to sign, but it will need our votes to ratify it.

e2_moscow_trials.endorse.unavailableSubtitle: Our own party would never stand for it.

content.content: The government issues a statement welcoming the "vigilance of the Soviet people against the agents of fascism and Trotskyism". Eleven refugees are put on a train to the Polish border, where Soviet officials are waiting.

content: The Soviet ambassador is delighted. Inside the

, a group of deputies around the old Reichstag President Löbe resigns the whip in protest, and the Reformist faction is in open revolt. In the factory councils, delegates have started to look over their shoulders before they speak.

e2_moscow_trials.title: The Moscow Trials
e2_moscow_trials.subtitle: Show trials in Moscow, and refugees at our door.

options.title: Condemn the trials publicly, and open our doors to their victims!
Why not go further, and grant Trotsky asylum?
Quietly take in the refugees, but say nothing in public.
Say nothing. The trials are an internal Soviet affair.
Endorse the verdicts, and send back the "Trotskyist wreckers".

content.content: Last August, Zinoviev and Kamenev stood in the October Hall of the House of Unions and confessed to plotting Stalin's murder on Leon Trotsky's orders. They were shot the next day. In January it was the turn of Pyatakov and Radek, and now the arrests have reached the Red Army itself. Marshal Tukhachevsky and seven other commanders are accused of spying for a foreign power, and the Soviet prosecutor has named the Reichswehr as their paymaster. The Bendlerblock calls the charge absurd—though it is true that Tukhachevsky worked closely with German officers in the twenties, when the Reichswehr and the Red Army cooperated in secret after Rapallo.

content: Every week, more people arrive at the Schlesischer Bahnhof with one suitcase and no papers: Soviet engineers recalled from German firms who refused to go home, the widows of executed officials, and foreign communists from the Comintern's offices in Moscow. Among them are a number of
members who had been working in the Soviet capital. Hermann Remmele and Heinz Neumann have not been heard from since the spring.

content.content: From Mexico, Leon Trotsky has written to the President of the Reichstag to ask for asylum. He made the same request in 1929, and the government refused it.

Leon Trotsky answers every verdict from his flat in Charlottenburg, usually within a day. *Pravda* says that he runs the conspiracy from Berlin with the help of the Reichswehr, and that the Republic is sheltering the chief of the wreckers. An American commission of inquiry under the philosopher John Dewey has asked permission to hear his evidence in Berlin.

On Föhr, Leon Trotsky is keeping to the letter of his promise and gives no interviews. His secretaries, however, send a statement to the foreign press after every verdict. *Pravda* says that he runs the conspiracy from a German island with the help of the Reichswehr, and that the Republic is sheltering the chief of the wreckers. An American commission of inquiry under the philosopher John Dewey has asked the police for permission to hear his evidence there.

content: leadership has endorsed the verdicts without reservation, and asks the government to do the same. Inside the party, some members are quietly asking where their missing comrades have gone.
leadership has refused to endorse the verdicts, and Moscow's loyalists in the party are demanding that it fall into line. Many communists are asking where their missing comrades have gone.
