e2_obituary.severing.subtitle: The former Prussian and Reich interior minister, trusted by the coalition partners.

content.content: Carl Severing is sworn in as Chancellor. The coalition partners welcome the choice, and the Left faction does not.
We stay home. The nationalists applaud, and our athletes are bitter. The Games go on without us, and the Ruhr Soviet sends a team of its own to the People's Olympiad being organized across the city.
The Games have been taken from Berlin.
The world is coming to Berlin.

options.title: Make it a festival of the Republic, whatever the cost!
Hold sober, inexpensive Games. There is still a Depression on.
Open the Games to the workers' sports movement!
Send a single German team to Barcelona, under the black-red-gold.
Boycott the Games that were stolen from us!

content.content: In 1931, in the depths of the slump, the International Olympic Committee awarded the Games of the Eleventh Olympiad to Berlin. Few on the Committee expected Weimar to still be standing by then. It is, and in August athletes from fifty nations will arrive at the Lehrter Bahnhof. The Organizing Committee needs to know what kind of Games the government wants, and how much it is willing to pay.

The Reichswehr has offered to stage a grand military review at the opening ceremony. Meanwhile, the workers' sports clubs, which have held their own Workers' Olympiads since 1925, want to know why they have been left off the guest list.

The Committee hesitated for months over whether a country so recently at war with itself could safely host the Games—there are still shell craters in the Grunewald. However, hosting the Games would be the clearest possible sign to the world that the fighting is over.

The Committee's president, Count Baillet-Latour, has made it plain that he does not care for "a Bolshevik festival". He will only keep the Games in Berlin if the government guarantees that the red flag stays off the stadium, and that the Workers' Sport movement stays out of the arena.

In 1931 the Committee chose Berlin over Barcelona. After our civil war, it changed its mind, and the Games of the Eleventh Olympiad will now open on the hill of Montjuïc instead. The German Olympic Committee, which now speaks only for the territory we hold, must decide whether to send a team—and under whose flag the athletes from the Ruhr and the Rhineland will march.

content: % of the Saarlanders have voted to return to Germany! Church bells ring from Saarlouis to Homburg, and the League commissioners pack their files.

content.content: However, the nationalists have claimed the victory as their own—the day belonged to the black-white-red flags and the old soldiers' songs, and Paris has noticed.
The miners' union marched under the black-red-gold, and for once the colors of Weimar were the colors of a national triumph. Our workers are proud of the campaign.
Under the terms of Versailles, we must buy back the mines from France in gold. This will strain the budget, but the pits are ours again.

German and Soviet arms travel together, on Soviet ships with German crews. The Thälmann Battalion of the International Brigades is the largest in Spain, and it is followed by German "advisers" whose real masters sit in Moscow.

content: It is a powerful show of proletarian solidarity, and
Moscow is delighted, although the <span style="color: #700000;">
. However, in Republican Spain, the men who decide who gets the guns increasingly answer to the Spanish Communist Party.

content.content: Exhausted, and with their foreign backers losing interest, the generals accept an armistice brokered in Geneva. The Spanish Republic survives as a federal state, with an amnesty for both sides and autonomy for Catalonia and the Basque Country. Franco takes a boat to Lisbon.
The Ebro offensive breaks the Nationalist front in two. Over the winter the generals' army falls apart, and in the spring Republican troops enter Burgos. Franco flees to Portugal, and Mola is dead.

content: The Spanish Republic survives as a parliamentary democracy, battered and bankrupt but free. Its victory is a blow to the reactionary right everywhere in Europe, and a boost for the democratic parties at home.

content.content: Our workers are proud of the part we played.
When the Legion Schwarz-Rot-Gold marches through Madrid, the crowds throw flowers at it. Madrid and Barcelona now look to Berlin, and Rome will not forget it.

e2_war_end.inquiry.subtitle: The army will not like it. The truth might stop a legend.

content.content: The Reichstag appoints a committee of inquiry, with the right to see the general staff's files and to call the generals as witnesses. After the last war, the Reichstag's inquiry sat for years and was ignored. This one has six months, and its hearings are broadcast on the radio. By the time it reports, the country has heard the generals explain their own orders.

e2_war_crisis.suppress.subtitle: The factories will work again. Nobody who saw it will forget it.

content.content: The President declares a state of siege in Berlin, Saxony and the Ruhr. Troops occupy the factories, and the strike leaders are arrested, our own shop stewards among them. The strike is over in four days. The Left faction meets in the evening, and some of its members do not go home.
The United Front is no longer in government.
Our own party would not stand for it.

Our delegate in Geneva votes against expulsion and speaks of "the legitimate security needs of Leningrad". Only three states vote with us. Finland loses its eastern provinces in March. In Stockholm and Copenhagen, the comrades of the Scandinavian labor parties stop answering our letters.

e2_winter_war.title: War in the Snow
e2_winter_war.subtitle: The Red Army marches on Finland.

options.title: Send arms and allow volunteers to go to Finland.
Vote to expel the Soviet Union, and send only humanitarian aid.
Work with Sweden for a quick negotiated peace.
Stay strictly neutral.
Defend Moscow's security interests in Geneva.

content.content: For two months Moscow demanded that Finland hand over the Karelian Isthmus and lease it the port of Hanko. Helsinki refused. On the last day of November, Soviet bombers struck Helsinki, and four armies crossed the frontier. Stalin expected the campaign to last a fortnight. Instead, the Finns are destroying whole Soviet divisions in the frozen forests north of Lake Ladoga, and the Mannerheim Line on the Isthmus is holding.

content: Finland has appealed to the League, which is preparing to expel the Soviet Union, and to every government in Europe for arms. Sweden is sending volunteers.

content.content: The Reichswehr, which helped found the Finnish army in 1918, is keen to help again. The right is keener still.
The Republic has few arms to spare, but the Finnish appeal has stirred something in a country that knows what it means to be invaded.

content: insists that the Red Army is liberating the Finnish workers from the White butchers of 1918. Even inside the KPD, not everyone believes it.
Only the Moscow loyalists who left the <span style="color: #700000;">
insist that the Red Army is liberating the Finnish workers from the White butchers of 1918. The KPD itself calls the invasion what it is.

content.content: Many in Berlin fear that Finland is a rehearsal, and that the next demands will be made of the Baltic states and Poland.

e2c_bredow_coup.foiled.title: The conspiracy is crushed before it begins.

content.content: At two in the morning, police trucks pull up outside forty addresses from Potsdam to Königsberg. Bredow is arrested at his desk, with the draft proclamation of the Reich Directory still in front of him. By breakfast, the Berlin papers are printing photographs of it.

content: On the morning of the ninth, the Potsdam battalions find the railway stations dark and the roads into Berlin blocked by streetcars that their drivers have parked across them. The radio tower is held by its own technicians and
a police company of former <span style="color: #c00000;">
. By noon the battalions are back in their barracks, and Bredow is arrested at Wannsee with the draft proclamation of the Reich Directory still on his desk.

content.content: The effect on the officer corps is remarkable. Generals who have hedged their bets since 1918 rush to sign declarations of loyalty, and the purge commission finds its work much easier. For the first time, the Reichswehr has learned that we are the stronger party.

The Council in Geneva hears our case and refers it to a commission, which refers it to a subcommittee. Italy backs France for its own reasons, and Britain abstains. A year later the French are still on the bridges, and the nationalists point out that we asked politely and were refused.

The columns reach the Oder bridges at Küstrin and find machine guns waiting for them. The Reichswehr commander gives three warnings over a loudspeaker, and then orders his men to fire over their heads. The front ranks break, and then the rest of the column breaks too. By Wednesday the marchers are walking home in groups of ten or twenty, and Strasser has been arrested at a farmhouse near Prenzlau.

The marchers reach Berlin to find no streetcars, no trains, no electric light, and no one who will sell them bread. Every factory gate is shut and guarded by workers with armbands. After two nights in the cold, the columns begin to fall apart. Strasser never gets to his balcony; he is arrested at a railway station, trying to buy a ticket to Copenhagen.

This was our greatest test since the civil war, and we have passed it. Thousands of people gather at the Reichstag to sing, and for the first time in years the crowd seems to believe in the government.

content: The rest of the country votes yes by large margins. The Ruhr does not. Fifty-three percent of its voters reject the Act of Reunification, in protest against the offensives, the blockade years and a decade of Berlin's broken promises. Under the rules the Assembly adopted, the result is binding there.

content.content: Strasser's ministers call it "the treason of the Ruhr" and demand that the army settle the matter.
The Assembly adjourns. Germany is closer to being whole than at any time since the civil war, and still not whole. The delegates agree to meet again within the year.

e2d_reunification.title: The Weimar Assembly
e2d_reunification.subtitle: For the first time since the civil war, every German land can send delegates to one assembly.

options.title: A federal Republic. The Ruhr and the Rhineland enter as self-governing Länder.
A unitary Reich. Commissioners will govern the returned territories until they are reintegrated.
Let the people decide. A referendum in every region, on the same day.

content: The delegates arrive at the National Theatre in Weimar by every road and railway in Germany. There are miners' delegates from Essen

content.content: who still wear the red armbands of the Land police
who came out of the Reichswehr's prisons only a few years ago

content: , wine-growers from the Moselle who have not seen a German official in years,

content.content: refugee representatives from the lost provinces, there as observers,

content: and the Berlin deputies who kept the Republic alive through its worst years. In front of the theater, the bronze Goethe and Schiller look down at a crowd that has come to see the end of the civil war.

content.content: The eastern frontier has been settled in a treaty, at a painful cost.
The plebiscite has brought East Prussia home.
The neutrality treaty with Warsaw has brought East Prussia home.

content: The Ruhr is quiet. What remains is to decide what kind of country the parts are joining. The <span style="color: #c00000;">

wants a federal republic with strong Länder, so that the Ruhr and the Rhineland come home as partners. The Reichswehr and the bourgeois right want Reich commissioners and a strong center, so that no region can secede again. A third group, including many of our own younger delegates, wants no deal at all until the people of every region have voted on it.

content.content: Strasser's ministers are demanding a "Reich of the German nation, one and indivisible", run from Berlin.

Unfortunately, the referendum fails. Turnout in the countryside is enormous, and the nationalist slogan "Keep the Field Marshal's sword" does its work. The decree power remains as it was—now with a plebiscite behind it. The Reformist faction blames us for provoking the President.
At least every future use of Article 48 will now be closely watched.
We will be left out of the government.
We will stay out of the government.

content: The Left faction will be furious.

content.content: We have agreed to tolerate a "cabinet of experts" that answers only to the President, in return for a written promise that the Reichstag will be recalled within a year. The troops return to their barracks, and there is no bloodshed.

content: However, the government is now in the hands of the President's men, led by

, and we have no place in it. The Left faction is furious, and many of our working-class voters feel that we have surrendered without a fight. The cabinet is already rewriting the rules for the promised elections.

content: signed three decrees. The first dismisses the government. The second dissolves the Reichstag and postpones new elections "until public order has been restored". The third hands executive power to a Reich Directory of five men—two generals, two senior civil servants and the President's state secretary.

Last night, troops of the Berlin garrison occupied the Reich Chancellery, the Interior Ministry and the radio station on the Masurenallee. A "Committee of National Concentration" of senior Reichswehr officers has announced that it is taking power "to save the Reich from chaos", and has asked President
This is a coup against the Republic, and against us. After months of crisis and fallen cabinets, the reactionaries have decided that the time has come.

content.content: Under the Emergency Powers Act, what has just been done is plainly illegal, and our jurists say the decrees are void. However, a law cannot stop soldiers on its own.
The constitutional lawyers are already arguing over whether Article 48 covers any of this. Unfortunately, the soldiers are not waiting for their verdict.
Our leaders have gathered with the trade union leadership in the ADGB headquarters on the Inselstraße. The telephone lines are still working, but we have perhaps an hour.

content: , a sober catalog of verdicts and sentences that sells 80,000 copies. It changes no laws. However, the judges now know that somebody is keeping count, and our standing among the voters has improved somewhat.

e2w_judiciary.title: Blind in the Right Eye
e2w_judiciary.subtitle: The judges who freed Hitler after nine months still sit on the bench.

options.title: Pass a judicial renewal law—a retirement age of 65, new judicial training, and the Radbruch code!
Create a Reich Constitutional Court, to guard the constitution against the courts as well as the cabinet.
Expand the lay assessors and the labor courts. Let the people sit beside the judges!
Judicial independence is a principle, even when the judges abuse it.
We are in opposition, but we can publish a new Gumbel report.

content.content: In 1922, the statistician Emil Julius Gumbel counted the political murders of the Republic's first years. The Right had committed more than 300 of them, and almost all went unpunished. The Left had committed 22, and 10 of the killers were sentenced to death. Gumbel's figures were never refuted; the Reich Justice Ministry confirmed them in a report that it then declined to publish.

content: Little has changed since. Most of our judges were appointed under the Kaiser, and the constitution says they cannot be removed. They gave Hitler five years for high treason in 1924, and let him out after nine months. Last month, a court in Breslau acquitted three <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
men who beat a trade unionist to death, on the grounds that they had acted "out of an honorable, if excessive, love of the fatherland". The verdict has set off protest strikes across Silesia.

content.content: Gustav Radbruch's draft criminal code, which would abolish the death penalty, has lain in a drawer since 1922. Meanwhile, the Association of German Judges has warned that any interference with the bench "will be resisted by every lawful means".

content.content: The bourgeois cabinet passes its conscription law over our votes. We fight it clause by clause, and win a single concession: conscientious objectors may serve in hospitals instead.
The generals have their army, and they have not forgotten who voted against it. However, the workers and the Left faction approve of our stand.

e2w_reichswehr.title: A State Within the State
e2w_reichswehr.subtitle: What should we do with the army that stood aside in the crisis?

options.title: Retire the old guard of Seeckt's officers, and open the officer corps to the sons of workers!

content: army with a short-service citizens' militia!

content.content: Leave the generals their professional army, in return for a parliamentary commissioner and a loyalty pledge.
Leave the officer corps alone, in return for a parliamentary commissioner and a loyalty pledge.

options.title: Give the generals their conscript army.
Oppose the cabinet's conscription bill from the opposition benches.

content.content: Hans von Seeckt built the Reichswehr to outlast the Republic. His 100,000 long-service men were meant to be the cadre of a future mass army, and his officer corps—drawn heavily from the old nobility and the Imperial General Staff—was taught that the army "stands above party". In practice, that meant it stood above the Republic. Reichsbanner members were refused enlistment, and the regimental messes still toasted the Kaiser's birthday. In the worst months of the crisis, the generals in the Bendlerblock openly debated whether the Republic was worth defending at all.

Now the question can no longer be put off. The disarmament talks in Geneva have conceded Germany equality of rights in principle, and the generals want to use it: 200,000 men, and a return to universal service. The Left faction wants the opposite—the old Erfurt demand for a citizens' militia in place of a standing army.

The Volkswehr Law has begun to turn the army into a people's militia. However, its regional units are still commanded by Seeckt's officers, and the generals are lobbying the Reichstag for universal service instead.

Conscription has given the generals the trained reserve they wanted. However, the officers who train it are still Seeckt's men, and the Left faction still wants the old Erfurt demand for a citizens' militia in place of a standing army.

content: Meanwhile, half the general officers on the active list were commissioned before 1914.

content.content: Our relations with the army command are better than they were. Some of the younger staff officers have even begun to speak of the Republic as "the state" without irony.
Unfortunately, the army command remains sullen and closed. Our ministers learn about its plans from the newspapers.

content: Out of the civil war, we built the most ambitious social state in Europe.

content.content: The constitution of the Second Republic, drafted while the barricades were still standing, guarantees economic rights alongside political ones.

content: The coal mines and steel mills of the Ruhr are in public hands. The Reichsbank answers to the Reichstag, and works councils sit on every board.
The bourgeois opposition is loud, but it has little influence.

content.content: The Junge Front still runs town halls in Lower Saxony, but it has never come near power.
Lifting the bans in the late thirties was a gamble—but it paid off, as the far right split into quarreling factions in public instead of plotting in secret.
Reconstruction is complete. The rubble has become housing estates, and the trenches have become parks.

agricultural_crisis.title: Agricultural Revolt
agricultural_crisis.subtitle: Small farmers are in revolt over debts and taxes...

options.title: There is nothing we can do.

We must increase financial support for the peasantry.

content.content: The German peasantry is beginning to wage a war against the Republic. Starting in the state of Schleswig-Holstein, the *Landvolkbewegung* (peasants' movement) has become increasingly brazen, conducting sabotage against local government offices. The peasants claim that they are being crushed by taxes and debts, and insofar as they have coherent demands, they demand unconditional economic relief. In addition, the movement is developing ties to the so-called "National Socialists", the Nazi party.

content: The trade slump has reached the countryside. Grain and pig prices have fallen again, and many farms that got through the last crisis on credit can no longer pay the interest. In Schleswig-Holstein the *Landvolkbewegung* (peasants' movement), which began there in 1928, is back: farmers are refusing to pay their taxes, and crowds are breaking up the auctions of foreclosed farms. The agrarian leagues demand a moratorium on farm debts.

content.content: The Nazis are sending their speakers into the villages again.

content: When the march arrives in Altona, they are immediately confronted by an angry crowd of communists and socialists, who throw objects at the Nazis. Gunshots are heard, reportedly from rooftop snipers. In response, the
engage the surrounding crowd and fire at the surrounding buildings. Dozens are killed, mostly civilians. The Nazis recruit off their dead martyrs.

bruning_joever.papen.title: Franz von Papen?
bruning_joever.papen.subtitle: An relatively unknown Catholic Conservative from the Center Party. Schleicher's preferred candidate.

content.content: With Goerdeler and Westarp out of the equation, Hindenburg has grasped the straw Schleicher offered and appointed a far-right Catholic Conservative, Franz von Papen, from the Center Party, as chancellor. Papen is relatively unknown, only whose political experience is limited to two terms in the Prussian Landtag. The two have been friends since their days in the Prussian military academy.

content: Papen's decision to take the chancellorship, despite
's urging and Papen's promise not to, Hindenburg has used the same tactic on him as he used on Brüning, convincing him to accept the position. Due to Papen breaking his promise to

just after he made it, expulsion proceedings and against him are interrupted by his resignation from the Center Party, forever ruining his relations with the party necessary for a parliamentary majority as they strongly denounce him as the "Ephialtes of the Center Party".

content.content: It's unknown of the exact reasons why Schleicher would choose a man like Papen as Brüning's successor, but we can assume he was trying to secure the support of the Center Party and Nazis, as he's a far-right member of the former, and that Papen would be an easy person to control.

content: Time will tell if the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
will honor its promises to Schleicher, which they'd purposefully refused to write on paper.

content: Brüning's days are numbered. The only reason President Hindenburg is keeping him around is solely by the fact of his foreign policy expertise, and his claim that he's only 'one hundred meters from the finish line' from achieving a huge breakthrough in terms of securing an abolishment of reparations at Lausanne and Germany's rearmament at Geneva, an issue close to Hindenburg's heart. The only hope for Brüning's political salvation rests in those conferences.

content.content: There is also no precedent of the President sacking a government that still enjoys a parliamentary majority.

However, General Kurt von Schleicher sees Brüning as the biggest obstacle in his 'taming strategy', as Brüning has refused to take serious efforts toward bringing the national opposition into government. The sense of urgency Schleicher has invoked onto the issue, along with his convincing of Hindenburg's State Secretary Otto Meissner and his son Oskar, has brought Hindenburg to make an early and rash decision on the matter.

content.content: President Hindenburg has made his dissatisfaction with the socialist presence in government clear and has forced Brüning's hand to reorganize the cabinet. Brüning, despite his conservatism, has demonstrated strong loyalty in sustaining our government. It seems like this decision wasn't a rash one, but rather a matter of finding the appropriate pretext.

The SPD remaining electorally resilient despite the radicalizing effects of the economic depression has thwarted Hindenburg’s plan to burden us with governance and erode our popularity. Realizing his strategy has failed, he now moves to dismiss us from government to prevent further socialist reforms from fueling our rising support.
Germany's economic crisis and our inadequate response have severely tested Hindenburg's patience, as he favors an austerity-driven approach.
The rapid rise of the far-right in local elections has pushed Hindenburg to appoint a government more in line with the national mood.
Kurt von Schleicher and the Reichswehr, outraged by our actions, have leveraged their influence over Hindenburg to push for our removal.
Business leaders, frustrated by our policies, have pressured Hindenburg’s inner circle to act against us.
This is a blatant violation of democracy, but we are powerless to stop it. Our only hope is to rally enough support in the next election to reclaim our mandate.

schleichers_schemes.subtitle: Chancellor Schleicher claims to have a plan to save Germany...

content.content: Chancellor Kurt von Schleicher claims to have a plan to save Germany, and he has reached out to the Social Democrats with vague promises. He claims that in order to govern, the Reichstag must be temporarily suspended to prevent the Nazis and Communists from disrupting government, in effect giving him and Hindenburg dictatorial powers. In the meantime, he is enacting a public works program and job creation plan, which he claims will stabilize the economy,

The trade unions are somewhat favorable to Schleicher's plan, as they see a commonality between Schleicher's economic plan and the ADGB's WTB-plan for debt-funded job creation. However, the rest of our party is vehemently against Schleicher.

Rumors are that Schleicher is also reaching out to the Nazis with similar promises of cooperation; he seems to believe that he can "tame" the Nazis. Most in our party do not trust him to not bring the Nazis to power. In addition, working with him would essentially mean the end of our claim to be a "democratic" party.

content.content: The Reichswehr signs a contract with Heinkel for a single-seat interceptor with two turbines. The drawings are stamped "Secret". The test pilots come from the "commercial flying schools", whose students all happen to be officers.

Pension claims that used to take nine months are paid in three weeks. The sickness funds find a million marks a year in double payments. For the first time, a widow in Bremen or Dresden can write to the insurance office and get an answer before Christmas.

The standard receiver drops to thirty marks, and the television set to three hundred. In the villages of the Eifel and East Frisia, families who never had a newspaper now listen to the news every evening.

The Workers' Welfare, Marie Juchacz's organization, sends midwives with penicillin to every rural district. Deaths from childbed fever, which once killed one mother in a hundred, almost disappear. The Catholic Caritas, after some hesitation, joins in.
Only the Reich government can fund this.

In the mornings, village schoolrooms watch chemistry lessons broadcast from Berlin. In the evenings, the People's University of the Air teaches bookkeeping, English and the history of the labor movement. A miner's son in the Erzgebirge passes the Abitur after three years of studying in front of the screen.
Only the Reich government can fund this.

Norsk Hydro sells its entire output of heavy water, at a price that makes the Finance Ministry wince. London and Paris want to know why Germany needs it. The first pile goes critical behind the walls of the Leipzig institute.
Only the Reich government can fund this.
The army specification is simple: a tonne of explosive, carried 250 kilometers. That is the distance from the Oder to Warsaw, or from the Rhine to Paris. Nobody at Peenemünde says this out loud.
We do not have enough resources.

The government signs a treaty of alliance with the Soviet Union. German divisions, now officially the People's Army, cross into the Corridor as the Red Army crosses the Bug. Within a week, France declares war on Germany, and Britain, even with its armies fighting in Burma, follows. This is the general war that everyone has feared since 1918. It is a war between two worlds, the capitalist and the communist, and the front runs from the Baltic to the Alps.

The government grants the Red Army transit rights and sends three divisions to occupy the Corridor and Danzig, "to protect the German population". France declares war, but the French army stays behind the Maginot Line, and on the Rhine nobody fires a shot. In the east, Poland fights on alone.

e2_eastern_crisis.title: The Eastern Crisis
e2_eastern_crisis.subtitle: Moscow's ultimatum to Warsaw and the Baltic capitals.

options.title: Call a conference of the powers before the guns start firing.
Declare armed neutrality and guard our own borders.
Stand with Poland and France, in a limited war of defense.
Stand with the Soviet Union.

content.content: The note was delivered to the Polish Foreign Ministry at six in the morning, and similar notes went to Kaunas, Riga and Tallinn the same day. Moscow demands that the three Baltic states accept "mutual assistance pacts" with Red Army garrisons on their soil. From Poland it demands the eastern borderlands, home to some six million Belarusians and Ukrainians, which it says Pilsudski seized by force in 1920. Poland has ten days to answer. Forty Soviet divisions are already moving to the frontier.
France has declared that it will honor its alliance with Poland.
Even the regime in Paris, for all its talk of reconsidering France's eastern alliances, has declared that it will honor its alliance with Poland against Bolshevism.

content: Britain, with its fleet in the Indian Ocean and its armies in Burma, can offer a few squadrons and its sympathy. Both Paris and Warsaw are asking whether Germany will stand with them. For all the bitterness of the last twenty years, a Polish army on the Vistula is the only thing between the Red Army and our own eastern border.

content.content: The Reichswehr is ready, and more than ready. The right, which has spent twenty years calling the Poles our hereditary enemy, has discovered overnight that they are a Christian bulwark against Bolshevism. Our own members remember 1914 and dread a second August.
Germany has had less than a decade to recover from its own civil war. Paris has let it be known that French troops on the Rhine "might be better employed elsewhere" if Germany helps.

content: Warsaw needs every soldier it has in the east. If the Republic joins the alliance, its ambassador says, Polish garrisons will leave East Prussia and Upper Silesia within the month.

content.content: After the Danzig talks, the treaty is already drafted.
Meanwhile, the Ruhr Soviet has declared its "unshakeable solidarity" with Moscow.
The Republic has only just put itself back together, and its army is small. A war in the east is the last thing it needs, and the first thing Warsaw asks of it.

content: Moscow has reminded the United Front of "the duty of proletarian solidarity" and asked for transit rights for the Red Army across German territory to East Prussia.
demands that we go further and stand openly with the Soviet Union.
is pressing hard for an alliance with Moscow. Most of our own party would rather resign.
, which broke with Moscow years ago, wants nothing to do with the Red Army's war.

content.content: Moscow has asked the bourgeois cabinet for transit rights for the Red Army across German territory to East Prussia, and has been told to wait.
The embassy in Moscow reports that Stalin has made up his mind, and that this time the Red Army means to march.
The embassy in Moscow thinks that Stalin is testing the West, and that a firm, united answer might still make him think again.
The troop trains come home through the winter, and the Reichstag cuts the war budget by two-thirds within the year.
The frontier guard is stood down and the special war levy repealed.

content: The money goes to housing, schools and the railways. The generals complain that the Republic is disarming in the face of the Bolshevik menace. The voters, on the whole, are glad of the houses.

content.content: The peace of Königsberg is put to the test.

options.title: Press for a general peace conference under the League.
Join France and Poland in a permanent Western defense pact.
Open the frontier to the refugees from the east.
Bind the Republic to the Soviet-led alliance.
Keep our distance from Moscow now that the guns are silent.
Bring the soldiers home and turn to rebuilding.

content.content: The Red Army's offensive broke on the Vistula in the first autumn. Polish cavalry, French tanks and German infantry held the line from Modlin to the sea through a terrible winter, and in the spring the counter-offensive drove the Soviets back to the Riga line of 1921. The armistice signed at Brest restores the old frontier. Lithuania, briefly occupied, is free again. Eleven thousand German soldiers lie in Polish cemeteries. It is a fraction of what a single month of the Great War cost, but every one of them was someone's son.

After eighteen months of fighting, the front has frozen along the Bug and the marshes of Polesia. Neither side can break through, and neither can afford to keep trying. The armistice signed at Brest leaves Poland its heartland and the Soviet Union most of the eastern borderlands it wanted. The Baltic states are now Soviet republics. German soldiers held their sector of the Narew to the end, and they come home to a country unsure whether to call it victory or defeat.

The line on the Vistula did not hold. The Red Army's second offensive broke through north of Warsaw, and German divisions fell back into East Prussia in disorder. The armistice signed at Königsberg partitions Poland at the Vistula. A Polish rump state survives in the west, and the Red Army stands on the borders of East Prussia. The nationalist press has already found its explanation, and it is not the Red Army.

Poland fought alone, with French arms and French officers, and it held. The Red Army's offensive stalled in the marshes east of the Bug, and after a year of slaughter Moscow accepted an armistice that gave it the Baltic states and nothing else. Germany sold to both sides and grew rich doing it. In Warsaw and Paris, few people have a good word to say about us.

Poland fought alone, and it fell. Warsaw surrendered after a four-month siege, and the armistice partitions the country at the Vistula. Soviet garrisons now hold Białystok and Lwów, and the Baltic states have become Soviet republics. Hundreds of thousands of Polish and Jewish refugees are camped along the German frontier. The Red Army is now a neighbor, and every German knows it.

The war between the two worlds has ended in victory for the East. In the spring the People's Army and the Red Army broke the French line on the Meuse, and by the autumn Soviet and German troops stood on the Atlantic at Brest and Bordeaux. The French government has fled to Algiers and the British have withdrawn behind the Channel. A vast new bloc of people's democracies stretches from Lisbon to Arkhangelsk. Germany is its industrial heart, and Moscow is its head. The cost in German lives runs to the hundreds of thousands.

Poland is partitioned. The Soviet Union takes everything east of the Vistula, and Germany has the Corridor and Danzig back, which no nationalist government ever managed. The French, who declared war and never fought it, accept an armistice with bad grace. The nationalists hardly know what to say. The rest of Europe now regards the Republic as Moscow's junior partner.

The bases at Paldiski and Liepāja did not stay bases for long. In 1944, "workers' governments" in Tallinn, Riga and Kaunas asked to join the Soviet Union, and the request was granted. Poland, though, has kept its borders, and the League's autonomy statute in Volhynia is holding. There has been no war. The Republic's diplomats can live with that bargain, and so can the country.
What should be Germany's course now?

content.content: Paul von Hindenburg, Field Marshal and Reichspräsident, has died at Neudeck at the age of eighty-six. For better or worse, an era closes with him. The Reichsgericht president serves as acting head of state while the country prepares to choose a successor.

The bourgeois parties are rallying behind

content.content: Carl Goerdeler, the conservative mayor of Leipzig and former price commissioner. He has sharp elbows and an even sharper pencil, and he promises "order without dictatorship".
Otto Gessler, the former Reichswehr minister. He presents himself as a man above party who can reconcile the army with the Republic.
Heinrich Brüning, who has returned from the political wilderness to lead a bourgeois bloc against "the Marxist experiment".

content: % of the Saarlanders voted to return to Germany. The rest chose League rule or France, or simply chose not to be part of whatever Germany has become.

content.content: The nationalists are in uproar. "Even our own blood rejects the Republic," runs one headline, and in the Reichstag the right demands to know who lost the Saar. Unfortunately, they are pointing at us. In Paris, the result is greeted with quiet satisfaction.

e2_saar.title: The Saar Plebiscite
e2_saar.subtitle: The Saarlanders vote on their future.

options.title: Campaign for the Saar's return to a democratic Germany!
Join the nationalists in a single patriotic "German Front".
Propose a European statute for the Saar, under joint Franco-German administration.
This is for the Saarlanders to decide, not us.

content: Versailles took the Saar from us for fifteen years. Its coal mines went to France, its government to a League of Nations commission, and its future to a single vote to be held in January 1935. That day has now come. Some half a million Saarlanders will choose between return to Germany, union with France, or the

No one seriously doubts the result—the Saar is German in speech and sentiment, and we have come through the Depression without a dictatorship. The real question is how the campaign is run, and who gets the credit for it. The nationalists of the "Deutsche Front" want torchlight parades and speeches about the bleeding border. Max Braun's Saar
wants a sober campaign for return to a democratic Reich.
The Saarlanders watched Germany fight itself in our civil war

content.content: , and French troops still stand on the Rhine a few hours' march away

content: . The Quai d'Orsay has let it be known that a vote for Germany would be "premature" while the Reich remains unsettled. Unfortunately, many miners' wives now see the *status quo* as the safe choice.

content.content: The Saar sits between the French-occupied Rhineland and a Ruhr ruled by the Red Army. Paris is pouring money into a campaign for the *status quo*, the Ruhr Soviet's agents are calling for a "Saar Workers' Republic", and we can promise little beyond goodwill. For the first time in living memory, it is not certain that the Saar will choose Germany.

The mine owners, the Catholic clergy and the Saar's small shopkeepers are campaigning hard against return to what they call "the Red Reich", and the pulpits warn that a vote for Germany is a vote for collectivization. We will have to convince a pious, conservative mining district that socialism in Berlin will not mean the closing of its churches.
How should we approach the vote?
Our coalition partners will not allow it.

content: We arm the Spanish Republic openly and at our own expense, and we send the volunteers ourselves, under German officers who answer to Berlin. The "Ebert Brigade", drawn largely from veterans of
, reaches the Madrid front in November.
complains that we are splitting the anti-fascist front. In truth, we are keeping Spain's arms out of Moscow's hands.
, which knows what Moscow's help costs, approves.
Across the trenches, our volunteers find exiled <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
At home, the Reichswehr resents an armed brigade it did not choose, and the Center Party protests loudly.

content.content: The talks collapse when the generals, sensing victory, refuse any amnesty.

content: The Ebro offensive bleeds the Republican army white, and Catalonia falls over the winter. Half a million refugees stream over the Pyrenees into French internment camps. In March, Madrid surrenders, and Franco proclaims a "New State" from the balcony of the royal palace.
The executions begin at once. Spain is now a dictatorship of the generals and the Church, on the model of Salazar's Portugal, and the nationalists at home have a new example to point to.

content.content: The German volunteers who survived come home to a hero's welcome from the labor movement, and a cold silence from everyone else. Unfortunately, the defeat has demoralized many of our workers.

content: The government opens camps for the people who fled

, and then, as the camps fill, houses families in requisitioned barracks across the Reich. Many of them are trade unionists, Social Democrats and Jews, who know what the new order means for them. The right complains about the cost. The refugees are soon earning their keep.

e2_war_crisis.exploit.subtitle: The war could be won here, at a price.

content.content: Every division the general staff can find goes into the gap. The armored columns drive on through the night, and by the end of the week they are eighty kilometers behind the enemy's old line. The casualty lists are long, and the newspapers print maps with arrows on them.

e2c_bredow_coup.bloody.title: The coup is defeated, at a terrible price.

content.content: The strike call reaches too few.

content: On the ninth, two battalions from Potsdam occupy the government quarter and the radio tower at Witzleben. For thirty hours, Berlin hears nothing on the radio but marches and the Directory's proclamations.
Then the city fights back. The railwaymen stop the trains bringing reinforcements from Pomerania,

barricades on the Spree bridges, and a loyal cavalry regiment from Brandenburg rides into the Tiergarten. On the third day Bredow surrenders at the Bendlerblock. He is shot that evening by a sergeant who does not wait for orders.

content.content: We have survived a second civil war. Unfortunately, there is rubble in the Wilhelmstraße again, and repairing the damage will cost us (-1 budget). The purge of the army that follows is thorough and bitter.
Speakers from the Center, the liberals and our own party share platforms from Flensburg to Passau under the slogan *The Republic Is Ours*.
Our Reconciliation Program offers housing loans, settler holdings and apprenticeships to the veterans of both sides of the civil war, and nobody asks which side they fought on.
The Interior Ministry dissolves the Junge Front and seizes its offices and its membership files.
From the opposition benches, we take the fight to the Junge Front ourselves. Our speakers follow its marches from town to town, and the union youth hold counter-rallies wherever it appears.
In the next elections the Junge Front wins 4% of the vote and a dozen seats, and its deputies soon find out how tedious committee work can be.
The forest rallies shrink, and the windbreakers go back into the wardrobes.

content: Zehrer writes a gloomy editorial about the "inertia of the masses" and leaves on a lecture tour of Sweden.

content.content: The grievances that fed the movement have not gone away. For now, though, the young men of the defeated have found jobs and other things to do, and our position is more secure.

The railwaymen of the Rhineland stop work, and the civil servants refuse orders from the French commissioners. The miners of the Aachen basin let their pits flood rather than dig coal for French requisition. The whole country rallies behind them, even the parts that hate us.

Unfortunately, Paris responds as it did in 1923, with arrests, expulsions and a customs border on the Rhine. The French troops stay, and the cost of supporting a striking province falls on a treasury that was already struggling.

e2c_rhineland.title: The Watch on the Rhine
e2c_rhineland.subtitle: Paris is ready to talk about the Rhineland, at a price.

options.title: Settle the reparations and sign a new Rhine Pact.
Why not offer Paris and London a defensive alliance?
Take our case to the League of Nations.
We will not negotiate under occupation! Call for passive resistance.

content: French infantry battalions have been on the bridges at Mainz, Koblenz and Cologne since the civil war.

content.content: They crossed the Rhine to help us win the war, and we could not have won without them. Now that the fighting is over, however, they show no sign of leaving.
Paris says they are there to protect France's security until Germany is stable.

content: Most Rhinelanders believe they are there to stay. The tricolor flies over the Ehrenbreitstein fortress, and every incident between soldiers and townspeople makes the front pages from Munich to Königsberg.

content.content: The French ambassador has told the Foreign Office that his government is willing to discuss a withdrawal. The Quai d'Orsay wants the Young Plan reparations that were suspended during the war paid in full, along with a new Rhine Pact that keeps the left bank demilitarized under League inspection. British diplomats have hinted that a French withdrawal could also be part of a wider defensive agreement among the three powers. Meanwhile, the nationalist press is calling for passive resistance, as in 1923.
Two Pomeranian regiments join the march, and the Oder bridges are surrendered without a shot.
The strike holds in the working-class districts, but the suburbs keep working, and the farmers along the road feed the marchers.

The government does not fall, but it gives way.

content: Strasser enters the cabinet as Reich Commissioner for the Lost Territories, and his men take over two ministries and the refugee administration. The parliamentary system survives, but everyone has now seen that it can be overpowered. The Left faction is furious with us.
The putsch is over in three days!

content.content: By noon on the first day, Berlin has stopped. The trams stand where their drivers left them, the power stations are cold, and the printers refuse to print the Directory's proclamations.

content: The militia battalions put up barricades across the Frankfurter Allee and the Müllerstraße, and the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
's lorries are stopped at every bridge over the Spree.

content.content: The Potsdam infantry regiment refuses to march, and the Prussian police retake the radio station in a sharp fight that costs eleven lives.

content: The Directory's support collapses as quickly as it appeared, and the garrisons that were waiting to see who would win now declare that they were always loyal.

Fritsch is arrested at Döberitz, and Rundstedt escapes to Switzerland. In the Bendlerblock, the police find files that name the conspiracy's backers: three Ruhr industrialists, a banker, the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
leadership, and several deputies of the
. Worst of all for the right, they find letters from bourgeois politicians who promised to "accept the facts" if the putsch succeeded. The conservative opposition is badly discredited.

content.content: The old officer corps is finished. What should we do with the traitors?

The Emergency Powers Act becomes law. Every decree must now be laid before the Reichstag within three days, can be canceled by a simple vote, and may not touch the budget or the electoral law. A power that was once limited only by the President's conscience is now limited by statute.
It is not the clean break our jurists wanted, however, and the Left faction grumbles that we have "regulated the guillotine instead of dismantling it".

content.content: Every resident of the Reich gets a number and a punched card, on which is recorded their name, address, occupation and religion. The police are delighted. The liberals and the party's own lawyers are not, and they ask what such a register would do in the wrong hands. Nobody has a good answer.

The unions and the employers' federation sign a five-year agreement that ties wages to output. When productivity rises, so do wages. It is not class struggle, and the party's left says so. But it does put money in workers' pockets every year.
Only the Reich government can introduce this.

The Health Service Act merges the sickness funds into a single national insurance, with free treatment for every resident and the funds' own clinics as its backbone. The doctors' association threatens a strike, then thinks better of it when it sees the polls. A London newspaper calls it "Beveridge with a German accent".

There is football on Saturdays, variety on Sundays, and Fritz Lang films on weeknights. On the evening of the Cup Final, the streets of every industrial town are empty. The party's educators are unhappy about it, but the voters are not.

The graphite pile in Dahlem is run as a factory as much as a laboratory. Radioactive iodine goes to the Charité for thyroid patients, cobalt goes to the cancer clinics, and tracer isotopes go to the chemical industry. The engineers at Leuna use them to find leaks in their pipelines. It is the first time the atom has paid its way.

The institute's papers go out to Robert Goddard in New Mexico and to the French rocket society in Paris. Goddard writes back a cautious letter, which is more than he has ever done before. The War Ministry protests that it is like handing out the plans of a field gun. The Foreign Office answers that this is a rocket without a gun.

It is a bright time for German democracy. After a period of struggle, inflation is finally under control, and the economy is expanding steadily. In foreign policy, we have reached agreements with the Western powers and the Soviet Union that might make genuine peace a reality.

Now, the task of Social Democracy is to prepare for the next election. The bourgeois-right government of Wilhelm Marx is unpopular, and we stand to gain. Perhaps the next government will have a socialist majority.
The current bourgeois-right government has fallen. The next elections are slated for May of this year.

content.content:
The impact of the last election to encourage cooperation between the two liberal parties have culminated in the creation of a parliamentary faction featuring the two parties. This is begrudgingly accepted by the extremes of both parties to increase their parliamentary influence with the declining liberal vote.

A new Liberal Association has been gaining traction with funding from both parties, and are expected to open up state and local chapters and to draft a policy program. This seems to be the prelude to the founding of a new liberal party, but it's not certain if both parties will consent to this.

Our calls for new elections just after the last one have pushed the liberal parties closer together, in order to not face any further decline. A new Liberal Association has emerged coordinating the efforts of the two parties and seems to be the prelude to the founding of a new liberal party, but it's not certain if both parties would fully agree.

The idea of a liberal parliamentary faction has gained considerable traction with both parties and they are likely to negotiate as a single bloc after the election.

His deflationary and austerity measures deepened the economic crisis, radicalizing the very social groups upon which these moderate parties relied for electoral support. content.content: The formation of the Austro-German customs union has prompted France to exert significant economic pressure on Austria. Leveraging its sizable influence over the Austrian economy, France is not only refusing to extend financial assistance to the country’s struggling major banks but is also deliberately withdrawing large sums of money, further destabilizing Austria's financial sector.

The major Austrian Bank Creditanstalt has declared bankruptcy, following French political and economic pressures aimed at undermining the plans for the Austro-German customs union. In that respect, they have certainly succeeded. We can only hope that this crisis does not spill over into Germany or, worse, spread across Europe.

content: Following Creditanstalt's bankruptcy, an event that has shaken international financial markets, investors are now rapidly withdrawing funds from German banks. Germany's heavy reliance on short-term foreign loans has turned Austria’s banking crisis into a direct threat to our own stability. In response, Reichsbank President

has implemented measures to curb capital flight by disincentivizing the transfer of money abroad. However, the effectiveness of these policies remains uncertain, and may cause unintended consequences.

content.content: Rumors have circulated regarding Center Party leader Ludwig Kaas's intention to resign, as he has privately expressed a desire to step down from his burdensome position. His frequent absences from Germany, often spent in Rome, have left his deputy leader Joos and parliamentary leader Brüning to effectively manage the party. Kaas also holds one of the worst attendance records in the Reichstag. However, Kaas has attributed his prolonged absences to poor health, and the considerable autonomy he has granted to his colleagues has quelled efforts to replace him with a more active, though controversial, leader.

Great Britain has abandoned the Gold Standard! The short-lived naval mutiny, caused by pay cuts, led to panic on the London Stock Exchange and a run on the Pound. The British government then adopted this policy as a means to stimulate industrial exports without the harmful side effects of deflation, achieved through the devaluation of the Pound. Germany's top economic experts viewed this as an act of desperation that would ruin England’s banks and insurance companies. Germany's citizens' fear of inflation, along with the obligation to preserve the mark’s value at 0.358 grams of fine gold under the Young Plan, has prevented Reichsbank President

from abandoning the Gold Standard. However, with both the United States and Britain showing sympathies toward our request for more flexible regulations, perhaps this decision was ultimately made on economic grounds after all.

Kaas has since departed for an extended convalescent leave in South Tyrol.

content.content: Chancellor Papen has ordered the German delegation to walk out of the Geneva Disarmament Conference after France issued a strong objection to Germany’s demand for equal armament rights. Papen declared that Germany will not return to the conference unless the other powers agree to his terms.

The new right-wing and non-partisan Prussian cabinet assembled by Reichskommissar Papen has launched a large-scale purge of socialist and democratic officials from the civil service, forcing them into early retirement. Most of their replacements are conservatives—many of them nationalists. The purge is particularly aimed at socialist provincial presidents and police officials. An estimated 69 republican officials have been stripped of their power. Safe to say, the democratic bulwark has been dismantled.

content.content: Perhaps the global recovery is finally on the horizon. Many economists now believe the slump has bottomed out, with the Frankfurt stock exchange climbing steadily—share and bond values have risen by over 30% since spring. But this resurgence remains abstract to the millions of unemployed Germans still trapped in poverty.

content: The aftermath of the Reichstag elections and the emergence of a Black-Brown majority has initiated negotiations between the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

General Schleicher has presented an enticing proposal to

In this arrangement, Gregor Strasser would serve as Interior Minister of both Prussia and the Reich, while Schleicher believes he can control the Nazis by taking the role of Defense Minister. However, the Nazi leadership's enthusiasm quickly fades when President Hindenburg refuses to appoint
as Chancellor. Papen, deeply offended by Schleicher's apparent willingness to abandon him, has used his growing rapport with Hindenburg to undermine Schleicher’s influence over the President.
Following the results of the Reichstag elections, Papen and President Hindenburg met with
to hear his demands for the party’s participation in government.

content.content: General elections were held in Sweden, resulting in a great victory for Per Albin Hansson and his Social Democrats, who now govern in a minority government. The Swedish Social Democrats have embraced the concept of a 'people's home', a form of reformist socialism aimed at reducing class divides while working in the capitalist framework. Perhaps we should consider following their 'nordic' model?

The main proceedings in the case against Papen’s unconstitutional Reichsexekution of the Prussian government have begun, with a verdict expected in the coming weeks. Yet, the historically reactionary leanings of the judiciary place us at a clear disadvantage—despite support from the state governments of Bavaria and Baden, who have joined us in challenging the decree’s legality.

Chancellor of Austria Engelbert Dollfuß has used the "War Economy Enabling Act", a law passed during the days of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, which allowed him to restructure the Creditanstalt without parliamentary approval. While the Austrian Social Democrats have protested, Dollfuß' actions are technically legal.

However, it is essentially a restatement of classical liberal ideology, tailored to appeal to a more nationalistic German middle class. The national democracy program also reaffirms the

With its electoral alliance with the DNVP, the

signaling his readiness to seek the support of other parties if he were to be made chancellor first. Calling

content.content: Democrat Franklin D. Roosevelt has defeated incumbent Republican President Herbert Hoover in a landslide in the United States presidential election. This is attributed by the Great Depression and Roosevelt's campaigning for a "New Deal", proposing expansive public works and government reform.
Rumors are circulating widely that General Schleicher intends to undermine the very chancellor he helped install. Among his contacts, he's already being referred to as the chancellor-designate.

content: to make one final attempt at forming a majority coalition. Reporting back the next day,

has suffered yet another crushing setback—this time in the local elections in Thuringia. The results show the party lost nearly a quarter of its vote share compared to the previous state election. While low turnout may be a factor, this and three other recent local elections have only reinforced the growing sense that the Nazis have peaked and are rapidly losing support.

content.content: Despite his ousting, Papen remains in far closer physical proximity to the President than the chancellor does. At Hindenburg’s personal request, he continues to reside in an apartment within the Interior Ministry building—just steps from Hindenburg’s own quarters—while Schleicher lives miles away in a private residence. This arrangement has enabled Papen to scheme full-time, without attracting public attention.

Once a close ally, Oskar von Hindenburg has become an implacable enemy of the new chancellor—reportedly over a tasteless joke that wounded his pride beyond forgiveness. In Prussian times, such insults could end in duels; this time, the fallout may claim the life of the Republic. Two members of the Camarilla now harbor intense hostility toward Schleicher, and are working to sway the President into reconsidering his appointment.

Shortly after Schleicher’s appointment, the Western Allies, following protracted negotiations at the Geneva Disarmament Conference, conceded in principle to Germany’s right to equality in arms. The practical terms of this concession remain unclear, but in Schleicher’s view, it opens the path toward establishing an official militia service.

During Schleicher's addresses to the nation, one central theme rings clear: "Create Work!" He has revived efforts to resettle the urban unemployed on rural homesteads carved from bankrupt estates in the sparsely populated East. Although the Reichstag remains dissolved and he cannot legislate, he has publicly opposed Papen’s changes to the unemployment insurance system, presenting himself as a proponent of neither capitalism nor socialism. His ideological ambiguity has earned him the nickname "social general"—a label he embraces, claiming it aligns with the army’s tradition of solidarity between officers and soldiers.

content: 's resurgence in the polls has led Dingeldey to become overconfident, unequivocally supporting Papen, then Schleicher, and even forming a parliamentary faction with the various splinter parties between it and the
. While this move has bolstered their influence, it has alienated Hugenberg and the
, on whom they still depend on as of their electoral alliance.
For some odd reason, von Schleicher came to believe that nothing came of
’s attempts to be appointed parliamentary chancellor simply because the man didn’t “at the bottom of his heart” want the office. By

, this suspicion had become a firm conviction; he repeatedly confided to journalists and his cabinet that the man simply doesn’t really want power. This belief is leading to Schleicher overestimating his chances of securing <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
Heavy electoral losses for the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

in local elections have further reinforced the disillusionment of the voters who have brought the movement to prominence, many who joined and donated to the party expecting to receive the spoils of victory are beginning to despair, withdrawing their donations. Admission fees for rallies, once a major source of income at the local level, have collapsed despite steep price reductions.

's failure to gain the chancellorship or enter government to constructively relieve Germany's economic woes has caused further frustration among the movement. However, Nazi leaders are quick to suppress any leaks of dissent or rumors of decline to the public.
The global economy is on the upswing—and with it, the erosion of the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
continues. The republican police force surveilling the

in Munich has noted clear signs of disintegration. Resignations are occurring daily, membership dues arrive irregularly, and expulsions over indebtedness are increasingly common. Every branch of the party appears run down. As for morale, the police report observed: “The view that the peak has passed and favorable prospects are missed is commonly held among many members.”
Schleicher still clings to the illusionary hope that the now powerless Strasser might somehow persuade
to allow Nazi participation in his cabinet, now that Strasser has returned from vacation. Strasser’s absence from the public eye has unsettled

, who now fears potential backroom plots to fracture the party—especially given the eagerness of Strasser’s remaining loyalists to do just that. In reality, all Strasser does is to warn former chancellor Brüning that Papen has arranged a secret meeting with Hitler—set to take place within a week or two—to conspire against their mutual enemy: Schleicher.

's financial situation is becoming dire. Increasingly, equipment and supplies are being acquired on credit—credit that's already drying up under the weight of the party's existing debts. Tensions have begun to flare between the

and the party leadership over how to divide dwindling donations, with some members resorting to begging in the streets or organizing lotteries to scrape together funds. One more election, and the party could face a full-blown financial crisis.

Despite promising President Hindenburg not to publicly criticize his favored former chancellor, Schleicher has done just that in a bid to distance himself from the deeply unpopular Papen. Hindenburg, displeased by the breach of trust, grows increasingly estranged from Schleicher. Papen, for his part, has shown little outward hostility toward his ouster—carefully masking his resentment and thirst for revenge beneath a façade of cordiality. In the meantime, Hindenburg has quietly authorized him to serve as his secret liaison to

content.content: Günther Gereke, the energetic special commissioner for public works, has grown frustrated with the chancellor after a request for intervention to clear bureaucratic obstacles was flatly rejected. His ambitious projects remain stalled. Gereke, disillusioned, has confided his disappointment to his close friend—none other than Oskar von Hindenburg.

content: Günther Gereke, the energetic special commissioner for public works, has had his project accelerated after his request for the chancellor to intervene and clear bureaucratic obstacles was approved.
Schleicher's eagerness to follow through on his promise to satisfy the unions and the <span style="color: #c00000;">

before their electoral base returns to work, has driven this decision.
Schleicher's eagerness to fulfill his promise to the unions, and to curb the growing <span style="color: #700000;">

content.content: The disastrous state of the German economy has made rearmament a pipe dream, and Schleicher is eager to get it back on track.

The campaign for the Landtag elections in the microscopically small Free State of Lippe has begun, with the Nazis investing a substantial amount of resources to sway just a hundred thousand voters. However, despite its small size, a victory here could dispel the growing belief that the Nazis are on the brink of a catastrophic decline.

content: At a private dinner with journalists, Chancellor von Schleicher repeatedly expressed confidence that the Nazi leader would eventually come around to tolerating his cabinet—despite

’s public affirmations of an all-or-nothing course. This, even as Schleicher made clear he would dissolve the Reichstag if needed, a move he believes would cost the Nazis further seats (though he seeks to avoid such a step, fearing the
would benefit most from their collapse). “They’ll soon be eating out of my hand,” were the chancellor’s exact words that evening. What Schleicher fails to grasp is that
is no ordinary politician. He will not respond rationally, nor prudently, to Strasser’s break or to the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
’s electoral collapse. He believes destiny is on his side.

Chancellor von Schleicher and his press secretary have deliberately “leaked” plans to appoint Strasser as Vice Chancellor, Interior Minister, and Minister-President of Prussia, alongside naming the Center Party labor leader Stegerwald as Labor Minister. The Agriculture and Economics Ministries were reportedly reserved for Hugenberg himself. It’s highly likely this is a bluff—an attempt to pressure the
into dropping its total opposition, lest they risk being sidelined entirely.
With Dingeldey's pretentiousness, fueled by the <span style="color: #C0A054;">

's uptick in polling, elevating it to the lead party on the "moderate" Right, Hugenberg is growing increasingly irritated by their independence and seeks to terminate their electoral alliance if new elections are called. While the
still hopes to renew the alliance, they begin exploring the possibility of an accommodation with the

and the bourgeois parties as a safeguard against near-certain annihilation if Hugenberg severs ties. Meanwhile, the DNV (German National Association), a non-partisan organization aiming to consolidate the German middle, is starting to repair its relations with the liberals after already securing the support of the non-liberal right, with politicians like Treviranus.

content.content: Von Schleicher's bluffs—such as proposing a cabinet that includes both Stegerwald and Hugenberg—have lost all credibility. The Center Party has publicly ruled out Stegerwald serving alongside Hugenberg, a notorious enemy of organized labor. Moreover, the leak about the President’s meeting with Strasser has led to a permanent break between the Nazi leader and Schleicher, ending any hope that Strasser might persuade him to support a cabinet involving Schleicher. His contradictory tactics and careless remarks have only deepened mistrust and furthered his political isolation. He only now condemns efforts to postpone elections—despite having supported the idea just a week earlier.

With progress stalled across nearly all sectors, Schleicher has attempted to shift focus by bringing the issue of rearmament back into the public eye. He announced plans to establish a compulsory militia within a year, alongside a renewed commitment to arming the Reichswehr with heavy weaponry and instituting universal conscription. However, the impact of this intended public relations triumph is minimal, as news of Schleicher’s political setbacks dominates public attention.

Having failed to extract concessions from the chancellor to turn Germany into a dictatorship, the more radical elements within his party have pressured him into adopting an all-out opposition to Schleicher. A strongly worded resolution has been released, accusing him of "vacillation" in his willingness to "reform" the constitution. Furthermore, his initiative to restart peasant homesteads on bankrupt eastern estates has drawn the ire of conservative elites. With the next vote of no confidence looming, it may well come down to Schleicher versus the entire chamber.

Dollfuß has abused his powers given in the "War Economy Enabling Act" to crack down on the workers in a railroad strike, which has resulted in all three presidents of parliament resigning amid a crucial vote. This crisis presented a perfect opportunity for Dollfuß to abolish the parliamentary system and restrict democratic rights, such as the freedom of the press and public protests. Another democracy has fell to authoritarianism.

Dollfuß's Austrofascist dictatorship has banned the Austrian Communists and the paramilitary of the Austrian Social Democrats, the Republican Protection League. He has also established the Fatherland Front, a party promoting a far-right fascist and corporate ideology.

content.content: The Austrian Civil War has begun and ended in a matter of three days, fought between the Republican Protection League and Austria's Austrofascist regime, resulting in a defeat for the socialists across the border. The uprising was sparked by efforts to suppress the remnants of the Austrian Social Democrats and their paramilitary wing. However, the poorly coordinated and weakened movement was swiftly crushed by the army. Perhaps things would have gone more differently if they have taken up arms earlier.

content: . The Reichswehr lends it instructors, officially on leave, and a squadron of fighters with Spanish markings painted over the crosses. The Legion lands at Cartagena under its own flag, the black, red and gold of 1848, and goes into the line at Madrid in November.

content.content: For the Reichswehr, Spain is the first chance since 1918 to test new aircraft and new tactics against a real enemy, and the officers who come home on leave talk about little else. For Rome, the Legion is an act of war in all but name. The Italian ambassador is recalled, and Mussolini's newspapers promise that the "Germans of Weimar" will pay for it.

e2_spain.title: The Generals Rise in Spain
e2_spain.subtitle: The Spanish Republic asks for our help.

Sign the agreement—and look the other way.
Send food, doctors and ambulances, but no arms.
Spain's government is lawful! Sell it arms openly.
Send arms, advisers and volunteers, together with Moscow.
Send arms and volunteers through our own channels.
Raise a Legion Schwarz-Rot-Gold, with Reichswehr instructors and aircraft.

content: On the seventeenth of July, the Army of Africa rose against the Spanish Popular Front government, and within days the mutiny had spread to garrisons across the peninsula. Generals Mola and Franco expected Madrid to fall in a week. It did not—workers' militias stormed the Montaña barracks, Barcelona's anarchists beat the soldiers in the streets, and the country is now split down the middle.

content.content: Mussolini, still bogged down in Ethiopia, can spare the rebels only a few dozen aircraft.
Italian bombers are already ferrying Franco's Moroccan troops across the Strait.

Britain and France have proposed a Non-Intervention Agreement, under which no power will supply either side. However, the Spanish ambassador has called on the Foreign Ministry to point out that his is the lawful government of Spain, and that under international law it is entitled to buy arms.

The Center Party has seen the photographs of burned churches in Catalonia and wants nothing to do with "the Spanish Reds". Our own left wing wants to know what our republic is for, if not to stand by other republics.

content: We know this story. Several thousand exiled veterans of the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">

We can spare little. The Ruhr Soviet has already announced that a "Rhine-Ruhr Column" will leave for Spain whatever Berlin decides, and exiled <span style="color: #3E88B3;">

The United Front sees itself in Spain. The <span style="color: #700000;">
has proposed that German aid be coordinated with the Comintern, which is already organizing International Brigades and has offered to route Soviet arms through Hamburg.
The United Front sees itself in Spain. The Comintern, which is already organizing International Brigades, has offered to route Soviet arms through Hamburg. However, the

The decision is not ours alone.

Our coalition partners will not let the Reich take sides in Spain.

content: At most, the cabinet will agree to keep its eyes shut, and only if the Foreign Office is ours.

content.content: As long as our Chancellor holds the coalition together, the Republic can sell arms to a lawful government. It cannot go further without breaking the coalition.
Nobody in the cabinet can stop us from going as far as we like.
The decision belongs to the government. What we can do is what the labor movement has always done for its own.

The Spanish Republic wins the war, but the Spanish Communist Party wins the Republic. Its commissars command the army that broke the generals on the Ebro, its police have already dealt with the anarchists and the dissident Marxists in Barcelona, and in the victory parade through Madrid the portraits are of Stalin and Dolores Ibárruri.

content: By the end of the year, Spain is a "people's democracy" in all but name. Lisbon, Paris and London are horrified, and every conservative in Europe now points to Spain as proof that the Soviets can win a war in the West. The Center Party and our Catholic voters are alarmed.
hails a great victory for the international working class, and asks why the United Front should not follow the Spanish example.

e2_spain_end.title: The Last Battles in Spain
e2_spain_end.subtitle: After two years of war, the end is in sight.

options.title: Send everything we can spare for the Ebro offensive!
Back Negrín's thirteen points, and press for a negotiated peace.
Stand aside, and prepare for the refugees.

content: The war in Spain has lasted two years, and it has settled into the grinding trench warfare of the Great War.

content.content: The Legion Schwarz-Rot-Gold has held the line on the Jarama and at the gates of Madrid, and its fighters have driven the Italian bombers from the sky over the capital.
German field guns and German volunteers have held the line on the Jarama and at the gates of Madrid.
The trickle of German arms has helped, but it has never been enough.
The Spanish Republic has fought with whatever Moscow and Mexico would sell it.
German field hospitals have treated its wounded since the first winter.
Mussolini's help to the generals has never amounted to much.
Italian divisions are fighting openly on Franco's side.

content: Now both sides are preparing for a decisive campaign on the Ebro. The Spanish prime minister, Juan Negrín, has published thirteen points for a negotiated peace, and the Vatican and Washington are both quietly sounding out the two camps.

content.content: Republican Spain is more and more dependent on the Spanish Communist Party, which controls the army's political commissars and the secret police.
With Moscow as its only real supplier, the Republic is more and more dependent on the Spanish Communist Party.
What will we do in the war's final act?

Germany joins the Council of the People's Democracies, with its joint command in Moscow and its planning commission in Berlin. The People's Army's general staff now takes its orders from Moscow. The councils, which once argued about everything, are learning that some questions are no longer open to discussion.

content: On the ninth, two battalions from Potsdam occupy the government quarter. This time, Berlin does not rise. The city is tired, hungry and disillusioned after years of war and inflation, and the workers stay at home.

By evening, the radio is reading out lists of arrested ministers. The Reich Directory dissolves the Reichstag, suspends the constitution and promises elections "once order has been restored". Nobody believes it. The leadership of the <span style="color: #c00000;">

The ninth is eleven days away.

content.content: Speakers from the Center, the liberals and our own party share platforms from Flensburg to Passau under the slogan *The Republic Is Ours*.
Our Reconciliation Program offers housing loans, settler holdings and apprenticeships to the veterans of both sides of the civil war, and nobody asks which side they fought on.
The Interior Ministry dissolves the Junge Front and seizes its offices and its membership files.
From the opposition benches, we take the fight to the Junge Front ourselves. Our speakers follow its marches from town to town, and the union youth hold counter-rallies wherever it appears.

The Junge Front does not take power, but it does not go away either. It wins a fifth of the vote in Schleswig-Holstein and Pomerania and runs town halls in Lower Saxony, and its marching columns have become a regular weekend sight in the provincial towns. The bourgeois parties no longer call it extremist. Now it is "the national opposition".
The Republic still stands. However, German politics has moved to the right, and some of our middle-class voters are drifting away with it.
