content.content: The Pomeranian regiments join the marchers at Küstrin, and by Tuesday the army is directing the columns into the capital.
Berlin does not strike. The city is cold and hungry, and it has had enough.

content: The columns enter Berlin through the Brandenburg Gate on Wednesday morning. Strasser speaks from the Chancellery balcony, as he promised, while the government's cars race north up the Hamburg road.

content.content: The first decree of the "Government of National Revolution" dissolves the Reichstag. The second opens camps for its political enemies, and our comrades are among the first to be sent there.

Their leaders announced in their own newspapers that they were coming to "dissolve the party state".

content: More columns are forming in Frankfurt an der Oder and Küstrin. The Pomeranian regiments of Wehrkreis II have been confined to barracks, but no one knows whether they will obey the order. Otto Strasser has promised to address the nation from the balcony of the Reich Chancellery on Wednesday.

content.content: The leading columns will reach the outskirts of Berlin by Tuesday night. What should we do?

Withdraw the government to Saxony and the Ruhr, and fight it out from there.
Accept Fritsch's terms. We must stop the bloodshed.

content.content: The putsch has neither won nor failed. The Directory holds the government quarter, the radio station and Tempelhof airfield. The workers hold the northern and eastern districts of Berlin, where barricades have gone up across the main roads. There is shooting along the Landwehr Canal.
Outside Berlin, the country is split. The Ruhr and Saxony are with us, Pomerania and East Prussia are with the generals, and Bavaria is talking about "neutrality".
The general strike has paralyzed the capital, but it has not stopped the soldiers.
The militia is fighting bravely, but it is outgunned, and every hour costs lives.
Half the army stands with us and half against us, and the officers are telephoning each other to negotiate a "resolution among comrades".

content: Through intermediaries in the bourgeois parties, Fritsch has offered terms: he will withdraw his troops if the <span style="color: #700000;">
leaves the government, the councils are curbed, the plotters are granted an amnesty, and the army is left to manage its own affairs.

The Cabinet of National Renewal has reopened the case files from the civil war, this time with our comrades as the defendants.

content.content: The result is that the Austrofascists have backed down! Caught in an untenable position domestically and abroad, they have agreed to restore the National Council and resign from government, holding new elections. Now begins the long work of reconstruction. Our countries are likely to be brought closer together as a result.
This is a great success of the new European Union, and its prestige is seen to rise internationally.

content.content: Now, Austria is entering a state of civil war. When the police attempted to seize weapons from the Republikanischer Schutzbund, the Schutzbund responded with force, shooting at the government troops. Fighting has sporadically broken out between Schutzbund and government forces all over Austria.

content: The government's attempts to suppress the socialist party and the Schutzbund were met with mass protest, supported by the

content: After several rounds of elimination voting at the <span style="color: #00C0FF;">

The moderate Frank Glatzel was the first to go, followed by Hans von Raumer, whose industrialist backers then fragmented between Treviranus and Hergt. In the penultimate round, Kuno von Westarp withdrew and threw his delegates behind Hergt rather than the centrist faction led by Gottfried Treviranus. Agrarian conservatives, church‑aligned delegates, and a sizable bloc of
conservatives gave him the edge over Treviranus in the final ballot.
Hergt’s victory has seen our relations with the <span style="color: #00C0FF;">

sour. His entrenched monarchism and hostility toward democratic processes have already led him to explore increased cooperation with the far right, including informal contacts with the Stahlhelm. Genuine legislative collaboration now seems all but impossible, making building coalitions in the future increasingly difficult.

content.content: The Center Party is internally split on this. Their ties to the Schleicher cabinet and the pro-Schleicher sentiment expressed by many of their party members have made joining the socialist-led boycott a hard pill to swallow. However, we have gained the sympathy of their left wing.

The Center Party is already a Blocpartei, so it's out of the question. However, we have some sympathetic voices on the party's left wing, like Wirth and Jakob Kaiser of the Christian labor unions, lending their support nonetheless.

content.content: But perhaps we can bypass this deadlock by targeting Hindenburg himself. With a two-thirds majority in the Reichstag, we could initiate impeachment proceedings under Article 59 or trigger a recall election under Article 43. If the recall election were to fail, the Reichstag would be dissolved for new elections.

Yet the reactionary nature of the courts renders impeachment unlikely to succeed. Recall, however, remains a narrow possibility—it requires only a majority of those who vote, not of all eligible voters. Still, to make either path viable, we must secure the backing of other parties.

The Reichsbank, long known for its strict fiscal conservatism and obsessive anti-inflation stance, had already slashed Schleicher's initial public works decree by 15%. So, it was no surprise when news of even greater government spending met with their disapproval.

However, the endorsement of the campaign by Hjalmar Schacht—a respected banker and former Reichsbank President credited with ending hyperinflation—has done much to calm the business community. Under government pressure, the Reichsbank is ultimately coerced into backing the plan.

content.content: But it is not all sunshine and rainbows. The civil war has devastated countless lives, and the costs of reconstruction and welfare have triggered the return of hyperinflationary nightmares. Hunger now exceeds levels seen during the Great Depression, and many are already growing disillusioned with their supposed saviors. Though the reactionary and far-right forces were defeated on the battlefield, it's only a matter of years before a new right-wing movement emerges and takes root among the weary and discontented populace.

content: No war as destructive as the Great War would come again. Slowly, Germany and the Western Allies began to rebuild relations, but the French reoccupation of the Rhineland has complicated efforts. Fascism never takes root as a dominant force, and the primary threat to European democracy becomes the resurgent Soviet Union. The Spanish Civil War ends in 1936 with a Republican victory.

content: Article 48 allows the Reichspräsident to take "the necessary measures" to restore public order, and to suspend seven of the basic rights while he does so. Its fifth paragraph promised that a Reich law would "determine the details"—but fifteen years on, no such law exists. Ebert used the article well over a hundred times to hold the young Republic together.

content.content: Brüning used it to govern without the Reichstag altogether, and in the worst months of the crisis, the Reich issued more decrees than it passed laws.
In the crisis years, many in Berlin came to see an emergency decree as an easier road than a Reichstag majority, and the bourgeois parties have not forgotten how convenient it was.

content: regards the emergency powers as the presidency's birthright. His state secretary has let it be known that the President will not sign away the "reserve constitution" quietly.
has told the cabinet privately that the President would rather lose the powers than be tempted by them.
has signaled that the presidency will accept whatever the Reichstag decides, as long as it is not left defenseless in a real emergency.

content.content: The Ministry of Justice has drafted two bills. The first amends the constitution itself: every decree lapses after 30 days unless the Reichstag confirms it, no basic right may be suspended for longer than two weeks, and a new Reich Constitutional Court may strike down any decree that oversteps. This needs a two-thirds majority. The second is the long-promised implementing law, which needs only a simple majority. It obliges the President to report each decree to the Reichstag and limits their scope, but leaves the article itself untouched.
The mood in the Reichstag is better than it has been in years. Even deputies of the bourgeois parties now admit in the lobbies that the emergency powers are too dangerous to leave unbound.
Unfortunately, the bourgeois parties are wary. Many of their deputies still see Article 48 as the last guarantee against a Marxist majority—and they can count as well as we can.

Perhaps we can buy ourselves some time—if we are willing to pay for it.

It is also the first aircraft in history built by countries that fought each other twenty-five years ago.

content.content: The licences have been bought and the American engineers have come and gone, but no German plant is yet making penicillin at scale. The hospitals still ration it by the milligram.
The Reich Penicillin Works is delivering.
The fermentation tanks at Höchst are delivering.

The drug is no longer the problem. The problem is the people who never see a doctor until it is too late: the miner with a cough, the girl too ashamed to go to the clinic, and the farmer's wife who gives birth on a kitchen table. The public health officers want a campaign, and they want us to choose which one.

The death rate from infectious disease has fallen faster in the last three years than in the previous thirty. The doctors' associations, the sickness funds and the trade unions now agree on one thing: the old patchwork of three thousand separate sickness funds cannot deliver modern medicine to everyone. They agree on nothing else.
The polyclinics run by the councils already treat a third of the working population, and the private doctors' association is furious about it.
Refugees from the occupied east are still crowded into camps around Berlin and Stettin, and tuberculosis has followed them.

The broadcasters of Germany, France, the Low Countries and Switzerland link their networks for the first time to show a single event, a cycling race from Paris to Brussels to Cologne. The commentary switches languages at every frontier. The newspapers start calling the network "Eurovision".

content.content: The first device is assembled in a bunker at Kummersdorf. It has never been tested, and the general staff intends to keep it that way. Its existence is the worst-kept secret in Europe. Within a year, Paris and Moscow both have uranium programs of their own, and Meitner refuses to speak to anyone who worked on it.

content.content: A cabinet order transfers Peenemünde from the War Ministry to a new Reich Space Research Agency. Dornberger resigns. Von Braun stays on, and within a year he is drafting plans for an artificial satellite. The generals are bitter about it, and they will remember.

content: in the wake of post-war optimism deeply divided the German left. As in 1920, leftist disunity once again produced a scenario where a "New Weimar Coalition"—composed of the

It was only through the formation of the German National Unity Front—a broad alliance of all bourgeois parties—and the election of Otto Gessler as president that Germany finally escaped its political deadlock. The resulting coalition of the
emerged as the new “natural governing bloc,” as persistent ideological rifts continued to paralyze the left. The

Only with the third wave of democratization in the 1990s did the long-divided German left begin to reunify. The gradual moderation and eventual merger of the <span style="color: #9B0000;">
culminated in the formation of the
, which at last returned to government after decades in opposition.

The current conditions are not favorable for us.
Our cause is popular in the West, but their sclerotic governments are reluctant to send us aid.
The Soviet Union has aided the Communists, but not the socialists and democrats, in an attempt to shape Germany's future government.
Poland and Czechoslovakia have sent some assistance against the fascists.

content.content: Rome sends two more divisions to Carinthia "at the request of the Austrian government".
Paris and London wonder aloud what Berlin thought it was doing.

The troop trains come home through the winter, and the Reichstag cuts the war budget by two-thirds within the year. The money goes to housing, schools and the railways. The generals complain that the Republic is disarming. The voters, on the whole, are glad of the houses.
The enemy has asked for terms.

options.title: Hold a victory parade through the Brandenburg Gate.
Hold no parade. Build a memorial to the dead.
Press for a general peace conference under the League.
Join France and Poland in a permanent Western defense pact.
Appoint a Reichstag inquiry into the conduct of the war.
Take in the people who fled the lost territories.
Bind the Republic to the Soviet-led alliance.
Keep our distance from Moscow now that the guns are silent.
Bring the soldiers home and turn to rebuilding.

content.content: The Red Army's last offensive broke on the Vistula, and the counter-offensive that followed did not stop at the Riga line. German and Polish armies crossed the Dnieper at Kiev in the autumn. A Ukrainian Rada met in Kiev for the first time since 1918 and proclaimed independence, and in Moscow the Politburo asked for an armistice. At the peace conference in Geneva, the Soviet Union recognized an independent Ukraine, and the Baltic states' independence under League protection. In Moscow, nobody seems quite sure who governs anymore.

The Red Army's offensive broke on the Vistula. Polish and German divisions held the line from Modlin to the sea through a terrible winter, and in the spring the counter-offensive drove the Soviets back to the Riga line of 1921. The armistice signed at Brest restores the old frontier, and Lithuania is free again. Tens of thousands of German soldiers lie in Polish cemeteries.

The front has frozen along the Bug and the marshes of Polesia. Neither side can break through, and neither can afford to keep trying. The armistice signed at Brest leaves Poland its heartland and the Soviet Union most of the eastern borderlands it wanted. The Baltic states are now Soviet republics. Our soldiers come home to a country that cannot decide whether to call it a victory or a defeat.

The line on the Vistula did not hold. The Red Army broke through north of Warsaw, and our divisions fell back into East Prussia in disorder. The armistice signed at Königsberg partitions Poland at the Vistula, and the Red Army stands on the borders of East Prussia. The nationalist press has already found its explanation, and it is not the Red Army.
Our counter-offensive crossed the Inn in the spring, and Salzburg fell in a week. In the summer, German troops entered Vienna, and the Viennese workers' districts hung out red flags to greet them.
Hitler was arrested by Austrian Social Democrats at a farmhouse near Linz, and he will be tried in Vienna, before an Austrian court.
Hitler escaped over the Brenner in a car with Italian diplomatic plates, and Mussolini has given him a villa on Lake Garda. Nobody expects Rome to hand him over.
The Heimwehr's leaders fled to Italy the night before.

content: Italy asked for an armistice at Innsbruck. The peace treaty restores the Austrian Republic, where the <span style="color: #A50034;">
is now the largest party, and leaves the future of South Tyrol to the League. In both capitals, people are talking about the Anschluss again.

content.content: The invasion broke on the Isar. After a winter in the Alpine passes, our counter-offensive drove the Italian and Austrian armies back across the Inn, and Rome asked for an armistice. Bavaria is free, and its government has thanked the Reich in a message that was read out in every church. The peace treaty restores the old frontier and puts the Austrian army under League inspection.

The front runs through the Bavarian Alps, and neither side can move it. The armistice leaves Berchtesgaden and the upper Inn valley under Austrian occupation "until a final settlement", and nobody expects that to come soon.

Munich fell. Under Italian and Austrian protection, a Bavarian assembly has proclaimed a Kingdom of Bavaria under Crown Prince Rupprecht, "free of Berlin and free of Marxism". The armistice recognizes it. Germany has lost an eighth of its people, and the nationalist press has already found someone to blame.

Our counter-offensive crossed the Rhine at Strasbourg, and by the autumn our armies stood on the Marne. Before they could reach Paris, the city rose. The Popular Front parties and the officers who had never accepted La Rocque restored the Republic, and the new government asked for an armistice the next morning. As a gesture, our armies are withdrawing behind the Rhine, and the peace treaty takes nothing from France. Léon Blum, the new premier, has thanked the German people, though not, in so many words, the German army.

The French offensive stalled in the hills of the Palatinate, and our counter-attack drove it back across the Rhine. The regime in Paris, which promised a short war, has asked for an armistice. The old frontier is restored, and the Rhineland stays German and demilitarized on both banks.
The front runs along the Rhine, with French bridgeheads at Kehl and Mannheim that we could never take back. The armistice leaves them in French hands "until a final settlement".

The Rhine did not hold. French troops occupy the left bank from Cologne to Landau, as they did in 1919, and Paris has announced a "Rhenish State" under French protection. The armistice leaves them there. The nationalist press speaks of 1923 again, and so does everyone else.

The war between the two worlds has ended in victory for the East. In the spring the People's Army and the Red Army broke the French line on the Meuse, and by the autumn Soviet and German troops stood on the Atlantic at Brest and Bordeaux. The French government has fled to Algiers, and the British have withdrawn behind the Channel. A vast new bloc of people's democracies stretches from Lisbon to Arkhangelsk. Germany is its industrial heart, and Moscow is its head. The cost in German lives runs to the hundreds of thousands.

Poland is partitioned. The Soviet Union takes everything east of the Vistula, and Germany has the Corridor and Danzig back, which no nationalist government ever managed. The French and the British, who could not break our line in the west, accept an armistice with bad grace. The rest of Europe now regards the Republic as Moscow's junior partner.

The Polish army held the Corridor, and neither we nor the French could break through in the west. Moscow has signed an armistice with Warsaw that gives it the eastern borderlands, and we have signed one that gives us nothing.

The Polish army held the Corridor, and the French and British broke through in the Saar and the Palatinate. In the spring, Moscow made a separate peace with Warsaw, took the eastern borderlands and left us to fight alone. The armistice puts the Rhineland and the Ruhr under Allied occupation until Germany has paid for the war, and the Allies have made it clear that they want a different government in Berlin.
Every victory has a price at home. The nationalist press speaks of the army that saved the Republic, and the army has begun to believe it. The war debts will take a generation to pay.
The front did not break so much as dissolve. Whole divisions went home on their own, and the general staff could not tell the cabinet where the line was.
The neutral powers' mediation brought both sides to a compromise that neither of them wanted.
The political truce ends with the war, and the party quarrels begin again on the day the armistice is signed.
The government will set the course, but it needs a majority in the Reichstag, and our votes count.
What should be Germany's course now?

content.content: The army falls back to a shorter line in good order, and blows the bridges behind it. The enemy's tanks reach the new line two days later and stop there. The nationalist press prints the names of the towns we have given up.

content.content: Three regiments of the Silesian division have refused to go back into the line. Their officers have sent the Chancellery a memorandum: the army will fight on only under a government it trusts, and without "political commissars of the Reichsbanner" at its headquarters. The Chief of the Army Command has not disowned them. In 1918 it was the sailors at Kiel who refused. This time it is the officers.

On Monday morning, the Berlin metalworkers walked out of the war factories, and by the evening the strike had spread to Leipzig, Hamburg and the Ruhr. Their demands are the ones the January strikers made in 1918: bread, and peace without annexations. Our own shop stewards are on the strike committee.
The Red Army's line has broken north of Warsaw.
The Austrian line has broken in the Chiemgau.
The French line has broken west of Kaiserslautern.
The Polish line has broken on the Vistula.
Our armored divisions are through, and for fifty kilometers there is nothing in front of them. The general staff wants to know whether to send everything into the gap.
Soviet tank armies have broken through on the Narew, and East Prussia is open.
The Italians have broken through at Kufstein, and the road to Munich is open.
The French have broken out of the Kehl bridgehead, and the road to Stuttgart is open.
The French have broken through in the Saar, and the road to the Rhine is open.
The general staff asks for a decision within the hour.
The Chancellor has called the party leaders to the Chancellery. The decision is the cabinet's, but the cabinet will not last the week without our votes.

content.content: The League of Nations is hosting a conference to discuss the state of the global economy and potential solutions to the ongoing depression. All parties want to reduce tariffs to encourage trade. However, the Western powers are at an impasse; France and to a lesser extent Britain are calling for fixed currency exchange rates, while President Roosevelt of the United States wants to print new money to stimulate demand, calling for "controlled inflation". The Europeans want to reduce their debts to the US, while America favors continued full payments.
Thanks to our own constitutional amendment, the president no longer has the power to call Reichsexekutions, and we are thus powerless to prevent this development.

Schreyer's valve machine works, when its valves do. It can do in an afternoon what a room of clerks does in a month.
The new machine works. It can do in an afternoon what a room of clerks does in a month.
Every ministry in Berlin wants time on it, and the question is which one gets it.

Calculating machines have stopped being a novelty. There are a dozen of them in Germany now, all built to different designs, and no two can read each other's programs. Zuse has written a programming language for them, the *Plankalkül*, which almost nobody understands.
The Planning Office's economists say they could balance the whole national plan by machine. The factory councils want to be sure that the machine does not end up making the decisions.
The Republic's statisticians cannot count what they cannot reach. The census figures for the Ruhr and the occupied Rhineland are still estimates.

Foreign journalists start writing about the "German miracle", and the shop windows on the Kurfürstendamm and the Jungfernstieg are as bright as Fifth Avenue's. Whether it is still socialism is a question for the next party congress.

content.content: The refrigerators are being built, but most of them are going to the Americans or the shops on the Kurfürstendamm. A working-class kitchen in Wedding or Chemnitz still has a cold cellar, a coal range and a tin bath.

The household goods are reaching ordinary homes at last, and the factories that make them are working three shifts. The next step is the big one: whether the Republic becomes a society in which every working family owns more than it needs. Some in the party think this is the point of socialism. Others think it is the end of it.

The shop windows are full, and so are the order books. Unemployment is the lowest anyone can remember. The trade unions want the next share of the boom to be paid in time off rather than money. The employers want it plowed back into the boom itself.

The signal now reaches most of the big cities, and the sets are getting cheaper. Now the question everyone is asking is what Germany will watch in the evenings.
The private stations already know their answer. They want variety shows, quiz games and anything else that sells soap.

A million German households now own a set, and the aerials on the tenement roofs look like a forest of bare trees. The regional stations are all still fed from Berlin by cable and relay, and their engineers say a proper national network is within reach.
The Planning Office has put television receivers on the consumer goods plan, between bicycles and sewing machines.
The transmitters on the western hills reach well into the occupied Rhineland and the Ruhr. Whatever Berlin broadcasts, people in Essen will watch.

content.content: Fission is now the most talked-about subject in physics. Every university with a neutron source is repeating Hahn's experiment, and the papers are piling up faster than anyone can read them. Nobody in Germany is directing the work, and so far nobody is paying for it either.
The Uranium Club has its uranium and its secrecy, and it is waiting for a decision on the moderator.
The physicists have uranium and a plan, and they are waiting for a decision on the moderator.

A chain reaction needs something to slow the neutrons down. Walther Bothe in Heidelberg has measured graphite and found it unsuitable, and the only other choice is heavy water. The only factory in the world that makes heavy water is the Norsk Hydro plant at Vemork in Norway.

In a pit lined with concrete, the reactor has gone critical: the first self-sustaining chain reaction ever achieved. It produced half a watt, which is not enough to light a torch bulb. Everything now depends on what the next machine is for.
The army's physicists have calculated how much uranium-235 a bomb would need. The answer is a few kilograms, not tonnes.
The Planning Office is drawing up a twenty-year electricity plan, and wants to know whether it should include uranium.
With the Ruhr's coal outside the Republic, the power ministry would happily take its energy from anywhere.

content: Under this agreement, the blue-collar Hirsch-Duncker, Christian, and the Strasserist

unions are merged into the new German Labor Front (DAF). White-collar and civil servant unions, including the DHV, are folded into their own section within the Front. The right to strike is curtailed, and all members are made to pledge full loyalty to the so-called "national interest"—however the state chooses to define it.

content.content: Local union leaders who refuse to join are having their offices raided, their funds confiscated, and themselves imprisoned. While membership in the German Labor Front is technically voluntary, access to benefits—and even basic protections—is now locked behind it, making participation all but mandatory. Furthermore, a new department is established in the DAF, tasked solely with spreading state propaganda and binding the workers more tightly into the Volksgemeinschaft.
The chancellor is also able to palate the industrialists, by placing their power significantly above that of labor in the newly established corporatist framework.

With the Center Party already on the verge of breaking with Schleicher's cabinet after the unconstitutional adjournment of the chamber, this latest undemocratic act has convinced its leaders that only a united republican front can restore Germany to normalcy.

Schleicher’s presidential cabinet now stands deeply delegitimized and increasingly unpopular in the eyes of the public, effectively ending his hopes of manipulating the party’s internal politics or using them to maintain even a façade of parliamentary democracy going forward.

Many neorevisionists consider the Weimar Constitution to be inadequate. They believe that the clauses of the constitution are in part responsible for the instability of the country, and must change in order to build a more stable democratic republic.

Under the Weimar Constitution, any coalition partner can bring down the cabinet without agreeing on a new one, and the President can dissolve the Reichstag at will. Between 1919 and 1928, no cabinet lasted two years. The Ministry of Justice has drafted amendments.

We may consider ideas from both socialists and liberals. A constitutional reform requires either a two-thirds supermajority in the Reichstag, or a constitutional referendum with support from a majority of the electorate. If we do not have a supermajority in the Reichstag, we must be assured of strong support from the other parties for the constitutional referendum.

content.content: Our party is wracked as to how to deal with the economic crisis. From the centrist faction, Hilferding argues that the economic crisis must be allowed to play out, because it is simply a part of the cyclic nature of capitalism.

The Labor faction is arguing for increased welfare spending to alleviate the suffering of the workers. Their economist, Wladimir Woytinsky, has voiced support for a public works campaign involving deficit spending, but it will take time to iron out the details. Furthermore, he will need the united support of the ADGB; otherwise, he won't have the power to challenge Hilferding's stance.

From labor, the economist Wladimir Woytinsky argues that we must pursue a massive public works program to reduce unemployment and stimulate demand, perhaps including deficit spending. His opponents, like Hilferding, argue that this plan will cause a return to hyper-inflation, and that it would not even help the economy. In addition, according to Hilferding, Woytinsky's strategy is opposed to Marxist principles.
The so-called WTB plan, after its chief supporters Woytinsky, Tarnow, and Baade, is receiving more attention within the party.

However, leftists in the party argue that the WTB plan is merely a bandage over the fundamental flaws of capitalism. They argue that the crisis is an opportunity to end capitalism through massive nationalizations of industry, and finally bring our country to socialism.

Meanwhile, moderates and reformists draw up proposals for a limited plan of job creation through public works, funded through taxes, that does not involve deficit spending or large-scale restructuring of the economy. Labor argues that the plan is inadequate in its scale and ambition.

content.content: Further increases in tariffs will not raise revenue, as we have already nearly reached economic autarky.

Increasing tariffs leads to higher prices for basic goods, increasing inflation and hurting consumption among the working class. Retaliatory tariffs reduce the competitiveness of German exports, raising unemployment among workers. They also lead to an atmosphere of international suspicion, reducing our ability to negotiate with other countries.

On the other hand, agricultural producers and some small businesses benefit from higher tariffs, as farmers can now command higher prices for grain, and formerly uncompetitive businesses are now able to function.

content: By 1939, a global recession—triggered by escalating instability across Europe and threats from the Soviet Union—obliterates the reconstruction progress made by the ruling

, plunging the country into yet another crisis. Following a March on Berlin, a "Third Positionist" regime seizes power, led by a new political party composed of former Nazis and disillusioned socialists.

content.content: Germany pivots toward autarky and radical self-reliance, sealing its borders to foreigners. The regime earns the moniker "Black Spot of Europe," ruling from 1940 to 1996. During this period, it successfully coerces the withdrawal of foreign troops from the Rhineland and reclaims its lost eastern territories—including the Polish Corridor—in 1946, capitalizing on Poland's distraction with the Soviet threat and the shifting priorities of the Western Allies as they fight war with Japan.

Today, Germany remains largely isolated from the rest of the world, with the successor to the dictatorship of old being not much better, being ruled by oligarchs and the wealthy who are relicts of the past regime. Now, the task of Social Democracy is to prepare for the next election. The incumbent government of Wolfgang Schäuble is unpopular, and we stand to gain. Perhaps the next government will have a socialist plurality.

content.content: President Hindenburg is, of course, running for re-election, and many in our party are prepared to support him as the last bastion of democracy against Hitler and the Nazis. The Hindenburg Mythos serves as a powerful rallying point for all parties, as he maintains high personal popularity despite everything Germany has endured. However, the more support he receives from the German left and center, the more Hindenburg views it as a stain on his personal honor. The refusal of August von Mackensen and other high-ranking officers with whom he served during the war to embrace his candidacy proved particularly painful to the Reich president.

In response, he may shift further to the right after the election in an effort to restore his sense of honor and to appease his former comrades and friends on the German Right. This urge has only been reinforced by the Harzburg Front’s refusal to support him without concessions, as they see Hindenburg as the greatest obstacle to their rise to power.

content: With the Nazi movement in decline following the end of the economic depression and an internal leadership struggle, and with the election of the nationalist Hergt alongside the appointment of the

Following the peaceful return of the Saarland via referendum in 1935, the Reichswehr suppressed an attempted uprising by the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

and purged the remaining Nazi elements from government. In the heavily managed 1936 elections, under the watch of "electoral monitors", the monarchist parties secured a manufactured mandate. Soon after, a secret rearmament program was launched, and shortly after, the crowning of Wilhelm III—blessed by his father—restores Germany's constitutional monarchy.

content.content: With ambitions focused on reclaiming lost territories in the East and Alsace-Lorraine in the West, Germany began courting allies for its revisionist aims. The restoration of Habsburg rule in Austria and the toppling of Mussolini in a royalist coup led by King Victor Emmanuel III drastically altered the balance of power in Europe. When Poland refused to return former imperial lands, the British, and more reluctantly the French, turned a blind eye to escalating German border skirmishes. The Communist victory in Spain, and the wave of revolutions it triggered across the continent, forced the imperial powers to prioritize containment of the Soviet threat above all else.

Africa remains colonized until the 1980s and 90s. Independence, when it comes, is negotiated largely on the terms of the colonizers. Exploitation persists under a different guise. The Cold War unfolds along different lines, as a "state capitalist" Soviet Union remains intact, forming a bloc with the authoritarian Kuomintang-ruled Republic of China and post-independence India, which fought a bloody war to escape British rule in the 1950s. This tri-polar alliance evolved into a global axis of its own, encompassing numerous Communist regimes worldwide.

content: Today, Germany is a dominant party state, ruled by the elites of the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">

However, cracks are beginning to show in the system. New, young, and popular

leaders are making inroads despite state repression, with Sahra Wagenknecht being the first to achieve a significant victory, having been elected Minister-President of Thuringia. Perhaps the next government will have a mere nationalist plurality.

Despite being hated by nearly 90% of the population, Franz von Papen's surprising victory—secured through the backing of the elites and the Reichswehr—brought him to power in a deeply fractured Germany. However, consolidating that power proved difficult. Despite the eradication of organized communist and social democratic resistance, the Ruhr remains ablaze with unrest. Meanwhile, ongoing conflict between Papen and Kurt von Schleicher, who still maintains significant influence within the military, further destabilizes his regime.

Papen's nationalist foreign policy has won him few friends abroad, and his goal of unshackling Germany from the chains of Versailles remains distant. In an effort to restore order, Papen forms a "National Regeneration Government", rooted in conservative Christian values, militarism, and monarchism. Following the death of President Paul von Hindenburg, Wilhelm III is crowned as a figurehead monarch, while real power remains concentrated in the hands of the political elite and industrial magnates. Germany is transformed into a dictatorship, with the "New State" envisioned by Papen centralizing authority in the executive.

After a period of economic recovery in the late 1930s, Papen turns his attention toward foreign policy, seeking to broker an entente with the French to combat Bolshevism in the East. When these efforts failed, he turned to cooperate with Austrofascist Austria and Mussolini’s Italy, who remained among Germany’s few continental allies.

content: However by the 1950s, however, the regime begins to decay. Corruption, unrest, and economic stagnation—coupled with Papen’s death—trigger a political thaw. The "Prussian Spring" ushers in a wave of democratic reforms, but the entrenched elites of the old system work to protect their interests. The military retains an active and unofficial role in politics, making it impossible for the reconstituted <span style="color: #c00000;">
to assume power without risking a coup.

content.content: Africa remains colonized until the 1980s and 90s. Independence, when it comes, is negotiated largely on the terms of the colonizers. Exploitation persists under a different guise. The Cold War unfolds along different lines, as a Soviet Union surviving intact but slightly liberalized, serving as the key pillar in a global alliance encompassing the Communist regimes worldwide.

Today, Germany is a multiparty democracy, following the ousting of the successor conservative party founded by figures of the former regime. Yet all is not well in the republic. Friedrich Merz, now President, has drawn criticism for invoking nostalgia for the old system, sparking fears of democratic backsliding and concentration of power in favor of the oligarchs. Now, the task of Social Democracy is to prepare for the next presidential election. Our Sahra Wagenknecht is considering running for another non-consecutive term; perhaps she is our only hope to topple Merz.

The coup failed. The abortive putsch was crushed by the proletarian masses and shattered the political landscape of Weimar. The far left of the

content: In a world largely hostile to socialism, we stand as a shining example: the economy is socialized, and economic control is placed directly in the hands of the proletariat. The Soviet Union remains distant, as does the West. We emerge as a beacon of socialism amid the growing tensions of a Cold War—between the
, an authoritarian Kuomintang-led China, and an independent India on one side, and the capitalist West on the other.

content.content: We maintain a strictly neutral stance, offering principled opposition to both blocs. In doing so, we inspire many nations to follow our political and geopolitical path. Our shining socialist republic manages to survive, until the end of an inconclusive Cold War in détente.
As a key neutral player throughout the Cold War, we reap the benefits—becoming a center for dialogue and commerce. With the arrival of détente, more and more nations join us in non-alignment.

All is not golden though. Our republic is prone to infighting, as the various proletarian groups represented in the economy often clash over resource allocation. Additionally, our council-centered system faces criticism for its inability to adapt to modern conditions, with growing signs of bureaucratic inefficiency. Nevertheless, as we enter the 2000s, the Deutsche Räterepublik remains a bastion of socialism and orthodoxy.

content: Our politics, culture, and economy are still deeply proletarian. Albeit third way and even capitalist parties remain on our right—and hardline vanguardists on our left—the

content: As the Constitutional Assembly convenes, it is gradually decided that the new socialist state will take inspiration from the Russian Revolution and the Soviet Union’s vanguardist model. The
—whether convinced, divided, or simply powerless to stop the shift—accepts it. The two
parties rapidly merge into a single party that monopolizes power in the new state, while allowing some minor parties to remain as bloc parties. The
The regime immediately begins aligning with the Soviet Union and puts forth its first

. Soon, the State becomes a member of the Eastern Bloc. World War II breaks out as a massive conflict between the capitalist and communist worlds. It ends with a vast Eastern Bloc stretching from Lisbon to Arkhangelsk. A Cold War begins against the United States, Britain, Kuomintang-led China, and the French government in exile.

assumes an important role in the Soviet Bloc as the leader of the second most industrialized country. Germany experiences decades of growth under the economic plans, calming most dissent within the country. To combat the remaining opposition, the Party establishes the Stasi, inspired by the Soviet Union’s NKVD.

In a meeting with Chancellor Brüning, Defense Minister Groener, General Schleicher, Finance Minister and Vice-Chancellor Hermann Dietrich, and our own Carl Severing, discussions focused on the upcoming presidential election and the organization of an effective propaganda campaign for Hindenburg. Severing outlined the threat that Nazism—particularly the
—posed to state authority and emphasized the election's critical role in keeping the Nazis in check.

content.content: All present agreed that a decisive victory for Hindenburg and a campaign free from violent disturbances would greatly accelerate Germany’s economic recovery and domestic political stabilization. Achieving this, however, would require the use of state funds. Dietrich himself passionately advocated for this, having secretly transferred 1.8 million marks to Severing and the Prussian government with the understanding that the funds would be distributed among various pro-Hindenburg organizations in the State of Prussia. This approach allowed Dietrich and the government to support pro-Hindenburg groups outside the right-wing United Hindenburg Committees.

Oh, you think the SPD betrayed the working class? That’s rich coming from the KPD, the self-proclaimed “vanguard of the proletariat” that spent more time attacking socialists than fighting fascists. Let’s talk about the real betrayal, comrade. While the SPD was trying to stabilize the republic and fend off fascist coups like the Kapp Putsch, where was the KPD? Oh, right—screaming about how social democrats were “social fascists” because they wouldn’t dismantle democracy overnight. You act like the SPD didn’t have its flaws. Sure, Ebert called in the Freikorps to crush the Spartacist uprising. Not a good look, but let’s not pretend the KPD’s adventurism and refusal to cooperate didn’t weaken the left. While the SPD was defending trade unions and passing labor reforms, the KPD was cozying up to Moscow and declaring the Weimar Republic dead on arrival. And don’t get me started on the KPD splitting the left vote in 1933. Was “class purity” worth letting Hitler come to power? But sure, keep calling the SPD sellouts while you play revolutionaries and fail to realize that burning the whole system down doesn’t magically lead to socialism. If anything, it just opens the door for reactionaries to walk right in. The SPD wasn’t perfect, but at least they tried to hold the line. The KPD? A textbook case of “owning the libs” gone horribly wrong. Congratulations, comrade, your ideological purity cost us the Republic. Hope you’re proud.

Out of all the various right-wing interest organizations, the endorsement of Germany's largest economic interest group, the RLB, with its million members and numerous influential state organizations, is undoubtedly the most significant. The Nazi strategy toward these organizations is not to attack them directly but to influence their rank-and-file members. content: With the 1932 German Presidential election coming up next month, we need to decide whether to run a candidate of our own or support one from another party.

content.content: Many are calling for us to support the incumbent Hindenburg, despite his reactionary tendencies. Contrary to fears, he hasn’t used his office to destroy the republic yet, so supporting him would hopefully prevent the Nazis, who actually support destroying the republic, from winning.

With Hindenburg's withdrawal, the German Right is in disarray, struggling to find a candidate who can attract support from the moderate right and middle, while also embodying the unifying character of Hindenburg. It’s likely that the candidate they put forward will have a military or industrial background and will be distanced from the partisan bickering of politics.
